  dramatic question or controlling idea as part of its mode, prioritizing
  voice, atmosphere, or structure over thematic assertion.
- Early drafts, before a manuscript's real center has emerged through the
  writing process itself, aren't yet evidence of a missing controlling idea
  — many authors discover theme through drafting rather than before it.
- Serialized fiction without a single planned ending may have arc-level
  dramatic questions without yet committing to a series-level controlling
  idea.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Identifying a manuscript's actual (as opposed to stated) dramatic question
and controlling idea requires reading and interpreting the whole
manuscript's causal structure and outcomes — a judgment no structured data
substitutes for. A coach can prompt the author to articulate both explicitly
but cannot infer them reliably from partial text alone.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Hollow resolution:* A story's dramatic question (will the protagonist
reclaim their throne) resolves cleanly with a coronation scene, but nothing
in the outcome demonstrates any change in how the protagonist rules
compared to how the deposed regime ruled — the plot question is answered,
nothing is asserted.

*Resolution with a controlling idea:* The same coronation instead follows a
story that has consistently shown power gained through manipulation
curdling relationships, and the protagonist's first act as ruler is to
publicly reject the same manipulative tactic that returned them to power —
the ending both answers the plot question and asserts something about the
story's subject.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The dramatic-question and controlling-idea framework draws on Robert
McKee's foundational writing on story structure and value
([[src.book.mckee-story]]) and John Truby's structural writing on premise
and moral argument ([[src.book.truby-anatomy-of-story]]); both are
long-established, widely taught texts, supporting a `high` confidence
rating for the core principles, while identifying either element in a
specific manuscript remains model-assisted.

records.title: Promise consistency
records.summary: A story's opening sets an implicit contract about the kind of experience it offers, and keeping that contract across a chapter and across a whole series may be the single highest-leverage concept connecting reader retention to long-term series quality.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)
Why Do Great LitRPG Series Fall Off? An Analysis of 1,147 Reddit Comments
Writing the Breakout Novel

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A story's opening chapters — sometimes its opening pages — establish an
implicit promise: what kind of experience this is, what tone it will hold,
what stakes it takes seriously, what it will and won't do to its characters.
Promise consistency is the degree to which the rest of the chapter, the rest
of the manuscript, and the rest of a series keep that contract. It operates
at every scale a coach has available: does this scene keep the chapter's
promise, does this chapter keep the opening's promise, does this book keep
book one's promise.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Two independent lines of evidence point at the same idea from different
angles. Reader-side analysis of long-running series names inconsistent
promise-keeping — a cozy opening that turns grim, or a desperate-stakes
opening that goes soft — as a throughline in series that lose readers over
time. Separately, early-chapter retention research treats poor chapter-one
to chapter-two retention as a promise mismatch rather than a prose-quality
problem: readers aren't leaving because chapter two is badly written, they're
leaving because chapter two isn't the book chapter one promised. Promise
consistency is the concept that connects a scene-level craft note to a
series-level retention outcome.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Tonal promise** — a story's emotional register (cozy, grim, comic,
  desperate) established early and either sustained or drifted from.
- **Stakes promise** — the level of consequence and risk a story establishes
  as its baseline, which readers calibrate their expectations around.
- **Structural promise** — the kind of plot a story signals it will deliver
  (a mystery that will be solved, a romance that will resolve, a quest that
  will complete), which readers track even when they can't articulate the
  signal that told them.
- **Series-level promise** — the contract a first book makes that later
  books either honor, deliberately and visibly evolve, or quietly abandon.
- **Deliberate promise subversion** — a story that signals one promise and
  breaks it on purpose, which can be a powerful effect when the break itself
  is the point, and a betrayal when it reads as drift rather than intent.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- An opening chapter's tone, stakes, and implied genre, compared against a
  chapter from the book's midpoint or a later book in a series.
- A cozy or low-stakes opening followed by sustained brutal violence with no
  signaled tonal shift.
- A story that promises a specific mystery or quest resolution and then
  quietly drops or indefinitely defers it across volumes.
- Reader reviews or comments (where available) describing a specific book or
  chapter as feeling like "a different story" from what came before it.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unintentional tonal drift**, where later installments of a long series
  gradually shift tone as the author's own interests or skills evolve,
  without the shift being signaled to readers as deliberate.
- **Confusing escalation with promise-keeping**, where rising stakes are
  mistaken for a stable promise even though the actual felt experience (cozy
  versus desperate, hopeful versus grim) has changed underneath the rising
  numbers.
- **Treating promise-keeping as "never changing anything,"** which
  overcorrects into stagnation; a story can evolve its promise deliberately
  and transparently without breaking faith with readers, and confusing that
  with rigid sameness is its own failure mode.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If a reader described this book's opening chapter in three words, would
  those same three words describe its climax?
- Has anything about this story's tone, stakes, or implied kind of ending
  changed since the opening — and if so, was that change signaled to the
  reader anywhere?
- In a series, does book three keep the promise book one made, or has it
  quietly become a different kind of book?
- If early chapters are losing readers, is that a prose problem, or is
  chapter two simply not the book chapter one promised?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write a one-sentence promise statement for the opening chapter (tone,
   stakes, implied kind of story) and check it against a sentence written the
   same way for the midpoint and the ending.
2. For a series, compare a scene from book one against a comparable scene
   from the most recent book, looking specifically at tone and stakes rather
   than plot content.
3. If a deliberate promise shift is planned, look for a scene that can
   explicitly signal the shift to the reader before it happens, rather than
   letting it arrive unannounced.
4. For a struggling early-chapter retention problem, reread chapter one
   asking only "what does this promise," then reread chapter two asking only
   "does this deliver on that," separately from any prose-quality read of
   either.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story built around a structural twist in its own premise — an opening
  that deliberately misleads the reader about what kind of book this is, as
  the twist itself — is using inconsistency as a technique, not failing to
  keep a promise.
- Long series legitimately evolve as their authors and audiences do; a
  transparent, gradual evolution acknowledged within the text is different
  from an unannounced drift.
- A single outlier chapter (a flashback, an interlude in a different voice)
  can depart from the main promise briefly without breaking it, provided the
  surrounding text signals the departure as intentional.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a specific scene, chapter, or book keeps or breaks an established
promise requires reading and comparing prose for tone, stakes, and implied
genre — an interpretive judgment with no deterministic substitute. A future
coach could shortlist an opening passage and a comparison passage as
evidence for the author's own review, but concluding that a promise was kept
or broken is model-assisted, not something structured data can settle.
Series-level promise-consistency claims additionally require access to
multiple books' worth of manuscript, which most coaching sessions will not
have simultaneously.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Promise kept:* A story opens with a character narrowly avoiding eviction and
worrying about a light bill. Its climax three hundred pages later still turns
on a resource shortage the character cannot simply out-power — the stakes
grew in scale but stayed the same kind.

*Promise broken without signal:* The same opening, but by the climax the
character commands an army and the story's central tension has become a
political succession crisis with no scene marking the shift from personal,
survival-scale stakes to political, systemic ones.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The series-longevity framing and the "consistently delivers on its initial
promise" finding come from a single vendor's coded analysis of Reddit
discussion ([[src.chapterchronicles.series-falloff]]), marked practitioner/
reader consensus rather than controlled research; that same source frames
promise consistency as a candidate connecting concept rather than a settled
conclusion, and `docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md` explicitly raises,
as an open question, whether promise consistency deserves to be the
library's organizing idea rather than one entry among many
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]). The general-craft framing
of reader promise and stakes escalation draws on established craft writing
about market-aware structure ([[src.book.maass-writing-breakout-novel]]).
This record treats promise consistency as a strong, cross-source hypothesis
worth prioritizing in coaching, not as a proven causal mechanism.

records.title: Continuity passes
records.summary: A dedicated read-through focused only on consistency — names, timelines, physical details, established facts — catches a different category of error than developmental or line-level revision, and trying to catch continuity errors during either of those passes usually means catching fewer of them.

citations.label: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A continuity pass is a dedicated revision read-through with a single,
narrow focus: consistency of names, dates, physical descriptions,
established facts, and timeline, rather than structure, prose quality, or
overall story assessment. It's a distinct pass from the developmental and
line-level revision covered in this library's triage record, because the
attention required is different in kind — a continuity pass asks "does this
match what was established earlier," not "does this work" or "is this well
written," and trying to hold both kinds of attention simultaneously tends
to mean neither gets done thoroughly.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Continuity errors — a character's eye color changing, a stated travel time
that doesn't match a later mentioned distance, a secondary character's name
shifting — don't usually break a story's structure, but they erode a
reader's trust in the manuscript's care and can pull a reader out of the
fictional experience at moments that have nothing to do with the story's
actual content. Because these errors are often invisible to an author deep
in developmental or line-level thinking (attention is elsewhere), they tend
to require their own dedicated pass to catch reliably.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Fact-tracking passes**, focused on concrete, checkable details (names,
  dates, physical descriptions, established rules) using an external
  reference document (a "bible") built alongside the manuscript.
- **Timeline passes**, focused specifically on chronology — travel times,
  seasons, the sequence and spacing of events — which can be harder to
  track than static facts because they require holding a whole sequence in
  mind at once.
- **Established-rule passes**, specific to genre fiction with explicit
  systems (magic rules, world logic), checking that stated limits and
  mechanics are honored consistently — closely related to several
  system-mechanic patterns' own consistency concerns.
- **Reader-facing versus author-only continuity**, distinguishing errors a
  reader would actually notice (a named character's described appearance
  changing) from ones that are technically inconsistent but unlikely to
  register (a very minor, unstated detail).

sections.title: What it can look like in an author's process
sections.content:
- A separate document or tracking system (character sheet, timeline,
  system-rules reference) maintained alongside drafting and checked during
  a dedicated pass.
- A revision pass conducted with no attention to prose quality or
  structure, purely cross-referencing details against earlier
  established facts.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: continuity checking folded into a
  general revision pass with no dedicated attention, or no external
  reference document at all for a manuscript with many trackable details.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **No dedicated pass at all**, relying on memory or general revision
  attention to catch continuity errors, which tends to miss more than a
  focused pass would.
- **Continuity tracking abandoned partway through a long project**, common
  in extended series or serialized fiction, where an initially maintained
  reference document falls behind the manuscript's actual state.
- **Over-scrupulous continuity checking that chases invisible errors**,
  spending disproportionate revision time on inconsistencies no reader
  would plausibly notice, at the expense of higher-priority developmental
  or line-level work.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is there a dedicated pass, separate from developmental and line-level
  revision, focused only on consistency?
- Is a reference document (character details, timeline, established rules)
  being maintained and kept current as the manuscript grows or changes?
- For a long or serialized project, has continuity tracking kept pace with
  the manuscript, or has it fallen behind?
- Is continuity-checking effort proportional to what a reader would
  actually notice, or is it consuming revision time disproportionate to
  its impact?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Before a continuity pass, build or update a reference document listing
   key names, dates, physical details, and established rules.
2. Conduct a pass focused exclusively on cross-referencing the manuscript
   against that document, with no attention to prose quality.
3. For a long or serialized project, schedule periodic continuity check-ins
   rather than relying on a single pass at the end.
4. Triage found inconsistencies by reader-visibility before spending
   revision time on the least noticeable ones.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very short manuscripts with few trackable details may not need a
  formalized continuity pass or reference document.
- Some genres or styles with intentionally loose, dreamlike continuity
  (certain literary or surrealist traditions) may not prioritize strict
  consistency as a value at all.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This is a practice pattern concerning an author's revision process; whether
a dedicated continuity pass occurred isn't observable from the finished
manuscript alone, though its *absence* often becomes visible through
inconsistencies a reader can point to directly. Where a project maintains
explicit structured data about names, dates, or established facts linked to
scenes, cross-referencing that data against the manuscript text could
identify candidate inconsistencies more directly than an unstructured
continuity pass could, though confirming an inconsistency's severity and
reader-visibility remains an interpretive judgment.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
Not applicable in the usual sense — this pattern concerns process rather
than manuscript content directly, though its failure is often visible in
the manuscript itself. An author-facing illustration: a serialized story
establishes a secondary character's hometown in chapter four; forty
chapters later, without a continuity pass or reference document, the same
character is described as being from a different town, with no narrative
explanation — an error a dedicated pass, cross-referenced against a
maintained character sheet, would likely have caught before publication.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The general practice of dedicated continuity checking as distinct from
developmental or line-level revision draws on Stephen King's writing on
revision process ([[src.book.king-on-writing]]), a single author's
practice and opinion presented as such; no dedicated craft-literature
source specifically addressing continuity-pass methodology was available
to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Developmental versus line-level revision
records.summary: Two different kinds of revision, working at different scales and in a costly order — polishing sentences in a scene that should be cut is the most common way revision effort is wasted.

citations.label: Self-Editing for Fiction Writers: How to Edit Yourself Into Print
Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft
Writing the Breakout Novel

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Developmental revision changes what the book is: which scenes exist, what
happens in them, who the characters are, what the story is about. Line
revision changes how it reads: sentence by sentence, word by word, at the
level of clarity and rhythm.

The distinction matters because the two interact asymmetrically. A
developmental change can delete a scene that took a day to line-edit; a line
change almost never affects structure. That asymmetry implies an order, and
this record is largely about the cost of ignoring it.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Readers do not encounter revision, only its results — but they encounter the
consequences of misdirected revision constantly. A manuscript that has been
polished sentence by sentence without a structural pass reads as
well-written and slow: nothing is wrong with any paragraph, and the book
does not move. Editors' craft literature returns repeatedly to this pattern,
because it is what a great many submitted manuscripts look like.

The reverse case is rarer and easier to fix. A structurally sound book with
rough prose can be improved by a line pass; a beautifully written book with
no shape usually cannot be improved without losing much of the writing.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The structural pass** — scene inventory, ordering, cutting, and
  rewriting at the level of what happens.
- **The character pass** — reading for one character's arc, motivation, and
  consistency across the whole draft.
- **The continuity pass** — facts, timelines, names, and established rules,
  treated separately in this library.
- **The line pass** — clarity, rhythm, repetition, and habitual
  constructions.
- **The read-through** — an uninterrupted reading with no editing at all,
  used to find where attention drifts rather than to fix anything.
- **Simultaneous revision** — doing all of it at once, which is what most
  drafts get and which reliably produces polished sentences inside unresolved
  structure.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A chapter with three well-turned paragraphs of description and no scene
  goal.
- Dialogue rewritten many times inside a conversation the book does not
  need.
- Conversely: a draft where a whole subplot has been cut cleanly, leaving
  rough seams that a later pass can smooth.
- A manuscript whose first fifty pages read noticeably better than the rest —
  usually a sign of repeated line passes that never reached the middle.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Line-editing a doomed scene.** The most expensive error available in
  revision, and the most common.
- **The endless first chapter.** Polishing the opening repeatedly instead of
  finishing or restructuring the book.
- **Structural avoidance.** Line work as a way of feeling productive while
  postponing a change the author already knows is needed.
- **Premature line-editing during drafting.** Which slows drafting and
  produces material that is harder to cut, because it now represents effort.
- **Treating a reader's line complaint as a line problem.** "The prose got
  bogged down here" is often a scene problem reported at the level the reader
  noticed it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is this scene definitely staying? If not, why is it being polished?
- What kind of change would the note I just received actually require —
  structural or sentence-level?
- Which pass am I on right now, and am I doing only that pass's work?
- Where has this manuscript received the most attention, and does that match
  where it needs the most?
- If the structure is not yet settled, what would it cost to leave the prose
  rough for one more pass?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Make a one-line-per-scene inventory of the draft and mark each scene keep,
   cut, or unsure. Do no line work in any scene marked cut or unsure.
2. Do a read-through with a pen you are not allowed to use except to mark
   where attention drifted, then diagnose those places before fixing
   anything.
3. Take one beta-reader note about prose and ask what structural cause could
   produce that symptom. Sometimes there is none; often there is.
4. Set an explicit pass order for the next revision and hold to it for one
   pass, even where a sentence is visibly annoying.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Writers whose process genuinely requires clean sentences to think, and who
  cannot draft forward over rough prose. This is a real working style; its
  cost is that more polished material eventually gets cut.
- Serialized publishing, where chapters are released as written and
  structural revision of published chapters is not available. The pass order
  is then a planning question rather than a revision one, which changes the
  advice substantially.
- Short work, where the scales collapse and a single pass is often adequate.
- Final proofreading, which is neither of these and should follow both.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This record is marked `practice`, and the mark is doing real work: it
describes an author's working process, not a property of the manuscript. A
coach cannot inspect a draft and determine what revision it has received.
Uneven polish between early and late chapters is sometimes visible, and even
that is weak evidence — a first chapter may simply have been written later.

Nothing here should be reported as an observation about a manuscript. The
coach's role with a practice record is to offer the distinction and let the
author recognize their own process in it, never to infer from the text that
the author has been revising in the wrong order.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Misdirected effort:* the tavern scene has been through eleven revisions. Its
dialogue is excellent. In the current outline the characters no longer go to
the tavern.

*Symptom reported at the wrong level:* three readers said chapter nine
"dragged." Chapter nine's prose is the cleanest in the book. Chapter nine is
where the protagonist has nothing to decide.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Renni Browne and Dave King ([[src.book.browne-king-self-editing]]) supply the
editorial account of what manuscripts typically need and the case for
distinguishing levels of revision; Janet Burroway
([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the general revision
framework and the read-through practice; Donald Maass
([[src.book.maass-writing-breakout-novel]]) supplies the argument that
structural weakness cannot be resolved at the sentence level.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. The
distinction between developmental and line revision is standard and
independently supported; the specific claim that misdirected effort
concentrates in line-editing doomed scenes is a widely repeated editorial
observation rather than a measured finding, and is presented here as
practitioner consensus. The serialized-publishing exception is drawn from
this library's own genre research, since none of the three sources addresses
publishing chapters as they are written — a context where much of this
record's advice simply does not apply.

records.title: Protecting the intended reader experience
records.summary: Revision advice is only useful relative to what a manuscript is trying to be for its intended reader — the same note (add more description, cut this scene, raise the stakes) can be exactly right for one book and exactly wrong for another with a different promise.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Protecting the intended reader experience means evaluating and applying
revision advice relative to what a specific manuscript is trying to
accomplish for its specific intended reader, rather than against a generic
standard of "good writing" that doesn't account for genre, register, or
authorial intent. The same piece of feedback — trim the description, slow
down here, raise the stakes, cut this subplot — can be exactly the right
call for one manuscript and actively wrong for another with a different
promise, and the difference isn't always obvious from the feedback alone.
This is less a single technique than a stance a coach or reviewer should
hold throughout revision: understand what the book is trying to be before
recommending changes to how well it's being it.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A manuscript revised against a generic standard rather than its own
intended promise risks losing what made it distinctive in the first place —
sanding a deliberately dense, atmospheric opening down to match
"industry-standard pacing" can strip a literary novel of its actual appeal;
adding unwanted interiority to a fast, plot-forward adventure can slow it
in ways its intended readers never wanted. This pattern exists to name the
risk directly: revision feedback that's technically sound in the abstract
can still be wrong for a specific book.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Genre-calibrated feedback**, evaluating pacing, description density,
  and structural choices against the conventions of the manuscript's
  actual genre and subgenre, not a generic standard.
- **Promise-calibrated feedback**, checking proposed changes against what
  the manuscript's own opening has promised (closely related to the
  promise-consistency pattern), rather than an external ideal.
- **Author-intent clarification**, explicitly asking what a specific choice
  is meant to accomplish before recommending it be changed, distinguishing
  deliberate craft choices from unintentional gaps.
- **Audience-calibrated feedback**, accounting for who the manuscript is
  actually written for — a middle-grade adventure and a literary novel for
  adults have different, equally legitimate standards for pacing,
  complexity, and content.

sections.title: What it can look like in a revision process
sections.content:
- A piece of feedback that names the manuscript's own genre or promise
  explicitly before recommending a change, rather than applying a
  one-size-fits-all standard.
- A revision note distinguishing "this doesn't work for what your book is
  trying to do" from "this doesn't work, full stop" — the two require very
  different responses from an author.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: revision feedback that would apply
  identically regardless of the manuscript's genre, audience, or stated
  intent, suggesting it wasn't actually calibrated to this specific book.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Generic feedback applied without calibration**, recommending changes
  that would improve an abstract "well-written novel" without checking
  whether they'd improve this particular book's actual promise.
- **Mistaking a deliberate choice for an oversight**, recommending a
  change to something the author did intentionally, without first asking
  why it's there.
- **Over-indexing on personal taste**, where a reviewer's own genre
  preferences shape feedback more than the manuscript's own stated or
  implied intentions do.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this piece of feedback account for what this specific manuscript is
  trying to be, or would it apply the same way to any manuscript?
- Is a proposed change addressing something that isn't working, or
  something that's working differently than a generic standard would
  expect?
- Before changing a specific choice, has its purpose been considered — is
  it possible this was deliberate?
- Would this manuscript's intended reader actually want the proposed
  change, given what the book has promised them so far?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Before applying a piece of revision feedback, state explicitly what
   genre, promise, and intended reader the manuscript is written for, and
   check the feedback against that statement.
2. For a proposed change to something that might be intentional, ask why
   the choice was made before recommending it be altered.
3. Distinguish, in writing, feedback that says "this doesn't achieve what
   you're going for" from feedback that says "what you're going for isn't
   working for me personally" — treat the two differently.
4. When multiple pieces of feedback conflict, check each against the
   manuscript's own stated promise rather than trying to satisfy all of
   them simultaneously.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Genuine craft errors (inconsistent POV, broken causality, unintentional
  continuity errors) aren't relative to intended reader experience in the
  same way — this pattern applies most directly to calibration-sensitive
  choices like pacing, density, and tone, not to outright mistakes.
- A manuscript still finding its own intended promise during early drafting
  may not yet have a stable standard to calibrate feedback against; this
  pattern is most useful once a manuscript's direction is reasonably
  settled.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a piece of feedback is properly calibrated to a manuscript's
intended promise, genre, and audience requires understanding that promise
in the first place — a judgment that depends on interpreting the
manuscript holistically and remains model-assisted; a coach cannot verify
"author intent" from text alone and should treat this as a question to ask
rather than an assumption to make.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Uncalibrated feedback:* A reviewer recommends cutting a fast-paced
adventure novel's brief, functional descriptions to add more sensory depth,
applying a standard suited to literary fiction without checking whether the
adventure novel's intended readers value pace over density.

*Calibrated feedback:* The same reviewer instead first identifies that the
manuscript is a tightly plotted adventure aimed at readers who prioritize
momentum, and recommends instead that one specific description — at the
story's most significant reveal — be expanded, since even a pace-forward
book can afford to slow down at its most important moment.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This pattern is this drafting pass's synthesis of the coaching-voice
standard already established throughout this library (the instruction to
offer options with different costs and to avoid unsupported universal
claims), informed by the broader craft-failure research's caution about
treating genre-specific conventions as universal flaws
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no single dedicated
craft-literature source addressing this exact framing was identified.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Revision triage and beta-reader signal
records.summary: Not all revision feedback is equally trustworthy or equally worth acting on — separating developmental concerns from line-level ones, and reader-reported symptoms from reader-diagnosed causes, is what makes a revision pass efficient rather than reactive.

citations.label: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Revision triage is the practice of sorting what a manuscript needs by scale
and order rather than addressing every issue as it's noticed: developmental
concerns (structure, character arc, pacing at the manuscript level) usually
need to be settled before line-level concerns (word choice, sentence
rhythm, individual dialogue) are worth polishing, since developmental
changes can make line-level work on an affected passage moot. Beta-reader
signal is the related practice of separating what a reader reports
experiencing (a symptom — "I got bored around chapter ten," "I didn't
believe the romance") from what they diagnose as the cause, since readers
are reliable narrators of their own experience but not always reliable
diagnosticians of why they had it.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
This pattern serves the author's process rather than directly shaping
reader experience, but it has an indirect and significant effect: a
manuscript revised out of order (polishing prose before structure is
settled, or restructuring based on a misdiagnosed symptom) tends to need
more revision passes, cost more author time and energy, and risk the kind
of burnout symptoms covered in the related pattern — all of which eventually
surface in what readers experience, even though the practice itself happens
off the page.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Developmental-first triage**, addressing structure, arc, and pacing
  concerns before line-level polish, the most commonly recommended default
  order.
- **Symptom-and-cause separation**, treating a beta reader's reported
  experience ("I got bored," "I didn't buy the reconciliation") as reliable
  data while treating their proposed fix ("you should cut chapter ten," "add
  a scene where they talk it out") as one hypothesis among several possible
  causes.
- **Pattern-across-readers triage**, weighting feedback that recurs across
  multiple independent readers more heavily than a single reader's specific
  reaction, which may reflect that reader's individual taste rather than a
  structural issue.
- **Targeted beta requests**, asking readers to focus feedback on a specific
  concern (pacing, a particular character, whether a twist lands) rather
  than open-ended reaction, trading breadth for depth on a known concern.

sections.title: What it can look like in an author's process
sections.content:
- A structural revision pass completed before a line-editing pass begins,
  rather than the two happening simultaneously on the same draft.
- Beta feedback organized by what readers experienced, with proposed causes
  tracked separately and checked against the author's own read of the
  manuscript before being acted on.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: line-editing a chapter that later gets
  cut or substantially restructured, or accepting a reader's proposed fix
  without checking whether it addresses the actual symptom they reported.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Line-editing before structure is settled**, wasting effort on passages
  that later change or disappear.
- **Treating a single reader's proposed cause as settled fact**, especially
  when it isn't corroborated by other readers or the author's own
  independent assessment.
- **Ignoring a recurring symptom because the proposed fixes seem wrong**,
  discarding valid signal (readers getting bored at the same point) because
  the accompanying diagnosis doesn't ring true, rather than looking for a
  different cause.
- **Revising reactively to every piece of feedback**, without triaging by
  scale or recurrence, which can fragment a manuscript's voice and
  coherence.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is structural revision (plot, arc, pacing) settled before investing in
  line-level polish on the same material?
- Does a piece of beta feedback recur across multiple independent readers,
  or is it a single reader's individual reaction?
- Is a reader's reported experience being treated as reliable while their
  proposed cause is checked against the author's own read of the
  manuscript, or is the proposed fix being accepted uncritically?
- Has a valid, recurring symptom been dismissed because the accompanying
  diagnosis didn't feel right, without looking for an alternative cause?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Before line-editing, confirm the manuscript's structure is stable enough
   that the chapter being edited won't be cut or substantially reordered.
2. For a piece of beta feedback, separate the reported experience from the
   proposed cause in writing, and generate at least one alternative
   hypothesis for the cause before revising.
3. Collect feedback from several readers on the same draft and look for
   symptoms that recur, weighting those over single-reader reactions.
4. If a recurring symptom's proposed fixes all seem wrong, revisit the
   affected section fresh and look for a cause none of the readers named.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very short revision cycles (a quick polish pass with no structural
  concerns) may not need the full developmental-first sequencing this
  pattern describes.
- Some authors' processes genuinely work better with simultaneous
  structural and line-level revision; this is a common default recommendation,
  not a universal requirement.
- A single trusted reader's feedback (an experienced editor, a
  longtime collaborator) may reasonably be weighted more heavily than the
  "multiple readers" corroboration standard would otherwise suggest.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This is primarily a practice pattern concerning an author's revision
process, not something a manuscript's current state can directly reveal;
whether a specific structural issue is genuinely settled, or whether a
piece of feedback has been triaged appropriately, is not verifiable from
text alone. A coach may teach this practice and, where a project explicitly
tracks revision-pass history, could report that history, but cannot verify
an author's process discipline from the manuscript itself.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Misdiagnosed feedback:* Several beta readers report losing interest around
chapter ten; readers who diagnose a cause disagree (too much description,
not enough dialogue, an unlikeable side character), and the author,
confused by the conflicting diagnoses, makes no change — missing that the
recurring symptom itself (attention drops at that specific point) is valid
signal regardless of the conflicting proposed causes.

*Triaged appropriately:* The same author instead treats the recurring
symptom as reliable and investigates chapter ten independently, discovering
the actual cause is a stalled subplot with no forward motion at that
point — a diagnosis none of the readers happened to name, but one the
symptom pattern pointed toward.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The developmental-before-line-level triage principle draws on Stephen
King's writing on revision practice ([[src.book.king-on-writing]]), a
single author's practice and opinion presented as such; the symptom-versus-
diagnosed-cause distinction for reader feedback is this drafting pass's
synthesis, informed by the broader craft-failure research's general caution
about distinguishing reader-reported experience from proposed explanations
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]). `source_confidence` is
`mixed` accordingly, and no dedicated source specifically on beta-reader
management practice was available to this drafting pass.

records.title: Scene entry and exit points
records.summary: Where a scene chooses to start and stop, independent of where its underlying events actually begin and end, is one of the most direct levers an author has over pacing — starting late and leaving early is usually stronger than covering everything.

citations.label: The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers
Helping Writers Become Authors (blog and structure guides)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A scene's entry and exit points are the moments an author chooses to begin
narrating and to stop, which don't need to match where the scene's
underlying events actually start and finish. A scene can be entered well
before its central conflict begins (showing full arrival, small talk, and
setup) or well into it (opening mid-conversation, mid-action); it can be
exited once every loose end is settled, or the moment its central turn
lands, leaving the aftermath to the reader's imagination or the next
scene's opening. The common advice to "start late and leave early" names a
default bias — enter as close to the point of interest as orientation
allows, exit as soon as the scene's essential work is done — without
making it an absolute rule for every scene.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Scenes that include their full run-up and full aftermath can feel padded,
asking the reader to sit through transitional material that doesn't carry
the scene's actual interest. Scenes that enter close to their point of
tension and exit at or near their turn tend to feel tighter and more
propulsive, because the reader's attention is directed at the material that
matters most. This is a different lever from narrative summary versus
scene — it's not about whether to dramatize an event at all, but about how
much of a dramatized event's edges to actually show once the decision to
dramatize it has been made.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Late entry**, opening a scene close to or inside its central action or
  conflict, with necessary orientation supplied economically rather than
  through a full run-up.
- **Early exit**, ending a scene at or shortly after its central turn,
  before every loose end (goodbyes, logistics, full emotional processing)
  is resolved on the page.
- **Full-coverage scenes**, including complete arrival, setup, and
  resolution — appropriate when the transitional material itself carries
  meaning, or when a slower pace serves the moment.
- **Cross-cut entry/exit**, where a scene is entered or exited via a jump
  cut from or to a different scene, compressing transitional time
  implicitly rather than narrating it.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A scene opening mid-action or mid-conversation, with context supplied
  through a few economical lines rather than a full establishing sequence.
- A scene ending at its emotional or plot turn, with the immediate
  aftermath left implicit or deferred to the next scene.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a scene that includes several paragraphs
  of arrival, greeting, and settling in before its actual point of interest
  begins, or lingers well past its central turn resolving minor,
  non-essential loose ends.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Full run-up on every scene**, including transitional material
  (traveling to a location, settling in, small talk) as a default habit
  rather than a deliberate choice, slowing pacing across the manuscript.
- **Exiting too early**, cutting a scene before its essential turn has
  actually landed clearly, leaving the reader confused about what happened
  rather than intrigued by what's left implicit.
- **Uniform application**, applying "start late, leave early" so
  consistently that scenes needing a slower approach (an intentional
  breather, a scene where the transitional material itself matters) get cut
  the same way as ones that don't.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Could this scene begin later — closer to its point of actual interest —
  without losing necessary orientation?
- Could this scene end earlier — at or near its central turn — without
  leaving the reader confused about what happened?
- Is a scene's run-up or aftermath included because it does real narrative
  work, or out of habit?
- Are there consecutive scenes in the manuscript that all follow the same
  entry/exit pattern, and would varying it sharpen the ones that matter
  most?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a scene that feels slow to start, identify the earliest point that
   still gives the reader necessary orientation and cut everything before
   it.
2. For a scene that lingers, identify the moment its central turn lands and
   test cutting everything after it, moving any essential remaining
   information to the next scene's opening.
3. Audit several consecutive scenes for entry/exit pattern uniformity; vary
   the treatment for the scenes carrying the most narrative weight.
4. For a scene where the transitional material seems worth keeping, name
   specifically what work it's doing (mood, characterization, pacing
   breather) to confirm the choice is deliberate.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Scenes where the transitional material itself is the point (a quiet
  arrival that reveals character, an ending's aftermath that needs space to
  land emotionally) should be given the room they need, not trimmed by
  default.
- Very short or fragmentary scene structures may not have a meaningful
  "full coverage" version to compare against.
- Some literary styles deliberately linger on transitional or liminal
  moments as part of their voice and pacing philosophy.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a scene's entry or exit point serves its content, or merely follows
habit, requires reading and interpreting the prose and its surrounding
context — a judgment no structured data substitutes for. Scene length is
directly observable from raw text.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Full run-up:* A scene opens with a character waking, dressing, eating
breakfast, and walking to a meeting before the meeting's actual
conflict — the scene's point of interest — finally begins on the third
page.

*Late entry:* The same scene instead opens on the meeting's first
contentious line of dialogue, with the character's morning routine omitted
entirely; any necessary context arrives economically, woven into the
conversation itself.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The "start late, leave early" principle is a widely repeated piece of
scene-craft guidance, drawn here from John Gardner's foundational writing
on pacing and the "vivid, continuous dream"
([[src.book.gardner-art-of-fiction]]) and K. M. Weiland's structural
pacing writing ([[src.book.weiland-helping-writers-become-authors]]); both
established craft resources. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because the
specific variant taxonomy presented here is this drafting pass's synthesis
rather than a direct claim from either source.

records.title: Scene goal, conflict, and outcome
records.summary: A scene built around a character wanting something specific, meeting resistance, and ending in a changed situation gives a reader a reason to keep reading the next one — the classic scene/sequel structural unit.

citations.label: Techniques of the Selling Writer
Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A scene, in this structural sense, is a unit built around three moving
parts: a character enters wanting something specific and attainable within
the scene (a goal), meets resistance to getting it (conflict), and the scene
ends with the situation changed from how it started (an outcome) — often, but
not always, worse than the character hoped. This is one of the oldest
formalized models in modern craft teaching, usually traced to the
goal-conflict-disaster / reaction-dilemma-decision pairing, and it remains
widely taught because it gives a concrete diagnostic for "why doesn't this
scene work."

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A scene with a clear goal gives a reader something to root for or worry
about from its first page. A scene with real conflict makes the outcome
uncertain enough to matter. A scene with a changed outcome — rather than a
character simply getting what they wanted cleanly — creates the causal link
that pulls a reader into the next scene, because something is now different
than it was.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Classic goal-conflict-disaster.** A concrete, attainable goal; active
  opposition; an outcome that denies, complicates, or twists the goal rather
  than granting it cleanly.
- **Goal achieved, cost incurred.** The character gets what they wanted, but
  the getting costs something else, keeping the outcome from being a clean
  win.
- **Discovery scenes.** The "goal" is understanding rather than acquisition —
  a character seeking information meets resistance (a reluctant source, a
  locked archive, a lie) and the outcome changes what they know, which
  changes what they can do next.
- **Sequel/reflection scenes.** A companion unit, not this pattern's subject
  directly: a character reacts emotionally to the prior scene's disaster,
  weighs a dilemma, and makes a decision that becomes the next scene's goal.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A scene opening with a character's clearly implied want, even if never
  stated in so many words.
- Escalating obstacles between the want and its pursuit, rather than a
  single easily-cleared hurdle.
- A final beat that changes the character's situation, knowledge, or
  relationships from where the scene began.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a scene where the character wants nothing
  in particular, meets no real resistance, and ends exactly where it began.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Goalless scenes** that exist for atmosphere or information delivery with
  no want driving them, which readers often describe as "nothing happened."
- **Conflict-free goals**, where the character wants something and simply
  gets it, removing any uncertainty that would make the outcome matter.
- **Outcomes that reset the situation**, ending a scene in the same state it
  began, which erodes momentum even when the individual scene reads fine in
  isolation.
- **Treating the model as a rigid formula** applied identically to every
  scene, which can flatten scenes that are doing different, legitimate work
  (mood, characterization, transition).

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does the point-of-view character want at the start of this scene, and
  is it specific enough to be pursued in the pages that follow?
- What is actively working against that want, and is it strong enough to
  make the outcome uncertain?
- How is the situation different at the end of this scene than at the start?
- If this scene were cut entirely, would the story lose a causal link, or
  only some texture?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a scene that feels flat, write one sentence naming its character's
   goal, one naming the opposition, and one naming the outcome; if any is
   hard to write, that's the gap to address.
2. Try converting a clean "goal achieved" outcome into a "goal achieved, cost
   incurred" outcome and see whether the scene gains tension.
3. For a scene with no clear resistance, introduce one obstacle — even a
   small one — and see whether the scene's stakes sharpen.
4. Trace the outcome of one scene forward: does it become the seed of the
   next scene's goal? If not, consider whether the causal chain has a gap.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Interlude, mood, and pure-transition passages can legitimately lack this
  structure, provided they're used sparingly and the surrounding scenes carry
  the causal weight.
- Literary fiction working in a more associative, non-causal mode may
  deliberately decline conventional goal-conflict-outcome structure as a
  stylistic choice.
- Very short scenes (a single beat, a fragment) may compress or omit parts of
  this structure without losing effectiveness.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a scene has a legible goal, real conflict, and a changed outcome
requires reading and interpreting the prose; there is no structured data
substitute. A future coach could shortlist a scene's opening and closing
passages as evidence for the author's own comparison, but concluding that a
scene lacks structure is an interpretive judgment, not a deterministic one.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Missing structure:* A scene opens with a character walking through a
market, observing goods and vendors for two pages, then leaving. No want is
stated or implied; nothing resists; the situation at the end matches the
start.

*Present structure:* The same market scene opens with the character needing
to sell a family heirloom before nightfall to cover a debt, a vendor refuses
the asking price and threatens to report the item as stolen, and the scene
ends with the character having pawned it for less than needed and now owing
someone a favor to make up the difference.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The goal-conflict-disaster / reaction-dilemma-decision model traces to Dwight
Swain's foundational text ([[src.book.swain-techniques-selling-writer]]),
still widely taught under various renamings. Robert McKee's scene-as-value-
shift framing ([[src.book.mckee-story]]) supports the outcome-must-change-the-
situation principle from a complementary angle. Both are established,
long-standing craft texts rather than recent or contested ones; confidence
is set to `high` on that basis, while individual application to any specific
manuscript remains model-assisted.

records.title: Scene turns
records.summary: A scene turn is the moment a scene's value charges from positive to negative or back — the pivot that makes a reader feel something actually changed, distinct from mere activity.

citations.label: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A scene turn is the point where a scene's emotional or situational charge
flips — from hope to dread, from safety to danger, from ignorance to
knowledge that can't be unknown — usually driven by a piece of new
information, an action, or a decision. The concept comes from screenwriting
craft, where a "value" (life/death, love/hate, freedom/captivity) is tracked
across a scene, and a scene without a turn is one where that value starts and
ends in the same place: nothing, in this specific structural sense, changed.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A reader tracks emotional charge even without naming it. A scene that turns
gives the reader the sensation that the story moved; a scene that doesn't can
feel busy — full of dialogue, action, description — while still landing as
inert. The turn is often smaller and more precise than "something happened";
it's the specific moment the situation's meaning flipped.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Single clean turn.** One clear pivot point, usually near the scene's
  back half, where the charge flips once.
- **Multiple turns.** Longer or more complex scenes can turn more than once —
  hope to dread to grim resolve, for instance — each turn raising or
  complicating the last.
- **Micro-turns within dialogue.** A conversation can turn line by line as
  information is revealed, negotiated, or withheld, with the scene's overall
  turn being the sum of several small ones.
- **The negated turn**, where a character expects a turn and it doesn't
  arrive — used deliberately for anticlimax, dread, or dark comedy, but risky
  if it reads as an author's oversight rather than a choice.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A specific line, action, or revelation that can be pointed to as the
  moment the scene's emotional charge changed direction.
- Dialogue that ends in a materially different relational position than it
  began (trust broken, an alliance formed, a secret revealed).
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a scene that ends in the same emotional
  register it started in, despite containing dialogue or action.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Activity without a turn** — fights, chases, and conversations that
  generate motion without changing what anything means.
- **A turn buried too early**, leaving the rest of the scene to coast on
  momentum that's already spent.
- **A turn that isn't earned**, where the pivot depends on information or a
  decision that hasn't been set up, landing as arbitrary rather than
  inevitable-in-hindsight.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Can you point to the specific line or beat where this scene's emotional
  charge changes direction?
- If a reader described the scene's opening and closing emotional state in
  one word each, would those words differ?
- Is the turn earned by what came before it, or does it depend on something
  the reader hasn't been given reason to expect?
- Does a long scene turn only once, and would a second turn partway through
  sharpen it?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Mark the exact line or beat where a scene's charge flips; if none can be
   found, that's the scene to revise first.
2. For a scene that turns too early, try moving the turning information or
   action later, and use the earlier pages to raise what's at stake in the
   turn.
3. Try adding a second, smaller turn partway through a long scene to keep its
   middle from sagging.
4. For a deliberately negated turn (an expected reveal that doesn't land),
   check that the surrounding text signals the anticlimax as intentional.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Mood, transition, and atmosphere passages can function without a turn,
  provided they're not doing the narrative heavy lifting of a full scene.
- Some literary styles work in a deliberately flat, plotless register where
  charge shifts are subtle or absent by design.
- Very short beats within a larger scene may not need their own individual
  turn if the containing scene turns as a whole.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Identifying a scene's turn — or its absence — requires reading and
interpreting the emotional charge of prose; no structured data substitutes
for this. A coach can highlight candidate turning points for the author's
own confirmation but cannot determine emotional charge from text alone with
certainty.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*No turn:* A scene opens with two characters cautiously trusting each other
and closes with them still cautiously trusting each other, despite three
pages of conversation in between.

*Clear turn:* The same conversation includes one character letting slip a
detail only the betrayer could know; the scene ends with trust broken and an
alliance in question — a specific, locatable pivot point.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The value-shift/turn concept is drawn from Robert McKee's screenwriting
craft text ([[src.book.mckee-story]]), adapted here for prose scene
structure rather than quoted directly; `source_confidence` is set to `mixed`
because the model, while widely taught, originates in screenwriting
pedagogy and its direct transfer to prose scenes is this drafting pass's
adaptation rather than a claim McKee makes about novels specifically.

records.title: Sequel and reflection
records.summary: The companion unit to a scene — a character's emotional reaction, a weighed dilemma, and a decision — gives the reader room to feel a disaster's weight before the next goal launches.

citations.label: Techniques of the Selling Writer
Helping Writers Become Authors (blog and structure guides)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A sequel (in the classic structural sense, unrelated to "sequel" meaning a
follow-up book) is the unit that follows a scene's disaster: a character's
emotional reaction to what just happened, a dilemma weighed among imperfect
options, and a decision that becomes the next scene's goal. Where a scene is
built on external action and conflict, a sequel is built on internal
processing — it's the connective tissue that keeps a string of disasters
from reading as a character simply being battered by plot with no interiority
in between.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A story that moves from disaster to disaster with no reflection can feel
relentless in a way that numbs rather than thrills — readers stop being able
to track why a character makes their next move, because they never see the
character actually choose it. A sequel gives the reader access to the
character's reasoning and lets the next goal feel like a decision rather than
a random new problem the author introduced.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Full reaction-dilemma-decision**, played out explicitly across a page or
  more: an emotional beat, a weighed choice among bad options, a committed
  decision.
- **Compressed sequel**, handled in a paragraph or even a sentence, common in
  fast-paced or serialized fiction where a full sequel would slow momentum
  too much.
- **Interleaved sequel**, woven into the opening of the next scene rather
  than standing alone, so the reaction and decision happen on the move.
- **Deferred sequel**, where the emotional reaction is intentionally
  withheld and paid off later — used for characters who compartmentalize, but
  risky if the deferral reads as the author forgetting rather than the
  character choosing.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A passage of interiority following a disaster, naming or implying the
  character's emotional response before the next action begins.
- A visible weighing of options, even briefly, before a character commits to
  a course of action.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: consecutive disasters with the character
  moving directly into the next goal with no visible reaction or reasoning.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Omitting the sequel entirely** in fast-paced fiction, leaving reader
  disorientation about why the character does what they do next.
- **Over-length sequels** that stall momentum by lingering on reaction and
  dilemma far longer than the preceding disaster's weight justifies.
- **Decisions that don't follow from the dilemma** — the character reacts,
  weighs options, and then chooses something the reflection didn't actually
  point toward.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- After this disaster, does the reader get any access to how the character
  feels about it before the next goal launches?
- Is the length of this sequel proportional to the weight of what just
  happened?
- Does the character's next decision follow logically from the dilemma just
  weighed, or does it feel like a fresh, disconnected choice?
- In a fast-moving stretch, would a single compressed line of reaction be
  enough to keep the reader oriented, even without a full sequel?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. After a major disaster, add one line of explicit emotional reaction if
   none currently exists, and see whether the next scene's goal reads more
   motivated.
2. For a sequel that feels bloated, try compressing the dilemma to its
   essential tension and cutting restated options.
3. Check that a character's next decision can be traced back to the specific
   dilemma just weighed; if not, either adjust the dilemma or the decision.
4. In a high-tempo action stretch, try an interleaved sequel (folded into the
   next scene's opening beat) instead of a standalone pause, to preserve
   momentum while still grounding the choice.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Fast, adrenaline-driven sequences (a chase, a battle) can legitimately
  compress or omit full sequels to preserve pace, provided the reader isn't
  left unable to track motivation.
- A character written as deliberately unreflective, or a story working in a
  close, externally-focused POV, may minimize interiority as a stylistic
  choice rather than an oversight.
- Very short scenes may not need a distinct sequel at all if the next scene's
  goal is self-evident from context.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a sequel is present, proportionate, and logically connected to the
following decision requires reading and interpreting prose; there is no
deterministic substitute. A coach can point to the passage following a
disaster as candidate evidence but cannot conclude, from structured data
alone, whether the emotional beat lands.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Missing sequel:* A character's mentor is killed on page forty. Page
forty-one opens on the character already three streets away, executing a
plan, with no line acknowledging the loss.

*Present sequel:* The same death is followed by a paragraph in which the
character sits with the body for one line too long, weighs whether to pursue
the killer alone or return for allies, and chooses to go alone specifically
because waiting feels like a second betrayal — a decision the reflection
visibly produces.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The reaction-dilemma-decision structure comes from the same foundational
source as its companion pattern, Dwight Swain
([[src.book.swain-techniques-selling-writer]]); contemporary application and
pacing guidance draws on K. M. Weiland's widely referenced structure writing
([[src.book.weiland-helping-writers-become-authors]]). `source_confidence`
is `mixed` because the compression and interleaving guidance is this
drafting pass's synthesis of established sources rather than a directly
sourced claim from either.

records.title: Setting as a source of pressure
records.summary: A setting can be scenery a story happens in front of, or a set of constraints that makes the story's problems harder; this record is about the second, and about how to tell which one a draft has.

citations.label: Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft
The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers
Steering the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Setting can operate at two very different levels of involvement. At one, it
is the place a story happens: rendered, atmospheric, and essentially
neutral toward events. At the other, it is a source of constraint — the
weather, the distance, the season, the law, the architecture, the customs
make some things impossible and others expensive, and the story's problems
are harder because of where they occur.

This record is about the second. It is distinct from the description and
specificity record, which is about how vividly a place is rendered on the
page. A setting can be beautifully described and exert no pressure at all,
and a setting can be sketched in a sentence and constrain every scene.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Pressure from setting makes a world feel real in a way description alone
does not. When a place costs the characters something — a journey that takes
weeks, a city where their accent is a liability, a winter that ends the
campaigning season — the reader infers that the world exists independently
of the plot's convenience. Conversely, a world that supplies whatever a
scene needs and withholds nothing tends to feel like a backdrop even when
it is richly painted.

Setting-as-pressure also generates plot cheaply. A constraint the author has
established can complicate a scene without any new character or coincidence,
which is often the difference between a story that escalates through events
and one that escalates through invention.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Physical constraint** — distance, terrain, climate, season, scarcity.
  The oldest and most reliable form: things take time, and time costs.
- **Social constraint** — law, custom, class, reputation, obligation. What a
  character *may* do in this place, and what it costs them to do otherwise.
- **Institutional constraint** — the schedule, hierarchy, or rules of an
  enclosing structure: a school, a ship, an army, a hospital.
- **Setting as antagonist** — the place itself as the primary opposing
  force, common in survival and expedition stories.
- **Setting as relief** — a place whose function is to be safe, which works
  as pressure in reverse: it matters because leaving it is costly.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A plan that has to change because of where it must happen.
- Travel that takes a stated, felt amount of time, and characters who make
  decisions around it.
- Characters behaving differently in different places — quieter in one city,
  franker in another — because the setting is exerting something on them.
- Conversely: a journey of unspecified duration; a season that never
  constrains anything; a city that is a name and a marketplace.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Scenery without cost.** Extensive description of a place that never
  makes anything harder, which readers often experience as a slowed pace
  without a clear reason.
- **Inconsistent constraint.** A distance that takes weeks when the plot
  needs delay and days when it needs speed, which teaches the reader not to
  believe the map.
- **Constraint stated but not felt.** The narration says the winter is
  brutal; no scene is shaped by it.
- **Setting as exposition delivery.** A place introduced primarily so
  someone can explain the world in it.
- **Over-constraint.** So many limits that the characters cannot act, and
  the story becomes a description of impossibility.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this place make harder, and for whom?
- If this scene were moved somewhere else in the same world, what would
  actually change?
- What can the characters not do here that they could do elsewhere — and has
  the reader been told, or shown?
- Which constraints has the story established, and has it kept faith with
  them under plot pressure?
- Is there a place in this world the characters are trying to reach or
  avoid, and does the reader understand why?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Pick a scene and move it to a different location in the same world. If
   nothing about the scene changes, the setting is currently decorative
   there — which may be fine, or may be a missed source of difficulty.
2. List the three constraints this world imposes most often, and check
   whether any scene in the draft violates one for convenience.
3. Take one long description and convert half its detail into difficulty:
   the same features, but as things characters must work around.
4. Write the journey times, seasons, or laws down as a short reference, then
   read the draft against it. Inconsistencies usually cluster where the plot
   was in a hurry.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Interior and psychological fiction where the setting is deliberately thin
  because the pressure is internal.
- Stories whose promise is comfort or wish-fulfilment, where a frictionless
  world is the point and adding constraint would break the contract.
- Allegorical, fabular, and dreamlike modes, where a place that behaves
  according to meaning rather than physics is the form.
- Scenes that deliberately provide relief. Not every scene should be made
  harder by where it happens.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe some of this: whether journey durations are stated
consistently, whether described features recur as obstacles, how much of a
chapter is description versus action, whether a stated constraint is ever
referenced again. Contradictions in stated distances or times are the
closest thing here to a deterministic check, and even those require reading
context to distinguish an error from a character's mistaken belief.

What cannot be determined is whether a setting *should* exert more pressure.
That depends on the book's intent, and a low-friction world may be exactly
right. A coach can say that a place has been described at length and has not
yet constrained anything, and ask whether that is intended. It cannot
conclude that the setting is failing.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Setting as scenery:* three paragraphs on the salt flats — the light, the
crust underfoot, the distant heat shimmer. The characters cross them in a
sentence and arrive unaffected.

*Setting as pressure:* the same salt flats, where water must be carried, the
crust will not hold a cart, and travelling by day is impossible. The
crossing now costs a decision about what to leave behind.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Janet Burroway's textbook treatment of setting and atmosphere
([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the core distinction between
setting as backdrop and setting as an active element of conflict; John
Gardner ([[src.book.gardner-art-of-fiction]]) supplies the argument about
concrete detail and the vividness of the fictional world; Ursula K. Le Guin
([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]) supplies the treatment of description
as something to be integrated into action rather than delivered in blocks.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense: the principle
that setting can be active rather than decorative is well supported by
multiple independent craft sources, while this record's specific framing —
setting as a constraint economy, the location-swap test, the taxonomy of
constraint types — is this drafting pass's synthesis. The related record on
systemic social consequences extends the same reasoning to power systems
specifically; readers of that record should treat this one as the general
case rather than a duplicate of it.

records.title: Chapter architecture and transitions
records.summary: Where a chapter starts, where it ends, and how it hands off to the next one shape a reader's momentum independent of what happens inside the chapter — a strong scene can still underperform if it's boxed badly.

citations.label: Helping Writers Become Authors (blog and structure guides)
On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Chapter architecture concerns where a chapter chooses to begin and end
relative to the scene or scenes it contains, and how the transition to the
next chapter is handled. A chapter's entry and exit points don't have to
match a scene's own natural start and end — starting mid-action or ending
before a scene's full resolution are both established techniques — and the
choice of where to cut shapes reader momentum independent of the underlying
content's quality.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A chapter that ends on an open question, an unresolved threat, or a sharp
turn tends to pull a reader forward into the next one; a chapter that ends
only once everything is settled gives the reader a natural, comfortable
stopping point, which is sometimes exactly what's wanted (a breather) and
sometimes a momentum leak the author didn't intend. In serialized and
platform fiction, chapter-ending hooks are reported to matter more directly
to whether a reader continues, since the reader is actively deciding whether
to open the next chapter rather than simply continuing to read.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Mid-scene cuts**, ending a chapter before a scene fully resolves,
  carrying its remaining tension directly into the next chapter's opening.
- **Full-scene chapters**, where chapter and scene boundaries align, giving
  each chapter a self-contained shape.
- **Hook endings**, deliberately closing on a turn, revelation, or threat
  specifically to pull the reader forward. Worth distinguishing two kinds:
  an *event* hook, where something has happened and its outcome is open, and
  a *withheld-information* hook, where the narration knows something and
  declines to say it. Both pull, but the second spends reader trust rather
  than tension, and wears out faster under repetition.
- **Settled endings**, closing after a scene's tension has resolved, giving
  the reader a natural pause point — useful for pacing breathers and act
  breaks.
- **In-medias-res openings**, starting a chapter mid-action rather than at a
  scene's natural beginning, compressing setup and raising immediate
  engagement.
- **Multiple-POV chapter alternation**, where chapter boundaries also mark
  POV shifts, adding an additional structural function to the chapter break
  itself.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A chapter ending on a specific unresolved question, threat, or revelation
  that the next chapter doesn't immediately resolve, sustaining tension
  across the break.
- A chapter opening mid-action, with orienting context supplied
  economically rather than through a scene-setting preamble.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a run of consecutive chapters that all end
  once their contained scene is fully settled, with no variation in the
  resulting rhythm.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Uniform chapter shape**, where every chapter follows the same
  entry-to-exit pattern regardless of the story's pacing needs at that
  point, flattening the effect any individual choice could have.
