  (See the related pacing-across-scales record for the broader principle
  this instantiates at the chapter level.)
  
- **Hooks that don't pay off**, ending chapters on artificially inflated
  cliffhangers that the next chapter resolves anticlimactically, training
  readers to distrust the hooks over time.
- **Slow chapter openings after a hook**, undercutting momentum by opening
  the next chapter with scene-setting or recap instead of addressing the
  tension the previous chapter's ending raised.
- **Withholding as a substitute for event** — "she read the letter, and what
  it said changed everything" — where the pull comes from the narration
  refusing to report what it already knows. Readers eventually register this
  as a small dishonesty rather than as suspense.
- **Running past the ending**, where a chapter's real close is followed by a
  paragraph or two of tidying, so the intended final beat is not the one the
  reader leaves on.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If you read only this manuscript's chapter endings in sequence, would you
  feel pulled forward, or would each one feel like a natural stopping
  point?
- Does the chapter immediately following a hook ending address that hook's
  tension promptly, or does it open with unrelated scene-setting?
- Is there variation in chapter shape across the manuscript, or does every
  chapter follow the same entry-to-exit pattern?
- If this is serialized fiction, do chapter endings specifically account for
  the reader's active choice to continue, rather than assuming continuous
  reading?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Read only the manuscript's chapter endings in sequence and note which
   ones create forward pull versus which settle into a natural pause;
   consider whether the pattern matches the story's pacing needs.
2. For a hook ending that doesn't pay off promptly, either strengthen the
   following chapter's immediate response to it or reconsider the hook's
   framing.
3. Try moving a chapter break earlier or later relative to a scene's natural
   boundary and compare the resulting momentum.
4. For serialized fiction, specifically audit chapter endings for their
   effect on a reader's decision to continue, distinct from their effect on
   a reader already committed to reading straight through. The gap between
   chapters is real elapsed time on a serial platform — a day or a week —
   which is a different decision from turning a page.
5. Take a withheld-information hook and rebuild it on an event instead: let
   the reader have the fact and end on what the character does about it.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Literary or slower-paced fiction may deliberately favor settled,
  contemplative chapter endings throughout, where sustained forward pull
  isn't the intended reading experience.
- Very short chapters (vignette-style structures) may not need the full
  entry/exit architecture this pattern describes.
- A deliberately disorienting structure (chapters that begin without clear
  orientation, as a stylistic choice) may use unclear entry points on
  purpose.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a chapter ending creates forward pull or a natural pause, and
whether that choice serves the surrounding pacing, requires reading and
interpreting the prose — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.
Chapter length and count are directly computable from raw text where
structure is explicit.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Uniform, settled chapters:* Ten consecutive chapters each open with brief
scene-setting and close once their contained conflict resolves, producing a
consistent, comfortable rhythm with no variation in forward pull.

*Varied architecture:* The same stretch instead alternates: a settled
chapter after a high-intensity sequence, followed by two chapters that end
mid-scene on a rising threat, followed by another settled chapter — the
variation itself creates a felt rhythm distinct from either pattern alone.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Chapter-ending and structural-signpost guidance draws on K. M. Weiland's
widely referenced structure writing
([[src.book.weiland-helping-writers-become-authors]]); general prose-craft
principles about maintaining reader momentum draw on Stephen King's writing
on craft and revision ([[src.book.king-on-writing]]), a single author's
practice and opinion presented as such. `source_confidence` is `mixed`
accordingly, and the serialized-fiction-specific framing is this drafting
pass's application of general platform reader-behavior concerns rather than
a directly sourced claim.

records.title: Opening pages and reader commitment
records.summary: The first page or two do a specific job — establishing whose story this is, what kind of book it will be, and why the reader should keep going — and they do it before the reader has any accumulated goodwill to spend.

citations.label: Hooked: Write Fiction That Grabs Readers at Page One & Never Lets Them Go
Writing the Breakout Novel
Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An opening is the stretch of a story — often a page, sometimes a chapter —
during which a reader is deciding whether to continue, and is doing so
without any accumulated investment to draw on. Everything the story will
later be able to rely on (attachment to a character, curiosity about a
question, trust that setups will pay off) does not exist yet. The opening's
job is to create enough of it to buy the next few pages, and then the next.

This record covers that stretch and the pressure it operates under. It is
distinct from the promise and genre-signaling patterns treated separately
here: those concern what a story commits to across a whole book. An opening
is where those commitments are first made — quickly, and usually
implicitly.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A reader arriving at page one is deciding, mostly below conscious thought,
what kind of experience is on offer and whether they want it. Craft
discussion converges on a few things a reader seems to want early: someone
to attach to, an indication of what trouble is in play, and a reason to
believe the writing will repay attention. A reader given none of these
rarely articulates a complaint — they simply stop.

Serialized publishing sharpens this considerably. A reader browsing a
platform's list is comparing openings, not books, and a story whose appeal
begins in chapter four is competing against stories whose appeal begins in
paragraph one. That is a market fact rather than a craft law, but it changes
what an opening has to do.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Opening in motion** — beginning during an event already underway, so
  that orientation arrives as the reader watches rather than before.
- **Opening on a character in ordinary difficulty** — establishing who this
  is and what their life costs them before the story disrupts it.
- **Opening on a question** — a situation whose explanation is withheld,
  buying attention against the promise of an answer.
- **Opening on voice** — carrying the first pages primarily on the
  distinctiveness of the narration, most viable where voice is the book's
  central pleasure.

Edgerton's craft treatment of openings distinguishes the *surface problem*
a scene presents from the deeper *story-worthy problem* the book is actually
about, and argues that an opening works better when the first gestures
toward the second rather than standing alone.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A first paragraph establishing a specific person in a specific situation,
  rather than a landscape, a history, or the weather.
- Orientation delivered inside action — who, where, and what is at stake
  emerging from what characters do and say rather than from a preamble.
- A first chapter that ends on a reason to continue rather than on a
  resolution.
- Conversely: several pages of world history, a dream sequence revealed as a
  dream, or a character waking up and describing themselves — all common
  enough that many readers recognize them as openings that have not yet
  started.

None of these signals proves anything on its own. A prologue of world
history is a real choice with precedent; it simply spends reader patience
early, and should be made knowingly.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Front-loading orientation.** Explaining the world so the reader will
  understand chapter three, at the cost of chapter one being interesting.
- **Opening before the story starts.** Beginning at the last ordinary
  moment rather than the first consequential one, so the reader waits
  through a preamble for the book they were promised.
- **A hook with nothing behind it.** An arresting first line that connects
  to nothing, which buys attention and then spends the credit immediately.
- **Withholding to create false mystery.** Concealing information the POV
  character plainly knows, which reads as evasion rather than suspense.
- **Signalling the wrong book.** An opening whose tone promises a different
  experience from the one that follows — the promise-consistency problem,
  seeded at page one.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If a reader stopped at the bottom of page one, what would they be able to
  say this book is about?
- What is the first thing on the page that a reader might actually want to
  know the answer to?
- Is the opening scene the first moment when something changes, or the last
  moment before it does?
- What does the opening promise about tone, pace, and subject — and does
  chapter ten still honor it?
- If the orientation in the first pages were cut entirely, what would a
  reader genuinely fail to follow?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Delete the first page and read from page two. If nothing is lost, the
   book was clearing its throat; if something is lost, note precisely what —
   it is usually smaller than a page.
2. Write a one-sentence statement of the story-worthy problem, then check
   whether anything in the first scene gestures toward it. If not, consider
   whether the opening is doing the book's work or its own.
3. Ask a first reader to stop at the end of chapter one and say what they
   expect from the book. The gap between that and the actual book is the
   promise the opening is really making.
4. For a serialized draft, compare the first chapter against the opening
   chapters of three stories in the same category — not to imitate them, but
   to see what job those openings do that yours may be deferring.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Literary and experimental traditions where a slow, ambient, or
  disorienting opening is the intended effect and the readership expects it.
- Later books in a series, where the reader arrives with attachment already
  built and an opening may reasonably spend time re-establishing rather than
  hooking.
- Any case where the intent is to filter for a particular reader rather than
  retain the widest one — a legitimate strategy with a known cost.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe structural facts: how far into the first chapter the
first conflict appears, how much of the first page is exposition or
backstory, whether a named character is present in the first paragraph,
whether the chapter ends open or closed. These are countable from the text.

Whether an opening *works* cannot be determined. Reader commitment is a
response, not a property of the page, and it varies by reader, platform, and
expectation. The absence of a conventional hook is not evidence of failure,
and its presence is not evidence of success. A coach should describe what
the opening is doing and what it appears to promise, and leave the judgment
of effect to the author and their readers.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Opening that defers:* "The Kesarin Empire had stood nine hundred years. Its
founding is recorded in the Third Chronicle..." — accurate, and the reader
has not yet met anyone.

*Opening in motion:* "Tomas had been told the vault door could not be opened
from the inside. He had eleven minutes to find out who had been wrong." —
a person, a situation, a limit, and a question, in two sentences.

*Hook with nothing behind it:* "I died on a Tuesday." — followed by four
chapters of school routine in which nobody dies and the line is never
explained. The attention it bought is gone by page three.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Opening craft is well covered by practitioner literature. Les Edgerton's
dedicated treatment ([[src.book.edgerton-hooked]]) supplies the
surface-problem versus story-worthy-problem distinction and the catalogue of
recognizable weak openings; Donald Maass
([[src.book.maass-writing-breakout-novel]]) supplies the argument about early
tension and reader investment; Janet Burroway
([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the scene-construction and
orientation principles. The three agree broadly on what openings do and
disagree on how prescriptive to be, which this record preserves rather than
resolves.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the sense the handoff defines: the craft
principles are well supported by multiple independent sources, while the
serialized-publishing application — that platform browsing makes openings
compete directly — is this drafting pass's synthesis from the genre research
and is marked as such rather than attributed to any of the three craft texts,
none of which discuss serial platforms. The claim that readers "decide" on
page one is a widely repeated practitioner belief; no reader-response study
is cited here, and none should be inferred.

records.title: Series and arc architecture
records.summary: A long work needs shape above the chapter and below the whole — arcs that close while the larger story stays open, and a plan for what the series is actually building toward.

citations.label: Writing the Breakout Novel
Super Structure: The Key to Unleashing the Power of Story
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Between the chapter and the whole work sits a layer most drafts handle by
instinct: the arc. An arc is a stretch of story with its own question and its
own closure — a tournament, a siege, a journey, an investigation — nested
inside a larger story that stays open.

This record is about that layer and the one above it: how arcs are shaped,
how they close, and what the series as a whole is building toward. It is
distinct from pacing across scales, which is about rhythm, and from chapter
architecture, which is about the unit below.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Long-form readers need periodic satisfaction or they leave. An arc that
closes gives them a payoff without ending the book, and it gives the story
somewhere to breathe and reset. A serial with no arc boundaries reads as an
undifferentiated stream: things happen, nothing concludes, and a reader who
puts it down has no natural place to pick it back up.

The layer above matters differently. A reader will follow a long story on
faith for a while, but they are also asking, quietly, whether the author
knows where this goes. Signs that the series has a destination — questions
raised early and answered late, consequences that persist across arcs — buy
patience. Their absence is what "it lost its way" usually means.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The nested arc** — a self-contained sequence with its own question,
  closing while the larger story continues.
- **The escalating ladder** — each arc raising the scale of the last, common
  in progression fiction and prone to running out of ladder.
- **The braided series** — several long threads advancing at different rates
  across arcs, so something always closes and something always continues.
- **The volume break** — an arc boundary treated as a book ending, with a
  larger closure and a deliberate gap.
- **The open-ended serial** — no planned destination, arcs generated as the
  story goes. Common, viable, and the structure most likely to sag.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- An arc that ends with a cost the next arc has to carry.
- A question raised in the first arc, still live in the fifth, and visibly
  moving.
- Conversely: arcs that end with everything restored, so nothing accumulates.
- A middle stretch where several arcs pass and nothing about the larger story
  changes — the sag readers describe without being able to locate.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Arcs with no residue.** Each closes cleanly and leaves nothing behind, so
  the series is episodic without meaning to be.
- **The ladder that runs out.** Escalation by scale until the stakes are
  cosmic by book three and there is nowhere left to go.
- **No standing question.** Nothing asked early enough and held long enough
  for the reader to feel a destination.
- **The unplanned middle.** Arcs generated to fill space, recognizable
  because they could be reordered without loss.
- **Closure deferred indefinitely.** Every arc ending on an opening, so the
  reader is never once paid.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What question does this arc ask, and is it answered by its end?
- What does this arc leave behind that the next one must deal with?
- What question has been open since the beginning, and has it moved
  recently?
- Could these three arcs be reordered? If so, is that a feature?
- What does the series build toward — and if the honest answer is "I don't
  know yet," what is the earliest point that has to change?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one line per arc: its question, its answer, and what it leaves
   behind. Blank third columns are where the series is losing accumulation.
2. Find the last time the standing question of the series visibly moved. If
   it was long ago, that gap is probably where readers felt the sag.
3. Try reordering two arcs on paper. If nothing breaks, ask what would make
   the order matter.
4. For an open-ended serial, name three things that must be true at the end,
   even without knowing how you get there. Destinations constrain usefully
   without requiring an outline.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Deliberately episodic work — procedurals, slice-of-life, comfort serials —
  where resettable arcs are the promise and accumulation would work against
  it.
- Standalone novels, where the arc layer collapses into the whole.
- Early serial chapters where the shape has not yet emerged and imposing one
  prematurely can flatten the discovery a serial's momentum depends on.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Given a chaptered manuscript, a coach can approximate arc boundaries from
where locations, casts, and stated goals change, chart arc lengths, and
identify entities or questions that recur across them. Arc-length variance is
computable; arc *boundaries* are an inference and will sometimes be wrong.

Whether an arc "leaves residue" is a semantic judgment. So is sag: a stretch
where little changes may be deliberate breathing room in a very long work.
The coach should present the shape it can see — arc lengths, gaps in a
recurring thread — and ask, rather than diagnose a lost way.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Arc without residue:* the siege is lifted, the wounded recover, the ally who
betrayed them is forgiven offstage, and the next arc opens with the same four
people in the same positions.

*Arc with residue:* the siege is lifted, and the granary is gone. Everything
in the next arc happens to people who are hungry.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Donald Maass ([[src.book.maass-writing-breakout-novel]]) supplies the
treatment of tension sustained across a long work and of stakes that
accumulate; James Scott Bell ([[src.book.bell-super-structure]]) supplies
structural vocabulary for signposts and mid-length units. This library's
genre research ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the
serial-specific observations about arc boundaries and reader drop-off.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. Both craft
sources address novels rather than long serials, so the arc layer as
described here — nested closure inside an open larger story, residue between
arcs — is this drafting pass's synthesis extending their principles. The
observation that readers need periodic closure in long serials comes from
genre research, not from a study; treat it as practitioner consensus.

records.title: Subplots and thread braiding
records.summary: A book usually runs several storylines at once; braiding is the work of deciding what each one is for, how often it surfaces, and whether it eventually touches the others.

citations.label: The Anatomy of Story: 22 Steps to Becoming a Master Storyteller
Writing the Breakout Novel
Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Most novels run more than one storyline. Braiding is the management of those
threads: what each one is for, how often it surfaces, how long it can be
absent before a reader loses hold of it, and whether it eventually connects
to the main line or simply runs alongside it.

This is distinct from complications, which are events that change the shape
of a problem inside one line, and from causal escalation, which is about how
events drive each other. Braiding is the level above both: the arrangement of
whole storylines against each other across a book.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Threads let a book breathe. A single line at constant pressure exhausts a
reader; cutting away to a second concern creates relief without stopping the
story, and returning to the first after an absence often makes it feel more
urgent than it did when the reader left. Threads also let a book say more
than one thing — a subplot can examine the same question the main plot is
asking, from a position the protagonist cannot occupy.

The cost is attention. Every thread a reader is asked to hold is a small
ongoing tax, and a thread that never repays it becomes something the reader
waits out.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The mirroring subplot** — a secondary storyline that poses the main
  plot's question in a different key, so that the two comment on each other
  without either explaining the other.
- **The contrasting subplot** — a line that shows what the protagonist's
  choice would look like made differently, often through a character who
  chose otherwise.
- **The convergent thread** — a line that runs separately and then collides
  with the main plot, usually near the climax.
- **The standing thread** — an ongoing relationship, obligation, or
  condition that surfaces regularly without ever becoming the book's centre.
- **The runner** — a small recurring element, sometimes comic, that provides
  rhythm and familiarity more than plot.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Chapters that alternate between threads at a rhythm the reader learns.
- A thread that is set up in the first quarter, disappears for two hundred
  pages, and returns needing reintroduction.
- Two lines that share a scene for the first time, and the scene's tension
  comes largely from that convergence.
- A subplot that ends quietly a third of the way in and is never referenced
  again — sometimes a dropped thread, sometimes a deliberate closure the
  reader reads as dropped.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The unconnected thread.** A well-written line that never touches
  anything else and could be lifted out cleanly, which readers often
  describe as "the parts I skipped."
- **Thread starvation.** A line surfacing so rarely that each return spends
  its space on reminding the reader who these people are.
- **Competition rather than braiding.** Two threads of equal weight and
  similar concern, so the book reads as two half-books.
- **The subplot that eats the book.** A secondary line more alive than the
  main one — worth noticing rather than fixing, since it sometimes indicates
  which book the author actually wants to write.
- **Convergence by coincidence.** Threads that meet because the plot needs
  them to rather than because anything in either made it likely.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What is each thread for — what does the book get from it that it could
  not get otherwise?
- Which threads eventually touch, and which are content to run in parallel?
- What is the longest gap in the book for each thread, and does the reader
  need reminding when it returns?
- If a thread were removed entirely, what else in the book would have to
  change? If the answer is nothing, that is information.
- Does any thread ask the same question as the main line, and would the book
  be stronger if one of them asked a different one?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Chart the threads by chapter — a simple grid of which line each chapter
   advances. Gaps, clumps, and the shape of the convergence usually become
   visible immediately.
2. Write one sentence per thread saying what it is for. A thread whose
   sentence is only a description of its events, not its function, may not
   have one yet.
3. Try removing the weakest thread in outline and see what collapses. What
   collapses is the thread's real contribution; if nothing does, consider
   whether its material belongs to another line.
4. Move a convergence earlier and see what it costs. Threads often meet
   later than they need to because the author is saving them.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Deliberately episodic or picaresque structures, where discrete,
  unconnected episodes are the form rather than a failure of it.
- Short works, where a single line is often the right amount of book.
- Serialized fiction with a long arc structure, where a thread may
  legitimately sleep for a hundred chapters because the reader is reading
  across a much longer span than a novel's.
- Stories whose subject is disconnection, where threads that never meet may
  be the point — provided the book gives the reader a reason to believe that.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can, given a chaptered manuscript, approximate which thread each
chapter advances by tracking which characters and concerns appear, and from
that produce gap lengths, distribution, and the location of convergences.
These are useful structural observations, and they are approximations: which
thread a chapter "belongs to" is an interpretive call, and chapters often
advance two.

What cannot be determined is whether a thread earns its place. That is a
judgment about what the book is for. A thread with long gaps and no
convergence is not thereby a failure — the coach should show the shape and
ask, rather than name a fault.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*A mirroring subplot:* the protagonist refuses to give up a dangerous
inheritance; in the second thread, her cousin accepts an equivalent one and
is slowly consumed by it. Neither line explains the other, and the book's
question is sharper for having two answers in it.

*An unconnected thread:* eight chapters follow a cartographer mapping the
northern roads. The chapters are good. Nothing in the book requires the map,
and no character ever consults it.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
John Truby ([[src.book.truby-anatomy-of-story]]) supplies the argument that
subplots work best when they pose the main story's moral question
differently rather than merely adding incident; Donald Maass
([[src.book.maass-writing-breakout-novel]]) supplies the treatment of
multiple storylines as a source of tension and momentum; Janet Burroway
([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the general structural
vocabulary this record uses.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense: the underlying
principle — that a subplot should do work the main line cannot — is supported
independently by two of the three sources, while the specific diagnostics
here (thread charting, gap length, the removal test, the taxonomy of forms)
are this drafting pass's synthesis. The serialized-fiction exception is drawn
from this library's own genre research rather than from any of the three
craft texts, none of which address serial publication.

records.title: Description and specificity
records.summary: A specific, well-chosen detail does more work than a longer list of generic ones — specificity is what makes description feel observed rather than assembled from category labels.

citations.label: The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers
On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Specificity in description means choosing the particular, telling detail
over the generic category label — "a chipped enamel mug with a faded rooster
on the side" rather than "a mug," or a character's exact gesture rather than
"she looked upset." The principle isn't that more description is better; a
single well-chosen specific detail often does more work, and does it more
efficiently, than several generic ones stacked together. Specificity also
extends beyond physical description to characterization, dialogue tags, and
world detail — anywhere a generic placeholder could be replaced with
something particular to this story's specific world and characters.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Generic description asks a reader to fill in their own mental image from a
category ("a forest," "a sad expression"), which is efficient but forgettable
— readers report that unspecific prose tends to blur together across a
manuscript. A specific detail gives the reader something particular to
picture and, often, to feel — a chipped enamel mug carries implications
(age, use, a story) that "a mug" doesn't, without needing to state those
implications directly.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Sensory specificity**, grounding description in a particular sight,
  sound, smell, texture, or taste rather than a general category.
- **Behavioral specificity**, replacing generic emotional labels ("she was
  nervous") with a specific physical or behavioral detail that implies the
  emotion without naming it.
- **World-specific detail**, grounding a setting in details particular to
  this story's world rather than generic genre furniture (a specific,
  invented local custom rather than "a market town").
- **Selective specificity**, choosing one or two telling details rather than
  exhaustively describing everything in a scene — specificity is not the
  same as thoroughness, and can be undermined by over-description as easily
  as by vagueness.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A single, particular detail doing the work several generic ones would
  otherwise need to do.
- Emotional states conveyed through specific physical behavior rather than
  named directly.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: description built entirely from category
  labels (a house, a forest, an angry expression) with no particular,
  observed detail anywhere in a passage.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Generic description**, relying on category labels instead of particular
  detail, especially common in fast first drafts.
- **Over-description**, piling on many details (some specific, some not)
  past the point where they're doing useful work, slowing pacing without
  adding proportional value.
- **Specificity without relevance**, choosing a vivid but irrelevant detail
  that doesn't connect to character, mood, or plot, functioning as texture
  with no deeper purpose.
- **Telling the emotion and showing the detail redundantly**, stating "she
  was nervous" and then also describing the physical signs of nervousness,
  when the detail alone would have been sufficient.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is there a passage using a generic category label (a house, a forest, an
  expression) that could be replaced with one particular, observed detail?
- Does a description pile on multiple details past the point where they're
  doing distinct work?
- Is an emotional state named directly and also shown through physical
  detail, when one or the other would be sufficient?
- Does a vivid, specific detail actually connect to character, mood, or
  plot, or is it decorative texture with no deeper purpose?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Find a passage relying on generic category labels and replace one with a
   single particular, observed detail.
2. For an over-described passage, cut details until only the ones doing
   distinct work remain, and compare the result.
3. For an emotional state stated directly, try replacing the direct
   statement with only the physical detail and see whether the emotion
   still reads clearly.
4. Check a vivid detail's connection to the story's character, mood, or
   plot; if it has none, decide whether it earns its place as pure texture
   or should be cut or replaced.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Fast-paced action sequences may deliberately minimize description,
  including specific detail, to maintain momentum — sparse prose here is a
  pacing choice, not a failure of specificity.
- Some prose styles (minimalist, spare traditions) use generic or minimal
  description deliberately, where the absence of detail is itself a
  stylistic signature.
- A first draft's generic description is a normal, expected stage of
  process, not a finished-manuscript failure — this pattern is most useful
  during revision.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a description relies on generic labels or particular detail, and
whether a given detail connects meaningfully to character or plot, requires
reading and interpreting the prose — a judgment no structured data
substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Generic:* "The old house looked abandoned, with an overgrown yard and a
sad, empty feeling to it."

*Specific:* "Ivy had pulled two shutters loose from their hinges, and a
child's bicycle, rusted through, lay where it had fallen against the porch
steps years before" — the same abandonment, conveyed through particular,
implication-carrying detail rather than category labels.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The specificity principle draws on John Gardner's foundational writing on
concrete detail and the "vivid, continuous dream"
([[src.book.gardner-art-of-fiction]]) and Stephen King's writing on
description and revision practice ([[src.book.king-on-writing]]), a single
author's practice and opinion presented as such. `source_confidence` is
`mixed` because the specific variant taxonomy (sensory/behavioral/world-
specific/selective) presented here is this drafting pass's synthesis rather
than a direct claim from either source.

records.title: Dialogue and subtext
records.summary: What characters say and what they actually mean often diverge, and dialogue that lets a reader feel that gap — rather than stating both layers outright — tends to read as more alive than dialogue that says exactly what it means.

citations.label: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting
Steering the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Subtext is what's actually driving a conversation beneath its literal
content — a desire, fear, or conflict characters don't state outright, often
because stating it directly would be too costly, too vulnerable, or
socially impossible in the moment. Dialogue that carries subtext lets the
reader infer this deeper layer through what's said, what's avoided, and how
characters respond, rather than having a character announce their real
feelings. Not all dialogue needs subtext — direct, plain communication is
sometimes exactly right — but a manuscript where dialogue routinely says
exactly what characters mean, with no gap between text and subtext, tends to
read as flatter than one where the gap is used deliberately.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Dialogue with subtext rewards attention: a reader who notices what a
character isn't saying gets a specific pleasure unavailable to a reader
skimming only the literal words. It also more closely mirrors how people
actually communicate under real social and emotional pressure — directness
is often costly, and characters (like people) frequently talk around what
they mean rather than stating it. Dialogue with no subtext at all can feel
like characters explaining themselves to the reader rather than talking to
each other.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Avoidance subtext**, where a character talks around a topic they're
  unwilling or unable to address directly.
- **Conflict-masked-as-politeness subtext**, where surface courtesy
  conceals real tension or disagreement.
- **Declaration-as-deflection subtext**, where a character states something
  emphatically specifically because they don't believe it, or are trying to
  convince themselves.
- **Shared-understanding subtext**, where two characters communicate through
  implication because directness isn't necessary between them — a marker of
  intimacy or long history.
- **Direct dialogue with no subtext**, appropriate and often necessary for
  functional exchanges (giving instructions, conveying urgent plot
  information) where subtext would slow or obscure a scene that needs
  clarity.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A conversation where a character's literal words and their evident
  emotional state or underlying want are in tension, with the gap left for
  the reader to notice rather than explained.
- Dialogue where what's *not* said (a topic avoided, a question deflected)
  carries as much information as what is said.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: characters stating their feelings,
  motivations, or intentions directly and completely in every exchange, with
  no gap between text and subtext anywhere in the manuscript.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **On-the-nose dialogue**, where characters say exactly what they mean and
  feel in every exchange, removing the inferential pleasure subtext
  provides.
- **Subtext so buried it reads as confusion**, where the gap between text
  and meaning is so wide or unclear that a reader can't reasonably infer
  what's actually happening in the scene.
- **Uniform subtext strategy**, using the same technique (deflection, for
  instance) in every tense conversation regardless of the specific
  characters or situation, making dialogue feel formulaic.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- In a key conversation, do the characters say exactly what they mean, or is
  there a gap a reader has to infer?
- If a character is avoiding a topic, is the avoidance itself legible, or
  does it just read as the topic never coming up?
- Is there a scene where direct, plain dialogue would actually serve better
  than subtext, because clarity matters more than inference in that moment?
- Does every tense conversation in the manuscript use the same subtext
  technique, or does it vary by character and situation?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Take a scene where dialogue states feelings or intentions directly and
   try rewriting it so the same information is conveyed through what's
   avoided or implied instead.
2. For dialogue that feels confusing rather than layered, check whether the
   underlying subtext is legible enough for a reader to infer, even if the
   characters themselves don't state it.
3. Read a tense conversation aloud, focusing only on what's not being said;
   if nothing is being withheld, consider what a character in this
   situation would realistically avoid saying.
4. For a functional, information-conveying scene, confirm that direct
   dialogue is the right choice rather than a missed opportunity — not every
   exchange needs subtext.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Functional dialogue conveying necessary plot or safety information
  (instructions during a crisis, for instance) often benefits from
  directness over subtext, where clarity is the priority.
- Some characters are written as unusually direct or unable to
  read/produce subtext (due to characterization, culture, or neurotype),
  and dialogue reflecting that directly is accurate characterization, not a
  craft failure.
- Very short or functional scenes may not have room for subtext to develop
  meaningfully.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether dialogue carries subtext, and whether the gap between text and
meaning is legible without being overexplained, requires reading and
interpreting the prose — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*On-the-nose:* "I'm still angry that you left without saying goodbye, and it
made me feel like our friendship doesn't matter to you," a character says
directly, stating the scene's entire emotional content outright.

*Subtext:* The same character instead asks, "Did you find good weather for
the trip?" in a tone the narration notes as too careful, and the friend's
overlong answer about the weather, avoiding any mention of the goodbye,
carries the same unresolved hurt without either character naming it.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The subtext principle draws on Robert McKee's writing on dialogue and value
beneath the surface of a scene ([[src.book.mckee-story]]) and Ursula K. Le
Guin's writing on voice and narrative control
([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]); both established craft texts.
`source_confidence` is `mixed` because the specific variant taxonomy
(avoidance/conflict-masked/declaration-as-deflection/shared-understanding)
presented here is this drafting pass's synthesis rather than a direct claim
from either source.

records.title: Humor as a craft element
records.summary: Comedy is constructible rather than innate — and in a long serial it does structural work beyond amusement, buying relief, characterizing quickly, and making darker material bearable.

citations.label: The Comic Toolbox: How to Be Funny Even If You're Not
Steering the Craft
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Humor in fiction is often treated as a temperament — some writers are funny
and some are not — but comedy writing has a craft literature that treats it
as constructible: built out of exaggeration, reversal, incongruity, timing,
and characters whose flaws produce trouble. This record treats humor as a
craft element with jobs to do, rather than as a personality trait an author
either has or lacks.

It sits alongside voice as a craft element rather than inside it. Voice is
the narration's overall sensibility; humor is a specific effect that can
operate through voice, through character, through situation, or through
structure, and each of those behaves differently under revision.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Humor buys relief, and relief is a pacing instrument. A story running at
sustained pressure exhausts readers; a moment of comedy releases it without
stopping the plot, in much the way a quieter scene does but faster.

It also characterizes efficiently. What a person finds funny, whether they
joke under pressure, and whether anyone laughs at them tells a reader a great
deal in very little space. And in darker material, comedy is frequently what
makes the dark parts bearable — a book with no lightness anywhere asks a lot
of a reader across a long serial.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Character humor** — funny because of who this person is, which is the
  most durable kind since it also does characterization.
- **Situational comedy** — funny because of what has gone wrong, usually
  built by escalation.
- **Voice humor** — funny in the narration itself, through phrasing, timing,
  and understatement.
- **Banter** — comedy in the exchange between characters, which carries
  relationship information alongside the joke.
- **Undercutting** — a comic beat placed immediately after a serious one,
  which either releases tension usefully or discards it, depending on
  placement.
- **The comic register that never breaks** — sustained comedy as the book's
  whole mode, which changes what its serious moments cost.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A joke that only this character could have made.
- A scene whose comedy comes from escalating a small problem rather than
  from anyone saying anything funny.
- Understatement in the narration doing the work no character has to do
  aloud.
- Conversely: a designated funny character whose lines could be redistributed
  to anyone, and a running gag repeated past the point where it stopped being
  a surprise.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The joke that costs the scene.** Comedy placed where tension was
  accumulating, releasing pressure the story needed.
- **The designated comic.** One character carrying all humor, which flattens
  them into a function — closely related to the exposition-companion pattern.
- **Tonal whiplash.** Comedy and gravity alternating without transition, so
  neither register is trusted.
- **The gag with no half-life.** A running joke repeated at the same
  intensity until the reader is waiting for it to stop.
- **Humor as an apology.** Undercutting every sincere moment, so the book
  never asks the reader to take anything seriously — sometimes a voice,
  frequently a defence.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What is the humor here *for* — relief, characterization, tone, or
  contrast?
- Could another character have made this joke? If yes, it may not be
  character humor.
- Is this comic beat releasing tension the story wanted released?
- Does the book have any lightness in it at all, and if not, is that a
  choice?
- Does the running gag change over its repetitions, or only recur?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Mark every comic beat in a chapter and note what each is doing. Beats with
   no answer are candidates for cutting or repurposing.
2. Move one joke a paragraph later, past the tension peak rather than into
   it, and see what changes.
3. Redistribute one of the designated comic's lines to a serious character
   and see whether it gets funnier.
4. Take a running gag and escalate or invert its third appearance rather than
   repeating it.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Work whose promise is unrelieved intensity — some horror, some tragedy —
  where lightness would break the contract deliberately made with the reader.
- Comic novels, where humor is the mode rather than an element, and the
  questions above invert: the interesting problem becomes when to stop being
  funny.
- Cultural and personal variation in what is funny is wide enough that
  "this isn't landing" is often about audience rather than construction, and
  a coach should be slow to call a joke a failure.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This is among the least detectable patterns in the library. Humor has no
reliable textual signature: a coach cannot identify a joke, and certainly
cannot tell whether one works. Some weak proxies exist — dialogue density,
the recurrence of a distinctive phrase that might be a running gag — and none
is trustworthy.

A coach should treat humor as something the author raises, not something the
system detects. If asked, it can discuss placement relative to tension, the
distribution of comic lines across characters, and the structural questions
above, all as reasoning about a passage the author has identified rather than
as detection.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Redistributable joke:* "'Well, that went well,' said Pell, who was the
funny one." — The line is fine and belongs to nobody.

*Character humor:* Roan, who had never in his life admitted to being
frightened, said the cave was structurally interesting and that he would
guard the entrance from out here, where the light was better for it.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
John Vorhaus ([[src.book.vorhaus-comic-toolbox]]) supplies this record's
central premise — that comedy is constructible from identifiable components
rather than being an innate gift — along with the roles of exaggeration,
reversal, and character flaw. Ursula K. Le Guin
([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]) supplies the treatment of timing and
rhythm this record applies to comic placement. Everything else is marked
synthesis ([[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]]).

`source_confidence` is `limited`, deliberately. Vorhaus writes for screen and
comedy writing, not prose fiction, so his framework is being transferred
rather than applied; Le Guin does not discuss humor specifically. No craft
source examined by this pass treats humor's *structural* role in long-form
prose — the relief, pacing, and bearability arguments here are this pass's
reasoning, not sourced claims. This is a revision-pass target: there is a
substantial theoretical literature on comedy, from Bergson onward, that a
later pass with access to it should bring in. Nothing here should be read as
a claim about what readers in general find funny, which varies far too widely
to generalize.

records.title: Narrative summary versus scene
records.summary: Compressing time through summary and slowing down into fully dramatized scene are both necessary tools — the craft question is whether a given moment's significance matches the amount of narrative time spent on it.

citations.label: The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers
Helping Writers Become Authors (blog and structure guides)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Narrative summary compresses time and event into a condensed report — "the
next three years passed quietly" — while scene dramatizes a moment in close
to real time, with action, dialogue, and sensory detail. Both are necessary
tools, and neither is inherently superior to the other; the recurring craft
question this pattern addresses is proportionality — whether the amount of
narrative time and detail spent on a given moment matches that moment's
actual significance to the story, rather than defaulting to one mode
uniformly.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A moment dramatized in full scene when it doesn't warrant that level of
detail can drag, wasting a reader's attention on something that doesn't
matter enough to earn it. A moment significant enough to deserve full
scene treatment but instead compressed into summary can leave a reader
feeling cheated of an experience the story implied would matter. Getting
this proportionality right is part of what makes a manuscript's pacing feel
controlled rather than arbitrary — not "everything important gets a scene"
mechanically, but a considered match between significance and treatment.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Full dramatized scene**, used for a story's most significant moments —
  turning points, confrontations, revelations — where the reader needs to
  experience the moment directly rather than being told about it.
- **Compressed summary**, used to cover time or events that matter for
  continuity or context but don't need moment-by-moment treatment.
- **Summary-with-a-detail**, a hybrid where a compressed passage is
  punctuated by one specific, dramatized beat, letting the reader feel a
  representative moment without dramatizing the entire span.
- **Scene interrupted by summary**, where a scene briefly compresses a
  less-important stretch (getting from one location to another) before
  returning to full dramatization.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A significant turning point rendered in close, moment-by-moment detail,
  with the surrounding, less critical time compressed around it.
- A passage of summary covering a span of time efficiently, without
  attempting false significance through unwarranted detail.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a pivotal emotional or plot moment
  compressed into a sentence or two of summary ("they fought, and by the end
  neither one trusted the other") when the story's stakes suggest it
  deserved to be dramatized directly.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Summarizing a moment that needed to be a scene**, especially common
  with emotionally significant turns (a reconciliation, a betrayal) that
  get reported rather than experienced.
- **Dramatizing a moment that didn't need to be a scene**, giving full
  scene treatment to routine or low-stakes events, diluting the impact of
  scenes that do matter by making them proportionally similar to ones that
  don't.
- **Uniform treatment throughout**, where a manuscript defaults entirely to
  either scene or summary regardless of a given moment's actual weight.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is there a significant turning point currently rendered in summary that a
  reader would benefit from experiencing as a full scene?
- Is there a routine or low-stakes event currently given full scene
  treatment that could be compressed without losing anything the story
  needs?
- Does the amount of narrative time spent on a given moment roughly track
  its actual significance to the story?
- If several consecutive scenes are dramatized in similar depth regardless
  of their relative importance, would varying the treatment sharpen the
  more significant ones?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the manuscript's most significant plot or emotional turns and check
   whether each receives full scene treatment; convert any that are
   currently only summarized.
2. Find routine or connective passages currently given full scene treatment
   and consider compressing them into summary, freeing narrative space for
   more significant moments.
3. Try the summary-with-a-detail hybrid for a span of time that needs
   coverage but not full dramatization — compress most of it, but let one
   specific beat stand out.
4. Read a chapter and mark each passage as scene or summary; check whether
   the resulting pattern matches the chapter's actual distribution of
   significant versus connective content.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Some literary styles deliberately summarize significant events for effect
  (understatement, distancing, a narrator's own avoidance) — a legitimate
  choice distinct from an unintentional mismatch between significance and
  treatment.
- Fast-paced genre fiction may deliberately compress even fairly significant
  events to maintain momentum, trading some emotional depth for pace as a
  genre-appropriate choice.
- Very short forms may not have room for the full scene/summary contrast
  this pattern describes.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a given passage's treatment (scene or summary) matches its actual
significance requires reading and interpreting the manuscript's stakes and
structure — a judgment no structured data substitutes for. Passage length
and the presence of dialogue or sustained action are more directly
observable proxies, but matching them to significance remains
model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Under-dramatized:* "Over the following months, their friendship slowly
fell apart" summarizes what the story has established as a central
relationship's central turning point, in a single sentence.

*Proportionate treatment:* The same relationship's decline is instead
rendered through two or three specific, dramatized scenes — a canceled
plan, a conversation that goes wrong, a final unanswered message — with the
quieter months between them compressed into a brief connecting summary.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The scene/summary distinction and its connection to maintaining narrative
significance draws on John Gardner's foundational writing on pacing and the
"vivid, continuous dream" ([[src.book.gardner-art-of-fiction]]) and K. M.
Weiland's structural pacing writing
([[src.book.weiland-helping-writers-become-authors]]); both established
craft resources. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because the specific hybrid
form (summary-with-a-detail) and proportionality framing presented here is
this drafting pass's synthesis rather than a direct claim from either
source.

records.title: Sentence rhythm and clarity
records.summary: The line-level layer — where sentences are followed or re-read, and where rhythm does work that no amount of structural planning can substitute for.

citations.label: Steering the Craft
Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace
The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Every story is delivered one sentence at a time, and sentences vary in two
ways that matter independently: whether a reader can follow them without
effort, and how they sound. Clarity is the first; rhythm is the second. A
sentence can be perfectly clear and lifeless, or beautifully cadenced and
impossible to parse.

This record is about that layer. It is distinct from voice as a craft
element, which is about the sensibility a narration projects, and from
description and specificity, which is about what detail is selected. Those
choices are expressed *through* sentences; this record is about the
sentences themselves.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Le Guin's argument for reading prose aloud rests on a claim worth taking
seriously: the physical properties of language — sound, rhythm, pace — carry
meaning rather than decorating it. A reader may not consciously notice that
four sentences in a row have the same length and shape, but they will feel
the flatness, and in a long serial they may feel it as fatigue.

Clarity has a different economy. Williams's composition work locates much
difficulty not in vocabulary but in structure: sentences whose grammatical
subject is not the thing doing the acting, whose old and new information
arrive in the wrong order, or whose emphasis falls in a place the writer did
not intend. A reader who has to re-read a sentence has left the story for a
moment, and the cost compounds.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Varied sentence length** — short sentences for impact and pace, longer
  ones for accumulation, with the contrast doing the work rather than either
  in isolation.
- **Front-loaded versus end-loaded emphasis** — English tends to place weight
  at the end of a sentence, which makes what a sentence closes on a real
  choice.
- **Deliberate monotony** — repeated structure used for pressure, exhaustion,
  or ritual, which is a technique and not a lapse.
- **Fragment and run-on** — grammatical departures used for voice, effective
  in proportion to their rarity.
- **Plain style** — prose that deliberately draws no attention to itself, so
  that the reader's whole attention goes to the story. Harder than it looks
  and easy to mistake for absence of craft.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A paragraph whose sentences all begin with the subject and run to a
  similar length, producing a flatness the content does not explain.
- A key revelation buried mid-sentence, with the sentence ending on a
  subordinate clause about something else.
- Filter constructions — *she saw that*, *he felt that*, *it seemed to her* —
  interposing a layer between the reader and the perception.
- Conversely: a passage where sentence lengths visibly contract as a scene
  accelerates, so pace is carried by the prose rather than only by events.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Uniform rhythm.** Technically correct prose with no variation, which
  reads as competent and inert.
- **Emphasis in the wrong place.** The most important word in a sentence
  buried, so the reader has to work out what to care about.
- **Clarity sacrificed to elegance.** A sentence admired by its author and
  re-read by everyone else.
- **Habitual constructions.** A tic — a favourite qualifier, a repeated
  syntax — invisible to the writer and increasingly loud to a reader across
  a long work.
- **Line-editing a structural problem.** Polishing sentences in a scene that
  should not be in the book, which is the most expensive way to revise.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Read a page aloud: where does the breath run out, and where does the
  rhythm go slack?
- What does each paragraph's final sentence end on, and is that the word
  worth landing on?
- Which constructions recur enough to be a habit rather than a choice?
- Where has a sentence needed re-reading, and is the difficulty doing
  anything?
- Is this passage unclear, or is it clear about something confusing? Those
  need opposite fixes.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Read a page aloud without stopping. Mark every place the voice stumbles;
   stumbles are data even when the cause is not yet obvious.
2. Chart sentence lengths for one paragraph. Long uniform stretches are
   easy to see and usually easy to fix.
3. Take the three most important sentences in a scene and rewrite each so it
   ends on its most important word.
4. Search for a suspected tic — a filter verb, a favourite adverb — and count
   it. Counting settles arguments that impressions cannot.
5. Before any line pass, confirm the scene is staying. Line work on doomed
   material is the most common misdirected revision effort.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Drafting. Attending to rhythm while generating material stops most writers
  from generating any; this is revision work.
- Deliberately flat or affectless styles, where uniformity is the effect.
- Voice-driven narration whose grammar is a character's, not the author's,
  and where "correcting" it would erase the character.
- Fast-turnaround serial publishing, where an author may consciously choose
  a lighter line pass in exchange for cadence — a legitimate trade with a
  known cost.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This is the one area of craft where mechanical measurement is genuinely
informative. Sentence lengths, their variance, paragraph lengths,
repeated sentence openings, filter-verb frequency, and adverb density are
all countable, and a coach can report them per scene or across a manuscript.

What the numbers cannot say is whether any of it is a problem. Low variance
may be a deliberate flattening; a high adverb count may be a narrator's
voice; a repeated construction may be a motif. Measurement here locates
candidates for attention and nothing more, and a coach that reports these
figures as faults will be wrong often and confidently.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Emphasis mislaid:* "He realized that his brother had been lying to him for
years, as he set the cup down on the table by the window." — The revelation
is in the middle; the sentence ends on furniture.

*Emphasis placed:* "He set the cup down on the table by the window. His
brother had been lying to him for years."

*Uniform rhythm:* "She opened the door. She stepped inside. She looked
around the room. She saw the body on the floor." — Four subjects, four verbs,
four similar lengths, and a body that lands like the furniture.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ursula K. Le Guin ([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]) supplies the
argument that the sound and rhythm of prose carry meaning and the practice of
reading aloud to test it; Joseph M. Williams
([[src.book.williams-style-clarity-and-grace]]) supplies the account of
clarity as a structural property of sentences — subject placement,
information order, end-weight — rather than a matter of simple vocabulary;
John Gardner ([[src.book.gardner-art-of-fiction]]) supplies the treatment of
prose that breaks the reader's absorption.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense, with one limit
worth naming: Williams writes about expository and academic prose, so
applying his clarity principles to fiction is an extension this drafting pass
is making, not a claim he advances about narrative. The measurable diagnostics
listed here — length variance, repeated openings, filter-verb counts — are
this pass's synthesis; none of the three sources proposes counting anything,
and the caution against reading those counts as faults is deliberate.

records.title: Tense and narrative person
records.summary: First or third, past or present — two choices made once and felt on every page, each with real costs that are easier to weigh before drafting than after.

citations.label: Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft
Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)
Steering the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Two grammatical choices shape every sentence of a narrative: person (first,
third, occasionally second) and tense (past, present). They are usually
settled early, often unconsciously, and are expensive to change later.

This is distinct from the POV records this library already holds. Viewpoint
is about *whose* experience the reader occupies; psychic distance is about
how close the narration sits to it. Person and tense are the grammar those
choices are delivered in — and the grammar constrains what the other two can
easily do.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The choices carry different promises. First person offers intimacy and a
voice the reader spends the book inside; it also caps what can be shown to
what the narrator knows, and implies a narrator who survived to tell it,
unless the story does something deliberate about that. Third person buys
flexibility and range at the cost of a degree of immediacy.

Tense works similarly. Present tense produces immediacy and a sense that
outcomes are not yet settled; sustained across a long work it can also
flatten, since everything arrives at the same urgency and the narration loses
the retrospective register that lets a past-tense narrator weigh events. Past
tense is the unmarked default in most prose traditions, which is itself an
advantage: readers do not notice it.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **First past** — the retrospective personal narrator; room for hindsight,
  irony, and a narrator who understands more now than they did then.
- **First present** — maximum immediacy, minimum retrospect; common in
  contemporary YA and in serialized fiction.
- **Third limited past** — the workhorse of most genre fiction: one
  viewpoint at a time, flexible distance.
- **Third limited present** — immediacy without the first-person voice
  commitment.
- **Third omniscient** — a narrator above the characters, with its own
  sensibility; unfashionable for a stretch and entirely viable.
- **Second person** — rare, marked, and immediately foregrounded; in
  progression fiction it also happens to be the register system interfaces
  speak in, which is worth knowing before adopting it for narration.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A first-person narrator who knows how the story ends, and lets that leak —
  a resource third person does not have.
- A present-tense passage where a summary of three weeks sits awkwardly,
  because present tense resists summary.
- Tense slippage during flashbacks, which is where most drafts lose control
  of a present-tense narrative.
- Conversely: a first-person story that repeatedly needs the reader to know
  something the narrator cannot, and reaches for contrivances to deliver it.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The unconsidered default.** A choice made by habit and never tested,
  usually surfacing as a persistent awkwardness the author cannot locate.
- **First person with an information problem.** A plot requiring knowledge
  the narrator has no access to, patched with overheard conversations and
  convenient letters.
- **Present tense across long time-skips.** The tense that resists summary,
  asked to cover months.
- **Inconsistent slippage.** Drifting between tenses or distances without
  intent, which readers feel as unsteadiness even when they cannot name it.
- **Retrospect wasted.** A past-tense first-person narrator who never once
  uses the fact that they already know what happened.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Why this person and this tense? If the answer is "it's what I write," is
  that working here?
- What does this story need the reader to know that the narrator cannot?
- Does the narration ever use hindsight — and if not, would past tense first
  person be earning its keep?
- How will time-skips be handled, and has that been tested at length?
- If the whole book switched, what would be gained and what would be lost?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Rewrite one scene in the other tense, and one in the other person. Ten
   minutes of this settles arguments that months of instinct do not.
2. Find the passage that has been hardest to write and check whether the
   difficulty is grammatical rather than structural.
3. For first person, list three things the reader needs to know that the
   narrator does not. That list is the cost of the choice.
4. For past-tense first person, add one sentence of retrospect and see
   whether the voice gets more interesting.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Established series, where the choice is locked by the volumes already
  published and consistency outweighs any gain.
- Deliberate tense-shifting as a technique — frame narratives, mixed-mode
  works — where variation is designed rather than drifting.
- Serialized work already deep into publication, where a change would read as
  a break in the contract with returning readers.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This record's `detectability` is `deterministic`, unusually for this library.
Person and tense are grammatical facts of the text: a coach can classify the
dominant person and tense of any passage with high reliability, and — more
usefully — can locate *inconsistencies*, since an isolated present-tense
paragraph inside a past-tense manuscript is detectable without interpretation.

What is not deterministic is whether the choice is right. Every combination
above has produced excellent books. The coach can report what the manuscript
is doing and flag drift; whether the intimacy of first person is worth its
information cost is the author's judgment about their own story.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Retrospect used:* "I thought Bel was joking. I want to be clear that
everyone thought Bel was joking, because of what happened after." — a
first-past narrator spending the one thing that tense gives them.

*Retrospect unused:* "I thought Bel was joking." — indistinguishable from
third limited, and paying first person's costs for none of its returns.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Janet Burroway ([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the standard
taxonomy of person and its effects; Orson Scott Card
([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supplies the treatment of first
person's information constraints and the reader-intimacy trade; Ursula K. Le
Guin ([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]) supplies the exercises and the
argument about tense and voice as things to be tested by ear rather than
chosen by rule.

`source_confidence` is `high`: three independent, established craft sources
address person and tense directly and agree on the substance, which is
unusual in this corpus and reflects that this is one of the most thoroughly
documented areas of prose craft. Two smaller claims are this pass's
extension and are marked as such here rather than attributed: the note that
present tense resists summary across long time-skips, and the observation
that second person is the register progression-fiction system interfaces
already use, which comes from this library's genre material rather than from
any craft source.

records.title: Voice as a craft element
records.summary: Voice — the distinctive rhythm, vocabulary, and sensibility that makes prose recognizably itself — operates at both the narrative and character level, and confusing the two is a common source of manuscripts where every character sounds like the author.

citations.label: Steering the Craft
On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Voice is the distinctive combination of rhythm, vocabulary, syntax, and
sensibility that makes prose recognizable as itself rather than
interchangeable with other prose telling a similar story. It operates on
at least two levels worth distinguishing: narrative voice is the sensibility
of the telling itself — the narrator's or the prose's own personality, even
in third person; character voice is how a specific character's dialogue and
(in close POV) interiority sounds distinct from other characters and from
the narration around them. A manuscript can have a strong, consistent
narrative voice while its characters all sound alike in dialogue, or vivid,
differentiated character voices inside a narration with no particular
personality of its own — the two are related but separable craft
achievements.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A distinctive narrative voice is often what readers describe when they say
a book feels alive on the sentence level, independent of plot — it's part
of what makes an author's prose recognizable across different books.
Distinct character voices let a reader track who's speaking in dialogue
even without tags, and make an ensemble cast feel like individuals rather
than mouthpieces for the same underlying sensibility. When both level fail
together — flat narration, interchangeable characters — a manuscript can
be structurally sound and still read as curiously impersonal.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Strong, consistent narrative voice**, maintained across an entire
  manuscript regardless of POV character, common in first-person narrators
  with a pronounced sensibility or in stylistically distinctive third-person
  prose.
- **Voice that shifts with POV**, where narration itself takes on qualities
  of whichever character's perspective it's currently following, common in
  multi-POV close-third structures.
- **Differentiated character voice in dialogue**, where distinct word
  choice, rhythm, and habitual phrasing let a reader identify a speaker
  without dialogue tags.
- **Homogenized character voice**, a common failure mode rather than a
  variant, where every character's dialogue is grammatically and
  rhythmically interchangeable, differing only in content.
- **Deliberately flat or neutral narrative voice**, used in some literary
  traditions specifically to foreground plot or character over narratorial
  personality — a legitimate choice distinct from an unintentionally flat
  voice.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Dialogue from two different characters, stripped of tags, still
  identifiable by rhythm, vocabulary, or habitual phrasing alone.
- A narrative voice with consistent, recognizable sentence-level qualities
  (rhythm, diction, attitude) across the manuscript.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: dialogue that reads identically across
  characters when tags are removed, or narration with no discernible
  personality distinguishing it from generic, unmarked prose.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Homogenized dialogue**, where every character speaks with the same
  vocabulary, sentence rhythm, and register, differing only in what they
  say rather than how they say it.
- **Narrative voice drowning character voice**, where a very strong,
  consistent narratorial style overwhelms any distinction between
  characters, especially in close POV shifts between multiple characters.
- **Voice inconsistency within a single character**, where a character's
  dialogue or interiority shifts register without a story reason (a
  formal, educated character suddenly speaking in a register established
  as belonging to someone else).

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If you stripped dialogue tags from a scene with two or more speaking
  characters, could a reader still tell who's talking?
- Does this manuscript's narration have a recognizable rhythm and
  sensibility, or does it read as generic, unmarked prose?
- In a multi-POV structure, does the narration's voice shift meaningfully
  between different characters' sections, or does it stay uniform
  regardless of whose perspective is active?
- Does any character's voice shift inconsistently without a story reason?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Strip dialogue tags from a multi-character scene and test whether a
   reader (or you, returning to it later) can still identify each speaker.
2. Read a passage of narration aloud and note whether it has a
   recognizable rhythm and personality, or reads as interchangeable with
   generic prose.
3. For a multi-POV manuscript, compare two different characters' POV
   sections directly and check whether the narration itself shifts to
   reflect each character's sensibility.
4. For a character whose voice feels inconsistent, list their
   established speech patterns and check a later scene against that list.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A deliberately restrained or minimalist prose style may intentionally
  keep both narrative and character voice understated, where the absence
  of pronounced voice is itself a stylistic choice.
- Very minor characters with little dialogue may not need fully
  differentiated voices developed.
- Technical or procedural writing embedded within fiction (in-world
  documents, reports) may intentionally use a flat, voiceless register as
  characterization of the document type itself.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a narrative or character voice is distinctive and consistent
requires reading and interpreting the prose directly — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Homogenized dialogue:* Two characters — one an aristocrat, one a street
