vendor — both say, "I don't think that's a good idea, and here's why,"
differing only in the reasoning that follows, with identical sentence
structure and register.

*Differentiated voice:* The aristocrat instead says, "I would counsel
against it, though I doubt that will stop you," while the vendor says, "Bad
idea. Real bad. But you're gonna do it anyway, aren't you?" — same
underlying objection, distinct rhythm and register revealing distinct
characters.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The narrative-voice/character-voice distinction draws on Ursula K. Le
Guin's dedicated craft writing on voice and narrative control
([[src.book.leguin-steering-the-craft]]) and Stephen King's writing on
voice and revision practice ([[src.book.king-on-writing]]), a single
author's practice and opinion presented as such. `source_confidence` is
`mixed` because the specific two-level framing presented here is this
drafting pass's synthesis rather than a direct claim from either source.

records.title: Diminishing returns, rarity gates, and catch-up mechanics
records.summary: Three design tools shape how advancement feels over a long story: diminishing returns slow late growth, rarity gates control access to powerful options, and catch-up mechanics keep a widening gap between characters from becoming permanent.

citations.label: A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Three related design tools shape the felt experience of advancement over a
long story. Diminishing returns mean each additional unit of investment
yields progressively less benefit, naturally slowing growth without a hard
stop (related to, but distinct from, a soft cap, which is one specific
implementation of diminishing returns). Rarity gates restrict access to
powerful options — items, techniques, mentors — behind scarcity, making
their acquisition a plot event rather than a routine transaction. Catch-up
mechanics give characters who have fallen behind a way to close the gap
faster than characters who are already ahead, preventing an early lead from
compounding into permanent, insurmountable dominance.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Diminishing returns keep a character's late-story growth from feeling
either impossibly fast or completely stalled, supporting a believable
mastery curve. Rarity gates turn acquisition into narrative event: a
character doesn't simply buy the best sword, they have to earn or discover
it, which is part of why rare items and techniques so often become plot
drivers rather than background detail. Catch-up mechanics matter
specifically for ensemble casts and rival relationships — without them, an
early advantage compounds indefinitely, which can produce the side-cast-
obsolescence problem or make a rival's continued relevance implausible.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Investment-based diminishing returns**, where continued effort in one
  area yields smaller gains the more has already been invested there.
- **Difficulty-based diminishing returns**, where each subsequent
  achievement requires disproportionately more effort or risk than the
  last, independent of cumulative investment.
- **Hard rarity gates**, where an item or technique simply doesn't exist in
  accessible quantity, making acquisition a significant plot event by
  necessity.
- **Soft rarity gates**, where an item or technique is technically
  available but at a cost (social, financial, moral) high enough to make
  routine access implausible.
- **Comeback mechanics**, allowing a character who has fallen behind to
  advance unusually quickly under specific conditions (a training
  breakthrough, a discovered shortcut) — needs a credible in-world reason to
  avoid feeling like an author's thumb on the scale.
- **Structural catch-up**, where the setting itself provides slower
  characters with advantages unavailable to the lead character (a mentor's
  undivided attention, resources the leader has outgrown needing),
  integrated into the world rather than treated as a special mechanic.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's growth visibly slowing as they approach mastery in an area,
  narrated through increasing effort for smaller gains.
- A rare item or technique's acquisition treated as a significant plot
  event — a quest, a trial, a sacrifice — rather than a routine purchase or
  discovery.
- A supporting character who started behind the protagonist closing the gap
  through a credible, dramatized catch-up mechanism, rather than simply
  appearing stronger later with no explanation.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
These three tools interact directly with cast dynamics: without diminishing
returns, a character who starts strong tends to stay proportionally
stronger indefinitely; without rarity gates, acquisition becomes routine
and loses its plot-generating potential; without catch-up mechanics, an
early gap between characters widens rather than narrows, which can strand
supporting characters in permanent irrelevance unless the story deliberately
wants that outcome (as in some dungeon-core or base-building structures
where the supporting cast's relative power isn't the point).

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **No diminishing returns at all**, letting a strong character's advantage
  compound indefinitely with no narrative or mechanical friction.
- **Rarity gates that are stated but not honored**, where an item described
  as unique or exceedingly rare turns out to be readily available later
  with no explanation.
- **Catch-up mechanics that feel arbitrary**, where a lagging character
  suddenly closes the gap with no credible in-world cause, reading as
  authorial convenience rather than earned progress.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this character's growth show any diminishing returns as they
  approach mastery, or does progress stay linear indefinitely?
- Is a stated rare item or technique's rarity honored consistently across
  the manuscript?
- If a supporting character needs to remain relevant, does the story give
  them a credible, dramatized way to close the gap, or does their relevance
  depend on the protagonist's advantage simply not compounding?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a character nearing mastery in an area, add a scene showing
   increasing effort for smaller returns, if that logic isn't currently
   present.
2. Audit a rare item or technique's stated scarcity against its later
   appearances for consistency.
3. For a supporting character who's fallen behind, design a credible,
   in-world catch-up mechanism (rather than an unexplained jump) if their
   continued relevance depends on narrowing the gap.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story deliberately depicting an unfair, compounding-advantage system as
  a critique (early privilege determining outcomes, examined directly) may
  intentionally omit catch-up mechanics.
- Very lightweight systems with no long-term advancement tracking don't
  need these tools developed explicitly.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks advancement rates and item acquisition
across characters, whether diminishing returns and stated rarity are
honored is close to deterministic. Whether a catch-up mechanism reads as
credible or arbitrary requires interpreting the prose and remains
model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Compounding advantage, unaddressed:* A protagonist's early lead over a
rival widens steadily across the whole manuscript with no diminishing
returns and no catch-up mechanism, and the rival's continued presence in
late chapters becomes increasingly implausible given the growing gap.

*Managed advantage:* The same protagonist's growth instead visibly slows
past a certain point, while the rival — freed from needing to catch up to
an ever-moving target — benefits from a mentor's full attention the
protagonist has outgrown needing, closing the gap enough to remain a
credible narrative presence.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The diminishing-returns and mastery-curve framing draws on established
game-design literature covering learning curves and progression balance
([[src.book.koster-theory-of-fun]],
[[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]); both established academic/
practitioner texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's
application to narrative cast dynamics (rather than competitive game
balance) is this drafting pass's adaptation rather than a direct claim from
either source.

records.title: Experience sources and milestone growth
records.summary: What actually generates advancement — combat, discovery, training, narrative milestones — shapes what kind of story a progression system rewards, and a mismatch between stated sources and depicted growth undermines a system's credibility.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
A Theory of Fun for Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Experience sources are whatever a system credits as generating advancement:
defeating enemies, discovering new information or places, completing
quests, training deliberately, surviving hardship, or reaching narrative
milestones regardless of specific actions. Milestone growth is a related but
distinct model, where advancement is tied to reaching defined story beats
(completing an arc, surviving a trial) rather than accumulating from many
small actions. What a system credits as advancement-worthy is a direct
statement about what the story values — a combat-only experience source
implies a combat-centric story; a discovery-and-training source implies
something broader.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A system's stated experience sources set an implicit contract about what
kind of actions matter in this story. When a story's actual events track
consistently with its stated sources — a character who trains hard visibly
grows, one who avoids conflict grows more slowly in combat capability but
perhaps faster in other areas — the system reads as coherent and the growth
feels earned. When growth happens inconsistently with the stated sources
(a character who's done nothing but travel gains several combat levels),
the mismatch undermines trust in the system's internal logic.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Combat-only experience**, tying nearly all advancement to defeating
  enemies — common in classic LitRPG, but narrows what kinds of scenes can
  credibly produce growth.
- **Broad, activity-based experience**, crediting combat, discovery,
  crafting, social success, and other activities individually, supporting a
  wider range of scene types as growth-worthy.
- **Training-based advancement**, requiring deliberate, dramatized practice
  rather than passive accumulation — supports montage and mentor-relationship
  scenes directly.
- **Milestone-only growth**, advancing only at defined story beats
  regardless of specific actions taken along the way, which can simplify a
  system considerably but removes fine-grained legibility about what
  specifically caused a jump.
- **Hybrid systems**, combining incremental activity-based growth with
  occasional milestone bonuses for major story beats.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's advancement following visibly from the specific activities
  the system credits — training scenes preceding a skill increase, combat
  preceding a combat-related level.
- A milestone-triggered advancement dramatized as tied to completing a
  specific, significant story beat, rather than arriving arbitrarily.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: advancement occurring with no discernible
  connection to any activity the system has established as a credited
  source.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Advancement disconnected from stated sources**, where growth happens
  without any narrated activity the system credits, undermining the
  system's internal logic.
- **A combat-only system applied to a story that spends significant time on
  non-combat activity**, leaving long stretches with no legible
  advancement mechanism at all.
- **Milestone growth used to paper over pacing problems**, advancing a
  character conveniently whenever the plot needs a boost, rather than at
  consistent, meaningful story beats.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Any rule about what earns advancement is also a rule about what a clever
character would farm, and a setting is more convincing when someone in it
has noticed. If killing grants experience, someone is breeding or
stockpiling things to kill; if discovery grants it, someone is
manufacturing novelty; if quests grant it, someone is issuing trivial
quests for a cut. The story does not have to dwell on this, but a world
where the obvious exploit has apparently occurred to nobody reads as a game
nobody else is playing.

Milestone growth avoids most farming problems and acquires a different edge
case: because it advances characters on story beats, it can hand a character
power they did not visibly earn, which is the same effect the fake-
progression pattern describes. It also interacts with any experience-
sharing rule — parties, mentors, contribution splits — where the question of
who gets credit is a social problem long before it is a mechanical one, and
usually a better source of conflict.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this system credit as generating advancement, and does the
  story's actual depicted growth track consistently with those sources?
- If a character spends significant time on activities the system doesn't
  credit, does their advancement stall accordingly, or does growth continue
  unexplained?
- For milestone-based growth, are the milestones meaningful story beats, or
  do they function as an arbitrary excuse to advance the character when
  convenient?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the system's stated experience sources and audit a chapter range
   for whether depicted advancement traces back to one of them.
2. For a stretch of non-credited activity (travel, social scenes) that
   still shows advancement, either explain the growth or adjust the pacing
   of when advancement is shown.
3. For milestone-based growth, check that each milestone is a genuinely
   significant story beat, not a convenient excuse to advance the plot.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight or narrative-only progression systems may not need
  explicit, trackable experience sources at all.
- A story deliberately depicting an opaque or unfair system (advancement
  that doesn't track any legible source, as a dark/horror LitRPG feature)
  is using the inconsistency as a deliberate unsettling device rather than
  an unexamined gap.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks experience gains linked to specific
scenes or activities, whether advancement follows the stated sources is
close to deterministic. Whether the narrative adequately dramatizes the
credited activity requires interpreting the prose and remains
model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Disconnected advancement:* A character spends five chapters traveling with
no combat, training, or notable discovery, and gains two full levels with
no explanation connecting the growth to any activity the system has
established as a source.

*Connected advancement:* The same travel stretch instead includes deliberate
training sessions with a companion, explicitly credited by the system as a
training-based experience source, and the resulting level gain traces
directly to those dramatized sessions.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The experience-source and milestone-growth framing draws on established
game-design literature covering progression triggers and mastery curves
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]],
[[src.book.koster-theory-of-fun]]); both established academic/practitioner
texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's application to
narrative credibility (rather than game balance) is this drafting pass's
adaptation rather than a direct claim from either source.

records.title: Oaths, contracts, and bindings
records.summary: Promises the system enforces — a mechanic that converts a character's word into a constraint with teeth, and that only pays off when the story makes keeping it genuinely costly.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A binding is a promise the world enforces: an oath that damages the breaker,
a contract that cannot be evaded, a geas that compels, a sect vow whose
violation the system detects. What distinguishes it from an ordinary promise
is that compliance is not a matter of character — the mechanism, not the
person, guarantees it.

That is the design tension the whole mechanic turns on. A promise kept
because a character chose to keep it characterizes them. A promise kept
because breaking it would kill them does not. The interesting versions
recover the choice somewhere else: in the decision to swear, in what the oath
costs to honor, or in a situation where honoring it is worse than dying.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Enforced promises make constraints legible. A reader who knows a character
cannot lie about a particular thing reads every conversation about it
differently, and a reader who knows what an oath will cost watches the
approach of the moment it comes due.

Bindings also solve a specific problem in high-power settings: they are one
of the few constraints that scale. A character strong enough that nothing can
stop them can still be bound by something they agreed to, which keeps a
story's conflicts available long after physical opposition has stopped
working.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The sworn oath** — voluntarily taken, enforced by the system, usually
  with a stated penalty.
- **The imposed geas** — placed on a character by another party, which makes
  the binding an antagonist's tool.
- **The contract** — negotiated terms with mutual obligations, where the
  interesting material is in the drafting and the loopholes.
- **The lifelong vow** — sect or order membership as a standing constraint,
  covered in part by the sects record.
- **The conditional binding** — active only under stated conditions, so the
  story controls when it bites.
- **The unbreakable versus the costly** — bindings that literally cannot be
  violated versus those that can, at a price. The second is almost always the
  more useful, because it restores the choice.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character choosing terms carefully, because the terms are the whole
  negotiation.
- An oath honored at a cost the reader has been shown in advance.
- A binding used against its holder by someone who read it more carefully
  than they did.
- Conversely: an oath introduced and never tested, which functions as
  worldbuilding decoration rather than as a constraint.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The untested oath.** A binding established and never brought into
  conflict with anything the character wants.
- **Compliance without character.** The oath removes the decision, so scenes
  that should be about choice become about mechanism.
- **The convenient loophole.** An escape discovered exactly when needed,
  which retroactively drains every earlier oath of weight.
- **Unstated terms.** A binding whose scope is vague, so the reader cannot
  anticipate when it applies and cannot feel it tighten.
- **Oath inflation.** Many bindings across a cast, individually interesting
  and collectively reducing the world to paperwork.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The failure state is the design. What happens on violation — death, power
loss, physical damage, expulsion, a curse, mere detection — determines what
kind of story the binding supports. Lethal enforcement makes oaths absolute
and removes them from play; survivable enforcement keeps them live, because a
character can weigh breaking one and the reader can wonder whether they will.

Visibility matters in two directions. Can others tell a character is bound?
A visible binding is a social fact — it makes the character trustworthy in a
specific way and exploitable in another, since anyone who knows the terms
knows what they cannot do. A hidden binding produces different scenes
entirely: pressure the other characters cannot see the source of.

Consequentially, a world where promises are mechanically enforceable has a
radically different legal and commercial order. Contracts need no courts,
trust between strangers is cheap, and someone has built an industry around
drafting, witnessing, and dissolving bindings. Settings with oath magic
usually leave this unexplored — a large piece of distinctive worldbuilding
sitting unused.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Any enforced promise invites lawyering: precise wording that satisfies the
letter, oaths sworn on false premises, delegating a forbidden act to someone
unbound, or arranging circumstances where the binding's conditions never
technically trigger. Coercion is the sharpest edge case — an oath extracted
under duress is enforced identically by most systems, which makes forced
swearing a weapon and raises a question about the mechanism's indifference
that a story can profitably notice. Bindings also interact with sacrifice and
cost mechanics, since many are priced in the same currency, and with
betrayal, which becomes structurally different when the system can detect it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this oath cost to keep, in a scene the reader will see?
- Could the character break it? If not, where does the choice live instead?
- Who wrote the terms, and did the other party read them as carefully?
- Can anyone tell this character is bound, and what do they do with that?
- What has a world with enforceable promises built that ours has not?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the scene where honoring the oath costs the character something
   they badly want. If the scene cannot be written, the binding is currently
   decoration.
2. State the exact terms in one sentence, then look for the loophole. If you
   find one easily, so will a reader.
3. Have a minor character exploit the binding's letter, and see whether the
   world feels more inhabited.
4. Try converting an unbreakable oath into a costly one and see what the
   story gains in choice.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Settings where oaths are ordinary social promises with no enforcement, in
  which case this is character material rather than system design.
- Stories where the binding is a background condition — a standing vow that
  is simply part of who someone is — and interrogating it would distract from
  the actual subject.
- Comedic treatments where absurd contract-lawyering is the joke and the
  costs are meant to be weightless.
- Premises where the binding *is* the antagonist, in which case the record's
  questions apply to the antagonist's design rather than the protagonist's
  choices.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Very little here is computable. A coach might locate oath-swearing scenes by
their vocabulary and check whether stated terms recur later in the
manuscript, which is a weak consistency check at best.

Whether an oath has been tested, whether keeping it cost anything, and
whether a loophole reads as clever or convenient are all semantic judgments.
An untested oath is not necessarily a fault — it may be waiting for a later
volume — so the coach should ask whether the test is coming rather than
report an absence as a problem.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Untested oath:* he swore on the Amber Rite never to raise a hand against a
Vashti, and in the following two hundred pages met no Vashti.

*Tested oath:* he had sworn never to raise a hand against a Vashti, and the
girl bleeding in the doorway was a Vashti, and the man who had put her there
would be back before dark. He sat down on the step to think about what
counted as a hand.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ernest Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies only
the general design principle that a rule-enforced constraint must be tested
to function as a constraint. Everything else in this record — the taxonomy of
bindings, the argument that enforcement removes characterization unless the
choice is relocated, the coercion edge case, the legal and commercial
consequences — is this drafting pass's synthesis, marked with
[[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]] rather than attributed to a source
that does not make these claims.

`source_confidence` is `limited`. No craft-literature or scholarly treatment
of enforced-promise mechanics in fiction was available to this pass. This is a
real research gap and a revision-pass target: oath, vow, and binding have
substantial treatment in medieval and folkloric scholarship that a later pass
should bring in, particularly before this record's claims about sect vows are
relied on. Read it as structured reasoning about a widely used device, not as
sourced analysis of one.

records.title: Luck, randomness, and probability
records.summary: Systems that include chance hand the story an engine of uncertainty and a standing hazard — because a reader who suspects an outcome was rolled rather than earned stops crediting the character for it.

citations.label: Uncertainty in Games
Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals
Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Many progression systems include chance: critical hits, drop rates, skill
activation percentages, an explicit Luck attribute, or a system that rolls
for outcomes the characters cannot control. This record is about designing
that chance deliberately — where it operates, who knows about it, and what
it is allowed to decide.

Games and fiction want opposite things from randomness. A game uses it to
produce uncertainty the player experiences as tension. A novel's outcome is
fixed before the reader arrives, so randomness in fiction is always a
*representation* of chance rather than chance itself. That difference is the
whole design problem.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Uncertainty is a real source of engagement — games scholarship treats it as
close to the substance of play — and fiction can borrow the effect. A world
where outcomes are not guaranteed feels less arranged, and a character who
can fail at something they are good at is more interesting than one whose
competence is deterministic.

The hazard is symmetrical and larger. When a favourable outcome is
attributed to chance, the reader cannot credit the character for it. A
protagonist who wins a fight through a lucky critical has not demonstrated
anything, and a story that resolves difficulties this way is spending the
credibility its progression system exists to build. Readers of this genre
are, by disposition, people who like watching things be earned.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Displayed probability** — the system states odds, so characters and
  readers can reason about risk explicitly.
- **Hidden randomness** — chance operates unseen and outcomes simply happen,
  which reads as fortune rather than mathematics.
- **The Luck attribute** — chance itself made a stat, which is a distinctive
  genre move and quietly makes fortune into something a character can invest
  in.
- **Bounded randomness** — variance around an outcome the character's skill
  determines, so chance colours results without deciding them.
- **Catastrophic tails** — rare, extreme outcomes either way: memorable, and
  dangerous used more than sparingly.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character choosing a risk with stated odds, so the decision is legible
  and the outcome — either way — lands as a consequence of the choice.
- A drop or a critical narrated as remarkable *because* the story has
  established how unlikely it is.
- Conversely: a fight turned by a fortunate roll the reader had no way to
  anticipate.
- Repeated improbable good fortune, which readers tend to notice in
  aggregate even when each instance passed unremarked.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Luck as plot armour.** Chance that consistently favours the protagonist,
  which is not randomness but authorial protection wearing its costume.
- **Rolled resolutions.** Climaxes decided by chance rather than by anything
  the character did, the sharpest version of the earned-resolution problem.
- **Odds without consequence.** Stated probabilities that never produce a
  bad outcome, teaching the reader that the numbers are decoration.
- **Unbounded variance.** A system where any outcome is possible at any time,
  which prevents the reader from anticipating anything.
- **Chance as an excuse for the improbable.** A convenient event justified
  after the fact by a system that permits it, which readers read as
  coincidence with paperwork.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Visibility is the central decision here, more than in most mechanics. If
probabilities are displayed, risk becomes a subject characters can discuss
and the reader shares the calculation — which converts chance into decision
material and is usually the safer choice for the earned-resolution problem.
If chance is hidden, outcomes read as fortune, which is atmospheric but gives
the reader no way to distinguish a designed system from an author's thumb on
the scale.

Progression interacts with chance in a specific way worth deciding
explicitly: does growth reduce variance or increase the ceiling? A system
where advancement makes outcomes more reliable produces a protagonist who
becomes steadier; one where advancement raises the top end produces a
protagonist who becomes more explosive and no more dependable. Both are
legitimate, and they feel entirely different.

Socially, a world with real randomness in it develops institutions for
managing risk — insurance, guarantors, hedging, sworn appraisals, gambling —
and people whose profession is absorbing variance for others. A setting with
drop rates and no economy of risk around them has left an obvious feature of
its own rules unused.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Any stated probability invites manipulation: reroll mechanics, luck-boosting
consumables, repeating a low-cost attempt until it succeeds, or arranging
many small trials rather than one large one. Where the system permits
grinding an improbable outcome, someone in the world is doing exactly that
for a living. Chance also interacts sharply with loot and economy — drop
rates are a supply curve, and a rare item's value depends on a probability
someone can compute — and with fake progression, since variance can disguise
a flat power curve by making outcomes look eventful.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What is chance allowed to decide in this story, and what is it never
  allowed to decide?
- Can the reader tell the difference between good luck and good judgment
  here?
- Does the protagonist's luck run both ways, and where is the scene that
  proves it?
- Does advancement make outcomes more reliable or more extreme?
- If the odds were stated aloud, would this scene become a decision instead
  of an event?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the last ten significant outcomes and mark each as skill, choice, or
   chance. A chance-heavy list is worth looking at even if each instance
   seemed fine.
2. Take one lucky outcome and rewrite it as a decision made under stated
   odds. The scene usually gains a beat and loses nothing.
3. Write the scene where luck runs against the protagonist at a cost that
   sticks, and see whether the system suddenly reads as real.
4. Decide, in one sentence, whether growth reduces variance or raises the
   ceiling — then check the draft against the answer.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Comedic and picaresque work where absurd fortune is the mode and
  scrutinizing it would break the register.
- Stories deliberately about fortune, fate, or the unfairness of chance,
  where a protagonist's luck is the subject rather than a mechanism.
- Systems with no randomness at all, where this record simply does not apply
  and its questions should not be imported.
- Gambling and risk-centred premises, where the failure modes above are the
  point and the reader is watching the variance on purpose.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a manuscript reports probabilities or roll outcomes in structured text,
a coach can extract them and compare observed frequencies against stated
odds — one of the few genuinely deterministic checks available anywhere in
this library, and a striking one when a system's own numbers do not match its
events.

Everything else is interpretation. Whether an outcome reads as earned or
lucky is a semantic judgment; a run of favourable results may be authorial
protection or may be a deliberately fortunate character. The coach can report
the ratio of stated-chance to skill-determined outcomes, and should present
that as a description rather than a verdict.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Rolled resolution:* the killing blow triggered a 2% critical, and the duel
he had been losing for six pages ended. He had done nothing differently.

*Chance as decision:* the appraisal put the ritual at one chance in five, and
told him what the other four did to the people who tried. He went ahead
anyway, and the book had already shown the reader what he was accepting.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Greg Costikyan ([[src.book.costikyan-uncertainty-in-games]]) supplies the
central treatment of uncertainty as the substance of engagement and the
taxonomy of its sources; Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman
([[src.book.salen-zimmerman-rules-of-play]]) supply the formal account of
chance within rule systems; Ernest Adams
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the design
vocabulary for randomness in progression and reward systems.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense, and the
disanalogy is central: all three sources describe uncertainty experienced by
a player making live decisions, while a reader faces a fixed outcome.
Everything this record says about *reader* response is this drafting pass's
synthesis, resting on the genre's earned-progression expectations from this
library's internal research rather than on a cited source.

records.title: Affinities, resistances, titles, and bloodlines
records.summary: Innate leanings, defensive traits, earned honorifics, and inherited lineage all shape a character before they make a single choice — worth distinguishing from each other because they carry different implications about agency, destiny, and social structure.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Four related but distinct character-architecture elements often appear
together in progression systems, and conflating them can blur what a
character actually controls versus what was given to them. An affinity is
an innate leaning toward a particular element, discipline, or type of power,
usually present from birth or awakening rather than chosen. A resistance is
a defensive trait, reducing vulnerability to a specific kind of harm or
influence, which may be innate or earned. A title is an earned or bestowed
honorific, usually reflecting an accomplishment or social recognition rather
than a raw capability. A bloodline is inherited lineage, implying traits,
obligations, or access passed down from ancestors rather than earned by the
character themselves.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
These four elements sit at different points on a spectrum from pure agency
(a title, usually earned) to pure inheritance (a bloodline, entirely
unchosen), and readers track that spectrum even without naming it
consciously. A character whose defining traits are mostly earned (titles,
developed resistances) reads as agentive; a character whose defining traits
are mostly inherited (bloodline, innate affinity) raises the chosen-one
agency questions covered in that trope's own record. Neither is
automatically better, but conflating them — treating an inherited bloodline
trait as though the character earned it, for instance — can undercut a
story's own agency claims.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Pure innate affinity**, present from birth or awakening with no
  in-story origin explaining why this character has it — often paired with
  the chosen-one trope's agency concerns.
- **Trained or discovered affinity**, where an innate leaning exists but
  requires the character's active effort to identify and develop, blending
  inherited potential with earned growth.
- **Innate resistance**, a defensive trait present from the start, often
  tied to species, bloodline, or origin.
- **Earned resistance**, developed through repeated exposure or deliberate
  training, more agency-forward than an innate version.
- **Bestowed title**, granted by an institution or authority in recognition
  of an accomplishment, carrying social as well as mechanical weight.
- **Self-claimed or informal title**, adopted by the character or their
  reputation rather than formally granted — implies a different, sometimes
  contested, source of legitimacy.
- **Bloodline with attached obligation**, where inherited status comes
  with social or narrative responsibility, not just capability — a common
  and productive complication distinct from bloodline as pure power source.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's innate affinity or bloodline established as a starting
  condition, with the story's actual tension located in what the character
  does with or despite it, rather than in the trait itself.
- A title's grant dramatized as a social event with witnesses and stakes,
  rather than simply appearing in a status readout.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an earned-sounding title or resistance
  that the character never actually did anything on the page to earn, or a
  bloodline trait treated narratively as though the character had
  accomplished something by simply possessing it.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
These elements interact directly with the systemic-social-consequences
record: a bloodline with social weight implies institutions (inheritance
law, aristocratic structures, prejudice or privilege) that a story can
choose to engage or leave unexamined. Titles interact with the found-family
and supporting-cast records, since a title's grant is often a social event
involving other characters whose recognition (or refusal to recognize it)
carries its own stakes. Affinities and resistances interact with the
classes-versus-skill-based-growth comparison, since an innate affinity can
function similarly to a soft class-gate, shaping what capabilities are
easily available to a character without formally restricting them.

The four elements differ in visibility, and the differences are where much
of their story value sits. Titles are usually the most public — they exist
to be seen, announced, and reacted to, which is what makes a title a social
mechanic rather than a statistical one. Bloodlines sit in the middle: often
known to institutions and families even when invisible on the body, which is
why they generate records, registries, and people who know what a character
is before the character does. Affinities and resistances are frequently the
most concealed, discovered only when tested, which is what allows a
resistance to function as a reversal in a scene rather than a stat. Deciding
which of these a stranger can perceive, which an institution can look up,
and which the character themselves knows will shape more scenes than the
traits' mechanical values do. The reader's view is a separate decision again:
a reader who knows about an unrevealed bloodline is being offered dramatic
irony, not information.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Treating inherited traits as earned accomplishments**, letting a
  bloodline or innate affinity carry the same narrative pride or
  significance an earned title would, without acknowledging the difference.
- **Titles granted with no social dramatization**, appearing as a status
  update with no scene showing the grant's social weight or the witnesses'
  reactions.
- **Bloodline privilege with no examined social consequence**, where an
  inherited advantage exists with no engagement with what that implies
  about the setting's social structure (see the related systemic-social-
  consequences record).

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is this character's defining trait innate, inherited, earned, or
  bestowed — and does the story treat it consistently with that origin?
- If a title is granted, is the grant itself dramatized as a social event,
  or does it appear only as a status change?
- If a bloodline carries social privilege or obligation, does the story
  engage what that means for the wider setting, even briefly?
- Does the character's agency-forward growth (earned resistances, trained
  affinities) get equal or greater narrative attention than their inherited
  traits?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Audit the character's key traits and label each as innate, inherited,
   earned, or bestowed; check whether the narrative weight given to each
   matches its actual origin.
2. For a title granted off-page, add a scene dramatizing the grant and its
   social reception.
3. For a bloodline with implied social weight, find or add one scene
   engaging its consequence for someone other than the protagonist.
4. Balance earned traits against inherited ones if the character's arc
   currently leans entirely on what they were born with.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Settings deliberately built around inherited status as their central
  subject (a story specifically about aristocratic bloodline politics) may
  appropriately foreground inheritance over earned traits throughout.
- Very lightweight systems may use these labels loosely as flavor without
  needing the full distinction developed.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a trait is treated consistently with its stated origin (innate,
inherited, earned, bestowed) requires reading and interpreting the
manuscript's characterization and worldbuilding — a judgment no structured
data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Conflated origin:* A character is praised repeatedly by other characters
for their "impressive fire affinity," discovered at birth, in language
identical to how the story praises a rival's hard-won mastery of a
technique they trained for years to learn.

*Distinguished origin:* The same fire affinity is instead treated as a
starting condition — other characters note it neutrally, and the story's
actual praise and narrative weight go to what the character chooses to do
with it, including the specific techniques they train to develop despite
(or because of) that innate leaning.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The four-element distinction (affinity/resistance/title/bloodline) and its
connection to the agency spectrum draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of genre conventions
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) and established game-design
literature on character trait systems
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]); the specific framing
connecting these traits to narrative agency is this drafting pass's
synthesis. `source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Attributes and soft versus hard caps
records.summary: Base attributes (strength, agility, and their equivalents) and whether a system caps their growth softly or hard sets a ceiling on how open-ended a story's power fantasy can be, and how that ceiling is written matters as much as where it sits.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
A Theory of Fun for Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Attributes are a character's foundational, usually numeric traits —
strength, agility, intelligence, and their setting-specific equivalents —
that other capabilities (skills, abilities, combat performance) are
typically built on top of. A soft cap is a point past which further
investment yields diminishing returns without becoming impossible; a hard
cap is an absolute ceiling that cannot be exceeded by any known means within
the story's established rules (until or unless the story explicitly breaks
it). Whether a system uses no caps, soft caps, hard caps, or a mix by
attribute is a foundational design choice with direct narrative
consequences for how "endless" the story's power fantasy can plausibly feel.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A system with no caps at all promises limitless growth, which can generate
excitement but also risks the fake-progression problem if the story can't
keep pace with ever-rising numbers. A hard cap creates a legible ceiling a
reader can use to calibrate expectations and stakes — once a character
approaches the cap, the reader knows further growth in that dimension is
implausible, redirecting anticipation toward other axes (see the related
vertical-vs-horizontal comparison). A soft cap sits between the two,
promising that growth remains possible but increasingly costly, which can
create a satisfying "grinding toward the ceiling" dynamic distinct from
either extreme.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Uncapped attributes**, with no stated ceiling, implying an open-ended
  power fantasy — carries the highest risk of eventually reading as
  unbounded or arbitrary if the story doesn't manage escalation carefully.
- **Hard-capped attributes**, with an absolute, stated maximum, providing a
  clear reference point the story can build tension and stakes around
  (how close is this character to their absolute limit).
- **Soft-capped attributes**, where investment past a threshold still
  works but yields progressively less return, encouraging horizontal
  investment in other attributes or systems once a soft cap is reached.
- **Per-attribute variation**, where different attributes use different
  cap models (a hard-capped physical attribute alongside an uncapped
  magical one, for instance), which can be a deliberate way to differentiate
  what kind of growth story is being told about which capability.
- **Breakable hard caps**, where a stated absolute ceiling can be exceeded
  through a specific, narratively significant event — effective when rare
  and earned, risky when it undermines the cap's credibility if overused.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's approach toward a stated cap treated as a meaningful
  narrative marker — increasing difficulty, increasing stakes, or a shift
  in strategy as the ceiling nears.
- Diminishing returns on continued investment shown through narrated effort
  (training harder for smaller gains) rather than only reported numbers.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: attributes that keep climbing steadily
  with no acknowledgment of any ceiling, even as the story's own logic
  implies one should exist.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Caps interact directly with the vertical-versus-horizontal progression
comparison: once an attribute approaches its cap, a system without other
growth axes risks stalling the character's sense of forward motion,
while a system with rich horizontal options (skills, tactics, equipment)
can keep growth feeling alive even after a core attribute plateaus. Caps
also interact with the multi-character cast: if supporting characters
operate under the same cap structure as the protagonist, their relative
standing can remain legible even as the protagonist advances, mitigating
the side-cast-obsolescence risk discussed in the vertical/horizontal
record.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **An implied but unstated cap**, where the story's own logic suggests a
  ceiling should exist but the manuscript never acknowledges one, leaving
  escalation feeling directionless.
- **A hard cap broken too casually**, undermining its credibility as an
  absolute limit if exceeded more than once or without sufficient narrative
  weight.
- **Soft caps with no visible diminishing returns**, where the story states
  that growth slows past a threshold but continues narrating identical-
  feeling gains regardless.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this system have a stated or implied ceiling for its core
  attributes, and is that ceiling ever acknowledged in the story?
- If a hard cap exists, has it been broken, and if so, does that moment
  carry proportional narrative weight?
- As a character approaches a soft cap, does the story show diminishing
  returns through narrated effort, or only through unstated numeric
  reasoning?
- If supporting characters operate under the same cap structure, does that
  keep their relative standing legible as the protagonist advances?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Decide explicitly whether the manuscript's core attributes are capped,
   and if so, state the cap somewhere the reader can register it, even
   implicitly.
2. For a character nearing a stated cap, add a scene showing the effort-to-
   reward ratio shifting, rather than only reporting numbers.
3. If a hard cap has been or will be broken, check that the moment receives
   narrative weight proportional to breaking an established absolute rule.
4. Audit whether horizontal growth options are available once a core
   attribute nears its cap, to keep the character's sense of progress alive.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Narrative-only power systems with no tracked numeric attributes don't
  need explicit cap logic.
- A story deliberately depicting a limitless, escalating power fantasy as
  its subject (with the absence of caps itself being examined) is using
  uncapped growth on purpose rather than by unexamined default.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks attribute values over time, whether
growth follows a stated cap model is close to deterministic. Whether the
narrative gives appropriate weight to approaching or breaking a cap requires
interpreting the prose and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unacknowledged ceiling:* A character's strength attribute climbs steadily
across a hundred chapters with no stated maximum, and by the story's end the
numbers have grown so large the story stops referencing them directly,
leaving the reader unsure what the numbers still mean.

*Acknowledged soft cap:* The same attribute instead is established to yield
sharply diminishing returns past a stated threshold; the character's late-
story training montages explicitly shift focus to a different attribute
once the first visibly plateaus, and a mentor character remarks on the
wisdom of that shift.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The soft-cap/hard-cap framing and its connection to diminishing returns
draws on established game-design literature covering progression curves
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]],
[[src.book.koster-theory-of-fun]]); both established academic/practitioner
texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's application to
prose narrative stakes (rather than interactive game balance) is this
drafting pass's adaptation rather than a direct claim from either source.

records.title: Perks, feats, and talents
records.summary: Discrete, chosen character upgrades — distinct from continuous stat growth — let a story dramatize specific, narratively legible moments of choice, but only if each pick actually does something a reader can notice later.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Perks, feats, and talents (terminology varies by setting) are discrete,
individually chosen character upgrades, distinct from continuous stat
growth — a character doesn't gradually accumulate them through use the way
a skill might improve with practice, but selects them at specific moments,
usually as a reward for a milestone (a level-up, a quest completion, a
tier advancement). Because each one is a discrete choice rather than a
continuous curve, they're a natural place for a story to dramatize a
character actively deciding what kind of capability to become, rather than
simply reporting that growth occurred.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A discrete choice moment is inherently more dramatizable than continuous
growth: a reader can watch a character weigh options and commit to one, and
that choice can reveal character (what does this pick say about what the
character values or fears) in a way passive stat growth can't. The risk is
that a system with many available perks can produce a wall of options that
functions more like an inventory list than a meaningful decision, unless
individual picks are shown to actually matter later.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Milestone-gated single picks**, where a character chooses one perk at
  each major advancement, keeping the decision moments rare and weighty.
- **Frequent, smaller picks**, chosen more often but each individually
  minor, trading dramatic weight per choice for a broader sense of
  accumulating customization.
- **Prerequisite-gated talents**, where later picks require earlier ones,
  creating build paths that commit a character to a developing specialty
  over time.
- **Situational or triggered perks**, unlocked by specific in-story
  achievements or choices rather than milestone advancement alone, tying
  the mechanical reward directly to a narrative event.
- **Respecable picks**, allowing a character to reallocate past choices —
  interacts with the same identity-stakes questions covered in the
  classes-versus-skill-based-growth record's respec discussion.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character weighing two or more specific options at a choice point,
  with the deliberation revealing something about their values or
  priorities.
- A previously chosen perk becoming the specific solution to a later
  problem, demonstrating that the choice mattered beyond the moment it was
  made.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a list of acquired perks reported in a
  status update with no scene ever showing any of them chosen deliberately
  or mattering to a later outcome.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Perks as inventory**, reported rather than chosen, with no dramatized
  decision moment and no later payoff.
- **A choice with no real tradeoff**, where one option is obviously
  superior, removing the meaningful-choice value the discrete-pick
  structure is meant to provide.
- **Chosen perks that never resurface**, where a dramatized choice moment
  is never paid off by the perk actually mattering to a later scene.

sections.title: Visibility, consequences, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Discrete upgrades are unusually easy to make visible, because they have
names. A named perk can be announced, listed, boasted about, recorded by a
guild, and recognized by an opponent who has fought someone with the same
one — which turns a mechanical choice into a social signature. If the story
prefers characters to be read through behavior rather than labels, the same
upgrades can stay private and surface only in what a character turns out to
be able to do. Both work; drifting between them is what confuses readers
about how legible this world is meant to be.

At the scale of a society, a system of named, selectable upgrades implies
training that teaches toward them, institutions that certify them, and a
market for the rare ones — and implies people whose chosen perks made them
unemployable, which is a texture progression settings often skip. Perks also
interact with specialization and respec: a system where selections are
permanent makes each one a commitment worth dramatizing, while freely
reassignable perks are closer to equipment, and are better treated as such
in the prose than given the weight of an identity choice.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- When a character gains a perk, feat, or talent, is the choice
  dramatized, or only reported?
- Do the available options at a choice point carry genuine tradeoffs, or is
  one obviously correct?
- Does a previously chosen perk resurface as the specific solution to a
  later problem?
- If the system allows respeccing, does that ever carry narrative weight,
  or is it treated as costless bookkeeping?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a reported-only perk acquisition, consider converting it into a
   dramatized choice scene, especially if it's narratively significant.
2. Audit a choice point's available options for genuine tradeoffs; add a
   cost to an option that's currently strictly superior.
3. Trace a chosen perk forward and find (or add) a later scene where it's
   the specific solution to a problem.
4. If respeccing is available, find a scene where using it carries a
   narrative cost, rather than functioning as free reallocation.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight systems where perks function as minor flavor with no
  narrative weight expected may not need dramatized choice scenes for every
  pick.
- A story deliberately depicting a character's growth as externally
  imposed rather than chosen (a system that assigns perks without consent)
  is using the absence of choice as its own narrative point.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks perk or talent acquisition linked to
scenes, whether a choice was dramatized or only reported is directly
observable from the text. Whether a chosen perk's later relevance is
adequately paid off requires tracing its use across the manuscript and
remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Perks as inventory:* A status update lists three new perks gained after a
level-up, with no scene showing any of them chosen or later used in a way
that matters to the plot.

*Dramatized, paid-off choice:* A character instead deliberates between a
perk that improves offense and one that improves a companion's safety,
choosing the latter at a personal cost — and two chapters later, that exact
perk is what saves the companion's life in a scene the earlier choice
directly set up.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The discrete-choice-versus-continuous-growth framing draws on established
game-design literature covering character progression systems
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]); no dedicated craft-
literature source addressing discrete character-upgrade choices in prose
fiction specifically was available to this drafting pass.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Skill acquisition and mastery
records.summary: How characters get skills and how skills get better — the mechanic that decides whether growth reads as work or as acquisition, and one of the few places a system can dramatize effort directly.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
A Theory of Fun for Game Design
The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Two related questions, often left implicit: how does a character come to have
a skill at all, and how does a skill they have get better? A system can grant
skills as rewards, sell them, teach them, or grow them through use — and can
improve them by repetition, instruction, insight, or expenditure.

This is distinct from the classes-versus-skills comparison, which is about
how progression is *structured*, and from perks and talents, which are
discrete selected upgrades. This record is about the continuous middle: the
slow part, where competence is built.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Skill acquisition is where a progression system can show effort. Levels and
rewards arrive; skills are practiced. If the system grows what a character
does repeatedly, then what they practice becomes characterization — a reader
learns who someone is from what they got good at.

Game design's mastery literature is useful here with a caveat: it describes
the pleasure of a player becoming competent, which a reader does not
experience. What transfers is the shape — early rapid gains, a long middle,
a plateau — and the emotional register it implies. What does not transfer is
the satisfaction; the reader has to be given that through the character's
experience rather than their own.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Use-based growth** — skills improve by doing, so the character's history
  is legible in their sheet. Rewards specialization and invites grinding.
- **Instruction-based** — skills taught by someone, which makes access a
  social question and puts teachers in the plot.
- **Insight or breakthrough** — advancement by understanding rather than
  repetition, common in cultivation and well suited to dramatization.
- **Purchased or granted** — skills bought with points or awarded by the
  system, the fastest and the least characterizing.
- **Ranked tiers** — named mastery levels (novice, adept, master) that make
  progress legible and create thresholds worth crossing.
- **Skill fusion or evolution** — skills combining into new ones, which
  rewards experimentation and needs rules or it becomes arbitrary.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A skill that improved because of something the reader watched the character
  do.
- A plateau the character has to solve rather than out-repeat.
- A master demonstrating the same skill at a level that reframes what the
  protagonist thought they had.
- Conversely: a skill list growing between chapters with no scene attached to
  any entry.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Acquisition without practice.** Skills appearing as rewards, so the sheet
  grows and no effort is ever shown.
- **The unearned prodigy.** A protagonist who masters in weeks what the
  setting says takes decades, with no stated reason — which quietly tells the
  reader that the world's rules are decorative.
- **Grinding narrated.** Repetition depicted at length because the system
  rewards it, which is accurate and inert.
- **Mastery without ceiling.** No plateau, no diminishing returns, so
  practice never poses a decision about what to spend time on.
- **The unused skill.** Entries acquired and never used again, which trains
  the reader to skim the list — related to the stat-block density problem.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Failure in a skill system is usually a plateau, and how the story handles it
determines whether skills are interesting. If effort always yields progress,
practice is a formality. If progress stalls and the character must find
another route — a teacher, an insight, a different approach — then the
plateau becomes a scene.

Visibility decides whether skill is social. If levels are legible to others,
skill is a credential: people can be hired, ranked, and doubted on it, and
concealing a skill becomes an act. If skill is invisible until demonstrated,
reputation must be built the slow way and underestimation is available. The
reader's view can differ from both, which is where dramatic irony lives.

Systemically, a world with teachable, rankable skills has schools,
certifications, guild examinations, apprenticeships, and a labor market
sorted by them — and a black market in forged credentials. If skills grow by
use, someone has industrialized the use: training halls, practice partners
for hire, safe monsters to grind against. That infrastructure is usually more
distinctive than the skill list itself.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Use-based systems invite the obvious abuse: repeating a trivial action safely
to farm progress, which every such world should have noticed. Other standard
edges are training against helpless targets, exploiting a skill that levels
faster than its cost, and stacking skills whose bonuses were never meant to
combine. Skill systems interact with experience sources — if both grant
growth, the story has two advancement economies and should know how they
relate — and with classes, since a class that gates skills makes acquisition
a question of permission rather than practice.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- How did this character get each of their significant skills, and did the
  reader see it?
- What does practice cost here — time, risk, money, opportunity?
- Where does progress stall, and what breaks the stall?
- Who else has this skill, and how did they learn it?
- If a skill has not been used in twenty chapters, is it still doing anything?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the protagonist's skills with the scene where each was acquired.
   Blank entries are where growth is being asserted rather than shown.
2. Write a plateau: a skill that stops improving, and a character who has to
   do something other than repeat.
3. Put the same skill in a master's hands for one scene and see what it does
   to the reader's sense of the protagonist's level.
4. Name the most efficient exploit in this system and decide who in the world
   is using it.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Systems with no skills, where growth is attribute- or tier-based and this
  record does not apply.
- Stories whose promise is rapid acquisition — power fantasy where watching
  the list grow is the pleasure readers came for.
- Cultivation settings where breakthrough rather than practice is the
  advancement model; the realms record governs that case.
- Short work, where an acquisition arc has no room to develop.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where skills and ranks are reported in structured text, a coach can extract
them, chart acquisitions against chapters, and identify entries that appear
once and never recur. Both are close to deterministic and genuinely useful —
the unused-skill list in particular is hard to see by reading and easy to
compute.

What cannot be determined is whether an acquisition was earned. That requires
reading the surrounding scene, and a skill granted without practice may be a
deliberate gift with its own consequences. The coach should report the shape
of the acquisition curve and ask.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Acquisition without practice:* "Skill acquired: Bladework (Novice). Skill
acquired: Tracking (Novice). Skill acquired: Herbalism (Novice)." — three
competences and no afternoons.

*Practice shown:* he had been throwing the knife at the same post for eleven
days, and the system had said nothing at all, and then on the twelfth day it
said Novice and he sat down in the dirt and laughed.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ernest Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the
design vocabulary for skill systems and advancement; Raph Koster
([[src.book.koster-theory-of-fun]]) supplies the mastery-curve account —
rapid early gains, long middle, plateau; Jesse Schell
([[src.book.schell-art-of-game-design]]) supplies the treatment of
challenge-and-skill balance this record applies to plateaus.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense, with the
disanalogy stated in the record itself: all three sources describe a *player*
acquiring competence, while a reader watches a character do it and gets none
of the mastery pleasure directly. The argument that practice characterizes,
and the social and economic consequences described here, are this drafting
pass's synthesis rather than sourced claims.

records.title: Specialization and respec
records.summary: Committing deeply to a narrow path and being able to undo that commitment are opposite design pressures, and how freely a system allows respeccing determines whether specialization functions as identity or as a costless, reversible loadout choice.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Specialization is the degree to which a character has committed to a
narrow path — a specific class, skill tree, or capability set — often at
the cost of breadth elsewhere. Respec (short for "respecialize") is the
ability to undo or reallocate that commitment, ranging from freely
available and costless to entirely impossible. Where a system sits on this
spectrum determines whether specialization functions as a meaningful
identity commitment (irreversible or costly to change, so the choice
carries real weight) or as a flexible, low-stakes loadout decision (freely
reversible, so the choice carries little more weight than picking an
outfit). This connects directly to, but is distinct from, the classes-
versus-skill-based-growth comparison, which addresses the structure of
progression; this record addresses the reversibility of commitment within
whatever structure is chosen.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A character's specialization choice reveals more about them when it costs
something to make and can't be casually undone — committing to a narrow,
demanding path says something about a character's values or priorities in
a way a freely reversible choice doesn't. Conversely, easy respeccing
supports a different kind of story, one where a character's flexibility
and adaptability are themselves the point, and where narrative tension
comes from other sources than the weight of an irreversible choice. A
mismatch between a story's tone (treating a build choice as
identity-defining) and its system (allowing that choice to be freely
undone) can undercut the story's own stated stakes.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **No respec available**, where a specialization choice is permanent once
  made, maximizing the weight of the initial commitment.
- **Costly respec**, available but at a significant price (a rare
  resource, lost progress, a narrative-significant sacrifice), preserving
  most of the commitment's weight while allowing for a dramatized course
  correction.
- **Freely available respec**, allowing characters to reallocate their
  build with minimal or no cost — supports flexible, experimentation-
  focused stories but removes specialization's identity-defining weight.
- **Narratively gated respec**, where reallocation is mechanically easy but
  requires an in-story event or teacher to access, blending mechanical
  flexibility with narrative significance.
- **Partial respec**, allowing some elements of a build to be changed while
  others remain permanently fixed, creating layered stakes where some
  choices matter more than others.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's specialization choice treated with narrative weight
  proportional to how reversible the system actually makes it — real
  hesitation and consequence for a permanent choice, lighter treatment for
  an easily reversible one.
- A costly respec used as a significant plot event — a character's
  deliberate reinvention of themselves, dramatized as a meaningful turning
  point rather than routine bookkeeping.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a specialization choice treated as
  deeply identity-defining in the narration, in a system where respeccing
  is trivially easy and unlikely to carry real stakes.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Respec availability interacts directly with the classes-versus-skill-based-
growth comparison's discussion of identity stakes, and with the
vertical-versus-horizontal progression comparison, since a freely
respeccable system makes horizontal experimentation lower-risk (a character
can try a build and abandon it) while a non-respeccable system makes each
horizontal choice carry the same weight as a vertical investment. It also
interacts with narrative pacing: a permanent specialization choice made
early can become a long-running constraint the plot has to work around or
through, while easy respec removes that particular constraint but opens
different story possibilities around adaptability and reinvention.

Visibility changes what specialization costs socially. If a character's
build is legible to others — through an appraisal ability, a guild record, or
simply a reputation that precedes them — then specializing means being known
for something, and being countered for it: opponents prepare, allies expect,
and a respec becomes a public act with consequences beyond the character's
own capability sheet. If builds are private, specialization is a secret
advantage and respec is a quiet reinvention, which supports very different
stories. Worth deciding separately: whether the *cost* of a respec is
visible. A character who can quietly rebuild themselves reads differently
from one whose neighbours can see what the change took from them.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Narrative weight mismatched to mechanical reversibility**, treating an
  easily undone choice as identity-defining, or treating a genuinely
  permanent choice as casually as picking a loadout.
- **Respec used to erase narrative consequences**, where a character
  reallocates their build specifically to sidestep a story's established
  stakes rather than as a meaningful, costly choice in its own right.
- **Inconsistent respec rules**, where the story's stated cost or
  availability of respeccing isn't honored consistently across different
  characters or scenes.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- How reversible is this system's specialization commitment, and does the
  narrative weight given to the initial choice match that reversibility?
- If respec is available, is it used as a meaningful, costly plot event, or
  does it function as an unexamined way to sidestep established stakes?
- Are the system's stated respec rules honored consistently across
  different characters?
- Does a permanent specialization choice function as a long-running
  constraint the plot has to engage, or does it fade into the background
  once made?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Check whether the narrative weight given to a specialization choice
   matches the system's actual reversibility; adjust one or the other for
   consistency.
2. For a respec event, treat it as a dramatized plot beat — what does it
   cost, and what does the character's decision to pursue it reveal —
   rather than routine bookkeeping.
3. Audit respec rules across the manuscript's characters for consistency.
4. For a permanent specialization made early, find a later scene where it
   still functions as a meaningful constraint on the character's options.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight systems with no tracked specialization mechanic don't
  need this distinction developed.
- A story deliberately depicting a character's fluid, ever-changing
  identity as its subject may intentionally use easy respeccing as a
  metaphor or mechanic supporting that theme.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks specialization and respec events linked
to scenes, whether stated rules are honored is close to deterministic.
Whether the narrative weight given to a specialization choice matches its
actual mechanical reversibility requires interpreting the prose and remains
model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Mismatched weight:* A character agonizes for a full chapter over choosing
a class, described in near-sacred terms, in a system where respeccing is
established two chapters later to be freely available at any town shop for
a small fee.

*Matched weight:* The same agonizing choice instead occurs in a system
where reallocation requires a years-long ritual few cultivators ever
survive attempting twice — the narrative weight given to the initial
decision matches the genuine, near-permanent stakes of getting it wrong.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The specialization/respec framing and its connection to build commitment
draws on established game-design literature covering character progression
systems ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]); no dedicated
craft-literature source specifically addressing respec mechanics in prose
fiction was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: Action economy in encounters
records.summary: Action economy — who gets to act, how often, and in what order — is the hidden logic behind whether a fight scene feels tactically legible or arbitrary, whether or not a story ever states a number.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Action economy describes who gets to act, how often, in what order, and with
what range or positioning constraints during a conflict — the underlying
logic tabletop and video games make explicit through initiative, turns, and
action points. Prose fiction rarely states this logic as numbers, but a
fight scene still has an implicit action economy: a reader can tell, even
without a number, whether one side is meaningfully outnumbered, whether a
character's "turn" makes tactical sense, and whether the story is applying
its own implied rules consistently.
