sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A fight whose implicit rules are inconsistent — a character taking several
actions in the time another gets one, with no explanation, or ignoring an
established range or positioning constraint when convenient — can register
as unfair or arbitrary even to a reader who couldn't name why. A fight with
a legible, consistently applied action economy lets tactical cleverness
actually read as clever, because the reader can follow the logic of why a
particular maneuver worked.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Implicit/prose-native**, where the story never states turn order or
  action counts explicitly, but consistently implies who can act when
  through pacing and description.
- **Semi-explicit**, where a LitRPG or system-driven story states some
  mechanical elements (an ability's cooldown, a stated range) without a full
  formal turn structure.
- **Fully explicit**, rare in prose but present in some LitRPG, where turn
  order, action counts, or initiative are stated directly as system
  information.
- **Numbers advantage / positioning play**, where the tactical interest
  comes from managing how many opponents can act on a character at once,
  independent of any individual character's raw power.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character using terrain, positioning, or timing to ensure they only face
  one opponent's action at a time, rather than being surrounded.
- A consistent implied rhythm to exchanges — attack, response, complication —
  that a reader can track even without stated numbers.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a character taking several unanswered
  actions in a row with no established reason (an ability, a
  speed advantage) while opponents simply wait their narrative turn.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Action economy interacts directly with progression: an ability that grants
an extra action, an interrupt, or a way to act out of turn is often far more
valuable than a raw damage increase, because it changes the fundamental math
of who acts how often — worth flagging explicitly if a system grants such
abilities, since they can trivialize encounters the story hasn't accounted
for. It also interacts with stakes: a character facing multiple opponents
simultaneously is facing a harder action-economy problem than raw
individual strength comparisons would suggest, which is part of why
"surrounded" reads as dangerous even against individually weaker
opponents.

Action economy is usually invisible to characters and only semi-visible to
readers, which is precisely what makes it easy to break without anyone
noticing at the time. Characters in a fight do not perceive turn order; they
perceive being outnumbered, being too slow, or having no opening. A reader
perceives the economy indirectly, through whether a scene's outcomes feel
earned. This asymmetry cuts both ways: an author can quietly cheat the
action economy and get away with it in the moment, and readers who cannot
articulate the rule will still register its violation as a fight that felt
unearned. In systems where characters *can* see the economy — visible
turn-based interfaces, initiative displays, speed statistics — it becomes a
tactical resource characters can reason about aloud, which is a distinctly
different kind of fight scene and a different promise to the reader.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unearned extra actions**, where a character acts more often than
  established rules would allow, with no in-story explanation (a granted
  ability, an opponent's choice to hold back).
- **Ignored numbers disadvantage**, where a character facing many opponents
  simultaneously fights as if facing them one at a time, with no
  acknowledgment of the tactical problem multiple simultaneous actors
  create.
- **Action-economy-breaking abilities introduced without consequence**,
  where an ability that should trivialize ordinary encounters (an extra
  action every turn, an interrupt) is granted without the story examining
  how it changes the encounters that follow.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- In this fight scene, is it clear who can act, how often, and why, even
  without stated numbers?
- If a character faces multiple opponents, does the scene acknowledge the
  tactical problem that creates, or treat it as equivalent to facing one at
  a time?
- Does any granted ability effectively give a character an extra action or a
  way to act out of turn, and if so, has the story accounted for how that
  changes future encounters?
- Would a reader tracking this fight closely be able to follow why a
  particular maneuver worked tactically?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a fight scene that feels arbitrary, sketch an informal turn order (who
   acts, in what sequence) and check whether the prose is consistent with
   it.
2. For a character facing multiple opponents, make the numbers disadvantage
   legible on the page — through positioning, exhaustion, or explicit
   acknowledgment of being outnumbered — rather than treating it as
   equivalent to a one-on-one fight.
3. If a character gains an action-economy-breaking ability, test one future
   encounter to see whether the story needs to escalate opponent numbers or
   tactics to keep the fight meaningfully contested.
4. Read a key fight scene aloud, tracking only who acts when, to catch
   unintentional inconsistencies in implied turn structure.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stylized, non-tactical action prose (some literary or impressionistic
  fight scenes) may deliberately avoid legible action economy in favor of
  sensory or emotional impact, and applying this pattern would work against
  the intended effect.
- Very short, one-sided confrontations (an ambush, an execution) may not
  need a tracked action economy if the scene's point is the mismatch itself
  rather than tactical exchange.
- Non-combat conflict scenes (negotiation, a chase) can have an analogous
  "turn" logic but this pattern's combat-specific framing may not transfer
  directly without adaptation.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a fight scene's implicit action economy is internally consistent
requires tracking who acts, how often, and under what stated constraints
across the scene — a close-reading task with no deterministic substitute.
Where a project explicitly tracks mechanical combat data (initiative,
cooldowns) linked to scenes, a coach could surface that data directly, but
judging whether the prose honors it remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Inconsistent action economy:* A character single-handedly exchanges blows
with four opponents in sequence, each waiting politely for their turn, with
no narrative reason given for why they don't simply attack together.

*Consistent action economy:* The same character deliberately backs into a
narrow corridor specifically so only one opponent can reach them at a time,
and the prose explicitly notes this as the reason the fight remains
survivable — the numbers problem is acknowledged and tactically addressed.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The action-economy framing draws on established game-design literature
covering turn structure, encounter design, and resource management in
formal game systems ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]],
[[src.book.salen-zimmerman-rules-of-play]]); both are established academic/
practitioner texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's
application of a formal game-design concept to prose fiction craft (where
it is rarely made explicit) is this drafting pass's adaptation rather than a
direct claim from either source about prose narrative specifically.

records.title: Death, respawn, and permadeath design
records.summary: Whether death is permanent, reversible, or something in between is one of the highest-leverage decisions a progression system makes, because it directly sets the ceiling on how much a reader can be made to fear for a character.
modifiers: dark-horror-litrpg: Permadeath or severe, durable penalties are conventionally central to this subgenre's promise; a soft-respawn system undercuts the genre's core appeal here more than in most other subgenres.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A death mechanic sits somewhere on a spectrum from fully permanent
(permadeath, no in-world reversal available) through costly-but-reversible
(a respawn with a durable, meaningful penalty) to soft (a respawn with a
minor, quickly recovered penalty) to functionally consequence-free (death
carries no lasting mechanical cost at all). Where a story's death mechanic
sits on that spectrum sets a hard ceiling on how much genuine mortal risk
the reader can ever be made to feel, regardless of how tense any individual
scene is written to be.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
If a reader knows, explicitly or through established precedent, that death
in this story carries no lasting cost, no individual combat scene can
generate real mortal stakes no matter how well it's written — the reader's
knowledge of the underlying system caps the achievable tension. Conversely,
a system with genuine, durable cost to death (or true permadeath) means even
a low-key scene can carry real weight, because the reader can't assume
survival is guaranteed by genre convention.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **True permadeath**, with no in-world mechanism to reverse death at all —
  the highest-stakes option, common in dark/horror LitRPG and used
  deliberately elsewhere for maximum tension.
- **Costly respawn**, where death is reversible but at a significant,
  durable cost (lost levels, a lasting debuff, a resource expenditure that
  takes real narrative time to recover) — preserves ongoing stakes without
  removing characters permanently.
- **Soft respawn**, where death carries a minor, quickly recovered penalty —
  common in lighter or more comedic LitRPG, where death functions more like
  a setback than a genuine risk.
- **Consequence-free death**, rare as a stated system but sometimes true in
  practice even when not stated, when a story never actually lets death
  matter mechanically or narratively despite nominal stakes.
- **Selective mortality**, where the protagonist has some form of protection
  or reversal unavailable to other characters — raising the question of
  whether other characters' deaths still carry weight even if the
  protagonist's don't.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's death (or near-death) followed by an explicit, lasting
  consequence that the story continues to reference in later chapters.
- A death or near-death treated as a minor inconvenience, quickly recovered
  from with no lasting narrative or mechanical trace.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a system that states death carries severe
  penalties, but no character in the story ever actually experiences those
  stated penalties, even after a near-fatal encounter.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Death mechanics interact directly with the tier-pacing and advancement-rate
patterns: a costly respawn that resets meaningful progression creates a
genuine setback the story can dramatize, while a consequence-free respawn
removes that tool entirely. They also interact with the multi-character
cast: if only the protagonist enjoys favorable death mechanics, the
disparity itself can become a plot-relevant fact (a source of guilt,
privilege, or narrative unfairness) if the story chooses to engage it, or an
unexamined inconsistency if it doesn't.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Stated stakes that are never actually paid**, undermining the system's
  credibility every time a character survives an established fatal scenario
  without the promised cost.
- **Protagonist plot armor inconsistent with stated world rules**, where the
  protagonist survives situations the system has established as fatal for
  everyone else, with no explanation.
- **Death used for shock with no lasting narrative weight**, where a
  significant character's death carries no visible consequence for the
  ongoing plot or the surviving cast's behavior.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does death actually cost in this system, and has a character
  actually paid that cost on the page?
- If the protagonist has more favorable death mechanics than other
  characters, does the story ever engage that disparity, or does it go
  unremarked?
- When a significant character dies, does the story show its effect on the
  surviving cast, or move past it quickly?
- Does the established death mechanic match the level of mortal tension the
  story wants a reader to feel during its combat scenes?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify the last scene where a character was established to be at
   serious risk of death; check whether the stated system's consequences
   were actually applied if the character died, or paid if they survived.
2. If death currently carries no lasting cost, consider introducing one
   deliberate instance where it does, to recalibrate reader expectations for
   future scenes.
3. For a story with protagonist-specific death protections, test a scene
   where a supporting character faces the same risk without that
   protection, to see whether the contrast is worth engaging directly.
4. Trace a significant character death forward several chapters and confirm
   its effects (grief, tactical loss, plot consequence) remain visible
   rather than fading immediately.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Comedic or low-stakes LitRPG may deliberately use soft or consequence-free
  death as part of its tonal promise, where mortal stakes were never the
  intended appeal.
- A story that explicitly interrogates its own death mechanic's fairness or
  unfairness as a theme (a protagonist troubled by their own safety relative
  to others) is engaging this pattern directly rather than failing to
  notice it.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks character death, revival, or associated
penalties as structured state, a coach could report whether stated
consequences were applied deterministically. Whether the resulting
mortality stakes feel earned to a reader, and whether a disparity between
characters is narratively engaged or merely present, requires reading and
interpreting the manuscript and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unpaid stakes:* The system states that death results in permanent loss of
one full level. A major character dies and is later shown at full,
unchanged power with no acknowledgment of any loss.

*Paid stakes:* The same death instead visibly and permanently weakens the
character; the following chapters show them relearning lost ground and
grappling with the loss in ways that shape subsequent decisions.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The subgenre framing (dark/horror LitRPG's centrality of genuine mortal
risk) draws on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s subgenre coaching profiles
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre material
as partly inferential; the stated-stakes-must-be-paid principle draws on the
broader craft-failure research on established limits staying established
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]], pattern P15).
`source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Summons, familiars, and bonded companions
records.summary: A companion the system grants rather than the plot introduces — which raises a question most such records never answer: is this a capability the protagonist owns, or a person?

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A bonded companion is a creature or entity the system attaches to a
character: a summoned beast, a familiar, a contracted spirit, a tamed
monster, a system-granted partner. What distinguishes it from an ordinary
ally is provenance — the relationship is mechanical, often exclusive, and
frequently something the protagonist acquired rather than earned socially.

Every such record faces the same fork, and the story is largely determined by
which way it goes: the companion is a capability the protagonist deploys, or
a person the protagonist is in a relationship with. Both work. Drifting
between them is what produces the genre's characteristic awkwardness, where a
creature with dialogue and preferences is nonetheless described as being
levelled up.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Companions are among the most beloved elements in this genre, and the reason
is not tactical. A bonded creature supplies uncomplicated attachment,
witnessed growth alongside the protagonist's, and a relationship whose terms
are clear — which is restful in a story otherwise full of negotiation.

They also solve a practical problem: a solitary protagonist has nobody to
talk to. A companion permits dialogue, reaction, and interiority made
external, without requiring the protagonist to trust another person.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The summon** — called and dismissed, existing at the character's
  discretion, which makes it closest to a capability.
- **The familiar** — persistent, usually with some autonomy and often a
  shared sense or link.
- **The contracted entity** — a bargain with terms, where the companion has
  its own agenda and the relationship is negotiated. Overlaps the oaths
  record.
- **The tamed or raised creature** — acquired young or defeated and kept,
  where the acquisition itself carries moral weight the story may or may not
  address.
- **The bonded equal** — a companion of comparable standing, closer to a
  party member than a possession.
- **The unwilling bond** — a companion who did not choose this, which is the
  most dramatically loaded version and the least often taken seriously.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A companion who wants something the protagonist does not, and says so.
- Growth on the companion's own track, with its own costs and choices.
- A summon deployed tactically and described in the same register as a spell,
  consistently.
- Conversely: a creature with a name, jokes, and opinions whose death or
  dismissal the narrative treats as a resource loss.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The talking tool.** A companion characterized enough to be a person and
  used exclusively as an ability.
- **Unexamined acquisition.** A bond formed by capture, coercion, or system
  fiat, in a story that has given its companion a mind and never asks whether
  it consented.
- **Power laundering.** The companion carries the protagonist's fights, so
  growth is displaced onto an asset rather than demonstrated.
- **The absent companion.** Present in exposition, forgotten in scenes,
  reappearing when useful.
- **No cost of bonding.** A companion that arrives free, costs nothing to
  maintain, and risks nothing — which makes it pure upside and structurally
  inert.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Whether the companion grows on its own track is the decision that most
changes the story. A companion that levels with the protagonist is a
capability; one that grows through its own experiences, choices, and
setbacks is a second character arc, and it will compete for the reader's
attention — often successfully.

The failure state deserves the same care. If a summon can be dismissed and
recalled intact, its defeat costs mana; if a bonded companion can die, every
fight it enters carries different weight. Systems frequently permit the first
while writing the companion as though the second were true, and readers feel
the mismatch even when they cannot name it.

Visibility is worth deciding too: can others perceive the bond? A visible
bond makes the protagonist legible — people know what they are and what they
can do — while a concealed one supports reveals and misdirection. And
socially, a world where creatures can be bound to people has an economy in
them: breeders, brokers, contracts, welfare arguments, and people who think
the whole practice is monstrous. That last group is almost always the most
interesting and almost never present.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Companions are an action-economy exploit by definition — they add actions per
turn — and any system that permits several has to price that. Other standard
exploits: using a summon as a disposable scout because it can be recalled,
bonding a creature purely for a passive bonus, or acquiring companions faster
than the story can characterize them. Where companions grant the protagonist
capabilities, the bond is functionally a perk and interacts with that record;
where companions are contracted, it interacts with oaths and bindings, and
the terms of the contract are worth writing out.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is this companion a capability or a person? Does the prose treat it
  consistently as whichever it is?
- What does the companion want that the protagonist does not?
- Did it choose this bond, and does the story ever ask?
- What does the bond cost — to form, to maintain, to break?
- If the companion died, would the loss be grief or expense? Does the book
  agree with itself about that?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write a scene where the companion refuses. If refusal is not possible,
   the story has answered the capability-or-person question already.
2. Give the companion one goal of its own and follow it for a chapter.
3. Remove the companion from a fight it usually decides, and see what the
   protagonist can actually do.
4. Write the character who objects to the practice of bonding, and see
   whether the setting gets more interesting.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Systems where summons are explicitly non-sentient constructs, and treating
  them as capabilities is both consistent and intended.
- Stories where the companion is the co-protagonist and the party record
  governs instead.
- Comedic treatments where a companion's personality is a running joke rather
  than a claim about its interiority.
- Cultivation settings with spirit beasts, where the tradition carries its own
  conventions about bonding that this record should not overwrite.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe whether a companion has attributed dialogue, how often it
appears in scenes relative to being mentioned, and whether it is described
using capability vocabulary or character vocabulary — that last is a genuinely
useful signal for the consistency question this record raises, though it is
an inference and not a measurement.

What cannot be determined is which treatment the author intends. A companion
described as a resource may be a deliberate portrait of a character who thinks
that way, which is a different book from one that has not noticed. The coach
should surface the inconsistency as a question about intent.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Talking tool:* Ash whined and pressed his head against her knee. Summoning
cost had dropped to 40 mana at Bond Rank 3, which made him considerably more
efficient to field.

*Person:* Ash would not go into the water, and no amount of coaxing moved
him, and in the end she went in alone and came out knowing something about
him she had not known before.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ernest Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the
general design vocabulary for companion units and their effect on action
economy; Jesse Schell ([[src.book.schell-art-of-game-design]]) supplies the
treatment of player attachment to game entities. This library's genre
research ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation
that bonded companions are a durable subgenre convention.

`source_confidence` is `limited`, deliberately. Neither game-design source
addresses the question this record is actually about — whether a
characterized companion is being treated as a person or a possession — and no
craft or scholarly source on that question was available to this drafting
pass. The capability-or-person fork, the consent observation, the failure
taxonomy, and the consequence reasoning are all this pass's synthesis. The
note about cultivation spirit beasts is a deliberate boundary rather than a
sourced claim about that tradition; a later pass should check it against the
cultivation sources this library already holds before the author vets it.

records.title: Systemic consequences: institutions, labor, and governance
records.summary: A power system reshapes who governs, who works at what, and how authority is organized — this record works through those three domains specifically, as a deeper application of the general systemic-social- consequences framework rather than a restatement of it.

citations.label: Writing Progression Fantasy
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
This record applies the general systemic-social-consequences framework to
three specific, closely related domains: institutions (the organizations —
guilds, sects, licensing bodies, military orders — that form around a
power system), labor (what work looks like in a society where some
fraction of the population has access to power that could replace,
augment, or devalue conventional work), and governance (who actually rules,
and whether that authority tracks personal power, institutional position,
or something independent of both). A setting that hasn't decided how these
three interact tends to produce inconsistencies a careful reader will
notice — a "kingdom" whose government never reckons with the fact that a
handful of its citizens could individually topple its army, for instance.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Institutions, labor, and governance are where a power system's abstract
implications become concrete, trackable social structure — a reader can
hold "the mages' guild controls licensing and therefore controls who gets
to practice" in mind much more easily than an abstract claim that "magic
has changed society." These three domains are also a rich, underused
source of plot material distinct from personal power conflicts: political
maneuvering over guild leadership, labor displaced or transformed by
magical automation, a government whose legitimacy is genuinely threatened
by individuals more powerful than its institutions.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Power-tracks-governance systems**, where political authority directly
  correlates with personal cultivation or magical power — the simplest and
  most common default, though one that raises its own questions about why
  weaker administrators would be tolerated at all.
- **Power-independent-of-governance systems**, where political authority
  is deliberately separated from raw personal power (a bureaucracy, a
  hereditary monarchy, an elected council) that maintains control despite
  not commanding the setting's strongest individuals — often more
  narratively interesting because it requires the story to explain how
  that separation is sustained.
- **Institution-mediated power**, where guilds, sects, or licensing bodies
  sit between individual power and formal governance, controlling access
  and legitimacy without being the government themselves.
- **Displaced-labor settings**, where magical or system-based automation
  has visibly changed what conventional work looks like, with characters
  or communities affected by that displacement.
- **Unexamined-default settings**, a failure mode rather than a variant,
  where institutions and governance simply mirror a real-world historical
  period with no adaptation for the setting's actual power system.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A political or institutional structure whose stability is explicitly
  addressed given the setting's power distribution — why the government
  hasn't been overthrown by more powerful individuals, or how it maintains
  legitimacy despite them.
- Labor or economic activity shown adapting to the presence of a power
  system — jobs that exist because of it, jobs displaced by it, workers
  whose livelihoods depend on navigating around it.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a kingdom, guild, or government whose
  structure and stability are never addressed despite the setting's power
  system implying they should be under obvious strain.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unexamined governance stability**, where a weak formal government
  persists despite the setting having individuals capable of overturning
  it, with no explanation for the persistence.
- **Labor untouched by the power system**, where an economy functions
  exactly as a non-magical historical setting would despite the story's
  own power system implying it shouldn't.
- **Institutions with no political stakes**, where a guild or sect exists
  as flavor with no actual competition, hierarchy dispute, or governance
  function affecting plot.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Institutions are where power systems get gamed, and a setting becomes
noticeably more solid once it admits that. Licensing bodies can be captured
by the people they license; guilds can restrict supply to keep prices high;
a governance structure that tracks personal power invites duels as
succession, and one that does not invites the strongest people in the
society to ask why they should obey it. Any credential a system can verify
can also be forged, rented, or inherited by someone who did not earn it —
and who has an interest in that forgery is often a better plot engine than
the forgery itself.

The sharpest edge case is labor. If power can replace work, someone owns
that power, and the question of whether it displaced workers, enriched a
few, or was quietly restricted to protect an existing order is usually more
interesting than the magic. This record interacts most directly with
universal-versus-class-bound access: who can reach the system determines
which of these exploits are available to whom, and a story that has settled
access has usually already answered half of this.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Given this setting's power distribution, why hasn't formal governance
  been overturned by more powerful individuals — or has it, and does the
  story engage that?
- Has labor or the economy visibly adapted to the presence of this
  setting's power system, or does it function as though the system doesn't
  exist?
- Do institutions (guilds, sects, licensing bodies) have genuine political
  stakes affecting the plot, or do they function as decorative setting
  detail?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence explaining why formal governance in this setting
   hasn't been overturned by its most powerful individuals, and check
   whether that explanation is legible anywhere in the text.
2. Find or add a scene showing labor or economic activity shaped by the
   presence of the power system.
3. Give an institution a genuine political stake — a leadership dispute, a
   resource competition — that affects a plot decision.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Small-scale, personal-stakes stories may deliberately keep their frame
  narrow enough that governance and institutional questions are outside
  scope, provided the setting doesn't imply a larger scale it never
  engages.
- A newly emerged power system (early system apocalypse, a recent
  awakening) hasn't had time to reshape institutions yet, and the absence
  of adaptation is accurate rather than an oversight.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a setting's institutions, labor, and governance plausibly reflect
its power system requires reading and interpreting the manuscript's
worldbuilding as a whole — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined governance:* A kingdom is ruled by a hereditary monarchy with
no magical ability at all, in a setting where several independent
cultivators could individually raze the capital, with no in-text
explanation for why this arrangement persists.

*Examined governance:* The same monarchy instead maintains power through an
explicit, dramatized arrangement — a mutual-destruction pact among the
realm's most powerful cultivators, brokered generations ago and actively
maintained by a dedicated institution whose collapse would immediately
destabilize the whole political order — giving the setting's power/
governance gap a legible, plot-relevant explanation.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The core principle — that a society living with transformative power
should show some trace of institutional adaptation — draws on Andrew
Rowe's progression-fantasy craft writing on society applying its own
powers ([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]), reinforced by the broader
craft-failure pattern research ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-
research]], pattern P13). Both are practitioner-level sources; this
record's specific application to institutions, labor, and governance as
three distinct domains is this drafting pass's synthesis and elaboration
of the general systemic-social-consequences record. `source_confidence` is
`mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Systemic consequences: medicine, religion, and crime
records.summary: Healing magic changes what medicine looks like, divine or spiritual power changes what religion claims and can prove, and any power system changes what crime is possible and how it's policed — three domains where an unexamined default tends to read as the least examined part of a setting's worldbuilding.

citations.label: Writing Progression Fantasy
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
This record applies the general systemic-social-consequences framework to
three more domains: medicine (how healing, disease, and mortality are
understood and treated in a setting where healing magic or restorative
power exists), religion (what a faith tradition claims, and how those
claims are complicated or confirmed by a setting where divine or spiritual
power is directly, verifiably real rather than a matter of belief), and
crime (what becomes possible, and what becomes policeable, when magic or
system-granted power can be used to steal, deceive, coerce, or kill in ways
mundane law was never built to address). These three are grouped together
because they share a common failure pattern: a setting's power system
exists, but medicine, religion, and crime all continue to function as
though it doesn't.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
These three domains touch daily life more directly than governance or
grand institutions do, which means an unexamined default is often more
immediately noticeable to a reader — a world with reliable healing magic
where people still die routinely of treatable illness, or a religion whose
central claims are directly, verifiably true or false and yet functions
exactly like a real-world faith built on unprovable belief, can read as an
oversight rather than a deliberate choice. Engaging even one of these
domains, even briefly, signals that the setting's power system has been
thought through past its immediate use to the protagonist.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Medicine transformed by healing magic**, where access to restorative
  power is itself an economic and social stratifier — who can afford
  healing, who has access, and what conventional medicine still handles
  because magic can't or won't.
- **Medicine untouched by magic**, a legitimate choice when a setting's
  power system doesn't include healing capability, or when healing magic
  is deliberately rare or limited — worth an explicit reason rather than
  simply being unaddressed.
- **Verified religion**, where divine power is directly, provably real,
  raising questions about what faith even means in a setting where belief
  isn't required to access divine favor — a rich and underused source of
  thematic material.
- **Contested or fragmented religion**, where divine power's reality is
  acknowledged but its meaning and moral implications remain genuinely
  disputed among different factions or traditions, preserving some of the
  interpretive uncertainty religion has in settings without verifiable
  divine power.
- **Magic-adapted crime and law enforcement**, where legal and policing
  structures have specifically evolved to address magically-enabled
  offenses (mind-reading as evidence, magical forgery detection,
  supernatural containment for dangerous offenders).
- **Unadapted crime and law**, a failure mode rather than a variant, where
  criminal law and enforcement mirror a non-magical historical system with
  no acknowledgment of what the setting's power system should have changed.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's access to healing magic (or lack of it) shown to carry
  social or economic weight, rather than functioning as a uniformly
  available convenience.
- A religious tradition whose claims are treated as directly verifiable
  within the story's own logic, with characters engaging what that
  verifiability actually means for faith and doubt.
- A crime or law-enforcement scene that specifically accounts for what the
  setting's power system makes possible, rather than functioning
  identically to a mundane historical equivalent.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Healing magic with no social stratification**, where restorative power
  exists but is treated as universally, freely available with no economic
  or access implications.
- **Verifiable divine power treated like unprovable faith**, where a
  religion's directly confirmable claims are narrated with the same
  uncertainty and doubt structure as a real-world faith based on belief
  alone, with no acknowledgment of the difference.
- **Law enforcement untouched by magic**, where crime and policing mirror
  a mundane historical system despite the setting's power system implying
  they should function differently.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Each of these three domains has an obvious abuse that a story gains texture
by acknowledging. Medicine: if healing is purchasable, then health tracks
wealth, and someone is rationing, insuring, or counterfeiting it — and a
healer who can restore anything is also someone who can withhold it.
Religion: if divine power is verifiable, then faith becomes falsifiable, and
the interesting characters are the ones whose authority depends on a claim
the system could test — as well as those who have found how to produce the
signs without the substance. Crime: every capability the system grants is
also a criminal method, and every detection ability is also a surveillance
tool, so a setting with mind-reading has either an unusually invasive state
or a very good reason it does not.

The common edge case across all three is verification. Where power is real
and testable, institutions will build tests, and those tests will be gamed,
bribed, and occasionally wrong about someone the reader knows the truth
about — which is frequently the most dramatically useful failure available
here.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If healing magic exists in this setting, does access to it carry social
  or economic weight, or is it treated as universally available?
- If divine or spiritual power is directly verifiable in this setting, does
  the story engage what that means for the nature of faith, or does
  religion function as though it weren't?
- Does crime and law enforcement in this setting account for what the
  power system makes possible, or does it mirror an unmodified historical
  equivalent?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. If healing magic exists, add or find a scene showing unequal access to
   it, and let that inequality matter to a character.
2. If divine power is verifiable, find a scene where a character grapples
   with what that verifiability means — for doubt, for worship, for
   moral obligation — rather than treating faith as functioning identically
   to a real-world belief system.
3. For a crime or legal scene, check whether the setting's power system
   would plausibly have changed how the offense is committed, detected, or
   punished, and adjust if it currently doesn't.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A setting deliberately keeping magic rare, hidden, or newly emerged
  hasn't had time for medicine, religion, or crime to adapt, and the
  absence of adaptation is accurate rather than an oversight.
- Very narrow, personal-stakes stories may deliberately keep their frame
  too small to engage these domains meaningfully, provided the setting
  doesn't imply a scale it never addresses.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a setting's medicine, religion, and crime plausibly reflect its
power system requires reading and interpreting the manuscript's
worldbuilding as a whole — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined medicine and religion:* A setting has reliable, common healing
magic, yet a secondary character dies of an easily curable illness with no
explanation for why magical treatment wasn't sought; the setting's temple
also preaches faith and doubt in a deity whose power is otherwise treated
as directly, unambiguously real and observable by everyone.

*Examined medicine and religion:* The same setting instead makes healing
magic's cost or scarcity explicit — the character who died couldn't afford
a healer, and that economic fact is shown to matter — and the temple's
teaching reframes "faith" as devotion and interpretation of a
verifiably real deity's ambiguous will, rather than belief in the deity's
existence itself.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The core principle — that transformative power should leave a visible
trace on a society's daily institutions — draws on Andrew Rowe's
progression-fantasy craft writing ([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]),
reinforced by the broader craft-failure pattern research
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]], pattern P13). Both are
practitioner-level sources; this record's specific application to
medicine, religion, and crime as three distinct domains is this drafting
pass's synthesis and elaboration of the general systemic-social-
consequences record. `source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Systemic social consequences of power systems
records.summary: A power system that reshapes what's possible — resurrection, teleportation, elemental magic, mass-accessible progression — should plausibly reshape the society that has lived with it for generations; a setting that looks otherwise unchanged reads as unexamined.
modifiers: crafting-and-economy: This pattern is especially central here — the subgenre lives or dies on whether society plausibly uses the goods and materials the economy produces.

isekai-portal: Closely related to the outsider's-advantage failure mode (P14): an outsider's edge only holds up if the society's own non-use of similar knowledge is explained, which requires the same systemic thinking this record asks for.

citations.label: Writing Progression Fantasy
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
If a setting's power system enables something transformative — reliable
resurrection, teleportation, mass communication via magic, or widely
accessible power progression itself — a society that has had access to that
capability for any meaningful length of time should show some trace of
having organized around it: institutions, economies, laws, religions, and
daily habits that would plausibly form in response. A setting where wizards
have existed for centuries but daily life, governance, and economy look
otherwise indistinguishable from a world with no magic at all reads, to
attentive readers, as unexamined rather than deliberately conservative.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Worldbuilding that traces a power system's second- and third-order effects
signals a setting that's been thought through, and it also opens genuine
plot material a purely personal-power-focused story leaves untouched:
institutions built around a mechanic can be corrupt, contested, or
collapsing in ways that generate conflict independent of any individual
character's strength. A setting that ignores these effects isn't
automatically bad, but it forecloses an entire category of story the system
itself was implicitly offering.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Institutional adaptation**, where governance, law, or religion has
  visibly organized around the power system (licensing for spellcasters, a
  church built around a resurrection mechanic's theology).
- **Economic adaptation**, where markets, labor, and class structures
  reflect who has access to power and who doesn't.
- **Military and political adaptation**, where warfare, diplomacy, and
  borders reflect what the power system makes possible or moot (walls matter
  less if teleportation is common, for instance).
- **Deliberately limited adaptation**, where the story explicitly explains
  why society hasn't organized around a capability as much as one might
  expect (the ability is new, rare, deliberately suppressed, or too
  dangerous to institutionalize) — a legitimate variant provided the
  limiting factor is stated rather than simply absent.
- **Uneven adaptation**, where some sectors of society have reorganized
  around the power system and others conspicuously haven't, which can itself
  be a source of tension (a magical elite alongside an unchanged peasantry).

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- An institution, law, custom, or economic structure explicitly shaped by
  the setting's power system, treated as unremarkable background by
  characters who live with it.
- A character's plan or problem running into a systemic consequence of the
  power system (a licensing law, a guild monopoly, a resurrection-related
  inheritance dispute) rather than only personal-scale obstacles.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a power capable of reshaping society
  (mass communication, resurrection, cheap teleportation) that the setting
  treats as though it barely exists outside the protagonist's own use of it.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
A power system's social consequences interact directly with its access
rules (see the related resource-lifecycle-design pattern): a universally
accessible power reshapes society very differently than one restricted to a
narrow elite. They also interact with the crafting/economy loop pattern,
since materials, goods, and services tied to the power system imply their
own markets, labor, and scarcity dynamics. Worth considering explicitly:
does the power system change warfare enough that borders, walls, or armies
function differently? Does it change medicine, education, or crime in ways
the story could engage even briefly?

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **An unexamined status quo**, where a transformative power exists but
  society looks unchanged from a version of the setting with no magic at
  all, with no explanation for why.
- **Isolated personal use**, where the power system matters only for the
  protagonist's individual advancement and never intersects with any larger
  social structure.
- **Inconsistent institutional logic**, where an institution is shown
  reacting to the power system in one scene and behaving as if it doesn't
  exist in another.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If this world's central power (magic, cultivation, the system itself) has
  existed for generations, what institution, law, or custom would plausibly
  have formed around it?
- Does this power change warfare, medicine, governance, or economy in ways
  the story ever shows, even briefly?
- If society hasn't organized around an available power, is there a stated
  reason (rarity, suppression, danger), or is the absence simply unexamined?
- Is there an institution in this setting whose corruption, contestation, or
  collapse could generate conflict independent of the protagonist's personal
  power level?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Pick one transformative capability in the setting's power system and
   sketch one institution, law, or custom that would plausibly exist because
   of it, even if it never becomes plot-central.
2. Find a scene where the protagonist's plan could plausibly run into a
   systemic consequence of the power system (a law, a guild, a market) and
   test adding that friction.
3. If society has deliberately not organized around an available power,
   make the limiting reason explicit somewhere in the text rather than
   leaving it implicit.
4. Consider one sector of society that would be most disrupted by the
   power system (labor, medicine, the military) and see whether even one
   scene could show that disruption in the background.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A young or recently emerged power system (a system apocalypse in its
  opening act, a newly awakened ability) hasn't had time to reshape
  institutions yet, and the absence of systemic adaptation is itself
  accurate rather than an oversight.
- Small-scale, personal-stakes stories may deliberately keep the frame
  narrow enough that broader systemic consequences are outside the story's
  scope, provided the setting doesn't imply a scale it never engages.
- A deliberately isolated or secret power (known only to a handful of
  characters) wouldn't be expected to have reshaped society yet, by design.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a setting's social, economic, and political structures plausibly
reflect its power system requires reading and interpreting a manuscript's
worldbuilding as a whole — a judgment no structured data substitutes for. A
coach can prompt the author with the diagnostic questions above but cannot
verify systemic plausibility from text alone.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined status quo:* A setting where resurrection has been reliably
available for three hundred years still has grief, funeral customs, and
inheritance law that read identically to a setting with no resurrection
magic at all, with no acknowledgment of the discrepancy.

*Examined consequence:* The same setting instead has an entrenched, wealthy
"Second-Life Guild" controlling resurrection access, inheritance law
explicitly rewritten to account for the possibility of a decedent's return,
and a black market in unauthorized resurrections that the plot can draw on
directly.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The core principle — that a society living with transformative power for
generations should show some trace of having organized around it — is drawn
directly from Andrew Rowe's progression-fantasy craft writing
([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]), reinforced by the broader craft-failure
pattern research ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]], pattern
P13). Both are practitioner-level sources rather than academic worldbuilding
scholarship; `source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly, and the specific
variant taxonomy (institutional/economic/military/uneven adaptation) here is
this drafting pass's synthesis.

records.title: Alchemy and pill refinement
records.summary: Pill refinement is cultivation fiction's characteristic crafting subtype — a non-combat advancement path with its own risk, skill, and economy — and it inherits the crafting-and-economy-loops record's consistency requirements while adding cultivation-specific stakes around dosage and side effects.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Alchemy in cultivation fiction typically refers to pill refinement (often
called dan refining, following common transliterations) — a specialized
crafting practice that converts rare materials into pills or elixirs
granting temporary boosts, accelerated cultivation, healing, or even direct
progress toward a breakthrough. It functions as cultivation's characteristic
crafting subtype, sharing the general crafting-and-economy-loops record's
concerns about material scarcity and market consistency, while adding
cultivation-specific stakes: a poorly refined pill can carry side effects,
a wrong dosage can harm rather than help, and pill quality is often tied
directly to the alchemist's own cultivation level or skill in a way that
makes alchemists a distinct, valuable, and vulnerable role within a
cultivation setting's social structure.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Pill refinement offers cultivation fiction a legitimate non-combat
advancement and support path, giving characters who aren't primarily
fighters a way to remain narratively central — a skilled alchemist can be
as valuable to a group's survival as its strongest combatant, without
ever entering combat directly. The risk and skill embedded in refinement
(a botched pill isn't just wasted materials, it can be actively harmful)
also creates natural tension around trust: taking a pill from an unknown
or unproven alchemist is itself a small but real risk a story can
dramatize.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Skill-based refinement**, where success depends on the alchemist's own
  developed expertise, independent of raw cultivation power — supporting a
  distinct non-combat specialization.
- **Cultivation-linked refinement**, where pill quality is tied directly
  to the alchemist's own cultivation realm, conflating the crafting skill
  with the general power system rather than keeping it separate.
- **Recipe-based refinement**, where specific, discoverable or
  inheritable recipes determine what's possible, making recipe scarcity
  and acquisition a source of plot material (echoing the crafting-and-
  economy-loops record's scarcity concerns).
- **Risk-graded refinement**, where higher-tier or more powerful pills
  carry proportionally greater risk of failure or side effect, creating a
  legible risk/reward curve for both the alchemist attempting the
  refinement and the cultivator consuming the result.
- **Advancement-shortcut pills**, a specific and narratively loaded variant
  that grants direct cultivation progress rather than a temporary boost —
  interacts directly with the advancement-rate pattern's caution against
  skipping to the end, since overreliance on shortcut pills can undercut a
  story's earned-progression stakes if left unexamined.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A pill's quality and effect shown as directly traceable to a specific
  alchemist's skill or materials, with variation in outcome depending on
  who made it.
- A character weighing the risk of taking an unproven pill against the
  benefit it offers, dramatizing the trust and risk this record describes.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: pills functioning as consequence-free,
  reliable power-ups regardless of who made them or under what
  conditions, with no risk or quality variation ever shown to matter.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Pill refinement interacts directly with the crafting-and-economy-loops
record's scarcity and market-consistency concerns, since rare materials
and recipes create the same kind of tracked-value stakes as any other
crafted good. It interacts with the advancement-rate pattern specifically
through shortcut pills, which — if used too freely — can flatten the
widening-interval pacing convention this library's cultivation records
describe as characteristic of the subgenre. Failure in refinement (a
botched pill, a wasted rare material, an accidental poisoning) is worth
deciding deliberately as a real, dramatizable cost rather than an
abstraction.

Pill quality is often only partly visible, and that partial visibility is
where alchemy generates plot. A buyer may be able to judge grade by color,
scent, or a formal appraisal, or may be entirely dependent on the seller's
word — which makes counterfeiting, adulteration, and reputation into
structural features rather than incidental ones. Whether a character can
perceive what a pill is doing to them matters too: a boost whose cost is
hidden until later supports a very different story than one whose cost is
stated on the label. For the reader, the question is whether they are told
the pill's true grade before the character learns it. Telling them early
buys dread; withholding buys surprise. A record of the choice is worth
keeping, since a story that switches between the two arbitrarily teaches
readers they cannot trust either mode.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Consequence-free pill use**, where pills function as reliable,
  risk-free power-ups regardless of source or quality, removing the trust
  and risk stakes the mechanic can otherwise provide.
- **Shortcut pills overused**, undermining the earned-progression stakes a
  cultivation story's advancement rate is otherwise built around.
- **An alchemist whose skill or role never actually matters to the plot**,
  present as a convenience (someone who produces useful items) without
  becoming a genuinely valued, vulnerable, or narratively significant
  character.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does pill quality and risk vary meaningfully based on who made it and
  under what conditions, or are pills uniformly reliable regardless of
  source?
- If shortcut pills exist, does their use interact with the story's
  broader advancement pacing, or do they let a character skip earned
  progression without consequence?
- Is there a scene where taking a pill from an unproven or unknown
  alchemist carries real, dramatized risk?
- Does an alchemist character's skill matter to the plot in a way
  comparable to a combat specialist's?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a pill consumed in the story, trace its source and check whether
   quality or risk is tied to that source in a way the scene reflects.
2. If shortcut pills are used, check their frequency against the story's
   broader advancement pacing and consider whether their use should carry
   a cost that preserves earned-progression stakes.
3. Give an alchemist character a scene where their specific skill
   (not just their product) is the direct solution to a problem.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A lighter cultivation-adjacent story using "pills" as a simple, reliable
  power-up mechanic with no intent to develop alchemy as its own subsystem
  may reasonably keep the mechanic simple.
- Very brief pill references (a single item used once) don't need the
  full risk-and-trust treatment this pattern describes.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether pill quality and risk vary meaningfully based on source and
conditions, in a way the narrative reflects, requires interpreting the
manuscript's worldbuilding and plot — a judgment no structured data
substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Consequence-free pills:* A character keeps a pouch of unlabeled pills
from various sources and consumes them freely whenever convenient, with
no scene ever showing a bad batch, a wrong dosage, or any variation in
quality or effect.

*Risk-engaged pills:* The same character instead hesitates before taking a
pill from a stranger, recalling a story about a cultivator who lost years
of progress to a poorly refined batch — and when they eventually do trust
a specific alchemist's work, that trust is shown to be earned through
established, demonstrated skill.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The pill-refinement subsystem and its characteristic risk/skill/economy
framing draw on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of
cultivation genre conventions ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]),
which marks its subgenre material as partly inferential; no dedicated
craft-literature source specifically addressing alchemy-as-crafting-
subsystem was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set
to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Body cultivation and soul cultivation
records.summary: Cultivation traditions frequently distinguish physical refinement from spiritual or mental refinement as separate, sometimes competing paths — treating them as interchangeable collapses a distinction that usually carries real narrative and philosophical weight.

citations.label: Introducing Daoism
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Many cultivation traditions, both historical and in modern genre fiction,
distinguish body cultivation (physical refinement — strengthening the
flesh, bones, and physical vessel to withstand and channel greater power)
from soul or spirit cultivation (refining consciousness, willpower, or the
non-physical self toward clarity, insight, or transcendence). The two are
often presented as complementary but distinct paths, sometimes pursued in
balance and sometimes specialized into, with a body-only cultivator and a
soul-only cultivator facing different strengths, vulnerabilities, and
philosophical implications about what they're actually becoming.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The distinction gives a cultivation system two genuinely different axes of
growth rather than one undifferentiated "power level," supporting the
multi-axis progression principle this library treats as generally healthier
than single-track advancement. It also opens specific narrative material:
a character who has neglected soul cultivation for raw physical power
raises different stakes (impulsiveness, spiritual instability, vulnerability
to certain attacks) than one who's inverted the imbalance (physically
fragile despite great insight or willpower) — imbalance between the two
paths can itself become a plot-relevant vulnerability or a source of
character tension.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Balanced dual cultivation**, where a character deliberately develops
  both paths in tandem, often framed as the wiser or more sustainable
  approach within the fiction's own internal philosophy.
- **Body-specialized cultivation**, prioritizing physical refinement,
  typically implying greater raw physical durability and combat capability
  at the cost of spiritual vulnerability or a ceiling that pure body
  cultivation can't exceed alone.
- **Soul-specialized cultivation**, prioritizing spiritual or mental
  refinement, typically implying stronger magical or willpower-based
  capability at the cost of physical fragility.
- **Sequential cultivation**, where a tradition prescribes developing one
  path to a certain point before the other becomes viable, creating a
  structured order a character can follow correctly or attempt to
  circumvent.
- **Body-soul conflict**, a narrative and sometimes mechanical tension
  where advancing one path too far ahead of the other creates instability
  or risk — a productive source of the bottleneck and deviation concepts
  covered in this library's other cultivation records.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character's specialization in one cultivation path shown to create a
  specific, consequential vulnerability the other path would have covered.
- A moment where balancing body and soul cultivation (or the failure to)
  directly affects a scene's outcome — a physically powerful character
  undone by a spiritual attack, or vice versa.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a cultivation system that names both
  body and soul cultivation but treats advancement in either identically,
  with no distinct capability, vulnerability, or philosophical
  implication attached to the choice.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **A distinction without a difference**, naming both paths but making
  them functionally interchangeable in the story's actual events.
- **Unbalanced specialization with no consequence**, where a character who
  has clearly neglected one path suffers no vulnerability traceable to
  that neglect.
- **Sequential cultivation violated with no acknowledgment**, where a
  tradition's stated order (body before soul, or vice versa) is
  circumvented with no narrative engagement of the risk that should imply.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and visibility
sections.content:
The two paths differ in how legible they are, which is much of their story
value. Body cultivation is usually visible: it is written on the frame,
the scars, the way a person moves through a doorway, and it can be
estimated by a stranger across a room. Soul cultivation is typically
unreadable to ordinary perception and legible only to specialists, to
spiritual senses the setting has defined, or to nobody at all — which is
why soul cultivators so often read as either serene or unsettling, and why
underestimation plots attach to them so naturally.

The asymmetry is worth using deliberately rather than inheriting. A world
where physical refinement is visible and spiritual refinement is not will
rank people by the thing it can see, and will be wrong about them in
consistent, exploitable ways. Failure states are similarly asymmetric:
body-cultivation setbacks tend to be injuries a reader can picture, while
soul-cultivation setbacks are internal — deviation, fracture, a change in
who the character is — and need the narration to make them perceptible, or
they will register as a stated consequence rather than a felt one.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this character's specialization in body or soul cultivation create
  a specific, consequential vulnerability the other path would have
  addressed?
- Is there a scene where the distinction between body and soul cultivation
  actually matters to the outcome, not just to the character's stated
  build?
- If a cultivation tradition prescribes a sequential order, and a
  character circumvents it, does the story engage the risk that implies?
- Does balancing both paths (where a character does so deliberately) carry
  a dramatized cost — slower overall progress, for instance — that
  specialization avoids?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a specialized cultivator, identify a specific vulnerability their
   neglected path would have addressed, and find or add a scene where it
   matters.
2. For a balanced cultivator, make sure the cost of balance (usually
   slower overall progress relative to a specialist) is shown somewhere in
   the story.
3. If a sequential cultivation order is established, and a character
   breaks it, dramatize the resulting risk or instability directly.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A lighter cultivation-adjacent system using the vocabulary loosely, with
  no intent to mechanically or narratively distinguish body and soul
  paths, may reasonably treat them as flavor rather than a functional
  design choice.
- A story focused entirely on one path (a setting where soul cultivation
  doesn't exist or isn't relevant) doesn't need the dual-path treatment
  this pattern describes.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether body and soul cultivation function as genuinely distinct paths
with different implications, or as an undifferentiated label, requires
reading and interpreting the manuscript's worldbuilding and plot — a
judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Distinction without difference:* A cultivator described as having
"neglected their soul cultivation for years" faces no vulnerability, penalty,
or narrative consequence traceable to that neglect anywhere in the story.

*Meaningful distinction:* The same neglect instead leaves the cultivator
vulnerable to a specific spiritual-domain attack that a soul-cultivated
opponent recognizes and exploits, forcing the protagonist to reckon with
the imbalance directly — the distinction does real narrative work.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Historical grounding for body/soul or physical/spiritual cultivation
distinctions in Daoist internal alchemy draws on an academic introduction
to Daoism ([[src.book.kohn-introducing-daoism]]); the modern genre-
convention framing draws on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general
survey ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its
subgenre material as partly inferential. `source_confidence` is `mixed`
accordingly, and this record is careful to note that specific mechanical
implementations (sequential order, instability from imbalance) are genre
convention rather than historical Daoist doctrine.

records.title: Cultivation realms and breakthroughs
records.summary: Named cultivation realms and their breakthroughs are dramatized narrative events, not simply levels with more evocative names — treating them as interchangeable with a generic tier system tends to lose what draws readers to the subgenre.
modifiers: cultivation: Western cultivation fiction conventionally compresses pacing relative to the Chinese source tradition and establishes meaningful stakes within the first few pages; treat this as a genre convention to weigh, not a rule.

citations.label: Introducing Daoism
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Xianxia

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Cultivation fiction (xianxia, xuanhuan, and their Western-authored
progression-fantasy descendants) structures power growth as movement through
named realms — commonly something like Foundation, Core Formation, Nascent
Soul, and onward, though specific naming schemes vary widely by author and
tradition — punctuated by breakthroughs: dramatized, often dangerous events
where a cultivator crosses from one realm into the next. This differs from a
generic numeric level system in two structurally important ways: realms are
usually qualitative and discontinuous (there is a categorical difference
between realms, not just a bigger number), and breakthroughs are narrated
as events with their own risk, cost, and often philosophical content, not as
an automatic threshold crossing.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Readers of this subgenre are reported to care more about *why* a
breakthrough happens and what it costs than about the raw number of realms
crossed — the reverse emphasis from classic LitRPG's number-forward appeal.
A breakthrough that arrives as narrated event, with tension, risk, and
often a moment of insight or choice, delivers on the promise that power in
this genre is inseparable from self-cultivation; a breakthrough that arrives
as an automatic threshold crossing (hit enough qi, advance a realm, no
further drama) reads as a generic level-up wearing cultivation vocabulary.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Insight-driven breakthroughs**, where advancing requires a genuine
  understanding, realization, or resolved internal conflict, not just
  accumulated resource.
- **Resource-threshold breakthroughs**, where sufficient accumulated qi or
  practice enables an attempt, but the attempt itself remains a risky,
  dramatized event rather than automatic.
- **Tribulation breakthroughs**, where crossing a realm boundary invites an
  external trial (a heavenly tribulation, a hostile response from the world
  itself) that must be survived, common in the genre's higher realms.
  Historical note: this specific mechanic (external, cosmically imposed
  trials at advancement) is a genre convention rather than a documented
  element of historical Daoist practice, and should not be presented as
  drawn from real internal-alchemy tradition.
- **Bottleneck breakthroughs**, where a cultivator plateaus at the edge of a
  realm for an extended period, unable to advance until a specific
  obstacle (internal or external) is resolved — a common source of
  extended tension in longer works.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A breakthrough scene with dramatized risk (failure could cause harm,
  regression, or death) rather than a guaranteed, safe threshold crossing.
- A named realm change accompanied by a qualitative shift in the character's
  capabilities, worldview, or social standing, not just a bigger number.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: realm changes announced with the same
  mechanical flatness as a numeric level-up, with no accompanying dramatized
  event or qualitative change.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and visibility
sections.content:
Failure at a breakthrough attempt is a genre-conventional and often
significant story beat: consequences can range from a wasted attempt
(try again later) to serious injury, power loss, or death, depending on the
realm and the author's established stakes. Whether a bottleneck or failed
breakthrough is visible to other characters (a cultivator's aura or
presence changing detectably) versus private is a design choice with real
social consequences — sect politics, marriage prospects, and standing in
many cultivation settings are explicitly tied to visible cultivation stage.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Common tensions worth deciding deliberately: can a cultivator's realm be
suppressed or disguised (a common plot device, and one with major social
implications if visible cultivation stage determines standing)? Can external
substances (pills, treasures) safely substitute for a "natural" breakthrough,
and if so, what's the tradeoff (often instability, later bottlenecks, or
"foundation" damage in genre convention)? Does the pacing of later realms
slow relative to earlier ones (a widely observed genre convention, related
to the advancement-rate pattern's widening-interval shape), and does the
story's stakes and prose weight scale to match, or does a later realm read
as narratively cheaper despite taking longer to reach?

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Breakthroughs as reskinned level-ups**, mechanically identical to a
  generic numeric system with cultivation vocabulary layered on top, losing
  the reason-over-numbers appeal the subgenre's readers are reported to
  want.
- **Unexplained realm significance**, naming realms without establishing
  what qualitatively changes between them, leaving readers unable to gauge
  what a breakthrough actually means.
- **Ignoring visible-cultivation social stakes**, treating realm as a purely
  personal-power metric with no bearing on the setting's social or political
  structures, in a subgenre where that connection is conventionally central.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What changes qualitatively, not just quantitatively, when a character
  crosses into a new realm?
- Is a breakthrough attempt ever genuinely risky, or does the character
  always succeed once resources are sufficient?
- Is a character's cultivation stage visible to others in this world, and
  does that visibility carry social or political weight?
- Does the pacing of later realms in this manuscript reflect the genre
  convention of slowing down, and if so, does the prose's weight and stakes
  scale to match the longer narrative investment?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For each named realm in the system, write one sentence describing what
   qualitatively (not just numerically) changes about a character who
   crosses into it.
2. Add genuine risk or cost to the next breakthrough scene if the current
   draft treats it as automatic once resources are sufficient.
3. Decide explicitly whether cultivation stage is visible to others in this
   world, and test one scene where that visibility (or its absence) creates
   a social consequence.
4. Check the pacing of the manuscript's later realms against its earlier
   ones; if later realms take much longer to reach, confirm the prose gives
   them proportionally more narrative weight.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Lighter, faster-paced cultivation-adjacent stories (some Western
  cultivation fiction explicitly) may compress breakthroughs deliberately
  for pace, trading dramatized risk for momentum — a legitimate genre
  variant, not a failure of this pattern.
- A story using cultivation vocabulary purely decoratively, with no intent
  to engage the subgenre's conventions around visible stage and social
  consequence, may reasonably simplify realms into a generic tier system.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a breakthrough is dramatized with genuine risk, and whether realm
changes carry qualitative weight, requires reading and interpreting the
prose; no structured data substitutes for this judgment. Where a project
explicitly tracks a realm or tier value linked to scenes, a coach could
report advancement intervals deterministically (see the related
advancement-rate pattern), but the qualitative and social dimensions this
record addresses remain model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Reskinned level-up:* "Kest's cultivation base reached sufficient density,
and she advanced to Core Formation" — mechanically identical to a numeric
level-up with a different label, no risk, no qualitative change described.

*Dramatized breakthrough:* Kest attempts the same advancement during a
three-day seclusion, nearly loses control of her qi in a moment the text
treats as genuinely dangerous, and emerges changed not only in power but in
a new, unsettling clarity about a compromise she made years ago to survive —
the breakthrough is an event, not a threshold.
