particular threat or tactic — an ability that punishes a specific attack
type, a technique that specifically negates a specific status effect.
Together these systems add tactical texture to combat beyond raw damage
exchange, but each raises its own design question about fairness: how does
a character escape or resist an effect once it's applied?

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Status effects and crowd control raise the tactical stakes of a fight
beyond simple damage races, since a character disabled by a status effect
faces a fundamentally different problem than one simply losing a damage
exchange — and readers track that difference. Counters create satisfying
"rock-paper-scissors" tactical moments when a character specifically
prepares for or exploits a known threat, but only if the counter's
existence and logic are established before the moment it resolves a
conflict, per the same fair-play principle covered in the heist and
prophecy trope records.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Damage-over-time effects** (poison, burning, bleeding), extending a
  fight's stakes across time rather than a single exchange.
- **Action-denial effects** (stun, paralysis, sleep), the most powerful and
  most fairness-sensitive category, since they can remove a character's
  agency entirely for their duration.
- **Debuffs and buffs**, altering a character's effective stats without
  fully denying action, a less extreme but still tactically significant
  category.
- **Area crowd control**, affecting multiple opponents simultaneously,
  raising the action-economy stakes of a fight considerably when it lands.
- **Escapable versus inescapable effects**, where some conditions can be
  resisted, cleansed, or broken through specific counterplay, and others
  simply run their course — a major design fork affecting how fair a status
  effect feels to be hit by.
- **Established counters**, techniques or items specifically built to
  answer a known threat, most satisfying when their existence is set up
  before they're used to resolve a conflict.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character disabled by a status effect facing a genuinely different
  tactical problem than a simple damage exchange would create — allies
  covering for them, a race against the effect's duration.
- A counter's existence established before the scene where it resolves a
  conflict, satisfying the fair-play principle.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an action-denial effect applied to a
  major character with no established way to resist or escape it, followed
  by an escape that isn't explained by any previously established
  mechanism.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Status effects interact directly with action economy, since a stunned or
disabled character functionally loses their turn or action for the
effect's duration — a powerful crowd-control effect landing on a key
character can single-handedly shift a fight's balance. They also interact
with the resource-lifecycle-design pattern, since resisting or cleansing an
effect often costs a resource of its own, creating a secondary economy
within the fight. Counters interact with the setup/payoff pattern most
directly, since an unearned counter (introduced only at the moment it's
needed) breaks the same fair-play contract that pattern addresses in plot
structure generally.

Whether a status effect is *visible* determines whether it can be countered,
and therefore whether it produces tactics or just outcomes. If a poison
announces itself — a visible mark, a system notification, a smell — then
allies can respond, enemies can exploit it, and the effect becomes a problem
characters solve. If it is hidden, it becomes a discovery, which is
powerful once and frustrating if repeated. The same holds for durations: a
character who knows a stun lasts six seconds fights differently from one who
only knows they cannot move. For readers, unannounced effects raise the risk
of an outcome reading as arbitrary — a fight lost to something they never
saw — so a story that hides effects from its characters often still shows
them to the reader, or plants the evidence early enough to be fair in
hindsight.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Inescapable action-denial with no established counterplay**, removing
  a character's agency for a stretch of the story with no way established
  in advance for them or an ally to resist it.
- **An unearned counter**, introduced at the exact moment it's needed to
  resolve a conflict with no prior setup.
- **Status effects applied inconsistently**, where an established
  condition's effects (a poison's damage rate, a stun's duration) vary
  without explanation across different scenes.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If a major character is hit by an action-denial effect, is there an
  established way (an ally, an item, a resistance) for them to escape or
  mitigate it?
- Is a counter's existence established before the scene where it resolves a
  conflict?
- Are a status effect's stated parameters (duration, potency) honored
  consistently across the scenes where it appears?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For a major character affected by crowd control or a debilitating
   status, check whether an established resistance or counterplay option
   exists; add one earlier in the manuscript if not.
2. Trace a counter's use backward to confirm it was set up before the
   moment it resolves a conflict.
3. Audit a recurring status effect's stated parameters against its actual
   depicted behavior for consistency.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story deliberately depicting an unfair, escape-proof threat as its
  actual subject (a dark/horror LitRPG's antagonistic system) may use
  inescapable effects intentionally, provided the story engages the
  resulting powerlessness directly rather than glossing over it.
- Very lightweight combat with no tracked status mechanics doesn't need
  this level of systemic detail.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks status effects and their parameters
linked to scenes, whether they're applied consistently is close to
deterministic. Whether a counter is fairly set up, and whether an
action-denial effect's resolution feels earned, requires interpreting the
prose and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unearned escape:* A major character is paralyzed by a venom established as
having no known cure, and two scenes later simply recovers with no
explanation.

*Earned counterplay:* The same paralysis instead is escaped because an
ally, established earlier as a healer with relevant training, applies a
specific remedy the story previously showed them preparing — the escape
traces to setup, not convenience.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The status-effect and crowd-control framing draws on established game-
design literature covering combat systems and tactical depth
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) and on uncertainty and
counterplay as engagement mechanisms
([[src.book.costikyan-uncertainty-in-games]]); both established academic/
practitioner texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's
application to prose fiction's fairness conventions (rather than
interactive game balance) is this drafting pass's adaptation rather than a
direct claim from either source.

records.title: The system as an agent
records.summary: Whether the System has intentions — a question most stories answer by accident, and one that decides whether it is a physics, a bureaucracy, or a character with a plan.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Fundamentals of Game Design
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Many stories in this genre feature a System that assigns levels, issues
quests, and announces outcomes. A question sits under all of it and is often
never asked: does the System *want* anything?

The possible answers are genuinely different worlds. A System can be a
physics — impersonal rules, no more intentional than gravity. It can be a
bureaucracy — built by someone, administered by something, following
procedures that may be obsolete or badly designed. Or it can be an agent with
purposes of its own, which makes it a character, and usually the most
powerful one in the book.

This record is distinct from system-as-narrator intrusion, which is about the
voice and frequency of system text on the page. This is about what, if
anything, is behind it.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The answer determines what kind of conflict is available. Against a physics,
the story is exploration and optimization; nobody can be argued with. Against
a bureaucracy, the story can include appeals, loopholes, obsolete rules, and
the discovery that someone wrote this badly. Against an agent, the story can
have an antagonist that is also the source of the protagonist's power, which
is an unusually rich position.

Readers also tend to accumulate this question whether or not the book intends
it. A System that issues suspiciously well-timed quests reads as intentional
even if the author meant it as scenery, and a story that never addresses the
implication is leaving a live question unanswered on the page.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The System as physics** — impersonal, consistent, uninterested. Cleanest,
  and forecloses the argument plots.
- **The abandoned mechanism** — built long ago, still running, its purpose
  lost. Supplies mystery without requiring a present antagonist.
- **The bureaucracy** — administrators, tiers of authority, procedures, and
  the possibility of appeal or exploitation of process.
- **The tutor** — a System that appears to be helping, whose curriculum
  implies a goal.
- **The adversary** — deliberate, opposed, and usually revealed rather than
  announced.
- **The multiple or fractured system** — competing systems, or one in
  disagreement with itself, which turns the question into a plot.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- System text with a register — dry, sardonic, formal — that implies someone
  chose the wording.
- A quest offered at a moment too convenient to be coincidence, and a
  character noticing.
- Rules that behave differently for different people, with no stated cause.
- Conversely: a System that speaks in personality for eighty chapters and is
  never once asked what it is.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Implied intent, never addressed.** A System that plainly behaves as though
  it wants something, in a book that never lets a character notice.
- **The System as whatever the plot needs.** Impersonal when the story wants
  physics, purposeful when it wants a twist, with no rule governing which.
- **Personality without accountability.** A voice with jokes and opinions
  that is never asked a question it might have to answer.
- **The unanswerable adversary.** A System revealed as hostile and so far
  above the characters that opposing it is not a plot but a wait.
- **Answering too early.** Settling the question in chapter three, spending
  the most durable open question the convention offers.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The useful design question is whether the System can be *wrong*. A physics
cannot; a bureaucracy can be out of date, mis-specified, or gameable; an
agent can be deceived or can lie. Deciding this settles a great deal — a
System that can be wrong makes its pronouncements evidence rather than fact,
which changes how a reader reads every notification in the book.

Visibility here is about intent rather than data: can anyone tell whether the
System means anything? A world where that is an open question develops
theology, scholarship, and factions — people who believe the System is a god,
people who think it is machinery, people who make a living claiming to know.
That disagreement is usually more interesting than the answer, and it is
available even in stories that never resolve it.

Consequentially, a System with intent implies a relationship with everyone,
not just the protagonist. If it selects, rewards, or targets, then societies
organize around its preferences, and the question of what it wants becomes
the central political question of the setting. Most stories grant the System
apparent intent and keep the politics local.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
If the System is a bureaucracy, it can be lawyered: satisfying a quest's
letter, exploiting a category error, registering something as what it is not.
If it is an agent, it can be deceived or bargained with, and someone will
try. The sharpest edge case is a System that rewards behavior it did not
intend to reward, which is both realistic and a strong engine for plot. This
record interacts with onboarding — who taught the world what the System is —
and with the visible-versus-hidden comparison, since a System's opacity about
its own nature is a specific kind of hiddenness.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does the System want anything, and does the story know?
- Can it be wrong? Has the reader ever seen it be wrong?
- Who in this world has a theory about what it is, and are any of them right?
- If the System has a voice, who chose that voice?
- Would the story change if the System turned out to be nothing at all?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence stating what the System is. If it cannot be written,
   that is the finding.
2. Have a character ask the question aloud and get no answer, and see what
   the silence does.
3. Make the System wrong once, in a way that costs something, and watch how
   it changes the weight of its later statements.
4. Write two characters who disagree about its nature and let neither win.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories with no System at all, where power is magical or physical and this
  record does not apply.
- Light or comedic work where the System is a joke delivery mechanism and
  interrogating it would flatten the register.
- Stories where the System's nature is the central mystery and answering it
  early would spend the book's main question.
- Established series where the answer is already fixed by published volumes.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe whether system text carries evaluative or personal
language, whether the same phrasing recurs, and whether any character
addresses the System directly. Those are weak signals for a strong question.

Whether a System reads as intentional is a semantic judgment, and readers
will differ. A story that leaves the question open is not failing — deliberate
ambiguity is one of the better uses of the convention. The coach should raise
the question rather than diagnose an absence, and should be especially slow
to treat an unanswered question as a fault.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined intent:* "Congratulations! You have earned a title you will
almost certainly regret." Nobody in eighty chapters asks who is talking.

*Examined:* "Congratulations!" the interface said, and Wen sat looking at it
for a while, because the last three quests had all pointed north, and she had
begun keeping a list.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This library's genre research ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]])
supplies the observation that a System with apparent personality is a genre
staple and that its nature is frequently left unexamined. Ernest Adams
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies only the general
design principle that a rule system's authority depends on its consistency.
The taxonomy, the can-it-be-wrong question, and the theological and political
consequences are this drafting pass's synthesis
([[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]]).

`source_confidence` is `limited`. This is a convention specific enough to
this subgenre that no craft or scholarly source available to this pass
addresses it, and the record is structured reasoning about a pattern rather
than sourced analysis. The nearest real literature is probably criticism on
unreliable and non-human narrators, which a later pass could bring in; the
genre's own critical writing is thin and mostly practitioner commentary.

records.title: Travel, territory, and fast movement
records.summary: How far things are and how quickly they can be crossed — a quiet mechanic that sets the cost of every plan, and that teleportation deletes in one decision.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Distance is a constraint, and the rules that govern crossing it — road speed,
mounts, portals, teleport skills, waypoint networks — determine what a
character can attempt in a week. This record treats travel as a system:
what it costs, who controls it, and what a setting looks like once it becomes
cheap.

The decision that matters most is whether fast travel exists. It is usually
granted for convenience, to stop the story spending chapters on roads, and it
is one of the largest worldbuilding decisions a setting can make almost by
accident.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Travel time is where a plan acquires a price. If reaching the capital takes
three weeks, then everything happening in the capital happens without the
protagonist, allies elsewhere are genuinely out of reach, and a decision to
go is a decision not to be somewhere else. Remove the time and you remove the
tradeoff.

Distance also produces one of the most reliable sources of tension available:
being far from something that matters. A message that takes ten days is a
plot; an instant one is a phone call.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Ordinary travel** — roads, mounts, ships, weather. Slow, textured, and
  the source of most incidental encounter structures.
- **Waypoint networks** — fixed points connected instantly, which preserves
  distance between points while collapsing it along the network. The most
  design-friendly form, because it creates a map of privileged places.
- **Personal teleportation** — a character-level ability, which is the
  version most likely to break plotting, since it removes distance for one
  person only.
- **Gated fast travel** — instant movement at a cost: money, mana, a
  consumable, a cooldown, a licence.
- **One-way or unreliable movement** — travel that cannot be reversed or
  cannot be trusted, which makes each use a commitment.
- **Territory control** — movement restricted by who holds the ground, which
  converts geography into politics.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A plan changed because of how long the road takes.
- News arriving late, and a character acting on information that is no longer
  true.
- A waypoint town that exists because the waypoint does.
- Conversely: distances that stretch and compress to fit the chapter, which
  teaches the reader not to hold the map in mind.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Elastic distance.** Journeys taking however long the plot needs, the
  single most common consistency failure in secondary worlds.
- **Teleportation without consequence.** Instant movement granted to the
  protagonist and to no institution, army, merchant, or courier in the
  setting.
- **Travel as dead time.** Weeks of road narrated because they happened,
  rather than because anything does.
- **The unused map.** Elaborate geography that never constrains a decision.
- **Logistics ignored.** Armies, caravans, and sieges that move as though
  supply were not the hardest part of any of them.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Travel is one of the few mechanics whose failure states are naturally
interesting: getting lost, arriving late, being cut off, having a route
closed behind you. A system with no way to fail at travel has converted its
geography into a menu.

Visibility matters mostly for fast travel. If waypoints are public, they are
infrastructure — taxed, guarded, queued, and closed in emergencies. If a
character's ability to move instantly is private, it is a weapon, and their
knowing they can leave any room changes how they behave in every room.

The consequences are the largest of any mechanic in this record set, because
cheap movement restructures everything: trade goes long-distance, perishables
become viable, empires become governable at a distance, armies concentrate
faster than they can be met, and local scarcity stops meaning anything.
Settings routinely grant teleportation and keep a medieval economy, which is
the clearest case in the genre of a system's implications going unexamined.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Cheap movement is an arbitrage engine: buy where a thing is common, sell
where it is rare, and any world with both teleportation and regional prices
has someone doing that at scale. Other standard edges are using fast travel
to escape any losing fight, scouting with impunity, and delivering something
dangerous instantly. Travel interacts directly with the currency and market
record — distance is what makes prices differ in the first place — and with
institutions, since whoever controls the network controls the economy that
runs on it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- How long does the most-used journey in this story take, and has that been
  consistent?
- What can the protagonist reach in a day, and what is out of reach?
- Who else has access to fast travel, and what have they built with it?
- What does it cost to move something heavy, and does anyone in the story
  care?
- If teleportation were removed, which plots would stop working — and are
  those plots better or worse for it?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write down the three most common journeys and their durations, then check
   the draft against the list. Elastic distance shows up immediately.
2. Take one instant journey and make it take a week. Note what the delay
   generates.
3. Write the merchant who uses the waypoint network professionally, and let
   the setting acquire an economy.
4. Close a route behind the characters and see what the map becomes when it
   is not fully connected.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Single-location stories — a city, a school, a tower — where travel is not
  a live mechanic.
- Deliberate convenience, where a story's promise is momentum and readers
  arrive for the scenes rather than the roads.
- Dungeon-centred fiction, where the interesting geography is bounded and
  vertical; the dungeon record governs that case.
- Comedic and picaresque work where impossible logistics are part of the
  register.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Stated journey durations are extractable and comparable, which makes elastic
distance one of the more genuinely detectable problems in this library: the
same route taking three days in one chapter and three weeks in another is a
contradiction a coach can surface without interpretation, subject to the
obvious caveats about differing conditions, routes, and unreliable narrators.

What cannot be computed is whether a journey should have been dramatized or
skipped, or whether cheap travel has cost the story more than it saved. Those
are judgments about the book's intent. The coach's useful contribution is the
consistency check and the question about who else uses the network.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Elastic:* the ride to Kell took most of a month in chapter nine. In chapter
thirty-one they need to be there by the festival, and it takes four days.

*Costed:* the waypoint to Kell cost eleven silver, which was most of what
they had, and it went one way, and they spent the ride to the platform
arguing about whether they would be able to afford to come back.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ernest Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the
design vocabulary for world traversal, fast-travel systems, and their effect
on pacing; Jesse Schell ([[src.book.schell-art-of-game-design]]) supplies the
treatment of space and how players read it. This library's genre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation that
waypoint and teleport systems are a recurring subgenre convention.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense: the game-design
material addresses player convenience rather than narrative consequence, so
the argument that travel time is where a plan acquires a price is this
drafting pass's synthesis. The economic and political consequences follow
this library's own systemic-consequences reasoning; no source cited here
makes claims about how cheap movement restructures a fictional economy.

records.title: Appraisal, identification, and system information
records.summary: Abilities that tell a character what something is — the most quietly powerful mechanic in the genre, because information decides what a scene can be about.

citations.label: Uncertainty in Games
Fundamentals of Game Design
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Appraisal is any ability that converts a thing into information: a skill that
reads an enemy's level, an identify spell that names an item's properties, an
interface that labels what the character is looking at. It is close to
universal in the genre and is very rarely designed rather than assumed.

The reason it deserves a record is that it decides what scenes are possible.
Every mystery, negotiation, ambush, and bad bargain depends on somebody not
knowing something. An unrestricted appraisal ability removes that condition
across the whole book, usually without the author noticing at the moment they
grant it.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Uncertainty is what makes a decision a decision. When a character can see an
opponent's exact statistics before engaging, the fight becomes arithmetic;
when they cannot, it becomes judgment. Neither is wrong — the first supports
tactical, planning-heavy stories and the second supports tense ones — but
they are different books, and the appraisal rules pick which.

Appraisal also determines whether the world can lie. In a setting where
identification is reliable and cheap, deception between characters largely
stops working, and with it a whole family of plots. Deciding what appraisal
*cannot* see is therefore one of the highest-leverage decisions in a system.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Level-reading** — seeing an opponent's tier or power. Fast, and the most
  likely to flatten encounters into comparison.
- **Item identification** — revealing properties of objects, often gated by
  cost, skill, or a specialist.
- **Graded appraisal** — information proportional to the appraiser's skill
  relative to the target, so strong things read as unknown. The most useful
  variant, because it preserves uncertainty exactly where the stakes are
  highest.
- **Professional appraisal** — no personal ability; identification is a
  service someone sells, which makes it an economy and a social relationship.
- **Fallible appraisal** — results that can be wrong, spoofed, or resisted,
  which restores deception without removing the mechanic.
- **Contextual limits** — appraisal that requires proximity, time, line of
  sight, or consent.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character choosing not to appraise, because doing so is detectable.
- An appraisal returning "unknown," and the scene reorganizing around that.
- A merchant whose whole living is knowing what appraisal does not show.
- Conversely: every encounter opening with a stat readout, so the reader
  learns the outcome before the fight does.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unlimited appraisal.** Granted early, never bounded, quietly deleting
  mystery, negotiation, and ambush for the rest of the series.
- **Appraisal as exposition delivery.** The ability existing so the narration
  can state facts, which makes it a device rather than a mechanic.
- **Selective forgetting.** The protagonist not appraising when the plot needs
  them surprised, which readers notice faster than almost any other
  inconsistency.
- **Information without cost.** No time, mana, risk, or detectability, so the
  ability is never a decision.
- **Nobody else has it.** A world where reliable appraisal exists and its
  economics — insurance, authentication, fraud — are untouched.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The single most useful design decision is what appraisal returns when it
fails: nothing, partial data, a wrong answer, or a warning that the target
exceeds the appraiser. Each produces different scenes, and "unknown" against
a stronger target is the version that keeps danger legible while preserving
tension.

Visibility runs both ways here, which is unusual and underused. Can the
target tell they are being appraised? If so, appraisal becomes a social act —
rude, aggressive, or revealing of the appraiser's own capability — and
characters will conceal that they are doing it. If not, it is silent
surveillance, and the story should consider what a world of undetectable
mutual assessment feels like to live in.

Consequentially, reliable identification restructures commerce and law.
Contracts need no trust, fraud requires defeating the system rather than a
person, insurers price by appraisal, and someone sells authentication.
Settings usually grant the ability and leave the institutions untouched,
which is a large piece of available worldbuilding.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
The standard exploits are appraisal-spoofing items, suppressing one's own
readable statistics, using a low-level proxy to appraise safely, and mass
appraisal to price a market faster than its participants can. Any resistance
mechanic immediately creates a counter-industry. Appraisal interacts most
sharply with the visible-versus-hidden-systems comparison — appraisal is the
in-world mechanism by which a "hidden" system becomes partly visible — and
with information asymmetry in encounters, since a party with one appraiser
has a knowledge distribution problem of its own.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What can appraisal not see, and was that decided or defaulted?
- What does using it cost, and can the target tell?
- What is the last scene that depended on someone not knowing something? Is
  it still possible under these rules?
- Who sells this service, and to whom?
- If appraisal is fallible, has the reader ever seen it be wrong?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the rule for what appraisal returns against something stronger than
   the appraiser. That one sentence usually settles the mechanic.
2. Take a scene that turns on a surprise and check whether appraisal should
   have prevented it.
3. Make one appraisal detectable by its target and see what the scene
   becomes.
4. Write the appraiser who does this professionally, and what they know that
   the skill does not tell them.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Settings with no appraisal mechanic, where knowledge is ordinary
  observation and this record does not apply.
- Deliberately tactical fiction whose promise is exactly the planning that
  full information enables — a real contract, worth honoring knowingly.
- Stories where the system's omniscience is the subject rather than a tool,
  and its intrusiveness is the point.
- Early chapters where the protagonist's inability to appraise is the
  situation being established.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where appraisal results appear as structured text, a coach can count them,
chart their frequency, and check whether stated limits hold — for instance,
whether something previously described as unreadable is later read without
explanation. That consistency check is close to deterministic and is the most
valuable thing available here.

Whether appraisal has flattened a scene is interpretive. A stat readout
before a fight may be doing legitimate work in a tactical story. The coach
should report where appraisal appears and where stated rules appear to bend,
and ask about intent rather than declaring a mechanic overpowered.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unbounded:* "Appraisal: Vashka Deepwarden, Level 61, Weakness: fire." He had
never met her, and now the fight had been decided in one line.

*Bounded:* "Appraisal: — ." The blank was itself the information, and it was
the only thing the skill had ever refused him.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Greg Costikyan ([[src.book.costikyan-uncertainty-in-games]]) supplies the
central argument that uncertainty is the substance of engagement, which this
record applies to the removal of uncertainty by information abilities; Ernest
Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies design
vocabulary for information in game systems; this library's genre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation that
appraisal-type abilities are near-universal in the subgenre.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. Costikyan
writes about players facing live uncertainty rather than readers facing a
fixed outcome, so the application to fiction is this pass's synthesis. The
graded-appraisal recommendation, the two-way visibility observation, and the
commercial and legal consequences are reasoning from this library's own
systemic-consequences pattern rather than sourced claims.

records.title: Introducing the system to the reader
records.summary: A story with a power system has to teach it, and the teaching happens in the same pages the story is trying to start — which makes onboarding a pacing problem before it is an explanation problem.

citations.label: The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A story built on a power system has to teach that system to its reader: what
the rules are, what the numbers mean, what is at stake when a value changes.
Onboarding is how and when that teaching happens. It competes for space with
everything else the opening chapters must do, which is what makes it a
design problem rather than a matter of writing a clear explanation.

The genre has a characteristic solution — the tutorial sequence, in which a
character new to the system is taught it in-world — and a characteristic
failure, in which the story stops so the system can be described.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Game design has converged on a principle worth borrowing carefully: players
learn a system best while using it, and worst while being told about it
outside of play. Koster's account of fun as the sensation of learning
suggests why — the pleasure is in acquiring a pattern, and being handed the
pattern outright removes it.

Fiction has the same shape and one extra constraint. A reader can put the
book down. A tutorial that pauses the story spends the reader's earliest and
least-secured attention on material that has not yet been made to matter.
Where onboarding works, the reader learns the rules from consequences they
cared about, and the teaching is invisible.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The naive protagonist** — a character who does not know the system
  either, so explanation is motivated. Effective and overused; the risk is a
  companion who exists only to answer.
- **In-world instruction** — an academy, a mentor, an orientation: justified
  exposition, at the cost of chapters spent in a classroom.
- **Learning by consequence** — the character misuses the system, something
  goes wrong, and the rule is legible in the wreckage.
- **Progressive disclosure** — introducing one mechanic at a time as the
  story requires it, so the system is never explained wholesale.
- **Deferred explanation** — rules withheld and inferred, trading
  comprehension for mystery; workable only while the stakes stay legible.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A first chapter that establishes one rule and its cost, rather than the
  system's full taxonomy.
- An interface panel appearing at a moment when the reader already wants the
  information it contains.
- A character asking the question the reader is currently asking, rather than
  asking one purely so it can be answered.
- Conversely: several pages of nested system description before anything has
  happened; a companion whose dialogue is entirely explanatory.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The rules dump.** The system explained comprehensively before the reader
  has any reason to care about any part of it.
- **Teaching what is not yet needed.** Mechanics introduced chapters before
  they matter, so the reader must hold them without use.
- **The explaining companion.** A character whose function is exposition,
  who is recognizable as such and rarely survives it as a person.
- **Unmotivated ignorance.** A protagonist who does not know things they
  plainly would, so that someone can tell them.
- **Onboarding that never ends.** New rules arriving at the same rate in
  chapter eighty as in chapter three, so the reader never reaches
  competence.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Onboarding has a natural end, and deciding where it falls is a real design
choice: the point at which the reader can predict what the system will do.
Past that point, further explanation reads as padding, and the story should
be spending on consequences instead. A system that keeps adding rules
indefinitely never lets the reader feel competent, which forfeits the
mastery pleasure the genre is largely built on.

Visibility determines what onboarding even means. A system visible to
characters can be taught in-world, and the tutorial is a scene; a system
visible only to the reader must be taught by inference, and the "tutorial"
is a matter of narration. Where the system is hidden from both, onboarding
becomes the mystery plot itself.

Socially, a system old enough to be understood implies teachers, manuals,
apprenticeships, and disputed interpretations. A system that arrived
recently — an apocalypse premise — has none of these, and its onboarding
problem belongs to every character in the world, which such stories usually
underuse.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
The obvious edge case is a protagonist who onboards faster than anyone else
in the world for no stated reason. If the system is teachable, someone has
taught it before, and the story should know why this character learns
differently — a real answer is usually more interesting than the tutorial. Onboarding also interacts directly with stat-block density: the
first appearances of an interface teach the reader how to read it, and a
story that front-loads dense panels is training the reader to skim exactly
the element it will later rely on.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What is the smallest set of rules a reader needs to follow chapter one?
- Is each mechanic introduced at the first moment it matters, or before?
- Does the reader learn this rule from an explanation or from a consequence?
- Who in this world already knows all of this, and why is the protagonist
  being told instead of having learned?
- At what chapter does the reader know enough to predict the system? Is that
  where the story wanted it?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List each mechanic and the chapter where it is first explained and first
   used. Gaps between explanation and use are candidates for deferral.
2. Take one explained rule and replace the explanation with a scene where
   getting it wrong costs something.
3. Cut the first system explanation in half and see whether chapter three
   still reads. Comprehension survives more cutting than drafts assume.
4. If a companion exists mainly to explain, give them one objective of their
   own and see whether the explanations survive the change.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Systems-heavy work whose readers arrive for detailed mechanics and treat
  the specification as a pleasure rather than an obstacle. A real readership
  and a real contract.
- Later books in a series, where the audience is fluent and re-onboarding is
  the greater risk.
- Stories where the system's opacity is the point, and a reader's confusion
  is a designed experience rather than a failure of teaching.
- GameLit and adjacent subgenres with no explicit interface, where there is
  little to teach.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can locate where system terms first appear, where structured
interface text occurs, how dense those passages are, and the interval
between a term's introduction and its next use. That gap is close to
deterministic where terms are used consistently.

What it cannot determine is whether an explanation was needed, whether a
reader was confused, or whether a passage read as a dump. A long early
explanation may be a genuine problem or a deliberate contract with a
systems-loving readership. The coach should describe the shape of the
teaching and ask what the author intended it to feel like.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Explained:* "Mana regenerates at a rate determined by your Attunement,
modified by rest quality and ambient density. Attunement rises with..." —
four paragraphs before anyone has wanted mana.

*Learned:* He spent everything he had on the second wolf and stood there
afterward with his hands shaking, unable to make even a spark, while the
third one watched him from the treeline. Nobody had to tell him what
regeneration rate meant after that.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Jesse Schell ([[src.book.schell-art-of-game-design]]) supplies the treatment
of teaching a system through play rather than instruction; Raph Koster
([[src.book.koster-theory-of-fun]]) supplies the account of learning as the
source of engagement, which underpins the argument against wholesale
explanation; Ernest Adams
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the design
vocabulary for progressive disclosure and tutorial structure.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. All three
sources independently support the game-design principles. Their transfer to
prose is this drafting pass's synthesis, and carries a disanalogy worth
stating: a player must act to proceed, while a reader only reads, so
"learning by doing" becomes "learning by consequence" — a weaker mechanism
than the sources describe. The systemic observations follow this library's
own consequences reasoning, not a cited source.

records.title: Parties, guilds, and group structure
records.summary: When a power system is built around groups, the group becomes a mechanic — with roles, contribution rules, and obligations that generate as much conflict as the monsters do.

citations.label: The Proteus Paradox: How Online Games and Virtual Worlds Change Us — and How They Don't
Fundamentals of Game Design
The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Many progression systems assume groups: a party that shares experience, a
guild that holds resources and rank, a raid that requires specific roles. As
soon as the system formalizes a group, the group is a mechanic — it has
composition rules, a way of dividing what it earns, a way of admitting and
expelling people, and a set of obligations members owe each other.

This record treats those structures as system design. It is distinct from
the ensemble-cast trope record, which is about how a story handles a group of
characters on the page, and from the teamwork material inside the encounter
records, which is about how a group functions inside a fight. This one is
about the rules the group runs on.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A formalized group converts social life into something with terms, and terms
can be disputed. Who gets the drop? Who was carried? Who is owed a favour?
Research on guilds in online games describes obligation and scheduling
pressure becoming real burdens for real players — play acquiring the texture
of work. Fiction that takes its group structures seriously inherits a rich
source of conflict that requires no antagonist at all.

Groups also solve a structural problem for progression stories: they supply
characters whose competence is legible on the same scale as the
protagonist's, which is one of the few reliable ways to keep a rapidly
advancing protagonist in scenes with genuine peers.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The fixed party** — a small group with complementary roles, usually the
  book's core cast, where composition is a character question as much as a
  tactical one.
- **The guild or clan** — a standing institution with rank, resources, and
  politics, which outlives any particular party and can outrank the
  protagonist.
- **Ad hoc grouping** — temporary alliances formed per objective, which
  produces negotiation, mistrust, and short-term incentives.
- **Formal role systems** — where the system itself names roles (tank,
  healer, support) and composition rules become explicit constraints.
- **The solo exception** — a protagonist the system disadvantages for
  working alone, or advantages, either of which is a strong statement about
  what the world rewards.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- An argument about a split that is really an argument about who matters.
- A character kept in the party for reasons that are social rather than
  tactical, and the cost of that.
- Guild rank determining who may speak in a scene.
- A group whose members never disagree about anything, which usually means
  the group is functioning as one character with several names.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The frictionless party.** A group with no disagreement about risk,
  reward, or direction — pleasant, and a large source of conflict left
  unused.
- **Roles as labels.** Characters named as tank or healer whose behavior in
  scenes is indistinguishable from each other's.
- **Undesigned distribution.** Loot and experience shared by unstated rules,
  so the reader cannot tell whether a division is generous or a slight.
- **The guild that never asks.** An institution that supplies resources,
  training, and status and never requires anything inconvenient in return.
- **Group as audience.** Companions present to witness and admire the
  protagonist's growth rather than to have any of their own.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
Group structures need failure states as much as individual ones. A party can
be wiped, disbanded, or hollowed out by a single loss; a guild can be
politically captured, bankrupted, or disgraced. Deciding in advance what a
group's failure looks like usually improves it, because a group that cannot
fail is scenery.

Visibility is largely social here. Rank, membership, and reputation are the
most public facts about most characters in these settings — a guild badge is
read at a glance in a way a stat sheet may not be — which makes group
identity the fastest way for a stranger to form an opinion. That in turn
makes expulsion a serious event and forged or bought membership worth doing.

Systemically, formal groups are institutions, and everything the
institutions record says about labor and governance applies: guilds set
prices, restrict entry, license practitioners, and lobby whoever governs.
A world with powerful guilds and no guild politics has left something on
the table.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Shared-reward rules are the classic exploit surface: leeching on a group's
work, inflating contribution, forming a party purely to qualify for a split,
or disbanding immediately before a payout. Where the system grants group
bonuses, characters will assemble to farm the bonus rather than to work
together. Group mechanics also interact sharply with action economy —
numbers are the most direct action-economy advantage available — and with
information asymmetry, since a party is a structure for sharing knowledge
and therefore also a structure someone can withhold within.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What are this group's actual rules about splitting what it earns, and does
  everyone in it agree on them?
- What does the guild want from its members, and what happens to someone who
  will not give it?
- If this party lost its least important member, what would break?
- Does anyone in this group want something the others do not?
- Why is the protagonist in this group rather than a better one — and does
  the group know that?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the party's distribution rule as one sentence, then find the scene
   where it is tested. If there is no such scene, there may be a good one
   available.
2. Give one companion an objective that conflicts mildly with the party's,
   and follow it for a chapter.
3. Draft the guild's requirements as a short list of obligations. Any
   institution that asks nothing can usually be made more interesting by
   asking for one thing.
4. Remove the protagonist from a group scene and see whether the others have
   anything to do.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Deliberately solo stories, where isolation is the promise and a party
  would dilute it.
- Stories where the group is a settled, unexamined comfort — a found-family
  promise that readers arrive for specifically, and which examining too
  hard would spoil.
- Early-series sections where the group is still forming and its rules have
  not yet been established in-world.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe group composition, how often each member speaks or acts,
which members appear in which scenes, and whether stated distribution rules
recur consistently. Speaking-share across a group is countable and often
revealing.

It cannot determine whether a companion is a character or an audience —
that is a semantic judgment about function. Nor can it conclude from
harmony that a group is underused: some books are deliberately about people
who trust each other, and the coach should ask rather than diagnose.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Group as audience:* "Nice one," said Bel. "That was incredible," said Roan.
The three of them looked at the crater he had made.

*Group as system:* Bel wanted the core sold and the money split four ways.
Roan wanted it kept for the guild's tithe, because Roan intended to be
promoted. The core sat between them on the table while they worked out which
of them was going to lose.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Nick Yee's research-based account of online-game guilds
([[src.book.yee-proteus-paradox]]) supplies the description of obligation,
scheduling pressure, and play acquiring the character of labor; Ernest Adams
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the design
vocabulary for role composition and shared reward; Jesse Schell
([[src.book.schell-art-of-game-design]]) supplies the treatment of player
motivation within groups.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. Yee describes
real players in real online games — not fictional depictions of them — so the
transfer to how a novel's guild should behave is this drafting pass's
synthesis, and no claim is made that fiction readers respond as players do.
The institutional and economic consequences follow this library's own
systemic-consequences reasoning. No source cited here addresses prose
fiction directly.

records.title: Advancement rate across a manuscript
records.summary: How fast tracked power grows relative to manuscript length shapes which progression promise a book is keeping — gradual-growth stories and compressed-growth stories are different, legitimate appeals, not a fast and a slow version of the same book.
modifiers: system-apocalypse: Front-loaded advancement in the opening act is the genre convention, not evidence of an unpaced curve; read this metric against the subgenre's expected shape rather than a flat baseline.
cultivation: Later realms conventionally take longer than earlier ones; a slowing curve across the manuscript is expected, not a warning sign.
time-loop: Compressed re-advancement across each loop is the structure, not a violation of it; this metric is not meaningful applied naively across loop boundaries.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)
How to Write Meaningful Progression in Progression Fantasy
Writing Progression Fantasy

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Advancement rate is how quickly a tracked power measure — level, tier, realm,
rank — increases relative to how much manuscript has elapsed. Where a project
explicitly tracks numeric or ordinal progression tied to scenes, the interval
between advancement events, and how that interval changes over the course of
a manuscript, is a number a coach can compute directly from stored data. What
that number *means* for a given book is an interpretive question this record
does not answer on its own.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Progression fiction readers describe a felt difference between watching a
character earn power gradually and watching them acquire it in a rush.
Neither is inherently better; they are different promises. A book that opens
with a rapid climb from nothing to competent and then studies competence for
four hundred pages is offering something different from a book that spends
the whole manuscript climbing. Readers who signed up for one and got the
other describe the mismatch as pacing trouble, even when the actual complaint
is a broken promise about *what kind* of progression story this is.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Steady climb.** Advancement events land at roughly even narrative
  intervals throughout.
- **Front-loaded climb.** Rapid early advancement (common in system-apocalypse
  and portal-fantasy openings) followed by a plateau where the story shifts
  from power acquisition to power application.
- **Back-loaded climb.** Slow accumulation followed by a late, rapid breakthrough
  — common where a manuscript is building toward a single defining
  transformation.
- **Widening-interval climb.** Advancement events grow steadily further apart
  as tiers get harder to reach — the conventional cultivation and
  tower-climbing shape, where later realms or floors cost much more
  narrative space than early ones.
- **Compressed reset climb.** Advancement resets and re-accelerates each
  cycle, as in time-loop structures, where the metric needs a different unit
  of analysis entirely (see modifiers above).

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Level-ups or realm breakthroughs clustered in the first quarter of a
  manuscript, followed by a long stretch with none.
- A single advancement event consuming a disproportionate share of the
  manuscript's midpoint.
- Roughly even spacing between tracked advancement events across acts.
- A widening gap between advancement events as the story progresses, with
  each new tier taking measurably longer to reach than the last.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Treating any one shape as correct.** The most common misuse of this
  metric is comparing a book's curve to an assumed "ideal" pacing shape
  rather than to the promise that book's opening chapters made.
- **Racing to the end of the tier system**, where levels 1 through 99 occur
  inside a single volume — a legitimate but different appeal from gradual
  growth, and one that can leave readers who wanted the gradual version
  feeling shortchanged. `docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md` (pattern
  P10) names this the most common version of the mismatch.
- **A late, unexplained acceleration** with no narrative cause, which reads
  as the author needing to catch the plot up to a planned ending rather than
  as an earned breakthrough.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- When this manuscript's advancement events are plotted against its page
  count, does the resulting curve match the promise the opening chapters
  made?
- Is a plateau in the middle of the book a deliberate shift from "getting
  strong" to "being strong," or did advancement simply stall?
- If advancement accelerates late, what in the story explains why it does?
- Would this manuscript's actual curve surprise a reader who only read the
  first three chapters?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Chart tracked advancement events against manuscript position and compare
   the shape to the promise set in the opening act.
2. If the curve front-loads more than intended, consider whether early
   advancement events can be spread out, or whether the plateau after them
   needs an explicit narrative turn (a shift from acquisition to
   application) to read as intentional rather than stalled.
3. If a late acceleration feels unearned, look for an earlier chapter where
   the seed of that acceleration (a discovered method, a removed limiter, a
   sacrifice) could be planted.
4. For a widening-interval structure, make sure each later, harder-won
   advancement event is given proportionally more narrative weight, not just
   more narrative time.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories where the tracked number is explicitly decorative — a game-world
  skin over a narrative that isn't really about the numbers — may not
  benefit from this analysis at all.
- Time-loop structures need a fundamentally different unit of measurement
  (per-loop, not per-manuscript-position).
- A book that never intends to resolve its progression arc within itself
  (an ongoing serial with no planned ending) may show a curve that only
  makes sense across a series, not within one volume.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
This is one of the few patterns in this cluster that can be fully computed:
where a project explicitly tracks tier, level, or realm changes linked to
scenes, the interval and its trend across the manuscript are deterministic —
no interpretation is required to produce the number. Judging whether the
resulting curve suits the story's promise, genre, and subgenre modifiers is
model-assisted, and a coach should present the curve and ask the diagnostic
questions above rather than declaring the curve correct or wrong on its own.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Front-loaded, intentional:* In a system-apocalypse draft, the protagonist
gains four levels in the first three chapters as the world collapses, then
none for the next twelve while the story becomes about holding a shelter
together. The plateau is legible because the opening explicitly promised
survival, not a power fantasy.

*Front-loaded, unintentional:* The same shape appears in a quiet cultivation
draft with no stated urgency, and the plateau reads as the story running out
of momentum rather than shifting its promise on purpose.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
`docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md` (Part B1, pattern P6 and P10) and
Jacob Tam's essay ([[src.tam.meaningful-progression]]) both describe the
"faster early, slower later" convention and the failure mode of skipping to
the end; Andrew Rowe's writing ([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]) supports
the general principle that advancement should feel earned rather than rushed.
The subgenre modifiers (system apocalypse, cultivation, time loop) are drawn
from `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s subgenre coaching profiles, which that
document itself marks as the author's own inference rather than a sourced
claim; this record inherits that same confidence level for the modifiers
specifically, while the core deterministic-metric framing is better
supported.

records.title: The decorative chapter test
records.summary: A diagnostic question for progression-driven chapters — did the chapter add a new capability, a new demand on the character, or only one of the two?
modifiers: tower-climbing: Consider applying the test per floor rather than strictly per chapter; a floor is often the natural capability/demand unit in this subgenre.
time-loop: Apply per loop rather than per chapter; a single loop is the unit that carries new capability and new demand in this structure.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)
How to Write Meaningful Progression in Progression Fantasy

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
At the end of a chapter, two questions are worth asking side by side: what can
the protagonist now do that they could not do at the start, and what does the
world now ask of them that it did not ask before? A chapter that answers only
the first question — capability grew, but nothing new presses on the
character — is functioning as decoration. The numbers moved; the story did
not.

This is a chapter-level test, not a scene-level one, and it is specific to
progression-driven fiction, where capability change is tracked explicitly
enough that a reader (and possibly a coach) can notice when it happens without
a matching rise in what the story demands.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Progression fiction sells a promise of forward motion. A reader who feels the
tier climb but not the stakes climb experiences the same sensation prose
readers describe as "nothing happened this chapter," except here it happens
inside chapters that are visibly full of events — fights won, loot gained,
levels announced. The chapter reads as busy and feels empty at the same time,
which is a harder problem to name than plain slowness, and one authors can
miss because activity is present.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Pure capability chapters.** A level-up, a new skill, a stronger weapon —
  with the next scene functioning exactly as the last one did, just with
  bigger numbers.
- **Pure demand chapters.** A new threat, obligation, or complication
  introduced with no accompanying growth — valid and common, especially early
  in an arc, but a chapter type distinct from the failure this pattern names.
- **The compounding chapter.** Capability and demand rise together: a new
  ability is gained and immediately required by a harder problem than the
  character has faced. This is the target shape, not a rule that every
  chapter must hit it — see "when this advice does not apply" below.
- **The delayed-demand chapter.** Capability is granted now and the matching
  demand arrives two or three chapters later. This can work as a deliberate
  set-up, provided the eventual payoff actually lands (see
  [[craft.general.plot.negative-space-problems-power-cannot-solve]] for the
  related question of what capability never gets used against).

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A skill or stat increase followed by a scene in which the previous
  difficulty ceiling still applies unchanged.
- A new tier or rank announced, with the subsequent conflict resolved as
  easily, or with the same tactics, as the one before the increase.
- Conversely: a threat escalates, and the protagonist's toolkit is
  unchanged from three chapters earlier, forcing an unearned reach or a
  convenient rescue.
- A training or grinding montage that ends with a number changing but no new
  scene, obligation, or choice attached to the new number.

None of these signals is proof by itself — a chapter can show a stat increase
and still be doing real narrative work that isn't visible in the increase
alone. The test is a prompt for author reflection, not a lint rule.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Numbers substituting for stakes**, especially in serialized fiction where
  a chapter is expected to contain visible progress on a regular cadence.
- **Escalating threats with no escalating toolkit**, which produces either
  suspiciously convenient solutions or protagonist competence that reads as
  plot armor.
- **Repeating the test too literally**, treating every single chapter as a
  failure if it doesn't hit both halves — some chapters exist to develop
  relationships, build dread, or let the story breathe, and forcing capability
  or demand into all of them flattens pacing rather than improving it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What did this chapter's protagonist gain, and what does the story now need
  from them that it didn't need before?
- If you can answer the capability half easily but struggle with the demand
  half, is that an intentional breather chapter, or did the demand get lost?
- Where is the next chapter or scene that will actually spend the capability
  this chapter granted?
- Are there chapters in this arc where the reverse is true — demand rising
  with no matching growth — and is that gap deliberate?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List, chapter by chapter across one arc, what was gained and what was
   newly demanded. Look for chapters where one column is empty.
2. For a chapter that reads as decorative, try moving its capability gain to
   land immediately before the scene that needs it, rather than in its own
   chapter.
3. Try converting one "pure capability" chapter into a "delayed demand" setup
   by seeding, in the same chapter, the shape of the problem this new
   capability will eventually meet.
4. If several chapters in a row show capability with no demand, consider
   whether the story has entered an extended plateau and needs either a
   compressing edit or a new complication introduced earlier than planned.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Rest, bonding, and worldbuilding chapters can be valuable without either
  half of this test, especially directly after a high-intensity arc.
- Subgenres with front-loaded power growth (system apocalypse, for example)
  legitimately compress this pattern into a shorter span; applying it
  chapter-by-chapter in the opening act may flag intentional structure as a
  problem.
- A slow-burn story that is deliberately withholding demand to build dramatic
  irony (the reader senses a threat the protagonist hasn't met yet) is using
  the gap on purpose.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Deterministic code can report the capability half where the project tracks
explicit state changes — a stat, skill, or level change linked to a scene.
It cannot determine, from that data alone, whether the world's demands
changed in the same chapter; that requires reading what actually happens in
the prose, which is a semantic judgment. A future coach could shortlist
chapters with a tracked capability change and flag them for the author's own
review against this question, but it cannot claim to have verified the demand
half from prose alone.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Capability with no demand (decorative):* Wren's spellbook gains a new tier
of fire magic in chapter twelve. Chapter thirteen opens on the same bandit
patrol difficulty Wren cleared in chapter nine, resolved the same way, just
faster.

*Compounding:* Wren's spellbook gains the same tier of fire magic, and the
chapter ends with a scout reporting that the bandits have called in a
fire-resistant mercenary company specifically because word of Wren's magic
reached them. The next fight has to be won a different way.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The core formulation — capability gained versus demand raised — comes from
Jacob Tam's progression-fantasy craft writing
([[src.tam.meaningful-progression]]), a practitioner essay describing this as
the single most operational diagnostic the source material identified; it is
practitioner consensus rather than an academic or quantitative finding.
`docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md` (Part B1, pattern P2) frames it as
the most checkable pattern in its candidate pool and notes the deterministic
half (capability, where tracked) versus the model-assisted half (demand,
always). This record adds the tower-climbing and time-loop scope modifiers
and the explicit caution against applying the test to every chapter
uniformly, which is this drafting pass's synthesis rather than a sourced
claim.

records.title: Fake progression (relative position never moves)
records.summary: A protagonist can climb an absolute power scale while their standing relative to the world around them never actually changes — readers respond to the relative gap, not the raw numbers.
modifiers: dungeon-core: Relative position works differently for an immobile protagonist whose "peers" may be invading adventurers rather than a social cohort; apply the underlying question (has the gap between capability and demand stayed alive?) rather than the literal peer-comparison framing.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)
How to Write Meaningful Progression in Progression Fantasy

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Fake progression is what readers describe when a character's absolute power
keeps rising on paper while their position relative to the world's challenges
never actually changes: overpowered against the surrounding cast in chapter
five, still just as overpowered — no more, no less — in chapter five hundred.
The tier numbers climbed. Only the numbers climbed; everyone and everything
around the character scaled up in step, so the *experience* of progression
never arrives even though its evidence is everywhere on the page.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The genre's core appeal is the felt sensation of getting stronger relative to
what's in front of you — outmatched, then even, then dominant, then facing a
new kind of outmatched. A story that keeps the character permanently in the
"comfortably dominant" band, just with bigger numbers attached, removes the
sensation the numbers exist to produce. Readers name this specifically as
"progression that doesn't progress," which is a description of their felt
experience of relative standing, not a complaint about the math.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Peer inflation.** Every antagonist, rival, and encounter scales up in
  lockstep with the protagonist, so the gap between them is constant across
  the whole manuscript.
- **Comfort-zone plateau.** The protagonist reaches a power level early and
  the story keeps generating challenges calibrated to exactly that level
  indefinitely, rather than letting the character outgrow a tier of problem
  entirely.
- **Cosmetic tier changes.** A rank or title changes (apprentice to journeyman,
  for instance) with no accompanying change in what kinds of problems the
  character can now solve that they couldn't before.
- **The inverse, done well:** three distinct relative positions across an
  arc — excluded from an activity, competing at its edge, and having
  absorbed the old limit into routine — which is the shape fake progression
  fails to deliver (see the three-stages pattern for the fuller treatment of
  this positive form).

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Encounters that consistently cost the protagonist the same relative
  effort across a long span of the manuscript, regardless of stated tier
  changes.
- A rank-up or level-up that changes no subsequent scene's difficulty,
  tactics, or stakes.
- Antagonists introduced late in the book who are narrated as comparably
  threatening to antagonists from early in the book, despite the stated power
  gap.
- A character who never gets to revisit an old challenge and find it trivial
  — the "absorbed into routine" beat that signals real relative growth is
  simply absent.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Mistaking bigger numbers for real progression**, especially in serials
  under pressure to show visible advancement every installment; escalating
  the number is easier than escalating the story's actual demands.
- **Escalating everything at once**, so relative position is preserved by
  construction — every threat is designed to be exactly hard enough,
  regardless of the character's stated tier.
- **Never letting a former ceiling become routine**, which denies the reader
  the payoff moment where visible growth is confirmed by an old problem
  becoming trivial.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If you removed every stated number from this manuscript, would a reader
  still be able to tell the character got stronger relative to the world
  around them?
- Is there a scene where an old obstacle is revisited and now trivial? If
  not, would one be possible to add?
- Are late-book antagonists actually harder for this character specifically,
  or are they simply narrated with bigger numbers attached to a
  similarly-costly fight?
- Across the manuscript, does the protagonist ever get to feel dominant
  before the story raises the ceiling again?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Chart, at several points across the manuscript, an approximate "relative
   standing" (dominant / even / outmatched) rather than the raw tier number,
   and look for a flat line.
2. Identify one early obstacle that could plausibly be revisited later in the
   book and made explicitly trivial, to give the reader concrete proof of
   growth.
3. For a late antagonist that feels no more threatening than an early one
   despite a stated power gap, consider raising the *kind* of challenge
   (a new axis of difficulty) rather than only its magnitude.
4. Try deliberately allowing one arc where the protagonist is dominant with
   no immediate new threat, before introducing the next ceiling-raiser, to
   let the reader register the change before erasing it.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story whose explicit premise is a treadmill or trap (a cursed loop, a
  simulation designed never to let the character win) can use flat relative
  standing on purpose, provided that stagnation is itself the narrative
  problem the story engages.
- Ensemble or community-focused subgenres (base building, dungeon core) may
  not have a single protagonist whose relative peer standing is the right
  lens; apply the underlying capability-versus-demand question instead of the
  literal peer comparison.
- Early-arc chapters legitimately keep a character in a comfort zone briefly
  before the story raises stakes; a single early plateau is not the pattern.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project tracks explicit numeric capability and something like
encounter difficulty, deterministic code can compare the two over time and
surface a flat or widening gap as a candidate signal. Whether that flat gap
is a craft problem, a deliberate structural choice, or simply an early-arc
stretch requires reading the actual prose and cannot be concluded from
tracked numbers alone; this pattern stays model-assisted even when a
partial metric is available.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Fake progression:* Across ten chapters, Kest advances from tier three to
tier seven. Each chapter's fight costs the same three combat beats to win,
regardless of stated tier, and no antagonist from tier seven reads as more
dangerous than the tier-three rival from chapter one.

*Real relative movement:* Kest advances the same tiers, but the tier-three
rival reappears at the story's midpoint and is dispatched in one paragraph,
explicitly because Kest has outgrown that entire category of threat — and the
new tier-seven antagonist introduces a kind of danger (political, not
physical) that Kest's old toolkit cannot touch at all.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The core formulation is Jacob Tam's ([[src.tam.meaningful-progression]]),
describing readers responding to relative position rather than raw numbers;
`docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md` (pattern P1) frames the partial
deterministic angle (comparing tracked capability against tracked encounter
difficulty) as available only where both are explicitly recorded. Both
sources are practitioner-level, not controlled research; the dungeon-core
modifier is this drafting pass's synthesis, extending the genre-profile
reasoning in `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md` rather than a directly sourced
claim.

records.title: Stat-block density and interval
records.summary: How often and how completely a story shows raw system numbers changes whether those numbers read as significant or as clutter — density and interval are measurable, but their felt effect is medium- and reader-dependent.
modifiers: gamelit: This pattern largely does not apply — a book with no obligatory stat screen has no stat-block density to manage.
progression-fantasy: Applies only if the project's power system is genuinely numeric; hard-tier systems without displayed numbers should not be evaluated against this pattern.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)
How to Write LitRPG: Integrating Game Systems Into Your Story Without Losing Readers
LitRPG Audiobook Tropes Readers Love and Hate

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Stat-block density describes two related, countable things: how often a
manuscript shows a full or partial system readout (skill lists, attribute
sheets, level-up summaries), and how much of each readout is actually
relevant to what just happened. A story can show numbers constantly, rarely,
or selectively — and the interval and completeness of those reveals shape
whether a stat block reads as a meaningful punctuation mark or as clutter the
reader learns to skip.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Reader discussions in the LitRPG community return to this complaint more
often than almost any other mechanical one: a full stat sheet reprinted after
