sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If asked, could you answer all six questions (source, storage, access,
  expenditure, recovery, limits) for this system's main resource, even
  informally?
- Has this system's stated limit ever been bent for plot convenience, and
  would a reader notice?
- Is resource depletion visible to other characters in the story, and does
  that visibility get used tactically?
- What is the most exploitative use of this resource a clever character in
  this world could devise, and does the story ever acknowledge that
  possibility?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence each for source, storage, access, expenditure,
   recovery, and limits for the manuscript's central resource; any sentence
   that's hard to write marks a design gap worth deciding on deliberately.
2. Audit scenes where the resource is depleted or recovers, and check
   whether the stated recovery method is consistently honored.
3. Consider the most exploitative use of the resource a rational actor in
   this world could devise, and decide whether the story should engage it,
   explicitly forbid it, or leave it as unaddressed background.
4. If the resource can be extracted from others, test one scene where that
   possibility is raised, even briefly, to see whether it changes the
   world's stakes.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A system deliberately left mysterious as a narrative technique (the reader
  and characters alike don't understand the rules yet) can defer answering
  these questions as long as the ambiguity is legible as intentional.
- Very lightweight, thematic magic systems (GameLit, some general fantasy)
  may not need explicit answers to all six axes if the system is never
  load-bearing for plot logic.
- Short fiction may reasonably leave several axes implicit if the resource
  never becomes a plot-critical constraint.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript's resource rules are internally consistent across all
six axes requires tracking every scene where the resource is used, spent, or
recovered, and comparing them — a task requiring close reading and
interpretation. A coach could shortlist scenes mentioning the resource as
candidate evidence where a project explicitly tracks a mechanics resource,
but concluding consistency or inconsistency remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined system:* A character's magic "runs on willpower" with no further
specification; in one scene, exhaustion stops them from casting, and two
chapters later they cast under equal or greater exhaustion with no
explanation for the discrepancy.

*Examined system:* A character's magic draws from a stored reserve
(storage: a bonded stone) that recovers only during specific ritual rest
(recovery: gated, not passive), with a hard cap tied to the stone's size
(limits: hard), and the story consistently shows characters checking the
stone's charge before a costly working — the system's edges are legible and
honored.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The six-axis framing (source, storage, access, expenditure, recovery,
limits) draws on established game-design literature covering resource
systems, economies, and progression more broadly
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]],
[[src.book.salen-zimmerman-rules-of-play]]); both are established academic/
practitioner texts in game design, and their core resource-economy
principles are well-supported, supporting a `high` confidence rating for the
framework itself, while its application to any specific manuscript's
consistency remains model-assisted.

records.title: Reputation and faction standing
records.summary: When a system tracks what groups think of a character, social consequence becomes a mechanic with values — which is powerful, and which risks converting relationships into a resource to be farmed.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
The Proteus Paradox: How Online Games and Virtual Worlds Change Us — and How They Don't
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A reputation system tracks how a person is regarded — by a faction, a
settlement, a guild, or the world at large — and makes that regard
mechanically consequential: prices, access, quests offered, doors opened or
closed. Some systems display it as a value; others keep it as an in-world
social fact the interface never mentions.

This record is about that machinery. It is distinct from the institutional
record, which is about the organizations themselves, and from titles and
honorifics, which are markers a system awards. Reputation is the standing
those markers sit on, and it changes.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Reputation is the mechanism that makes a world respond. A protagonist whose
past actions are remembered inhabits a place with continuity; one who arrives
everywhere unknown inhabits a series of disconnected locations. That
continuity is much of what makes a long serial feel like one world rather
than a sequence of arcs.

It also creates a rare kind of stake. Most progression systems only go up.
Reputation can be lost, and lost in ways no amount of capability recovers,
which gives a story consequences that power cannot solve — a scarce and
valuable thing in a genre where power usually solves everything.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Numeric standing** — a value per faction, legible and easy to game.
- **Tiered regard** — named states (hostile, neutral, honored) that behave
  like thresholds rather than pools.
- **Reputation as rumor** — no system value at all; standing is what people
  say, which travels imperfectly and can be wrong.
- **Mutually exclusive allegiance** — gains with one faction costing standing
  with another, which forces choice and is where the mechanic earns its keep.
- **Notoriety** — reputation that rises with infamy, opening some doors while
  closing others.
- **Localized versus global renown** — known in one town versus known
  everywhere, which changes what anonymity is worth.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A merchant's price changing because of something the protagonist did
  chapters ago in a different city.
- A faction remembering a slight the protagonist has forgotten.
- A character declining a profitable job because of what taking it would cost
  them elsewhere.
- Conversely: standing that rises monotonically with every quest completed,
  so the mechanic never asks anything.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Reputation as a second experience bar.** Standing that only accumulates,
  with no opposed factions and nothing to lose.
- **Relationships as a farmable resource.** Characters treating people as
  standing dispensers, which the mechanic invites and the prose should
  notice.
- **Rumor that travels perfectly.** Everyone knowing everything instantly,
  which removes the interesting middle where a reputation is contested or
  outdated.
- **Standing without texture.** A number that changes nothing about how
  anyone speaks to the protagonist.
- **Unearned infamy.** A notoriety the story asserts but never dramatizes —
  no one crosses the street, no prices change, no doors close.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The design question that matters most is whether standing can fall, and how
far. A system with no downward path is a reward track wearing a social
costume. A system where reputation can be destroyed — and where destruction
is not simply repaired by later heroics — makes social consequence real, and
gives a protagonist something they can genuinely lose.

Visibility is unusually rich here because reputation is inherently social.
It can be visible to the character (a displayed value), visible to others but
not to them (everyone knows what is said about them except them), or visible
only to the reader. The second is the most useful and least used: a
protagonist operating on a stale understanding of their own standing is a
reliable source of scenes.

The consequences reach into everything the institutional records describe.
Where standing determines access, someone is selling it — letters of
introduction, sponsorships, cleared records — and someone else is
manufacturing it. A world with formal reputation and no reputation trade has
skipped the obvious.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Numeric standing is among the most gameable mechanics in the genre: repeating
small favours, farming low-value tasks for a faction, buying goodwill,
laundering a bad reputation through an intermediary, or exploiting factions
that do not communicate. Where two factions oppose each other and both track
standing, playing both sides is the obvious move and someone in the world is
doing it professionally. Reputation also interacts with party and guild
structure — a group's standing and an individual's may diverge, which is a
strong source of internal conflict — and with titles, which are usually
reputation crystallized into something portable.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Can this character's standing fall, and has it?
- Which two factions in this world make gains with one cost standing with the
  other?
- Does anyone treat the protagonist differently because of their reputation
  in a scene where it is inconvenient?
- How fast does news travel here, and who benefits from its being slow?
- What does the protagonist believe their reputation is, and are they right?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the scene where reputation costs something the protagonist wanted,
   and see whether the mechanic starts carrying weight.
2. Name two factions whose regard is genuinely opposed. If none exist,
   reputation is currently a single accumulating track.
3. Give one character a stale or mistaken view of the protagonist's standing
   and let a scene run on the gap.
4. Trace one rumor's route through the world explicitly — who told whom — and
   see whether the setting's information economy holds up.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Wandering or episodic structures where the protagonist deliberately leaves
  consequences behind, and continuity of regard would work against the form.
- Stories with no formal standing system, where reputation is ordinary social
  fact and needs no mechanical treatment.
- Early chapters where the protagonist is genuinely unknown and the absence
  of standing is the situation being established.
- Solo and isolated premises where there is no society to be regarded by.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where standing is reported numerically, a coach can extract values, chart
them over the manuscript, and note whether any faction's value ever
decreases — a near-deterministic check, and a revealing one, since
monotonic reputation is the failure mode this record names first.

Beyond that, interpretation. Whether characters *treat* the protagonist
consistently with their stated standing is a semantic judgment requiring the
scenes to be read. The absence of a reputation value is not evidence that a
world lacks social consequence; many settings handle it entirely in prose,
and handle it well.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Second experience bar:* Reputation with the Ashford Concord: 4,200
(Honored). It had risen after every job. Nothing in the town had changed
except the greeting.

*Standing with a cost:* the Concord raised him to Honored the same week the
river guilds stopped answering his letters, and the river guilds owned the
only boats going north.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Ernest Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies the
design vocabulary for faction and reputation systems and their reward
structures; Nick Yee ([[src.book.yee-proteus-paradox]]) supplies the
research-based account of social status and standing operating within online
game communities; this library's genre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation that
displayed reputation values are a recurring subgenre convention.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. The mechanical
design vocabulary is sourced; Yee describes real players rather than fictional
depictions, so using him to reason about how a novel's factions should behave
is an extension. The narrative arguments here — that reputation supplies
stakes power cannot solve, that a stale self-understanding is a scene engine —
are this drafting pass's synthesis. The consequence reasoning follows this
library's own institutional records rather than a cited source.

records.title: Accelerated training and time dilation
records.summary: Spaces where time runs differently — a mechanic that buys the story plausible mastery without spending chapters on it, and that quietly costs the protagonist years of everyone else's life.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Fundamentals of Game Design
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A time-dilation mechanic lets a character spend more subjective time than
the world does: a training chamber where a day is a year, a dream space, a
secluded cultivation retreat, a pocket realm. The genre reaches for it to
solve a specific problem — mastery takes time the plot cannot spare — and it
solves it well.

The reason it needs designing is that it does two things at once. It buys
plausible competence, and it separates the protagonist from everyone else's
timeline. The second is usually unintended and is often the more interesting
half.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Readers of this genre want growth to be earned, and time is the most
legible currency effort comes in. A protagonist who spends four subjective
years learning the sword has done something the reader can credit, without
the book spending four years of pages.

The cost is separation. Someone who has lived years the people around them
have not is out of step with them: friendships fall behind, the person who
returns is not who left, and a character who repeats this becomes
progressively harder to keep in relationships. Stories reach for the mechanic
for its convenience and often discover the loneliness afterwards, which is
worth designing for deliberately rather than tripping over.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The training chamber** — a bounded space with a stated ratio and usually
  a limit on how long can be spent inside.
- **The secluded retreat** — cultivation's version, where time passes
  normally but the character withdraws from the world for years.
- **The dream or mental space** — subjective time only, so the body does not
  age and the gain is knowledge rather than conditioning.
- **The stolen year** — dilation with a price paid in lifespan, health, or
  sanity, which restores the tradeoff.
- **Shared dilation** — a group entering together, which preserves
  relationships and is much less isolating.
- **Involuntary dilation** — time running differently without consent,
  closer to a captivity structure than a training one.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character emerging older than the friends they left, and the scene
  registering it.
- A hard limit — one use, or one per tier — that makes the decision to spend
  it matter.
- A skill that visibly could only come from years of repetition.
- Conversely: repeated dilation used as a plot solvent, so any capability gap
  is closed by a chapter in the chamber.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unbounded access.** No queue, no cost, no ceiling, so any capability gap
  is closed by a chapter in the chamber.
- **The frictionless return.** Years spent inside and nothing changed about
  the person who comes out or the people who waited.
- **Dilation as plot solvent.** Reached for whenever the protagonist is
  outmatched, which converts a mechanic into a get-out.
- **Growth asserted, not shown.** The chamber standing in for the scenes
  that would have demonstrated the growth — the fake-progression problem
  arriving through a door marked training.
- **A world that has not noticed.** A setting containing a device that
  manufactures expertise, whose institutions are organized as though it did
  not exist.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The mechanic needs a limit or it eats the story's difficulty curve. Limits
come in a few shapes: access (rare, expensive, controlled), duration (a
ceiling on subjective time), diminishing returns (later stays give less), or
cost (lifespan, health, memory, sanity). Any of them restores the decision;
none of them is a natural default, so it has to be chosen.

Failure states are usually underused. What happens if someone stays too long?
Emerging unable to relate to anyone, having practiced an error for years, or
having lost the thread of why they went in are all more interesting than a
uniformly successful retreat.

Consequentially, dilation is the most economically explosive mechanic in this
record set if it can be shared. If a chamber exists and can be rented, then
whoever controls it produces experts on demand, and every institution in the
setting reorganizes around access to it. Most stories give the protagonist a
chamber and leave the world untouched, which is the same unexamined-implication
pattern the travel and appraisal records describe.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
The obvious exploit is stacking: entering repeatedly to compress decades. If
the system permits it, someone in the world has done it and is very old
inside. Others include using dilation to out-plan opponents rather than
out-train them, mass-producing specialists, and — where the body does not age
— treating it as free time with no cost at all, which is the version most
likely to break a setting. Dilation interacts directly with advancement rate,
since it is a way of decoupling growth from chapter count, and with
diminishing returns, which is the cleanest available brake.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What limits access to this, and who enforces the limit?
- What does the character lose by going in?
- Who came out wrong, and does anyone in the setting tell that story?
- If this is available to institutions, what have they built with it?
- Could the same growth have been shown in half a chapter of ordinary time,
  and would that have been better?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. State the ratio, the limit, and the cost in three sentences. Missing
   entries are where the mechanic is currently unbounded.
2. Write the reunion scene: the character comes out, and someone who did not
   go in is waiting. Follow what that costs.
3. Give one earlier use a lasting consequence and see whether later uses gain
   weight.
4. Ask what a wealthy family does with this mechanic, and let the setting
   answer.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Settings with no time mechanic, where this record does not apply.
- Time-loop structures, which are a different form with their own record —
  loops repeat the same interval rather than extending it.
- Stories where the dilation is a single, plot-critical event rather than a
  recurring resource.
- Comedic treatments where an absurd chamber is a joke and its economics are
  not the subject.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where the story states ratios or durations, a coach can extract them and
check internal consistency — subjective years claimed against ratio and
elapsed time is arithmetic, and mismatches are detectable. It can also chart
how often the mechanic is used and whether uses cluster before difficulty
spikes, which is a suggestive pattern rather than a finding.

Whether the mechanic has been overused is a judgment about the story's
promises. A book whose subject is compressed mastery may use it constantly
and correctly. The coach should report frequency, stated limits, and
arithmetic inconsistencies, and leave the rest as a question.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unbounded:* he went into the chamber before each tier and came out ready.
The chamber had no queue, no cost, and no other users.

*Costed:* he went in for what the chamber called a year and came out to find
that Bel had married someone, and that the argument they had been having when
he left had been settled without him, in his absence, against him.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This library's genre research ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]])
supplies the observation that accelerated-training spaces are a recurring
subgenre convention, particularly in cultivation and tower structures. Ernest
Adams ([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]) supplies only the
general principle that an unbounded resource collapses the decisions a system
was built to create. Everything else — the taxonomy, the separation argument,
the failure states, the economic consequences — is this drafting pass's
synthesis ([[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]]).

`source_confidence` is `limited`. No craft or scholarly treatment of this
convention was available to this pass. The strongest claim here, that
repeated dilation isolates a character from their relationships, is
reasoning rather than a documented observation about how readers respond, and
should be read as a design prompt rather than a finding.

records.title: Trope inversions and combinations
records.summary: Inverting a familiar trope or combining two familiar ones can produce a genuinely new reader promise — but only if the inversion or combination is legible as deliberate, and only if it still delivers some version of satisfaction rather than simply negating the original's appeal.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A trope inversion takes a familiar convention and reverses one of its
defining assumptions — a chosen one who was never actually needed, a
dungeon whose "monster" protagonist is more sympathetic than the
adventurers "rescuing" the world from it. A trope combination pairs two
familiar elements that don't conventionally appear together, producing a
promise distinct from either element alone — a heist structured as a
found-family story, a cultivation narrative crossed with a formal mystery.
Both techniques depend on the same underlying requirement: the reader
needs to recognize what's being inverted or combined for the technique to
register at all, and the result still needs to deliver its own satisfying
promise rather than functioning only as commentary on the original.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A well-executed inversion or combination offers a specific pleasure
distinct from either straightforward execution or simple subversion for
its own sake — the reader gets the recognition of the familiar element
alongside the surprise of its new context, and when it works, the result
feels both fresh and legible rather than arbitrary. This only works if the
reader can actually recognize the trope being inverted or combined; an
inversion of an element the reader doesn't know well enough to notice as
inverted just reads as an ordinary, unremarkable choice.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Role inversion**, reversing an established character-role trope's
  usual dynamic (the mentor who's actually less capable than the student,
  the antagonist who's more sympathetic than the protagonist).
- **Structural inversion**, reversing a plot structure's usual shape (a
  quest where the object should never have been sought, a tournament where
  losing is the actual goal).
- **Promise inversion**, subverting what a genre or trope conventionally
  promises the reader (a chosen-one story where being chosen is a curse
  rather than a gift) — most effective when this subversion is itself
  handled as a serious, examined choice rather than only an ironic gesture.
- **Cross-genre combination**, pairing conventions from two genres not
  conventionally combined (a cultivation heist, a LitRPG mystery),
  producing a new set of reader expectations neither genre alone would
  generate.
- **Cross-trope combination**, pairing two specific tropes from within the
  same broad genre (a found-family dungeon core, a trickster chosen one)
  in a way that generates fresh tension between their usually separate
  logics.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- An inverted or combined element clearly recognizable as a specific,
  familiar convention before its inversion or combination becomes evident,
  giving the reader the recognition needed for the technique to register.
- A story that delivers real satisfaction through its inverted or combined
  form, not just commentary on or negation of the original convention.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an "inversion" so far removed from the
  original trope's recognizable shape that readers unfamiliar with the
  specific convention being inverted simply experience it as an ordinary
  choice with no particular resonance.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unrecognizable inversion**, where the original trope isn't established
  clearly enough for its inversion to register as a deliberate choice.
- **Inversion as pure negation**, where subverting a trope removes its
  satisfaction without replacing it with a different, equally real
  satisfaction — the story ends up delivering neither the original promise
  nor a new one.
- **Combination where one element dominates**, where a cross-genre or
  cross-trope combination ends up functioning as one convention with
  decorative trace elements of the other, rather than a genuine synthesis.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If a reader unfamiliar with the specific trope being inverted read this
  story, would the inversion still register, or would it just look like an
  ordinary choice?
- Does this inversion deliver its own satisfaction, or does it only negate
  the original convention's appeal without replacing it?
- In a cross-genre or cross-trope combination, do both elements
  meaningfully shape the story, or does one dominate while the other
  provides only decoration?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Establish the trope being inverted clearly enough, early enough, that
   an attentive reader recognizes it before the inversion lands.
2. For an inversion that feels like pure negation, identify what new
   satisfaction it could offer in place of the original, and strengthen
   that element.
3. For a combination where one element dominates, find scenes specifically
   built to foreground the underrepresented element's own logic.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Straightforward, uninverted execution of familiar tropes remains a
  legitimate and often preferred choice, as covered in each individual
  trope record's own "when straightforward execution is the right choice"
  section — inversion is a tool, not an obligation.
- A very subtle or minor inversion, not central to the story's identity,
  doesn't need extensive setup to register.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether an inversion or combination is legible, and whether it delivers
its own satisfaction rather than only negating the original, requires
reading and interpreting the manuscript's genre signaling and execution —
a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unrecognizable inversion:* A story features a mentor character who turns
out to be less skilled than their student, but the mentor's competence
was never established clearly enough for the reveal to register as an
inversion of the usual mentor-competence assumption — it just reads as an
underwritten mentor.

*Legible, satisfying inversion:* The same story instead establishes the
mentor's reputation and apparent competence clearly across several early
scenes, making the eventual reveal — that the reputation was built on the
work of students who came before, not the mentor's own current
ability — a legible inversion that also opens a new, examined story about
earned versus inherited authority.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This record's framing draws on general trope-taxonomy reasoning informed by
the broader craft-failure research's treatment of reader-fatigue and trope
handling ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated
craft-literature source specifically addressing trope inversion and
combination technique was available to this drafting pass.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Fantasy genre conventions
records.summary: Fantasy readers bring specific expectations about internal consistency and earned wonder that differ from other genres' promises — a fantasy world's magic doesn't need to follow real-world rules, but it does need to follow its own rules once it's established them.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Fantasy as a genre convention promises a world that operates by different
rules than the reader's own, with wonder and strangeness as part of the
core appeal — but readers of fantasy specifically also expect internal
consistency: a world's magic, creatures, and cosmology don't need to
follow real-world physics or history, but once the story establishes its
own rules, readers hold it to them with a rigor genres without an explicit
magic system often don't face. This is closely related to, but broader
than, this library's resource-lifecycle-design and systemic-social-
consequences patterns, which address the mechanical and social
implications of a magic system specifically; this record addresses
fantasy's broader genre contract, including elements (mythology, secondary-
world geography, non-human cultures) that aren't strictly mechanical.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Fantasy's appeal often depends on a world feeling large and coherent
enough to sustain genuine wonder — the sense that there's more to this
world than what's on the page, and that what is on the page holds
together. A worldbuilding inconsistency (a stated rule violated with no
explanation, a culture that behaves inconsistently with its established
values, a geography that doesn't hold together) can break immersion more
sharply in fantasy than in genres where the reader isn't tracking an
internally consistent secondary world in the same way.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **High or epic fantasy**, set in a fully secondary world with its own
  history, geography, and cosmology, typically expecting the most
  sustained internal consistency.
- **Low fantasy**, set in a world close to the reader's own with limited
  magical elements, where consistency expectations may be narrower
  (focused tightly on the magic system) but still real.
- **Mythic or fairy-tale-adjacent fantasy**, drawing on established
  folklore logic (rule of three, symbolic causality) rather than a fully
  systematized magic system, with its own, looser consistency
  expectations rooted in mythic rather than mechanical logic.
- **Portal or contemporary fantasy**, blending a real-world setting with
  fantastical elements, requiring consistency both within the fantastical
  logic and in how it interacts with the established real-world rules.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A stated worldbuilding rule (a magic limit, a cultural taboo, a
  geographic fact) honored consistently across the manuscript, even at
  moments when it would be convenient to bend it.
- A non-human culture or society whose behavior and values remain
  internally consistent even as the story explores their differences from
  human norms.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an established magical limit, cultural
  rule, or geographic fact quietly violated later in the story with no
  acknowledgment.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Rules bent for plot convenience**, violating an established magical or
  worldbuilding limit with no explanation, undermining the internal
  consistency fantasy readers specifically track.
- **Inconsistent non-human cultures**, where a culture's established values
  or behaviors shift depending on what a given scene needs rather than
  remaining coherent.
- **Geography or history that doesn't hold together**, where travel times,
  historical dates, or spatial relationships contradict earlier
  established facts.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Has a stated magical, cultural, or geographic rule been violated
  anywhere in this manuscript with no explanation?
- Does a non-human culture behave consistently with its established values
  across every scene it appears in?
- Do this world's geography and history hold together across the whole
  manuscript, or are there contradictions a careful reader might notice?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the manuscript's key established worldbuilding rules (magical
   limits, cultural taboos, geographic facts) and audit later chapters for
   consistency.
2. For a non-human culture, write a short list of their core values and
   check their depicted behavior against it across the manuscript.
3. Build or check a rough timeline and map for the manuscript's key events
   and locations to catch geography or history inconsistencies.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Mythic or fairy-tale-adjacent fantasy operating on symbolic rather than
  mechanical logic may reasonably have looser, more associative
  consistency expectations than a fully systematized secondary world.
- A story deliberately depicting an unreliable or unstable world (where
  inconsistency is itself a plot element, such as a setting under active
  magical corruption) is using apparent inconsistency intentionally,
  provided that's legible as a choice.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical secondary-world fantasy with clearly established, consistently
honored rules remains a satisfying and reliable structure — its
familiarity doesn't require subversion, and consistency itself is often
the primary craft achievement readers are responding to when they describe
a fantasy world as feeling "real."

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript's established worldbuilding rules are honored
consistently requires tracking those rules across the manuscript's full
length — a close-reading task with no full deterministic substitute,
though where a project explicitly tracks canon facts as structured data,
some consistency checks could be partially automated.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Broken consistency:* A magic system establishes that resurrection is
impossible in this world; a beloved character is resurrected two hundred
pages later with no explanation for the violated rule.

*Honored consistency:* The same rule instead holds firm even at the
story's most emotionally costly moment, and the story's resolution
explicitly depends on characters finding a different way to address their
loss — the established limit does real narrative work by staying
established.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The internal-consistency-as-genre-contract framing draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of fantasy conventions
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre material
as partly inferential; no dedicated fantasy-craft literature source was
available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Horror genre conventions
records.summary: Horror's reader promise is managed fear — dread that builds, releases, and ideally means something — and conventions borrowed into horror from other genres (a LitRPG system, a mystery structure) need to serve that promise or they compete with it.
modifiers: dark-horror-litrpg: See the dark/horror LitRPG subgenre profile for how horror conventions interact specifically with progression-fiction death and resource mechanics; this record covers general horror genre convention independent of any progression system.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Horror as a genre convention promises managed fear: dread that builds
through withheld or ambiguous information, releases through confrontation
or revelation, and ideally carries meaning beyond the fear itself — a
monster that represents something, a violation of safety that says
something about vulnerability, a survival ordeal that tests character.
Readers bring genre-specific expectations to horror distinct from a
general story's suspense: they expect the threat to feel genuinely
dangerous (not defeatable through simple competence), they expect some
ambiguity or unknowability to persist rather than being fully resolved
and explained, and they expect the story to be willing to let bad things
actually happen rather than rescuing every character from meaningful
harm.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A reader who opens a story signaled as horror and finds a threat that's
fully explained, easily defeated, and costs nothing real feels the genre's
central promise broken, even if the resulting story is well executed on
its own separate terms. Conversely, applying horror conventions
(sustained dread, ambiguous threat, real cost) to a story that hasn't
signaled itself as horror can feel like a tonal betrayal in the other
direction. The convention exists because it names a real, distinct reader
expectation, not because horror is inherently "about" any specific content
like gore or jump-scares.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Psychological horror**, where dread comes primarily from uncertainty,
  perception, and internal experience rather than physical threat.
- **Visceral or body horror**, where dread comes from physical violation,
  transformation, or vulnerability made concrete and graphic.
- **Cosmic or unknowable horror**, where dread comes from confronting
  something beyond human understanding or control, often deliberately
  resisting full explanation.
- **Survival horror**, where the threat is escapable or defeatable in
  principle but genuinely, consistently dangerous, emphasizing resource
  management and vulnerability.
- **Horror-adjacent hybrids**, combining horror conventions with another
  genre's structure (horror-mystery, horror-LitRPG) — workable when the
  hybrid genre's other conventions don't undercut horror's core promise of
  genuine, sustained danger and some irreducible ambiguity.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A threat that remains genuinely dangerous across the manuscript, with
  competence and preparation mitigating but not eliminating risk.
- Some element of the story's central threat or mystery that resists full,
  tidy explanation, preserving irreducible unease even after a climax.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a story signaled as horror whose central
  threat is fully explained, fully defeated, and imposes no lasting cost
  by the story's end.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Over-explained threats**, where a horror story's central menace is
  fully rationalized and demystified, removing the ambiguity that
  sustains dread.
- **A threat rendered toothless by competence**, where the protagonist's
  established capability makes the danger feel manageable rather than
  genuinely threatening, undercutting horror's promise.
- **Borrowed conventions that compete with horror's promise**, where a
  hybrid genre's own conventions (a LitRPG system's helpful, reassuring
  interface; a mystery's tidy, fully-resolved reveal) work against
  sustained dread and ambiguity rather than supporting them.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this story's central threat remain genuinely dangerous throughout,
  or does the protagonist's growing competence make it feel manageable
  well before the climax?
- Is there some element of the story's central threat or mystery that
  resists full explanation, preserving unease even after resolution?
- If this story hybridizes horror with another genre's conventions, do
  those conventions support or compete with horror's core promise?
- Has the story signaled itself as horror clearly enough that a reader's
  genre expectations are correctly calibrated from the opening pages?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Audit the central threat's danger level across the manuscript; if it
   becomes fully manageable well before the climax, consider whether that
   serves the story's actual promise.
2. Identify one element of the central threat or mystery and test leaving
   it deliberately unresolved or ambiguous rather than fully explained.
3. For a horror-hybrid story, check whether the non-horror genre's
   conventions (a reassuring system voice, a fully tidy resolution)
   undercut sustained dread, and adjust if so.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story using horror imagery or aesthetics without pursuing the genre's
  core promise of managed, sustained dread (a comedic or ironic use of
  horror trappings) is using the convention differently, not failing to
  achieve it.
- Very brief horror interludes within a non-horror story don't need the
  sustained ambiguity and irreducible danger this pattern describes for a
  full-length treatment.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical horror structure — sustained dread, a genuinely dangerous and
not-fully-explained threat, real cost paid by the story's end — remains a
satisfying and reliable structure that doesn't require subversion to
deliver its core promise effectively.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a threat remains genuinely dangerous throughout, and whether
enough ambiguity is preserved to sustain dread, requires reading and
interpreting the manuscript's plot and pacing — a judgment no structured
data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Toothless threat:* A horror story's central menace is fully explained by
the midpoint and defeated through the protagonist's established combat
skill with no cost, leaving the remaining chapters without genuine danger.

*Sustained dread:* The same menace instead remains only partially
understood even after a costly confrontation, and the story's final
chapter includes a small, unresolved detail suggesting the threat — or
something like it — persists beyond the story's ending.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The genre-convention framing draws on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s
general survey, particularly its treatment of dark/horror LitRPG's
distinguishing conventions ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which
marks its subgenre material as partly inferential; no dedicated horror-
craft literature source was available to this drafting pass.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Mystery genre conventions
records.summary: Beyond the mystery plot's fair-play structure, the mystery genre carries its own sub-conventions — cozy, noir, procedural — each promising a different relationship to violence, moral complexity, and the detective's own competence, and mismatching them creates a different failure than a simply unfair reveal.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
This record addresses mystery as a genre with distinct sub-conventions
carrying their own reader promises, complementing this library's separate
mystery-plot record, which addresses the structural fair-play mechanics
that apply across all mystery variants. A cozy mystery promises a
relatively gentle relationship to violence (death often happens off-page
or is treated lightly), a community-embedded amateur detective, and a
restoration of order at the end. Noir promises moral ambiguity, a
compromised or world-weary detective, and often an ending that doesn't
fully restore order. A procedural promises institutional competence and
process — the mechanics of investigation itself as much of the draw as
the eventual answer. These aren't the only sub-conventions, but they
illustrate how "mystery" as a label covers genuinely different reader
promises that a story needs to calibrate to and signal clearly.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A reader who picks up a story signaled as cozy and encounters noir's moral
compromise and unresolved order (or vice versa) experiences a specific
kind of genre-promise violation distinct from an unfair mystery reveal —
the puzzle can be perfectly fair-played and the sub-genre mismatch will
still frustrate readers who came for a specific relationship to violence,
morality, and resolution that the story isn't delivering.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Cozy mystery**, gentle violence, community setting, amateur detective,
  restored order — promises comfort alongside puzzle-solving.
- **Noir**, moral ambiguity, a compromised detective, often unresolved or
  bittersweet order — promises atmosphere and complexity alongside puzzle-
  solving.
- **Procedural**, institutional process and competence as central
  interest, often with a professional detective operating within a
  system — promises methodical engagement alongside puzzle-solving.
- **Hardboiled**, closely related to noir but often more action-forward
  and terse in style — promises a specific voice and pace alongside
  puzzle-solving.
- **Genre-hybrid mystery**, combining mystery's puzzle structure with
  another genre's conventions (a fantasy mystery, a LitRPG mystery),
  requiring both genres' promises to be calibrated together rather than
  one undercutting the other.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A story's early tone, violence level, and detective characterization
  consistent with a specific, legible sub-convention throughout.
- A resolution whose degree of restored order (full, partial, or absent)
  matches what the story's sub-convention promised from the start.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a story opening with cozy signals
  (light tone, community warmth, gentle stakes) that shifts into
  noir-level moral compromise and unresolved consequence with no
  signaled transition.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Sub-convention drift**, where a story begins signaling one mystery
  sub-genre and ends delivering a different one, without the shift being
  a deliberate, signaled choice.
- **A hybrid mystery where the other genre's conventions overwhelm the
  puzzle**, leaving readers who came for the mystery half feeling
  shortchanged.
- **Mismatched detective characterization**, where a detective's
  established competence, morality, or worldview doesn't match the
  sub-genre's usual expectations, creating a subtle but persistent
  friction.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Which mystery sub-convention (cozy, noir, procedural, or another) does
  this story's opening actually signal, and does the rest of the
  manuscript deliver consistently on that signal?
- Does the ending's degree of restored order match what the opening
  promised?
- If this is a genre hybrid, do both genres' conventions get calibrated
  together, or does one undercut the other?
- Is the detective's characterization (competence, moral outlook)
  consistent with the sub-convention the story is otherwise signaling?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify which mystery sub-convention the opening chapters signal, and
   audit the rest of the manuscript for consistency with that signal.
2. For a story that drifts between sub-conventions, either adjust the
   opening to signal the eventual tone, or add a legible transition point.
3. For a genre hybrid, check that neither genre's conventions are
   silently overwhelming the other.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story deliberately subverting its own established sub-convention (a
  cozy mystery that reveals genuine, unresolved darkness beneath its
  comfortable surface, as its actual subject) is using the shift
  intentionally, provided it's legible as a choice.
- Very light or brief mystery elements within a larger, non-mystery story
  don't need a fully calibrated sub-convention.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical, consistently executed cozy, noir, or procedural mystery,
without genre-blending or subversion, remains a satisfying and reliable
structure — genre readers specifically seeking one of these established
promises are well served by a story that delivers it cleanly.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a story's tone, violence level, and resolution consistently match
a specific mystery sub-convention requires reading and interpreting the
manuscript's overall register — a judgment no structured data substitutes
for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Sub-convention drift:* A mystery opens in a small, warm village with a
gently curious amateur detective and light stakes, then shifts by the
midpoint into unresolved moral compromise and permanent, unmourned loss,
with no signal in the opening preparing readers for the tonal shift.

*Consistent sub-convention:* The same opening instead is followed by a
resolution that, while solving the central puzzle, restores the village's
sense of order and safety — consistent with the cozy promise the opening
made, even as the mystery itself involves real stakes along the way.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This record's sub-convention framing draws on general genre-taxonomy
reasoning informed by the broader craft-failure research's caution about
treating genre-specific conventions as universal
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated mystery-
subgenre craft source was available to this drafting pass.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Progression fiction reader expectations
records.summary: Readers who seek out progression fiction specifically want visible, trackable growth as a primary pleasure, not just a plot ingredient — a well-written story that treats progression as incidental can underperform for this readership even when it succeeds by other standards.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Readers who specifically seek out progression fiction — whether numeric
LitRPG or narrative progression fantasy — want visible, trackable growth
as a primary source of satisfaction, not merely as a plot ingredient
serving some other story. This distinguishes the genre's core readership
from readers of, say, epic fantasy generally, where a character's growth
might be present but isn't the central, load-bearing appeal the way it is
here. A well-crafted story that happens to feature power growth
incidentally to a differently-centered plot can succeed as a novel while
still disappointing readers who came specifically for the progression
genre's particular promise — this is a genre-calibration issue distinct
from general craft quality.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
This genre's readers track growth actively, often keeping mental (or
literal) tallies of a character's advancement, comparing builds, and
anticipating the next threshold. A story that treats growth as
backgrounded — happening, but not shown, tracked, or made satisfying in
its own right — asks this specific readership to accept a promise-
substitution: get an interesting plot instead of the growth-tracking
pleasure they came for. That can work if handled deliberately and
signaled early, but treated as an afterthought, it tends to read as a
missed opportunity specific to this genre's readership rather than a
general craft failure.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Growth-as-primary-pleasure**, where progression is dramatized in
  detail and given significant page time as a satisfaction in its own
  right, the genre's default and most reliable form.
- **Growth-in-service-of-plot**, where progression exists and matters but
  is deliberately kept lighter-touch in favor of a differently-centered
  story — workable, but benefits from clear early signaling so the right
  readers self-select in.
- **Growth-as-mystery**, where the specific mechanics of advancement are
  deliberately obscured or gradually revealed as their own source of
  interest, satisfying progression readers' tracking instinct through
  discovery rather than transparency.
- **Multi-character growth tracking**, where an ensemble cast's
  progression is tracked comparatively, appealing to readers who enjoy
  cross-character comparison as much as single-protagonist advancement.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Advancement events given dedicated narrative attention and space
  proportional to genre readers' expectation that growth is a primary
  draw, not an aside.
- A clear early signal (in tone, structure, or explicit framing) when a
  story is deliberately keeping progression lighter-touch in service of a
  different central focus.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: infrequent, minimally dramatized
  advancement events in a story otherwise signaling itself as core
  progression fantasy or LitRPG, without an apparent reason for the
  mismatch.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Progression treated as afterthought in a story signaled as
  progression-central**, disappointing the specific readership the
  signaling attracted.
- **No early signal when progression is deliberately backgrounded**,
  leaving readers to discover the mismatch mid-read rather than being able
  to self-select accurately from the outset.
- **Inconsistent growth-tracking density**, where advancement receives
  heavy attention early and then fades from narrative focus with no
  acknowledged shift in the story's priorities.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this manuscript's advancement receive narrative attention
  proportional to what its genre signaling (title, opening chapters,
  cover-adjacent framing) has promised?
- If progression is deliberately backgrounded in favor of a different
  focus, is that choice signaled early enough for readers to accurately
  self-select?
- Has the density of dramatized advancement events changed noticeably
  across the manuscript, and if so, is that shift acknowledged or
  unexplained?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Compare the manuscript's opening signals (tone, structure, explicit
   framing) against its actual advancement-event density; adjust
   whichever is out of alignment with the other.
2. If progression is deliberately secondary to another focus, add an early,
   clear signal (in tone or structure) that lets progression-primary
   readers self-select accurately.
3. Chart advancement-event density across the manuscript and investigate
   any unexplained drop.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories not signaling themselves as progression fantasy or LitRPG at all
  (general fantasy with incidental power growth) aren't subject to this
  genre's specific reader expectation.
- A story deliberately subverting progression-genre expectations as its
  actual point (a "progression fantasy" that reveals itself to be about
  something else entirely) is using the mismatch intentionally, provided
  it's a legible authorial choice rather than an unexamined drift.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical progression-fiction structure with growth as a consistently
dramatized, central pleasure throughout doesn't need subversion or
downplaying to succeed — delivering cleanly on this specific genre promise
is exactly what its core readership is looking for.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks advancement events linked to scenes,
their frequency and narrative space is directly observable. Whether that
density matches the story's genre signaling, and whether readers would
experience the balance as satisfying, requires interpreting the manuscript
and genre context and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Mismatched promise:* A story titled and opened in classic LitRPG
conventions — a stat screen shown in chapter one — features almost no
further advancement tracking for the next thirty chapters, which instead
focus entirely on political intrigue with power growth treated as
incidental.

*Signaled and consistent:* The same political-intrigue-focused story
instead opens by establishing its actual balance explicitly — a slower,
narrative-only progression system introduced without heavy stat-tracking
conventions — so readers calibrate their expectations correctly from the
outset rather than being promised one experience and given another.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The progression-as-primary-reader-pleasure framing draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of genre reader promises
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) and the broader craft-failure
research's treatment of promise consistency
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); both mark relevant
material as partly inferential or vendor-sourced. `source_confidence` is
`mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Science fiction genre conventions
records.summary: Science fiction readers expect speculative elements to be extrapolated with some rigor from a stated premise, and expect the story to actually explore the premise's implications rather than using it as decoration — the genre's core promise is thinking through a "what if," not just setting one dressing.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Science fiction as a genre convention promises that its speculative
elements — a technology, an alien contact, a changed physical law — will be
extrapolated with some rigor rather than treated as arbitrary set dressing.
Readers expect the story to actually think through a premise's
implications: if faster-than-light travel exists, what does that do to
politics, economics, and warfare; if a technology can read minds, what
does that do to law, privacy, and relationships. This is the genre's
version of the internal-consistency contract fantasy readers hold stories
to, applied specifically to extrapolated implication rather than
established magical rules — the difference being that science fiction's
promise is less about never breaking a stated rule and more about actually
following a premise's logic where it leads, including into places the
author might not have originally intended to go.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A science fiction premise that's introduced but never followed through —
a technology that changes nothing about how society functions, an alien
contact that has no lasting effect on humanity's self-understanding —
reads as a missed opportunity specifically because science fiction readers
are primed to expect and value that follow-through as the genre's central
pleasure. This is distinct from fantasy's consistency expectation: a
science fiction story isn't just avoiding contradiction, it's actively
expected to explore consequence.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Hard science fiction**, extrapolating with close attention to
  established physical science, holding itself to a high standard of
  technical plausibility.
- **Soft science fiction**, prioritizing social, psychological, or
  political extrapolation over strict technical rigor, still expected to
  follow its premises' implications even without hard-science grounding.
- **Space opera**, often treating some technological elements as
  convention rather than rigorously extrapolated, while still expected to
  follow through on its story's actual central premises (a galactic
  empire's politics, a specific technology's social effect).
- **Near-future or speculative fiction**, extrapolating from current
  trends or technologies, where readers may hold the story to an even
  higher standard of plausible consequence given the smaller conceptual
  distance from the present.
- **Science-fantasy hybrids**, blending SF's extrapolation-driven promise
  with fantasy's internal-consistency promise, requiring the story to
  honor both conventions where they apply.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A central speculative element whose social, political, or personal
  implications are traced through multiple scenes rather than remaining
  static background.
- A technology or premise's introduction followed by the story actually
  grappling with unintended or complicated consequences, not just the
  intended, convenient ones.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a technology or premise established
  early with dramatic implication, that the story then treats as static
  set dressing for its remaining length, never engaging what it would
  actually change.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Premise as decoration**, introducing a speculative element for
  atmosphere or plot convenience without extrapolating its implications.
- **Consequence-free technology**, where a stated capability (mind-
  reading, instant travel, resurrection-adjacent tech) never actually
  reshapes the plot, society, or relationships around it.
- **Inconsistent extrapolation**, where a technology's implications are
  followed through in one scene and ignored in another with no
  explanation.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this story's central speculative element actually change about
  society, politics, or daily life — and is that change shown, not just
  asserted?
- Is there an unintended or complicated consequence of the story's premise
  that hasn't been explored yet?
- Does the extrapolation stay consistent across the manuscript, or does
  the technology's implications get followed through in some scenes and
  ignored in others?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For the story's central speculative element, list three social,
   political, or personal consequences it would plausibly cause, and check
   how many are actually shown in the manuscript.
2. Find a convenient use of the premise and consider adding an
   inconvenient, complicating consequence nearby to balance it.
3. Audit the premise's application across the manuscript for consistency
   in how thoroughly its implications are followed.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Space opera and other convention-forward SF subgenres may deliberately
  treat some background elements (interstellar travel, translator
  technology) as genre furniture without extrapolation, provided the
  story's actual core premise still receives real follow-through.
- Very brief or minor speculative elements, not central to the story,
  don't need the full extrapolation treatment this pattern describes.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical hard-SF or soft-SF structure that rigorously follows its
premise's implications to a well-reasoned conclusion is a reliable and
satisfying structure that doesn't need to subvert genre expectations —
delivering on the extrapolation promise cleanly is often exactly what
science fiction readers are there for.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a speculative element's implications are adequately extrapolated
requires reading and interpreting the manuscript's worldbuilding and plot
as a whole — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Premise as decoration:* A story establishes that a device can transfer
memories between people, uses it once for a plot-convenient reveal, and
never explores what such a technology would do to law, identity, grief, or
relationships more broadly.

*Followed-through premise:* The same device instead drives a subplot about
a black market for stolen memories, a legal case over memory-based
inheritance disputes, and a character's crisis about whether a memory they
now hold is genuinely "theirs" — the premise's implications ripple outward
rather than staying contained to a single plot beat.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The extrapolation-as-genre-contract framing draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of genre conventions
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre material
as partly inferential; no dedicated science-fiction-craft literature source
was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: Serial fiction conventions
records.summary: Chapter-by-chapter serialized publishing shapes reader expectations that differ materially from a complete-book reading experience — each installment needs its own local satisfaction while the larger story keeps developing, a balance a manuscript written for one format doesn't automatically strike in the other.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Serial fiction — published and read chapter by chapter, typically online,
often with real-time reader engagement — carries its own set of reader
expectations distinct from a complete book read in one sustained session.
Each installment needs to offer some local satisfaction (a completed beat,
a forward-pulling hook, a reason the chapter was worth the reader's time
today specifically) even as the larger story continues developing across
many installments, and the gap between publication of one chapter and the
next changes how readers experience pacing, memory, and anticipation
compared to a reader who can turn the page immediately.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A serial reader's relationship to the text is fundamentally different from
a book reader's: they may wait days or weeks between installments, they
often engage with other readers' reactions and theories between chapters,
and they're actively deciding, chapter by chapter, whether to continue —
a decision a book reader mid-novel rarely faces in the same way. A
manuscript written with book-reading assumptions (long stretches with no
local payoff, expecting readers to hold complex information across many
undifferentiated chapters) can underperform in serial format even if it
would read perfectly well as a complete book, and vice versa.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Chapter-ending hook conventions**, where serial chapters conventionally
  end on a forward-pulling beat to encourage continued reading, distinct
  from a book chapter's freedom to end on a settled note.
- **Recap and memory-management conventions**, where serials often need to
  more actively remind readers of earlier context than a book would,
  since readers may return after a significant gap.
- **Real-time reader engagement**, where author awareness of reader
  reactions (comments, theories, requests) between installments can
  create pressure — productive or distorting — on ongoing plot decisions.
- **Episodic-with-throughline structure**, balancing local, chapter-level
  satisfaction against a larger arc's development, a structural challenge
  distinct from a book's more uniform pacing expectations.
- **Format-crossover works**, serials later compiled into books (or vice
  versa), which often benefit from revision to smooth conventions specific
  to one format that don't serve the other.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A chapter that offers both a completed local beat and a forward-pulling
  hook, balancing immediate satisfaction with continued anticipation.
- Strategic, economical reminders of earlier context placed where a
  returning reader would benefit from them, without over-explaining for
  readers who remember.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a serial chapter that ends on a fully
  settled note with no forward pull, or a chapter that assumes total
  recall of complex information established many installments earlier
  with no refresher.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Book-paced serials**, where chapters lack local satisfaction or hooks,
  reducing a reader's motivation to continue chapter by chapter.
- **Serial-paced books**, where a compiled book retains excessive
  recapping or overly frequent hook-chasing that reads as repetitive or
  manipulative outside the original serialized context.
- **Over-responsiveness to real-time reader reaction**, letting immediate
  audience feedback override a story's own planned direction in ways that
  compromise its longer-term coherence.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If this is serial fiction, does each chapter offer some local
  satisfaction alongside its forward pull, or does momentum depend
  entirely on hooks with no chapter-level payoff?
- Does the manuscript economically remind returning readers of context
  they might have forgotten, without over-explaining for readers who
  remember?
- If this serial is being compiled into a book, has it been revised to
  smooth serial-specific conventions (excessive recapping, hook-chasing)
  that don't serve continuous reading?
- Is real-time reader feedback shaping plot decisions in a way that
  serves the story's own planned direction, or working against it?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Audit a stretch of serial chapters for local satisfaction — does each
   one complete something, not just extend toward the next?
2. For a long-running serial, test whether a returning reader would have
   enough context reminders to follow a given chapter without rereading
   everything before it.
3. When compiling a serial into a book, identify and trim serial-specific
   conventions (frequent recaps, chapter-ending hooks that don't suit
   continuous reading) that don't serve the new format.
4. Review recent plot decisions for signs of over-responsiveness to
   reader feedback, and check them against the story's own original
   planned direction.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A manuscript written and intended only for complete-book publication
  doesn't need to adopt serial-specific conventions.
- A deliberately experimental serial structure (irregular chapter lengths,
  minimal hooks, literary pacing) may intentionally forgo standard serial
  conventions as part of its identity, provided that choice serves the
  work's actual intended audience.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript's pacing and structure are calibrated to serial or
book-reading conventions requires reading and interpreting its chapter-by-
chapter structure — a judgment no structured data substitutes for. This
pattern also touches on practice concerns (real-time reader responsiveness)
that aren't observable from the manuscript text alone.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Book-paced serial:* A serial chapter ends with its scene fully resolved,
no open question, no forward pull, and no local payoff distinct from
simply continuing the previous chapter's momentum — a reader has little
specific reason to return for the next installment versus reading it
later.

*Calibrated serial chapter:* The same scene instead resolves its immediate
local conflict (giving the chapter its own sense of completion) while
ending on a specific new complication that wasn't present at the chapter's
start — satisfying on its own terms while still pulling the reader
forward.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The serial-versus-book reading experience distinction draws on the
broader craft-failure research's platform-conventions material, itself
sourced from vendor-reported and forum practitioner discussion
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated academic
or literary-craft source specifically addressing serial fiction structure
was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: A cluster of fatigue-sensitive LitRPG conventions
records.summary: Five conventions one working author ranks as the genre's most-fatigued — an overpowered lead with no real struggle, large ensemble romantic casts, a secret lost class or item, an exposition-delivering comic-relief companion, and a uniformly attractive supporting cast — are each commercially viable and each reported as a source of reader fatigue at the same time, and this record treats both facts as true rather than resolving the tension.

citations.label: Top 5 Overused LitRPG Tropes
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A working LitRPG author, writing candidly for peers about his own
observations of the genre, ranked five conventions as the ones he sees
most often drawing reader fatigue: an overpowered main character who never
struggles meaningfully, a harem or large ensemble romantic cast, a secret
lost class or item no one else in the setting has heard of in centuries, an
exposition-dispensing comic-relief companion, and a supporting cast of
uniformly attractive women. This is one author's personal, ranked opinion
about his own reading experience — not a survey, not a study, and not
this library's judgment about any of these conventions' inherent worth.
Every item on this list is also, demonstrably, commercially successful:
these conventions appear constantly in the genre's bestselling work.
Holding "readers report fatigue with this" and "this sells extremely
well" as simultaneously, unresolvedly true is this record's actual
position — a coach that tells an author not to write what sells is wrong;
a coach that pretends there's no fatigue risk at all is useless. The goal
here is descriptive: naming what each convention promises, what produces
fatigue when it's handled unexamined, and what freshens it when an author
wants to use it deliberately.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Each convention below is popular for a specific, real reason — readers
seek out and enjoy all five, and this genre's bestselling work proves it.
Fatigue, where it's reported, comes from a specific mechanism particular
to each convention (named per item below), not from the convention's mere
presence. A coach that only names "this is popular" or only names "this
tires some readers" gives an author half the picture; both facts matter to
a deliberate choice.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
The five conventions below are this record's forms; each is treated in its
own section rather than compressed into a list, because their promises and
their fatigue mechanisms are genuinely different from one another and a
single summary would flatten them. Two variations cut across all five.
First, intensity: most appear on a spectrum from a light touch that few
readers notice to a saturated version that becomes the book's identity, and
fatigue reports cluster at the saturated end. Second, subgenre: what reads
as overused in classic LitRPG may be the expected promise elsewhere — a
power fantasy's overpowered protagonist is doing the job that subgenre's
readers arrived for. Deliberate inversions of all five are common and are
treated in the inversions-and-combinations record rather than repeated here.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
Common forms and variants for each of the five conventions, and the
specific mechanism that produces reader fatigue when the convention is
handled without individual development, are addressed together below,
convention by convention, rather than as separate generic sections — the
five items are different enough from each other that a single shared
"forms and variants" list would blur distinctions worth keeping separate.

sections.title: The overpowered protagonist with no real struggle
sections.content:
**What it promises:** an uncomplicated power fantasy — competence without
anxiety, a reader who gets to relax into watching the protagonist win.
**What produces fatigue:** when "no real struggle" extends to no stakes at
all, removing the tension this library's stakes and agency patterns
depend on; readers describe this specifically as boredom, not offense.
**What freshens it:** relocating the story's actual tension to a different
axis — social, moral, relational — so the character's overwhelming combat
or magical competence doesn't have to be the source of drama the plot
needs (see this library's negative-space-problems-power-cannot-solve
pattern).

sections.title: Harems and large ensemble romantic casts
sections.content:
**What it promises:** abundance, and for some readers, a lower-pressure
alternative to a single, exclusive romantic arc's usual obstacles. **What
produces fatigue:** when the ensemble functions as interchangeable
romantic options with underdeveloped individual identity, undercutting the
character-development stakes this library's supporting-cast-purpose and
romantic-subplot-conventions patterns describe. This is a structural
critique about characterization depth, not a judgment about the
relationship model itself — a large ensemble cast where each member has a
distinct, developed want and relationship to the protagonist doesn't
generate the same fatigue as one where they don't. **What freshens it:**
applying this library's supporting-cast-purpose pattern rigorously to each
member of the ensemble, so the cast's size doesn't come at the cost of
individual development.

sections.title: The secret lost class or item no one has heard of in centuries
sections.content:
**What it promises:** specialness and destiny, tying into the chosen-one
trope's core appeal. **What produces fatigue:** when the secrecy and
