rarity are asserted rather than earned, and when "no one has heard of it
in centuries" starts to feel like a convenient absence of competition
rather than a meaningful worldbuilding fact — closely related to this
library's chosen-one and competent-others patterns. **What freshens it:**
giving the secrecy an in-world cause (the knowledge was deliberately
suppressed, lost in a specific catastrophe, or requires an unusual
circumstance to rediscover) rather than leaving it as an unexplained
absence, and letting the discovery cost something.

sections.title: The exposition-dispensing comic-relief companion
sections.content:
**What it promises:** levity and accessible information delivery. **What
produces fatigue:** when the character has no function beyond those two
roles, exactly the failure this library's companion and mentor records
describe as "the exposition dispenser" — present to explain things and
lighten the mood, with no independent want or arc. **What freshens it:**
giving the character a want unrelated to their functional role, per this
library's supporting-cast-purpose pattern, so their comic timing and
explanatory usefulness sit on top of an actual person rather than
substituting for one.

sections.title: A supporting cast of uniformly attractive women
sections.content:
**What it promises:** a specific aesthetic register some readers
explicitly enjoy. **What produces fatigue:** when physical uniformity
substitutes for the differentiated characterization this library's voice
and supporting-cast-purpose patterns describe — readers report fatigue
specifically when a cast reads as interchangeable, and physical uniformity
is one visible symptom of that deeper interchangeability, not
necessarily its cause. This record makes no claim about what any
individual reader finds appealing in a cast's appearance; the craft
concern is specifically whether appearance-level similarity correlates
with — or substitutes for — deeper character-level similarity. **What
freshens it:** the same fix as the harem item above — distinct wants,
voices, and relationships to the protagonist, independent of any
description of appearance.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
The failure modes worth naming here run in both directions, and the second
direction is the one a coach is more likely to cause.

Using a convention unexamined: adopting it because the genre supplied it
rather than because the story wants what it offers, which tends to produce
the saturated version by default, since nothing in the draft is deciding how
much of it to use. Related: keeping the convention's shape after the story
has outgrown its purpose — a companion who is still explaining mechanics the
reader mastered twenty chapters ago.

Overreacting to fatigue talk: dropping a convention the author actually
wants to write, on the strength of a list like this one; treating
"subverted" as automatically better than "executed well," which produces
its own recognizable fatigue; or hedging a convention so thoroughly that the
book delivers neither the original promise nor a clear alternative. A
reader who came for this convention and found a half-hearted apology for it
has been served worse than one who found it done wholeheartedly.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- For any of these five conventions present in this manuscript, does the
  fatigue-producing mechanism (no real stakes, interchangeable cast
  members, unearned secrecy, function without personhood) actually apply
  here, or has the convention already been handled with the kind of
  individual development that avoids it?
- Is this convention being used because it serves this specific story, or
  because it's expected of the genre?
- If a convention here is core to what this book is trying to be, would a
  reader who's fatigued by the convention in its unexamined form still
  find something distinct in this particular execution?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For any convention from this cluster present in the manuscript, apply
   this library's relevant cross-referenced pattern (supporting-cast-
   purpose, negative-space, chosen-one, companion) directly and check
   whether the specific fatigue mechanism named above is actually present.
2. If a large ensemble cast is present, write one distinct want for each
   member independent of their relationship to the protagonist.
3. If a secret lost class or item is present, add an in-world reason for
   its obscurity rather than leaving the rarity unexplained.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Every convention in this cluster has a straightforward, well-executed
  form that doesn't require subversion — this record's purpose is naming
  the fatigue mechanism precisely enough that an author can choose
  deliberately, not steering authors away from commercially proven,
  reader-loved conventions.
- A story deliberately and knowingly leaning into one of these conventions
  for its established audience, with full awareness of both its appeal
  and its fatigue risk, is making an informed choice this record supports
  rather than overrides.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a specific instance of any of these conventions triggers the
fatigue mechanism described, or avoids it through individual
characterization, requires reading and interpreting the manuscript
directly — a judgment no structured data substitutes for, and one this
library is careful not to present as a verdict on the convention's
inherent worth.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
Not included as a single pair here, given the cluster's five distinct
sub-conventions each already illustrated by its own "what freshens it"
guidance above; see this library's related supporting-cast-purpose,
chosen-one, and companion records for fuller worked examples of the
underlying mechanisms this cluster shares.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This entire record is built on a single working author's candid, ranked,
first-person list of what he personally observes as overused
([[src.oster.overused-tropes]]) — explicitly a lead, not a finding, per
this corpus's confidence-marking standard, and `docs/research-litrpg-
craft-failures.md` treats it the same way
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]], pattern P23), naming the
open question of how opinionated trope coaching should be about
commercially successful but fatigue-associated conventions. This record
does not resolve that open question; it deliberately holds "fatigued" and
"commercially successful" as both true rather than picking one.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` to reflect the single-source basis
for the entire cluster's framing.

records.title: Amnesia and lost memory
records.summary: A protagonist without their own past, which hands the story a natural reason to explain the world and a standing question about who this person will turn out to have been.

citations.label: Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An amnesiac protagonist has lost access to their own history — entirely, or
in a specific gap — and the story proceeds while that history is recovered,
replaced, or permanently lost. The convention does two things at once. It
justifies explanation, since a character who knows nothing may be told
things, and it poses a question the reader carries throughout: who was this
person, and will they want to be that again?

It is adjacent to hidden identity, treated separately here. The difference is
where the ignorance sits: in a hidden-identity plot the protagonist knows and
the world does not; in amnesia the world may know and the protagonist does
not, which reverses the direction of tension.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The convention offers a clean version of a pleasure the genre runs on: a
protagonist and reader learning the world together, with no artificial
reason for the character to be uninformed. It also creates a rare structural
situation in which the protagonist's own identity is the mystery, so
characterization and plot advance in the same movement.

The deeper appeal is a question about the self: whether a person is their
history or their present conduct. A recovered past that contradicts the
character the reader has come to know forces that question rather than
merely posing it.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Total amnesia** — no past at all, the most convenient for exposition and
  the most likely to leave the protagonist thin until a past arrives.
- **The specific gap** — one period missing, usually the one that matters,
  which keeps the character intact while withholding the crucial fact.
- **Suppressed or stolen memory** — memory removed by another party, which
  supplies an antagonist and a reason.
- **Recovered-in-fragments** — memory returning in pieces the reader
  assembles, closest in structure to a mystery plot.
- **Permanent loss** — the past never recovered, so the story is about
  building an identity rather than restoring one. The least common and often
  the most interesting.
- **The unwelcome past** — recovery reveals someone the protagonist does not
  want to be, converting the arc into a choice rather than a restoration.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character asking questions the reader also has, without the story
  contriving a reason for their ignorance.
- Skills or reflexes that survive the memory loss, which characterize the
  lost self before the story reveals it.
- Other characters who knew the protagonist before, whose behavior tells the
  reader what the protagonist cannot remember.
- Conversely: an amnesiac whose condition affects nothing except how much
  exposition they receive.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Amnesia as an exposition license.** The condition exists so the world
  can be explained, and does nothing else to the story.
- **The blank protagonist.** No past and no formed present, so there is no
  one for the reader to attach to during the stretch before recovery.
- **Convenient recall.** Memory returning precisely when the plot requires a
  fact, which teaches the reader that the condition is a device.
- **The unearned identity.** A revealed past that arrives as information
  rather than as a problem, changing nothing about who the character is
  choosing to be.
- **Restoration without consequence.** Memory recovered and the character
  simply resumes, so the intervening chapters turn out not to have mattered.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
The plain version works, and it works often. A protagonist who has lost their
past, learns the world alongside the reader, and eventually discovers
something about themselves is a durable structure with a clear promise, and
readers who pick up such a book are asking for exactly that.

Straightforward execution asks for one thing: that the character be someone
during the gap. An amnesiac with present-tense preferences, fears,
competences, and a way of treating people is not blank, and everything else
the convention offers rests on that. The version that disappoints is not the
familiar one — it is the one where nobody is home until the past arrives.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Who is this character *now*, independent of what they have forgotten?
- What does the amnesia cost them, beyond information?
- Who else knows, and what do they want from a person who cannot remember?
- When the past returns, does it change what the protagonist does — or only
  what the reader knows?
- If memory were never recovered, would this story still have an ending?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write a page of the protagonist making an ordinary decision, with no
   reference to the missing past. If it is hard to write, the character may
   currently be a gap rather than a person.
2. Give the lost self a trait that survives — a skill, a fear, an instinct —
   and let it appear before any explanation.
3. Move a memory recovery earlier and see what the story does with the extra
   time. Recoveries often sit late because they are being saved rather than
   used.
4. Draft the version where recovery is unwelcome, and see whether it makes a
   better ending than restoration.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Mystery and thriller structures where the amnesia is the case being
  investigated and the protagonist's blankness is the premise the reader
  signed up for.
- Comedic treatments, where memory loss is a device for farce and examining
  its costs would break the register.
- Stories about dementia, injury, or trauma, where memory loss is a
  represented condition rather than a plot convention — the questions in this
  record are about a narrative device and should not be applied to those
  books without care.
- Portal and reincarnation premises where an unfamiliar world, not lost
  memory, supplies the learning-alongside-the-reader effect.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Very little here is computable. A coach might locate memory-recovery scenes
by their vocabulary and note where they fall in the manuscript, and might
observe whether the protagonist is given non-plot preferences and habits
during the gap. Neither is reliable, and both misfire in books where memory
is discussed for other reasons.

Whether an amnesiac protagonist is a person or a gap is a semantic judgment
of exactly the kind this library treats as model-assisted at best. A coach
should raise the question rather than answer it, and should be especially
careful not to treat a deliberately blank protagonist as an error, since
that is a real technique with its own tradition.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*A gap rather than a person:* he did not know his name, his home, or his
trade, and so he listened while Maera explained the six kingdoms, the war,
and the succession. He asked a follow-up question about the succession.

*A person during the gap:* he did not know his name, but he knew he could not
stand being lied to, and he knew it the way you know a burn — before he had
worked out why, he had already stood up and walked out of Maera's kitchen.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Orson Scott Card's treatment of characterization and reader attachment
([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supports this record's central
argument: that a protagonist must give the reader something to attach to in
the present, independent of backstory. The remainder of the record — the
taxonomy of variants, the failure modes, the diagnostics, and the
hidden-identity contrast — is this drafting pass's synthesis, marked
explicitly with [[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]] rather than
attributed to a source that does not make these claims.

`source_confidence` is `limited`. No dedicated craft-literature or scholarly
treatment of the amnesia convention was available to this drafting pass, and
the record should be read as structured reasoning about a widely recognized
device rather than as sourced analysis of it. This is a revision-pass target:
memory and identity in narrative have a real critical literature, and a later
pass with access to it should revisit this record before the author vets it.
The note above about dementia and trauma is a deliberate boundary, not a
sourced clinical claim, and nothing here should be read as guidance about
representing real memory disorders.

records.title: Betrayal
records.summary: A trusted character acts against the protagonist's interests — its impact depends almost entirely on whether the reader can trace the betrayer's choice back to an established, coherent motive once it's revealed.

citations.label: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A betrayal occurs when a character the protagonist trusts acts against
their interests, whether through a single decisive act or an accumulating
pattern of deception. The trope's emotional force comes specifically from
the violated trust, which means its craft success depends heavily on
whether the betrayer's motive is coherent and, ideally, traceable in
hindsight to behavior the story already showed — a betrayal that reads as
an arbitrary personality flip rather than a revealed, consistent
motivation undercuts the emotional payoff the trope is built to deliver.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Betrayal weaponizes a reader's own investment in a relationship the story
has built — the more genuine the trust seemed, the more the violation
lands. This makes betrayal one of the highest-risk, highest-reward tropes
in terms of setup: a well-earned betrayal recontextualizes everything the
betrayer did before it, often improving the reader's retrospective read of
earlier scenes; a poorly set-up one can retroactively damage the reader's
trust in the story's characterization generally, not just their trust in
the specific betrayer.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Ideologically motivated betrayal**, where the betrayer acts from a
  genuine, differing value system rather than personal gain — often the
  most sympathetic and complex variant.
- **Self-interested betrayal**, motivated by personal gain, safety, or
  advancement, straightforward but requiring the stakes of that
  self-interest to be established credibly.
- **Coerced betrayal**, where the betrayer acts against their will under
  threat or manipulation — shifts some of the moral weight onto whoever is
  doing the coercing.
- **Long-game betrayal**, revealed to have been planned or building for a
  substantial portion of the story, requiring careful retroactive
  consistency across many earlier scenes.
- **Impulsive betrayal**, a single decisive act under pressure rather than
  a sustained plan — different craft demands (the impulse needs to be
  consistent with an established weakness, rather than long-game
  consistency across many scenes).
- **Betrayal revealed to be misunderstood**, where what looked like
  betrayal turns out to have a different explanation — effective when fair-
  played, risky when it undercuts real stakes established earlier.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A betrayal's reveal that recontextualizes earlier scenes, with the
  betrayer's prior behavior rereadable as consistent with the revealed
  motive.
- The betrayed character's reaction given real narrative space, not
  resolved or moved past too quickly given the relationship's established
  weight.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a betrayal that requires the betrayer to
  have acted inconsistently with everything previously established about
  them, with no acknowledgment of the discontinuity.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The unmotivated betrayal**, where the betrayer's turn serves the plot's
  needs with no coherent motive traceable in their established
  characterization.
- **Retroactively inconsistent characterization**, where earlier scenes
  don't actually support the revealed motive on a reread, breaking rather
  than deepening on reexamination.
- **An under-processed emotional aftermath**, where the betrayed
  character's reaction is resolved too quickly given the relationship's
  established significance.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If a reader rereads the betrayer's earlier scenes knowing what's
  revealed, are they consistent with the eventual motive, or does the
  reveal require ignoring earlier characterization?
- Does the betrayed character's reaction receive narrative space
  proportional to the relationship's established significance?
- Is the betrayer's motive coherent and traceable, or does the betrayal
  serve the plot's convenience more than the character's established
  nature?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Reread the betrayer's earlier scenes with the eventual reveal in mind
   and check for consistency; add or adjust earlier details if the motive
   doesn't hold up on a reread.
2. Expand the betrayed character's reaction if it currently resolves too
   quickly given the relationship's weight.
3. For a long-game betrayal, trace the betrayer's actions across the whole
   manuscript and confirm none of them require them to have acted against
   their revealed motive.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A very minor betrayal (a small deception with limited stakes) doesn't
  need the full retroactive-consistency treatment this pattern describes.
- A story deliberately depicting an inexplicable, senseless act of betrayal
  as its subject (examining how trust can be violated without a fully
  legible reason) may use motivational ambiguity intentionally, provided
  that ambiguity itself is engaged rather than simply unaddressed.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical betrayal with a clear, well-established, self-interested or
ideological motive remains a satisfying and reliable structure — it doesn't
need moral complexity or ambiguity to land, provided the betrayer's
established characterization actually supports the turn when it happens.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a betrayal's motive is traceable to established characterization
requires rereading and comparing the betrayer's actions across the whole
manuscript — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unmotivated betrayal:* A loyal companion suddenly reveals they've been
working against the protagonist for unstated reasons, with nothing in
their prior appearances suggesting any conflicting loyalty or motive.

*Earned betrayal:* The same companion's earlier scenes instead show
repeated, small moments of unease around a specific topic (their family's
debt to the antagonist), each individually explainable but retrospectively
clear once the betrayal is revealed — a reread confirms the motive was
present all along.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The retroactive-consistency principle for character reveals draws on Robert
McKee's general writing on characterization and reveal structure
([[src.book.mckee-story]]); no dedicated craft-literature source
specifically addressing betrayal-plot structure was available to this
drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Hidden identity and secret heritage
records.summary: A protagonist's true name, lineage, or nature is concealed — from other characters, the reader, or both — and its reveal is only as strong as the consequences it triggers, not the surprise itself.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A hidden identity or secret heritage conceals something true and
significant about the protagonist — a royal bloodline, a forbidden power, a
past life, a connection to the antagonist — from some or all of the story's
characters, the reader, or both. The concealment can be a source of dramatic
irony (reader knows, characters don't), mystery (neither knows yet), or
both in sequence as the reveal is staged across the narrative.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A concealed identity creates a specific kind of anticipation: the reader
watches other characters interact with the protagonist without full
information, aware that the dynamic will shift once the truth surfaces.
The trope's payoff depends heavily on what changes once the secret is known
— readers report the strongest satisfaction when the reveal has real social,
relational, or plot consequences, and the weakest when the reveal changes
surprisingly little about how the story proceeds.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Reader-known, character-blind**, where the reader is let in on the
  secret early, generating sustained dramatic irony as other characters
  remain unaware.
- **Mutual mystery**, where the protagonist themselves doesn't know their
  own heritage, and the reveal is a discovery for character and reader
  together.
- **Character-known, reader-blind**, rarer, where the protagonist
  consciously conceals something the reader isn't told until later —
  requires careful POV management to avoid feeling like a cheat (see the
  related information-control pattern).
- **Partial concealment**, where some characters know and others don't,
  creating layered dramatic irony and differing stakes depending on who's
  present in a given scene.
- **Cursed or dangerous heritage**, where the concealment exists specifically
  because revelation carries genuine risk (persecution, obligation,
  targeting by enemies), giving the secret's protection real narrative
  weight beyond simple mystery.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Scenes where other characters' behavior toward the protagonist would
  plausibly change if they knew the secret, creating tension the reader can
  feel even before any character reacts.
- A reveal scene followed by visible, lasting change in relationships, plot
  direction, or the protagonist's own choices.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a reveal that generates a brief reaction
  scene and then changes essentially nothing about how the story proceeds.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The inconsequential reveal**, where the secret's disclosure doesn't
  meaningfully alter relationships or plot direction, undercutting the
  buildup that preceded it.
- **Concealment maintained past plausibility**, where characters who would
  reasonably have discovered or suspected the secret remain unaware for
  implausibly long, straining credibility rather than building tension.
- **A reveal used only for shock**, without the story engaging its
  consequences in the chapters that follow.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- When this secret is finally revealed, what specifically changes about how
  other characters treat the protagonist, or how the plot proceeds?
- Is the concealment maintained at a pace that stays plausible given what
  characters would reasonably notice or suspect?
- If this is a mutual mystery, does the protagonist's discovery process feel
  earned, or does the information simply arrive?
- Does the reveal's aftermath get real narrative space, or does the story
  move on quickly once the surprise has landed?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one paragraph describing what specifically changes — in
   relationships, plot, or the protagonist's own choices — once the secret
   is revealed; if the answer is thin, the reveal may need more
   consequence built in.
2. Check the plausibility of continued concealment against what characters
   in close contact with the protagonist would reasonably notice, and
   adjust either the concealment's carefulness or its duration.
3. Add a scene in the aftermath of the reveal that shows a specific,
   lasting consequence, rather than moving directly back to the main plot.
4. For a mutual-mystery structure, check that clues available to the
   protagonist are also fairly available to the reader, so the eventual
   discovery doesn't depend on offscreen information.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story where the "secret" is genuinely low-stakes and known to function
  as light dramatic irony rather than a major plot engine doesn't need
  heavy reveal consequences to succeed.
- Very short concealment periods (a secret revealed within the same
  chapter it's introduced) don't need the sustained plausibility management
  longer concealments require.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical hidden-royal or secret-heritage reveal, executed with a clear
and consequential aftermath, remains a satisfying and reliable structure —
its recognizability doesn't require subversion, provided the reveal actually
changes something the reader can see.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a reveal generates meaningful, lasting consequence, and whether
continued concealment remains plausible, requires reading and interpreting
the manuscript's characterization and plot structure — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Inconsequential reveal:* A protagonist is revealed to be the exiled heir to
a kingdom; the surrounding cast expresses surprise for one scene, and the
story continues exactly as it would have otherwise.

*Consequential reveal:* The same revelation instead triggers a companion's
quiet withdrawal (they'd been protecting the protagonist out of pity, not
respect, and the truth reframes their whole relationship), and a faction
that had been sheltering the protagonist now has to weigh the political risk
of continuing to do so — the reveal changes the shape of several
relationships and a plot thread at once.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The reveal-consequence framing draws on the broader craft-failure pattern
research's general treatment of setup, payoff, and reader trust
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated source on
hidden-identity structure specifically was available to this drafting pass.
`source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly, and a revision pass
should add a stronger dedicated source before author sign-off.

records.title: Resurrection
records.summary: A character returns from death — the trope's credibility depends on whether death's stakes are restored afterward, since a world with easy resurrection needs a different relationship to mortal danger than a world without it.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A resurrection trope brings a character back from death, whether through
magic, technology, divine intervention, or a system mechanic. Its central
craft challenge is downstream rather than immediate: once a story has
established that death can be undone, it has changed what death means for
every character going forward, and the story needs a deliberate answer for
how mortal stakes work afterward — otherwise resurrection can quietly
drain tension from every future life-or-death scene, since a reader who's
seen one death undone will reasonably wonder whether the next one will
stick.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A resurrection can be one of a story's most emotionally significant
moments — reversing grief, restoring a relationship, offering a second
chance. But that same power, once established, becomes information the
reader carries into every subsequent dangerous scene. If resurrection is
easy, cheap, or reliably available, later deaths (or near-deaths) need to
either explain why this specific case can't be resurrected, or accept that
mortal stakes have permanently changed for the story going forward — a
story that ignores this shift and expects future deaths to carry the same
weight as before the first resurrection is asking for something it hasn't
earned.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Rare, costly resurrection**, available but at a steep price (a finite
  resource, a significant sacrifice, a narrow window), keeping death mostly
  meaningful while allowing this specific exception.
- **Common or reliable resurrection**, available with modest cost or
  limitation, requiring the story to actively redesign what stakes mean
  going forward (see the related death-and-respawn record).
- **Incomplete or costly-return resurrection**, where the returned
  character comes back changed, diminished, or marked by the experience —
  keeping the resurrection itself consequential even if death's finality is
  compromised.
- **One-time or unique resurrection**, established as a singular event that
  cannot be repeated, preserving normal mortal stakes for every death after
  this one.
- **Resurrection with social or systemic consequence**, where the returned
  character's status, legal standing, or relationships are complicated by
  their having died and returned — engaging the systemic-social-
  consequences pattern directly.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A resurrection's cost, limitation, or uniqueness established clearly
  enough that the reader understands why future deaths won't necessarily
  follow the same pattern.
- The returned character shown to be affected by their death and return —
  physically, psychologically, or socially — rather than restored exactly
  to their prior state with no trace.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a resurrection with no stated cost or
  limitation, followed by later scenes that expect the reader to feel full
  mortal stakes for other characters with no acknowledgment of the
  precedent.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unaddressed precedent**, where a resurrection's implications for future
  mortal stakes are never engaged, leaving later "deaths" feeling
  provisional by association.
- **A costless, traceless resurrection**, where the returned character is
  restored with no lasting effect, understating an event that should carry
  real weight.
- **Resurrection used repeatedly without escalating cost or scrutiny**,
  cheapening the mechanic each additional time it's used.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Once this resurrection has occurred, what does the reader now understand
  about how permanent death is in this world going forward?
- Does the returned character show any lasting effect of their death and
  return?
- If a later character's death needs to carry full mortal stakes, does the
  story explain why this later case can't follow the same path as the
  earlier resurrection?
- Has resurrection's cost or difficulty stayed consistent, or has the
  system been used more freely as the story progressed?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Establish explicitly what the resurrection cost, and audit later
   life-or-death scenes to confirm the reader would understand why this
   precedent doesn't apply (or does).
2. Add a lasting effect — physical, psychological, or social — to the
   returned character if they're currently restored with no trace.
3. If resurrection recurs, check whether its cost or difficulty escalates
   or stays consistent, and adjust if it's being used too freely.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story explicitly built around a setting where death is never permanent
  (a genuinely consequence-light or comedic register) doesn't need to
  preserve traditional mortal stakes at all — this pattern applies when a
  story wants both an emotional resurrection and continued high-stakes
  mortality elsewhere.
- A single, clearly unique resurrection with no repetition and an explicit
  "never again" framing largely sidesteps the ongoing-precedent concern.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A single, costly, clearly unique resurrection used once at a story's most
significant moment, with the rest of the narrative maintaining normal
mortal stakes, is a reliable and emotionally powerful structure that
doesn't require extensive systemic examination — the uniqueness itself is
what preserves the precedent problem from ever arising.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a resurrection's precedent is adequately addressed in later scenes
requires tracking mortal-stakes scenes across the whole manuscript for
consistency — a judgment no structured data substitutes for. Where a
project explicitly tracks character death/revival events, their frequency
and stated cost are directly observable.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unaddressed precedent:* A beloved mentor is resurrected through a costly
ritual in the story's first act; by the climax, a different character's
death is played for full, permanent grief with no acknowledgment that
resurrection is a known possibility in this world.

*Addressed precedent:* The same resurrection is instead established as
requiring a specific, non-repeatable artifact destroyed in the process, and
when the climactic death occurs, a character explicitly notes that the
artifact is gone and no comparable option exists — the reader's
understanding of the world's rules is honored rather than contradicted.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The precedent-and-stakes framing draws on the broader craft-failure
research's general treatment of established limits staying established
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]], pattern P15, applied here
specifically to resurrection); no dedicated craft-literature source
specifically addressing resurrection-plot structure was available to this
drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: The double and the impostor
records.summary: Someone who is not who they appear to be, or who appears to be someone else — a convention whose tension lives entirely in the gap between what the reader knows and what the characters do.

citations.label: Morphology of the Folktale
Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)
Craft-library editorial synthesis

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A double is a duplicate — a twin, a shapeshifter, a copy, a mirror-self. An
impostor is someone occupying an identity that is not theirs. The two are
often treated as one convention because they produce the same structural
situation: a person in the story is not who the people around them believe,
and the story's tension comes from that gap.

It is adjacent to hidden identity, which this library treats separately.
There, a character conceals something true about themselves. Here, someone is
actively presenting as another specific person — which raises a different
question, since a real person is being displaced.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The convention is a pure information-control instrument, and it works in
either configuration. If the reader knows and the characters do not, every
ordinary scene acquires dread: watching someone confide in the wrong person
is uncomfortable in a way little else reproduces. If the reader does not
know, the eventual reveal reframes everything they have read, which is a
distinct and stronger single-use pleasure.

Beneath that sits the older appeal: the double asks what a person actually
consists of. If someone has your memories, your capabilities, and your face,
what is missing — and does the story think the answer matters?

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The replacement** — the original removed and someone installed in their
  place, with the question of what happened to them running underneath.
- **The infiltrator** — an impostor with an objective, where the tension is
  whether they will be caught before achieving it.
- **The unwitting double** — a duplicate who believes they are the original,
  which makes them sympathetic and the situation tragic rather than sinister.
- **The mirror self** — a double who represents what the protagonist could
  become, closer to a thematic device than a deception plot.
- **The system copy** — a genre-specific version where duplication is a
  mechanic rather than a magic, which raises the ownership and identity
  questions explicitly.
- **The suspected impostor** — nobody is a double, and the fear that someone
  might be does the work. Cheap to set up, and surprisingly durable.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Small wrongnesses noticed by one character and dismissed by everyone else.
- A test someone devises, and what it costs to administer it.
- A scene the reader watches through their knowledge of the deception, where
  nothing overt happens.
- Conversely: an impostor who is never nearly caught, which converts the
  situation from tension into a waiting period.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The undetectable double.** A duplicate so perfect that no one could ever
  find out, which removes the possibility of near-misses and therefore most
  of the tension.
- **The idiot ball.** Characters failing to notice what the reader can see
  plainly, which makes them look foolish rather than deceived.
- **The reveal with no aftermath.** The impostor exposed, and the story
  moving on without the damage — the trust broken, the decisions made on
  false information.
- **The vanished original.** A person displaced and never accounted for,
  which the story usually owes an answer to.
- **Duplication without a question.** A copy that raises no issue about
  identity in a story where it plainly should.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
The plain infiltrator plot is durable and needs no reinvention. Establish the
impostor, let the reader know before the characters do, give one person
suspicions nobody credits, and let the pressure build toward exposure.
Readers know the shape and the recognition is part of the pleasure.

The one requirement is that catching them be possible. A double who could be
found out — through a detail, a relationship, a test — generates tension in
every scene; a perfect one generates none, because nothing is at stake in any
individual moment. That is the difference between a working version and a
frustrating one, and it is a design decision more than a writing one.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Who could find out, and what would it take?
- Does the reader know? Should they, and from when?
- What happened to the person being impersonated, and does the story answer?
- What does the impostor want that requires being this specific person?
- After the reveal, what is broken that cannot be repaired by knowing?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Give one character a genuine reason for suspicion and no way to prove it,
   and follow them for a chapter.
2. Write the near-miss: the impostor almost exposed, and what it costs them
   to recover.
3. Try the other information configuration — tell the reader early instead of
   late, or the reverse — for one scene, and see which story you would rather
   write.
4. Write the aftermath scene where someone realizes what they said to the
   wrong person.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Comedy, where mistaken identity is farce and scrutinizing detection would
  break the machine.
- Thematic doubles that are not deception plots at all — a mirror-self used
  as a device about the protagonist's nature, where nobody is fooled.
- Settings where duplication is ordinary and untroubling, and the identity
  question genuinely does not arise.
- Very short work, where the tension has no room to accumulate.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Almost nothing here is detectable. A coach cannot identify an impostor plot
from the text without understanding the story, and attempts to infer one from
surface features would be guessing.

Where an author raises the subject, the coach can reason about the questions
above: who could detect, what the reader knows and when, whether the
displaced original is accounted for. It should not diagnose an "idiot ball"
from the text — whether a character's failure to notice is plausible depends
on characterization the coach is reading interpretively, and readers
routinely disagree about exactly this.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Undetectable:* the copy had his memories, his mannerisms, and his mana
signature, and there was no test in the world that could tell them apart. The
next forty chapters are a wait.

*Detectable:* the copy had his memories up to the night of the fire, which
was enough for everyone except his sister, who had spent that night with him
and had never told anyone what he said.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Vladimir Propp ([[src.book.propp-morphology-of-the-folktale]]) supplies the
structural observation that false-hero and unrecognized-hero functions recur
as distinct narrative roles, used here as a lens rather than a claim about
all traditions — the same limit this library applies to Propp elsewhere.
Orson Scott Card ([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supplies the
reader-knowledge framing behind the dramatic-irony argument. The taxonomy,
the detectability requirement, and the failure modes are this drafting pass's
synthesis ([[src.synthesis.craft-library-editorial]]).

`source_confidence` is `limited`. The double has a substantial critical
literature — the Gothic doppelgänger, the uncanny, questions of identity and
duplication — none of which was available to this pass, and a later pass
should bring it in. This record reasons about the convention as a working
structure rather than analyzing it, and the identity questions it raises are
posed rather than answered.

records.title: The antihero and the redeemed enemy
records.summary: A protagonist whose methods or morality diverge from conventional heroism, and an antagonist whose arc bends toward redemption — both promise moral complexity, and both fail the same way when the story asserts change it hasn't dramatized.

citations.label: Aspects of the Novel
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An antihero is a protagonist whose methods, values, or moral center diverge
from conventional heroism — pragmatic, self-interested, violent, or morally
compromised in ways a traditional hero typically isn't, while still holding
the reader's central sympathy or interest. A redeemed enemy is a character
introduced as an antagonist or threat whose arc bends toward reform,
alliance, or moral complexity over the course of the story. Both tropes
promise a reader something conventional heroism doesn't: the pleasure of
watching moral complexity resolve, or refuse to resolve, in a character the
story asks you to keep caring about regardless.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
An antihero offers permission to root for someone who doesn't behave the way
a reader might expect a "good" protagonist to behave, which can feel more
honest or more thrilling than conventional heroism. A redeemed enemy offers
the pleasure of watching an established threat become something else,
testing whether change is possible and what it costs. Both tropes fail the
same specific way when the reader is told a character has changed or is
sympathetic without the story dramatizing the specific choices or costs that
would earn that read.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Pragmatic antihero**, whose divergence from conventional heroism is
  primarily methodological (willing to do what "heroes" won't) rather than
  a difference in ultimate goals.
- **Morally ambiguous antihero**, whose actual goals, not just methods, are
  genuinely mixed or self-interested, leaving the reader to judge rather
  than simply root.
- **Slow-redemption antagonist**, whose shift from enemy to ally or
  sympathetic figure unfolds gradually across many scenes of demonstrated
  change.
- **Sudden or unearned redemption**, a common failure variant where a
  character's shift happens abruptly with no dramatized cause — worth
  naming explicitly as the form to avoid, not a legitimate variant.
- **Redemption that fails or reverses**, where a character's arc toward
  reform doesn't complete, or completes and then breaks — a legitimate,
  sometimes more resonant structure than guaranteed success.
- **Antihero who never softens**, remaining morally compromised throughout
  without a redemption arc at all — a valid structure distinct from this
  record's redeemed-enemy half.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Specific, costly choices that demonstrate an antihero's or reforming
  enemy's actual values, rather than the narration or other characters
  simply asserting sympathy or change.
- A redemption arc that includes setbacks, relapse, or genuine difficulty,
  rather than a single clean turning point.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a character's sympathetic or reformed
  status stated by other characters or the narration with no dramatized
  choice supporting the claim.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Unearned sympathy**, where an antihero's likability is asserted through
  narrative framing (cool dialogue, aesthetic presentation) without
  dramatized choices that would justify it.
- **Unearned redemption**, where an antagonist's turn happens abruptly, often
  triggered by a single event, with no accumulated demonstration of change.
- **Consequence-free moral compromise**, where an antihero's harmful actions
  never cost them anything narratively, undermining the moral complexity the
  trope is meant to explore.
- **Redemption that erases prior harm**, where a reformed character's past
  actions are narratively forgotten rather than remaining part of how other
  characters (and the story) continue to relate to them.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Can you point to a specific, costly choice that demonstrates this
  antihero's actual values, rather than relying on narrative framing to
  generate sympathy?
- If this is a redemption arc, is the turn gradual and demonstrated across
  multiple scenes, or does it happen at a single, unearned moment?
- Does the antihero's moral compromise ever cost them something concrete?
- Does a redeemed character's past harm remain part of how other characters
  relate to them, or does the story quietly move past it?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Find the scene most responsible for establishing audience sympathy for
   an antihero, and check whether it's built on a costly choice or on
   narrative style alone; add a costly choice if the latter.
2. For a redemption arc, list the specific scenes that demonstrate change
   over time; if the arc currently turns on one event, add intermediate
   steps.
3. Introduce a real cost for the antihero's morally compromised choices,
   even a small one, if none currently exists.
4. After a redemption arc completes, find a scene where a character who was
   harmed by the reformed character's past actions responds honestly,
   rather than the harm being narratively forgotten.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very short or comedic treatments (a lightly antiheroic protagonist in a
  low-stakes adventure) may not need the full moral-complexity apparatus
  this pattern describes.
- A story deliberately depicting a failed or false redemption — where the
  point is that the change was never real — is using unearned-seeming
  redemption as its actual subject, not failing to earn it.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A morally consistent antihero, whose divergence from conventional heroism is
clear and stable rather than evolving, is a reliable structure that doesn't
require a redemption arc or moral resolution to work — some of the trope's
most effective uses keep the character exactly as compromised at the end as
at the beginning.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether sympathy or redemption is earned through dramatized, costly choice,
or asserted through narrative framing alone, requires reading and
interpreting characterization across the manuscript — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unearned redemption:* An antagonist who has committed serious harm across
many chapters apologizes in a single scene and is fully reintegrated into
the protagonist's trust by the next chapter, with no intervening
demonstration of change.

*Earned redemption:* The same antagonist instead spends several chapters
making small, costly amends — returning something stolen at personal risk,
warning the protagonist of a danger at the cost of exposing themselves — and
even after these actions, a character they harmed remains rightly wary,
which the story treats as reasonable rather than as an obstacle to be
narratively overcome.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The characterization principle (change and sympathy earned through
demonstrated, costly choice rather than assertion) draws on E. M. Forster's
foundational writing on character
([[src.book.forster-aspects-of-the-novel]]) and the broader craft-failure
pattern research's treatment of character consistency and established
limits ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]).
`source_confidence` is `mixed` reflecting the combination of a foundational
literary-craft source and practitioner-level pattern research.

records.title: The chosen one
records.summary: A protagonist marked by prophecy, birth, or destiny as uniquely suited to a task — a trope readers report fatigue with specifically when destiny substitutes for choice, not simply because it's recognizable.

citations.label: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A chosen-one protagonist is marked, by prophecy, bloodline, or some external
force, as uniquely capable of or responsible for a central task others
cannot perform. The marking usually arrives before the story tests whether
the character actually deserves or has earned that role, which is the
structural tension the trope creates: does the story treat the choosing as a
starting condition to be complicated and earned, or as a substitute for
demonstrated agency and growth.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise of being chosen is powerful — recognition, purpose, and
significance handed to a protagonist who may otherwise feel ordinary. The
fatigue with this trope, where it exists, tends to come from a specific
failure rather than the premise itself: when destiny does the story's work
instead of choice, the protagonist's actual decisions stop mattering,
because the outcome was guaranteed by birth or prophecy rather than earned.
A chosen one whose choices still carry real risk and consequence keeps the
trope's promise intact.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Reluctant chosen one**, who resists or doubts the role, creating
  internal conflict between destiny and personal will.
- **Willing chosen one**, who embraces the role readily — a legitimate,
  less common variant that shifts the tension elsewhere (proving worthiness,
  managing others' expectations).
- **False or manipulated chosen one**, where the "prophecy" is revealed to
  be constructed, misinterpreted, or manipulated by someone with an agenda —
  a common and effective subversion.
- **Shared or distributed destiny**, where the chosen role is split across
  multiple characters or an ensemble, undercutting the single-savior
  framing.
- **Self-chosen protagonist**, an explicit inversion where a character
  claims significance without any external marking, often written as a
  direct response to fatigue with the traditional form.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A prophecy or marking established early, followed by scenes where the
  protagonist's actual choices meaningfully diverge from what destiny
  implied was guaranteed.
- A chosen-one status that creates social or political consequences (being
  hunted, worshipped, resented) rather than only personal significance.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a protagonist who succeeds primarily
  because of their marked status, with choices that don't meaningfully
  affect outcomes already guaranteed by destiny.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Destiny substituting for agency**, where the outcome feels
  predetermined regardless of what the protagonist actually chooses (see the
  related agency pattern).
- **Unexamined exceptionalism**, where the chosen one's uniqueness is
  asserted without ever being tested against genuine competition or doubt.
- **The prophecy that explains everything**, using destiny as a
  catch-all justification for coincidences and plot conveniences rather than
  a specific, bounded narrative device.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- If the prophecy or marking were removed, would the protagonist's choices
  still matter to the plot's outcome?
- Does the chosen-one status create real complications (being hunted,
  distrusted, burdened) or only benefits?
- Is there a point where the protagonist's own choice diverges from what
  destiny implied, and does that divergence have consequences?
- Would a reader who's tired of this trope specifically recognize this
  version as doing something different with it, or as a straight repetition?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify one major plot outcome currently guaranteed by the protagonist's
   chosen status, and rewrite it so a specific choice, not destiny, decides
   it.
2. Add a genuine cost or complication to the chosen-one status that isn't
   simply "great power, great responsibility" in the abstract.
3. Consider whether the prophecy itself could be wrong, incomplete, or
   manipulated, and what that would open up narratively.
4. For a willing chosen one, find the tension elsewhere — in proving
   worthiness to skeptical others, or in the burden of living up to
   expectation.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Myth-adjacent or fable-like registers may use destiny straightforwardly
  and effectively, where the pleasure is in the shape of the journey rather
  than in subverting its inevitability.
- Ensemble or communal-stakes stories (base building, some cultivation
  fiction) may distribute or de-emphasize individual destiny in ways that
  make this trope's usual tensions less relevant.
- A story explicitly about the burden and unfairness of being chosen,
  without resolving into empowerment, can use the trope's traditional
  shape while subverting its usual payoff.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical chosen-one arc, played without irony or subversion, remains a
reliable structure for straightforward adventure or myth-influenced fiction
— the trope's recognizability is not itself a flaw, and a reader who wants
that specific promise is not being poorly served by a story that delivers it
well, with real stakes attached to the protagonist's choices along the way.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a chosen-one protagonist's outcomes are genuinely contingent on
their choices, or predetermined by their marked status, requires reading and
interpreting causal structure across the manuscript — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Destiny substituting for agency:* A prophecy states the marked child will
defeat the dark lord; every subsequent obstacle resolves in the
protagonist's favor regardless of their specific choices, and the final
confrontation is won because the prophecy said it would be.

*Choice within destiny:* The same prophecy exists, but the protagonist's
specific choice to spare an enemy the prophecy never mentioned creates the
actual condition for victory — the prophecy set the stage, the choice
decided the outcome.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The mythic-destiny structure draws on Joseph Campbell's comparative
synthesis ([[src.book.campbell-hero-with-a-thousand-faces]]), contested by
later scholars as overgeneralized; the fatigue-and-agency framing draws on
the broader craft-failure pattern research's treatment of character agency
and reader complaint patterns
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]). `source_confidence` is
`mixed` reflecting both sources' limitations.

records.title: The companion
records.summary: A character who travels with the protagonist without being a mentor, rival, or romantic interest — the role most vulnerable to becoming pure company with no independent function, which is exactly what separates a memorable companion from a forgettable one.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A companion travels or works alongside the protagonist across a sustained
stretch of story without occupying one of the more specifically defined
supporting roles this library covers elsewhere — not a mentor (who
teaches), not a rival (who competes), not a romantic interest (whose
relationship carries its own distinct arc), not necessarily part of a
found-family structure (which implies a fuller ensemble). A companion's
defining feature is sustained proximity without a sharply defined
function, which makes the role simultaneously easy to include and easy to
leave underdeveloped — this library's general supporting-cast-purpose
pattern applies to the companion role with particular force, since
"someone who's around" is the least automatically purposeful function a
character can have.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A well-developed companion gives a protagonist someone to talk to, react
against, and be witnessed by across the story's full length, which can
carry significant narrative weight even without a sharply defined
function — companionship itself, sustained over time, is a real and
valued relationship readers respond to. The risk is specific to this
role's lack of built-in definition: a companion with no independent want,
perspective, or arc can become furniture, present in every scene but
contributing nothing a reader would miss if they were replaced by a
different character entirely.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Contrast companion**, whose personality or worldview differs
  meaningfully from the protagonist's, generating low-grade ongoing
  friction or complementary balance.
- **Similar companion**, sharing the protagonist's outlook or background,
  offering solidarity and shared perspective rather than contrast — a
  different but legitimate register.
- **Skill-complementary companion**, whose distinct practical capabilities
  fill a gap the protagonist has, giving the role a functional as well as
  relational purpose.
- **Witness companion**, whose primary narrative function is to observe and
  react to the protagonist, sometimes serving as an audience surrogate —
  effective when the reactions themselves reveal character, weaker when
  they only exist to prompt exposition.
- **Independent-arc companion**, who has their own developing want and
  storyline running alongside the protagonist's, distinct from a companion
  whose entire arc is defined by proximity to the protagonist.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A companion whose specific perspective, skill, or want shapes a scene's
  outcome independent of the protagonist's own choices.
- A companion's absence from a scene creating a specific, nameable gap —
  information, skill, or perspective only they would have provided.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a companion present in scene after scene
  who could be silently removed with no effect on plot, dialogue, or the
  protagonist's decisions.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The furniture companion**, present without independent want, skill, or
  perspective, functioning as company rather than character.
- **The exposition-only companion**, whose primary function is prompting
  the protagonist (or being prompted) to explain things to the reader, with
  no other narrative purpose.
- **An independent arc introduced late and never developed**, where a
  companion is given a hint of their own story that never actually
  receives page time or resolution.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this companion want, independent of their proximity to the
  protagonist?
- If this companion were removed from a chapter range, what specifically
  would be lost — information, skill, perspective, or nothing?
- Does the companion's presence in scenes serve a function beyond company,
  or could their dialogue be reassigned to any other character with no
  loss?
- If the companion has an independent arc, does it receive dedicated page
  time, or does it remain a gestured-at but undeveloped thread?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence describing the companion's want that has nothing to
   do with the protagonist, and find a scene where it surfaces.
2. Test removing the companion from a chapter range; if nothing changes,
   identify what specific function (skill, perspective, information) could
   be added to make their presence necessary.
3. For an exposition-only companion, replace at least one instance of
   prompted exposition with a moment revealing the companion's own
   perspective or stake in what's happening.
4. If an independent arc is gestured at but undeveloped, either commit
   page time to it or scale back the gesture to match what the story
   actually delivers.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very minor, single-scene companions don't need full independent
  development.
- A story deliberately depicting a protagonist's isolation, where a
  companion's flatness reflects the protagonist's own failure to really
  see the people around them, may use an underdeveloped companion as
  characterization of the protagonist — provided that's a legible,
  examined choice.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A loyal, consistent companion whose primary narrative function really is
steady presence and support — without a fully independent arc — remains a
satisfying and reliable structure in many registers, particularly
lighter or more episodic ones, as long as they have at least one
distinguishing want or perspective that keeps them from reading as
interchangeable.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a companion has independent narrative function, or exists purely
as proximity, requires reading and interpreting characterization across
the manuscript — a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Furniture companion:* A character travels alongside the protagonist for
twenty chapters, speaking only to ask questions that let the protagonist
explain the plot, with no stated want, skill, or reaction that isn't
directly prompted by the protagonist's own concerns.

*Purposeful companion:* The same character instead has a specific,
established skill (reading terrain) that solves a problem the protagonist
couldn't have solved alone, and a private worry about a family member back
home that surfaces in a quiet scene, unprompted by the protagonist — the
companion exists as a person, not a presence.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The companion role's vulnerability to becoming purely functional draws on
this library's general character-purpose reasoning, informed by the
broader craft-failure research's treatment of underdeveloped supporting
casts ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated
craft-literature source specifically addressing the companion role was
available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Ensemble cast dynamics
records.summary: A team of characters who work together over time — distinct from found family's emotional-bond focus — is a structural convention with its own logic: roles that complement rather than duplicate, and a balance of screen time that doesn't quietly reduce most of the cast to furniture.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An ensemble cast is a group of characters who function together as a
structural unit — a party, a team, a crew — distinguished from this
library's found-family trope by its emphasis on functional structure
rather than emotional bond specifically (the two frequently overlap, but
an ensemble can be a functioning team without being emotionally close, and
a found family can exist without functioning as a coordinated team). The
trope's core craft challenge is balance: each member needs a role distinct
enough from the others to justify their inclusion, and narrative attention
needs to be distributed such that most of the cast doesn't quietly become
furniture while one or two characters absorb nearly all the story's actual
development.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A well-balanced ensemble gives readers multiple characters to invest in
simultaneously, each bringing something distinct to the group's shared
problems — this is part of what makes team-based fiction (heists, party-
based adventures, base-building casts) satisfying in a way a solo
protagonist story structurally can't replicate. The risk scales with cast
size: the more characters a story includes, the more likely some will
receive disproportionately little development, and readers notice when a
"main cast" functions, in practice, as one or two developed characters
plus several undifferentiated others.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Role-complementary ensembles**, where each member's distinct skill or
  perspective is functionally necessary to the group's shared problems
  (closely related to this library's healing-teamwork-and-information-
  asymmetry system-mechanic record for combat-specific team dynamics).
- **Personality-complementary ensembles**, where members' distinct
  temperaments and values create productive friction or balance,
  independent of functional skill differentiation.
- **Rotating-focus ensembles**, where narrative attention shifts between
  members across the story (often via multi-POV structure), ensuring each
  gets dedicated development over the manuscript's full length rather than
  simultaneously.
- **Core-and-periphery ensembles**, where a smaller inner group receives
  full development while a larger surrounding cast remains more lightly
  sketched — a legitimate structure, provided the periphery doesn't
  overpromise development it never delivers.
- **Unbalanced ensembles**, a failure mode rather than a variant, where a
  nominally equal cast in practice functions as one or two developed
  characters with several interchangeable others attached.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Each ensemble member's distinct skill, perspective, or personality
  solving a problem or shaping a scene in a way no other member could have.
- Narrative attention distributed across the cast over the manuscript's
  full length, even if not evenly within any single scene.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an ensemble where most members'
  dialogue and function are interchangeable, and removing any one of
  several characters would leave the plot and dynamics largely unaffected.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The furniture ensemble**, where several nominal team members
  contribute no distinct function or development across the manuscript.
- **Uneven development with no acknowledgment**, where the story implicitly
  promises an equal ensemble (introducing several characters with
  apparent significance) but delivers development to only one or two.
- **Redundant roles**, where two or more ensemble members serve
  functionally identical purposes, diluting the significance of each.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does each member of this ensemble have a distinct skill, perspective, or
  personality that solves problems or shapes scenes in a way no other
  member could?
- Across the manuscript's full length, does narrative attention reach
  every significant ensemble member, even if not evenly in any single
  scene?
- If two ensemble members could be merged with no loss to the story, is
  that intentional or a sign of redundant roles?
- Does the cast's actual size match what the story delivers, or does it
  introduce more characters than it develops?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List each ensemble member's distinct function and check for overlap;
   merge or differentiate any two members serving nearly identical roles.
2. Chart narrative attention (scenes, dialogue, POV time) across the
   ensemble over a chapter range and identify anyone receiving
   disproportionately little.
3. Test removing a minor ensemble member from a stretch of the story; if
   nothing changes, decide whether to develop their distinct function or
   scale back their apparent significance.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A deliberately large, loosely developed ensemble (a whole settlement's
  population, a large military unit) may reasonably keep most members
  lightly sketched, provided the core cast that does receive development
  is clear.
- Very short works may not have room to develop a full ensemble and can
  reasonably focus on one or two members with the rest kept functional.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical, well-balanced small ensemble — three to five members, each
with a clear, distinct function — remains a reliable and satisfying
structure across many genres, and doesn't need an unusually large cast or
structural innovation to deliver real ensemble satisfaction.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether ensemble members have genuinely distinct functions, and whether
narrative attention is adequately distributed, requires reading and
interpreting characterization and structure across the manuscript — a
judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Furniture ensemble:* A party of five adventurers is introduced with
distinct names and brief descriptions, but three of them never speak more
than a line of dialogue across the following twenty chapters and
contribute nothing a reader could distinguish from any other minor
character.

*Balanced ensemble:* The same party instead has each member solve a
distinct problem across those twenty chapters — one navigates a social
negotiation the others couldn't, one identifies a magical trap by
specialized knowledge, one's combat approach specifically counters a
threat the others can't — with narrative attention rotating enough that
each has at least one chapter centered on their own stake in events.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This record's framing draws on this library's general character-purpose
reasoning, informed by the broader craft-failure research's treatment of
supporting-cast development and side-cast obsolescence
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated craft-
literature source specifically addressing ensemble-cast balance was
available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Found family
records.summary: A group of characters, unrelated by blood or initially by choice, who come to function as family for each other — a structure that promises belonging earned through shared experience rather than assumed through origin.
modifiers: base-building: Especially central here — the settlement's recruited cast often *is* the found family, and their individual stakes in the community are frequently the subgenre's real subject.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Found family describes a group of characters who come to occupy family-like
roles for each other — loyalty, obligation, unconditional-feeling support,
shared history — without being related by blood and often without initially
choosing each other deliberately. The trope's core promise is that belonging
can be built rather than only inherited, which gives it particular resonance
for protagonists who are orphaned, estranged from origin family, or
otherwise displaced from a conventional family structure.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Found family offers emotional stakes that don't depend on romantic pairing
or blood ties, letting a story build deep relational investment across an
entire cast rather than concentrating it in one or two central bonds. It
also allows a wide range of relationship types — sibling-like rivalry,
parent-like protection, chosen loyalty — to carry weight typically reserved
for biological family in other narrative traditions.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Party or crew found family**, built through shared adventure or
  survival, common in quest and progression-fantasy structures.
- **Institutional found family**, formed within a shared institution (a
  school, a guild, a military unit) whose structure brings characters
  together before affection develops.
- **Adoptive found family**, where an existing family unit deliberately
  takes in an outsider, blending inherited and chosen family structures.
- **Found family in tension with biological family**, where the found bonds
  compete with or heal a fractured relationship to origin family, adding a
  second layer of stakes.
- **Found family under strain**, where the group's cohesion is tested by
  disagreement, betrayal, or diverging goals — necessary for the bond to
  read as earned rather than assumed.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Small, specific acts of care or sacrifice between characters that
  establish the relationship's weight without requiring a formal
  declaration.
- Conflict within the found-family group that gets resolved through
  continued commitment rather than through the group simply agreeing on
  everything.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: characters who are told to be close (a
  narrator stating they're "like family") without scenes that dramatize why.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Declared rather than earned closeness**, asserting the bond exists
  without dramatizing the specific experiences that built it.
- **Conflict-free family**, where the group never disagrees or tests the
  relationship, making eventual displays of loyalty feel unearned because
  nothing was ever at risk.
- **Flattened individual identity**, where found-family members exist mainly
  to support the protagonist rather than having their own wants and stakes
  the family dynamic serves.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Can you point to a specific scene where the found-family bond was tested
  or built, rather than simply stated?
