- Does each member of this found family have a want independent of their
  role in the group?
- Is there a moment of real conflict within the group that gets resolved
  through continued commitment, rather than the group avoiding disagreement
  entirely?
- If this found family formed within an institution, does the institution's
  structure create any tension with the group's chosen loyalty?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Find the earliest scene establishing found-family closeness and check
   whether it's dramatized through specific action or only asserted through
   narration.
2. Introduce a genuine disagreement or diverging goal between two found-
   family members and let it play out without an easy resolution.
3. Give one supporting found-family member a want unrelated to the
   protagonist, and find a scene where it surfaces.
4. If found family exists in tension with biological family, find a scene
   that puts the two loyalties in direct conflict.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very early chapters establishing a group before bonds have had time to
  form are not yet evidence of unearned closeness — this pattern applies
  once closeness is asserted, not before it develops.
- Short-form or fast-paced structures may compress found-family formation
  into fewer scenes without losing effectiveness, as long as the compression
  still shows rather than only tells.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A found-family structure that plays warmly and without much internal
conflict can work well in comfort-read or lower-stakes registers, where the
promise is specifically the pleasure of found belonging rather than tested
loyalty — provided the group still has individually distinct members rather
than reading as an undifferentiated support system for the protagonist.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a found-family bond is dramatized or merely asserted, and whether
members have independent wants, requires reading and interpreting
characterization across the manuscript — a judgment no structured data
substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Declared closeness:* A narrator states that a group of adventurers has
"become like family" after two chapters together, with no scene showing a
specific act of care or sacrifice between them.

*Earned closeness:* The same group instead includes a scene where one
member gives up a hard-won reward to cover another's debt, without being
asked, and a later scene where that same generosity is remembered and
returned under different circumstances.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This trope's genre relevance (party-based found family in progression
fantasy and LitRPG, its centrality to base-building) draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s subgenre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre-profile
material as the author's own inference. No dedicated craft-literature
source for found-family structure specifically was available to this
drafting pass; `source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly, and an
author revision pass should add a stronger craft or reader-response source
if this record is retained past initial review.

records.title: The heir and the succession plot
records.summary: A character positioned to inherit power, position, or legacy, and the plot generated by contested or uncertain succession — a structure that works best when the inheritance carries genuine obligation, not just entitlement.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An heir is positioned, by birth, appointment, or circumstance, to inherit
power, position, or legacy — a throne, a business, a magical lineage, a
sect's leadership. A succession plot generates conflict from uncertainty or
contest around that inheritance: rival claimants, a testing period before
the inheritance is confirmed, or the heir's own reluctance or unfitness for
what they're set to inherit. The trope's strongest versions treat
inheritance as carrying genuine obligation and cost, not simply as an
entitlement the heir is owed — an heir who merely receives is a weaker
story than one who has to prove, sacrifice, or reckon with what they're
inheriting.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Succession plots offer built-in structural stakes: a contested inheritance
has a natural deadline (a coronation, a testing period's end) and a natural
comparison set (rival claimants), both of which generate legible dramatic
tension. The trope also invites a specific kind of character examination —
what does it mean to be shaped by, worthy of, or in conflict with a legacy
you didn't choose — that purely self-made protagonist structures don't
offer in the same way.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Rightful heir contested by rivals**, where the succession conflict is
  primarily external (other claimants, political maneuvering).
- **Reluctant heir**, who doesn't want the inheritance, generating internal
  conflict alongside or instead of external contest (closely related to the
  reluctant-hero trope, applied specifically to inheritance).
- **Unworthy or untested heir**, whose fitness for the role is genuinely in
  question, raising stakes around whether they'll rise to it or fail.
- **False or displaced heir**, where the "rightful" line of succession is
  itself uncertain or manipulated, adding a mystery element to the
  succession plot.
- **Heir who rejects the inheritance**, choosing a different path entirely
  — a legitimate subversion, provided the rejection carries real
  consequence rather than being cost-free.
- **Collective or shared succession**, where inheritance is distributed
  rather than concentrated in one heir, common in ensemble or
  institution-focused settings.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A succession conflict with a legible deadline or testing structure,
  giving the plot clear escalating stakes.
- The inheritance itself shown to carry real obligation or cost, not just
  benefit, once claimed.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an heir who receives their inheritance
  with no meaningful test, cost, or contest, reading as entitled rather
  than earned.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Inheritance with no obligation**, where the heir gains power or
  position with no accompanying cost, duty, or complication.
- **A succession contest resolved by simple birthright with no genuine
  test**, undermining any tension the contest was meant to generate.
- **A reluctant heir whose reluctance has no real stakes**, where their
  eventual acceptance carries no cost distinguishable from having wanted it
  all along.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this inheritance actually cost the heir once they receive it?
- Is the succession conflict resolved through a genuine test, or does
  birthright alone settle it with no real contest?
- If the heir is reluctant, does their eventual choice (to accept or
  reject) carry a distinguishable cost either way?
- Does the story examine what it means to be shaped by a legacy the
  character didn't choose, or does the inheritance function only as a plot
  device?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List what the inheritance specifically obligates the heir to do or give
   up, and check whether that obligation is dramatized on the page.
2. For a succession conflict resolved by birthright alone, add a genuine
   test — a trial, a rival's legitimate claim, a condition that must be
   met — to raise the stakes.
3. For a reluctant heir, find the specific cost of their eventual choice
   (whichever way it goes) and make sure it's shown, not just implied.
4. If the succession plot feels thin, consider adding a rival claimant with
   a genuinely legitimate case, not simply a villainous pretender.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story using succession as background context rather than a central
  plot engine (a minor detail about a character's family) doesn't need the
  full obligation-and-contest treatment this pattern describes.
- A satirical or deliberately shallow treatment of inheritance-as-
  entitlement (critiquing hereditary privilege directly) may intentionally
  show inheritance with no earned cost, as the point being made.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical rightful-heir-overcomes-rivals structure, played without
subversion, remains a satisfying and reliable plot engine — its
recognizability doesn't require inversion to work, provided the
inheritance still carries genuine stakes and the heir's eventual claim
feels earned through the story's events, not simply assumed from the
start.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether an inheritance carries genuine dramatized obligation, and whether a
succession contest is genuinely tested rather than assumed, requires
reading and interpreting the manuscript's plot and characterization — a
judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Entitled inheritance:* A protagonist is crowned at the story's end simply
by virtue of being the late ruler's only child, with no test, rival claim,
or cost attached to the transition.

*Earned inheritance:* The same protagonist instead must survive a
formal succession trial their late parent instituted specifically to
prevent unworthy heirs from inheriting, and passing it costs them a
close relationship with a sibling who believed themselves better suited —
the crown arrives with a specific, dramatized price.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The obligation-over-entitlement framing for succession plots is this
drafting pass's synthesis, informed by the broader craft-failure research's
general emphasis on earned outcomes over unearned ones
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated craft-
literature source specifically addressing succession-plot structure was
available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: The mentor
records.summary: A more experienced figure who trains, guides, or challenges the protagonist — a near-universal role across genres, whose staleness comes from function without friction, not from the role itself.

citations.label: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers
The Hero with a Thousand Faces

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A mentor is a character positioned as more experienced, skilled, or wise
than the protagonist, who provides training, guidance, resources, or
challenge that the protagonist could not easily access alone. The role is
functional rather than fixed to a single character type — a mentor can be
an ally, a rival who teaches through opposition, an institution, or even an
absent figure whose past teaching still shapes the protagonist's choices.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A mentor relationship gives a reader a legible structure for a
protagonist's growth: skills and understanding arrive through a
relationship the reader can track, rather than appearing unexplained. It
also offers built-in emotional stakes — a mentor's approval, disappointment,
limitations, or eventual departure (through death, conflict, or the
protagonist simply outgrowing them) can carry real weight distinct from the
external plot.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The classical wise guide**, imparting both skill and moral or
  philosophical direction, common across myth-influenced traditions.
- **The flawed or compromised mentor**, whose guidance is genuinely useful
  but whose own failures or blind spots the protagonist must eventually see
  past.
- **The rival-as-mentor**, where an antagonistic figure inadvertently
  teaches through opposition rather than instruction.
- **The absent or posthumous mentor**, whose influence persists through
  memory, letters, or established teaching after the mentor is gone from the
  story.
- **The peer mentor**, closer in age or status to the protagonist but ahead
  in relevant experience — common in academy and progression-fantasy
  settings where formal age-based hierarchy isn't the organizing structure.
- **The institutional mentor**, where guidance comes from a system,
  organization, or tradition rather than a single named character.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A scene where the mentor's specific guidance directly enables a later
  choice or capability, creating a traceable causal link.
- A mentor whose own flaws or limitations become visible and relevant to the
  protagonist's arc, rather than remaining an idealized source of wisdom.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a mentor who exists mainly to deliver
  exposition, with no personal stake, flaw, or relationship dynamic beyond
  information transfer.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The exposition dispenser**, a mentor whose only narrative function is
  explaining the world or system to the protagonist (and reader), with no
  independent motivation or characterization.
- **The mentor who is never wrong**, removing any friction or growth
  opportunity from the relationship and making the protagonist's eventual
  independence feel unearned.
- **Fridging the mentor purely for stakes**, killing off a mentor solely to
  motivate the protagonist with no other narrative function served by the
  death, which readers increasingly recognize and discount as a stakes
  shortcut.
- **The mentor who never actually mentors**, present in name but absent from
  the protagonist's actual skill or understanding growth.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does the mentor want, independent of their function in the
  protagonist's arc?
- Is there a point where the mentor is shown to be wrong, limited, or
  flawed, and does the protagonist's growth involve recognizing that?
- If the mentor is removed from the story (through death, departure, or
  conflict), does the protagonist's later growth trace back to something
  specific the mentor taught, or does the mentor's absence go unfelt?
- Does this mentor exist mainly to deliver information, or do they have a
  relationship with the protagonist independent of exposition?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one want or need for the mentor character that has nothing to do
   with the protagonist's development, and find a scene where it surfaces.
2. Identify a moment where the mentor's guidance is wrong, incomplete, or in
   tension with what the protagonist actually needs, and dramatize the
   friction.
3. If the mentor's function is mostly exposition, try converting one
   information-delivery scene into a scene built around what the mentor
   wants or fears instead.
4. If the mentor's death is planned as a stakes-raising device, check
   whether it also serves the protagonist's actual internal arc, not just
   external motivation.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very short works may not have room for a fully developed mentor and can
  use the role functionally, as a plot device, without weakening the story.
- A story deliberately depicting a hollow or purely functional mentor
  relationship as part of its critique of found-wisdom narratives is using
  the flat form on purpose.
- Ensemble stories may distribute mentor functions across multiple minor
  characters rather than concentrating the role in one figure.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical, largely reliable mentor with a warm relationship to the
protagonist is not a failure mode by default — a story whose focus lies
elsewhere (plot-forward adventure, ensemble dynamics) can use a
straightforward mentor role without needing to subvert or complicate it, as
long as the relationship still carries some specific, felt texture rather
than being purely functional.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a mentor relationship carries genuine narrative and emotional weight,
or functions purely as an information-delivery device, requires reading and
interpreting the manuscript's characterization and causal structure — a
judgment no structured data substitutes for. A coach could shortlist scenes
featuring a character in a mentor-like role as candidate evidence, but
cannot determine the depth of the relationship from that alone.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Exposition-only mentor:* An older sorcerer explains the rules of a magic
system across several scenes, expresses no personal want, and disappears
from the plot once the explanation is complete.

*Full mentor relationship:* The same sorcerer instead withholds one crucial
piece of teaching out of old guilt over a past student's death, and the
protagonist's eventual discovery of that withheld knowledge — and the
reason for it — becomes a turning point in both characters' arcs.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The mentor role's mythic and structural grounding draws on Joseph Campbell's
comparative-mythology synthesis
([[src.book.campbell-hero-with-a-thousand-faces]]), itself contested by
later scholars for overgeneralizing across cultures, and Christopher
Vogler's popularization of that structure for contemporary writers
([[src.book.vogler-writers-journey]]). Both are treated here as one
influential lens on the role rather than a universal template; the
fridging/exposition-dispenser failure-mode framing is this drafting pass's
synthesis from general contemporary craft discussion rather than a direct
claim from either source. `source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: The reluctant hero
records.summary: A protagonist who resists the call to act before eventually committing — the resistance itself does narrative work if it's grounded in a specific, legible reason, and reads as a stalling device if it isn't.

citations.label: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers
The Hero with a Thousand Faces

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A reluctant hero resists taking on a central task or role before eventually
committing to it, in contrast to a protagonist who accepts a call to action
readily. The resistance is a structural beat with its own name in several
influential story-structure traditions (often called the "refusal of the
call"), and its narrative function depends on the resistance being grounded
in something specific about the character — a fear, a competing loyalty, a
past failure — rather than existing only to delay the plot.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Reluctance that's specifically motivated deepens characterization: the
reader learns something true about the protagonist through what they're
afraid of or unwilling to risk. Reluctance that exists only to stall the
plot until the story is ready to begin in earnest can read as padding,
especially in serialized fiction where an extended refusal can cost real
reader patience before the story's actual engine starts running.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Fear-motivated reluctance**, where the protagonist doubts their own
  capability or fears failure or harm to themselves.
- **Loyalty-motivated reluctance**, where accepting the call would mean
  abandoning or endangering something else the protagonist values.
- **Principle-motivated reluctance**, where the protagonist objects to the
  task or role on moral or ideological grounds, not fear.
- **Trauma-informed reluctance**, where a past failure or loss specifically
  explains the resistance, giving it concrete narrative weight.
- **Brief or minimal reluctance**, where the refusal beat is compressed to a
  scene or a line rather than an extended arc — common and effective in
  faster-paced or serialized structures.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A specific, nameable reason for the protagonist's resistance, distinct
  from generic reluctance or plot-mandated stalling.
- A scene where the protagonist's eventual commitment is triggered by
  something that directly addresses or overcomes their stated reason for
  refusing.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an extended refusal period with no
  specific reason given, or a reason that never actually connects to why the
  character eventually changes their mind.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Refusal without motivation**, resistance that exists only to delay the
  plot's actual start, unmoored from any specific character trait.
- **A commitment trigger disconnected from the stated reluctance**, where
  the character finally agrees for a reason unrelated to what was actually
  holding them back, leaving the earlier refusal feeling unresolved.
- **Reluctance dragged out past its narrative usefulness**, particularly
  costly in serialized fiction, where readers following chapter by chapter
  may lose patience before the central story begins.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What specifically is the protagonist afraid of, unwilling to risk, or
  opposed to, and is that reason stated or clearly implied on the page?
- Does the moment the protagonist finally commits directly address the
  reason they were resisting, or is the trigger unrelated?
- If this is a serialized work, how much of the opening is spent on
  reluctance before the central plot engine actually starts, and is that
  proportion sustainable for reader patience?
- Would cutting the refusal beat entirely lose anything about who this
  character is?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence naming the specific reason for the protagonist's
   reluctance; if it's generic ("they were scared") rather than specific
   ("they promised their mother they'd never fight again"), sharpen it.
2. Check whether the commitment trigger addresses that specific reason; if
   not, revise the trigger or the stated reason so they connect.
3. For a serialized work, measure how many chapters pass before the
   protagonist commits, and consider whether that length serves reader
   patience or tests it.
4. Try compressing an extended refusal arc into a single strong scene and
   see whether the story loses meaningful characterization or only pacing
   weight.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A story explicitly about the cost of prolonged refusal (a character whose
  reluctance itself causes real, examined harm) can extend this beat well
  past its usual length as its actual subject.
- Ensemble stories may distribute reluctance and readiness across different
  characters, using the contrast between a reluctant and an eager character
  rather than centering reluctance in a single protagonist.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A brief, clearly motivated refusal-and-commitment beat, handled in a scene
or two, is a well-established and reliable opening structure that doesn't
need subversion to work — its familiarity is part of what makes it legible
quickly, freeing the story to spend its length elsewhere.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a protagonist's reluctance is specifically motivated, and whether
the eventual commitment addresses that motivation, requires reading and
interpreting characterization and causal structure — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unmotivated stalling:* A protagonist refuses a quest for three chapters
with no stated reason beyond general hesitation, then abruptly agrees when a
mentor insists, with no connection between the insistence and the earlier
refusal.

*Motivated reluctance:* The same protagonist refuses specifically because
accepting means breaking a promise to a dying parent never to leave their
younger sibling alone; they commit only once a solution for the sibling's
safety is found — the refusal and its resolution are causally linked.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The "refusal of the call" structural beat draws on Joseph Campbell's
comparative-mythology synthesis
([[src.book.campbell-hero-with-a-thousand-faces]]) and Christopher Vogler's
popularization for contemporary writers
([[src.book.vogler-writers-journey]]); both are treated as one influential
lens rather than a universal template, and Campbell's cross-cultural
generalizations are contested by later scholarship. The serialized-fiction
pacing caution is this drafting pass's application of general platform
reader-patience concerns rather than a directly sourced claim.
`source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: The rival
records.summary: A character pursuing a similar goal or standing to the protagonist, often without being an enemy — a rivalry does its best work when it reveals something about the protagonist that opposition alone can't.

citations.label: Writing Progression Fantasy

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A rival pursues a similar goal, status, or standing to the protagonist —
often within the same institution, competition, or field — without
necessarily being their enemy. A rival differs from a true antagonist in
that their success doesn't require the protagonist's defeat in the way an
antagonist's often does; a rival can lose the specific competition at hand
and remain narratively present, even become an ally, in a way a fully
opposed antagonist typically can't without a full redemption arc. The
comparison a rival invites is the trope's real engine: by pursuing a
similar goal differently, the rival reveals what the protagonist's own
approach actually is.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A rival gives a reader a direct point of comparison for the protagonist —
someone facing similar obstacles with a different method, different values,
or different resources, letting the story dramatize what makes the
protagonist's specific approach meaningful rather than simply asserting it.
This works especially well in progression and academy-adjacent structures,
where a rival's parallel advancement gives concrete, trackable stakes to an
otherwise abstract question of "who's better."

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Friendly rival**, where competition coexists with genuine respect or
  even friendship, common in academy and tournament structures.
- **Hostile rival**, where the competitive relationship carries real
  animosity, closer to antagonism but still distinguished by shared goal-
  pursuit rather than direct opposition to the protagonist's existence or
  survival.
- **Rival-to-ally**, where sustained competition eventually produces mutual
  respect and cooperation, a common and satisfying arc.
- **Rival-to-antagonist**, the inverse, where competitive pressure curdles
  into genuine enmity — effective when the escalation is dramatized rather
  than sudden.
- **Superior rival**, who is ahead of the protagonist for most or all of the
  story, functioning as an aspirational benchmark rather than a peer.
- **Inferior-but-persistent rival**, who never quite matches the
  protagonist but remains narratively relevant through determination,
  cleverness, or a different specialization.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Parallel advancement or achievement between protagonist and rival, shown
  concretely enough that the reader can track how the comparison is
  shifting over time.
- A moment where the rival's different approach to a shared problem
  reveals something about the protagonist's own method by contrast.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a rival who exists mainly to lose to the
  protagonist repeatedly, with no genuine threat or distinct approach that
  illuminates anything.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The disposable rival**, present only to be defeated, with no
  independent goals or approach that contrasts meaningfully with the
  protagonist's.
- **A rivalry with no real stakes**, where neither character's standing
  ever seems genuinely at risk, removing tension from their shared pursuit.
- **An unexamined shift from rival to antagonist (or vice versa)**, where
  the relationship's nature changes with no dramatized cause.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does the rival's approach to their shared goal reveal about the
  protagonist's own approach, by contrast?
- Is there a point where the rivalry's outcome is genuinely uncertain, or
  does the protagonist always win?
- If the rivalry shifts (to alliance or to enmity), can you trace the
  specific cause?
- Does the rival have goals and stakes independent of their function as a
  comparison point for the protagonist?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write one sentence describing what the rival's approach to their shared
   goal reveals about the protagonist by contrast; if nothing comes to
   mind, the rivalry may need sharper differentiation.
2. Find a scene where the rival's outcome is genuinely uncertain, and check
   whether the story lets that uncertainty register.
3. For a shift in the relationship's nature, trace back to the specific
   cause and make sure it's dramatized on the page.
4. Give the rival one goal that has nothing to do with the protagonist, and
   find a scene where it surfaces.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very brief or minor rivalries (a single competitive scene within a larger
  story) don't need the full comparative development this pattern
  describes.
- A story deliberately depicting a one-sided or unfair rivalry as its point
  (a protagonist who never sees a lesser rival as a real threat, examined
  as a character flaw) is using the imbalance intentionally.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical friendly or hostile rivalry, sustained without a shift to
alliance or enmity, remains a satisfying and reliable structure — not every
rival needs to become a friend or a foe by the story's end, and a rivalry
that simply continues, with its comparison intact, can carry a story's full
length without needing resolution.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a rival's approach genuinely illuminates something about the
protagonist by contrast, and whether the competitive stakes feel real,
requires reading and interpreting characterization across the manuscript —
a judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Disposable rival:* A tournament rival is introduced, loses decisively to
the protagonist in their first meeting, and never appears again with any
narrative weight.

*Illuminating rival:* The same rival instead pursues the tournament through
calculated risk-avoidance where the protagonist takes bold risks; their
final match is close enough that either could plausibly win, and the
protagonist's eventual victory specifically validates the risk they took —
a validation the story couldn't have earned without the rival's contrasting,
credible approach.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The rival's function as a comparison point that reveals protagonist
character draws on general progression-fantasy practitioner discussion
([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]); no dedicated craft-literature source
specifically addressing rival-character structure was available to this
drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: The outsider and belonging
records.summary: A protagonist positioned outside a community's norms — by origin, status, or difference — whose arc often turns on whether and how they find belonging; the trope's strength depends on the outsider status costing something real, not functioning only as a sympathetic label.
modifiers: academy-story: Outsider status is especially common here (a commoner among nobles, an underdog admitted unconventionally); see the academy-story profile's outsider-at-the-academy variant for the institutional framing.

citations.label: LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
An outsider protagonist stands apart from a community's norms — by origin,
social status, species, ability, or some other marker of difference — and
the trope's arc often turns on whether, and on what terms, they find
belonging. This differs from the reluctant-hero trope (which centers
resistance to a call to action) and from the chosen-one trope (which
centers destiny and marked significance), though all three can overlap:
an outsider can be reluctant, or chosen, or neither. The outsider trope's
specific engine is the tension between difference and belonging, and its
strength depends on the difference carrying a real, felt cost — exclusion,
misunderstanding, a genuine barrier to acceptance — rather than
functioning only as a sympathetic character label with no actual social
consequence.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Outsider stories offer a distinctive emotional throughline many readers
recognize from their own experience: the specific ache of wanting to
belong somewhere that doesn't automatically accept you, and the question
of what belonging actually costs or requires. The trope's payoff comes in
different forms — full acceptance, belonging on the outsider's own terms
rather than by conforming, or a clear-eyed decision that this particular
community was never the right fit — and readers track which resolution a
story is building toward as much as whether belonging is achieved at all.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Earned acceptance**, where the outsider is gradually, credibly
  accepted by the community, often through demonstrated value or shared
  hardship.
- **Belonging on one's own terms**, where the outsider achieves connection
  without fully conforming to the community's original norms, sometimes
  changing the community's norms in the process.
- **Chosen non-belonging**, where the outsider ultimately decides this
  community isn't the right fit and moves on — a legitimate and sometimes
  more honest resolution than forced acceptance.
- **Perpetual liminality**, where the outsider remains between full
  belonging and full exclusion by the story's end, examined as its own
  meaningful state rather than resolved cleanly either way.
- **Outsider-transforms-the-community**, where the outsider's difference,
  rather than being erased or accommodated, actually changes what the
  community values or how it operates.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- The outsider's difference creating a specific, dramatized cost —
  exclusion from an activity, a misunderstanding with real consequence, a
  barrier that isn't easily overcome.
- A resolution (acceptance, belonging-on-own-terms, or chosen departure)
  that traces to specific events and choices across the story, not an
  assumed default.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an outsider status that's stated
  (the character is described as different, an outcast, unwelcome) but
  never actually costs the character anything concrete across the story.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Stated but costless outsider status**, where difference is named but
  never produces a real social or narrative consequence.
- **Acceptance that arrives too easily**, undermining the tension the
  outsider's difference was meant to generate.
- **A resolution that erases the difference entirely**, where belonging is
  achieved only by the outsider becoming indistinguishable from the
  community, without the story examining what (if anything) was lost or
  gained in that assimilation.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this character's outsider status cost them something specific and
  dramatized, or is it stated without real consequence?
- Is the eventual resolution (acceptance, belonging on their own terms, or
  departure) traceable to specific events, or does it arrive by default?
- If the outsider achieves belonging by conforming to the community's
  norms, does the story examine what that conformity cost them?
- Could this character's outsider status be removed with no effect on the
  plot or their relationships?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Find a scene where the character's difference produces a real,
   dramatized cost, and add one if none currently exists.
2. Trace the eventual resolution (belonging or departure) back to specific
   causes across the manuscript.
3. If belonging is achieved through conformity, add a scene examining what
   that conformity cost the character.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A brief, single-scene use of outsider status (a character new to a
  setting for one chapter) doesn't need the full belonging-arc treatment
  this pattern describes.
- A story deliberately depicting outsider status as permanent and
  unresolved, examined directly as its subject, is using perpetual
  liminality intentionally rather than failing to resolve the arc.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical outsider-earns-acceptance arc, played without subversion,
remains a satisfying and reliable structure — its familiarity doesn't
require complicating, provided the difference costs something real along
the way and the eventual acceptance is traceably earned rather than
assumed.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether outsider status carries a real, dramatized cost, and whether a
resolution is earned rather than assumed, requires reading and
interpreting the manuscript's characterization and plot — a judgment no
structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Costless outsider status:* A character is repeatedly described as an
outcast in their community, but every scene shows them treated with
ordinary courtesy and included in group activities with no friction
traceable to their difference.

*Costly, earned belonging:* The same character instead is excluded from a
specific communal ritual early in the story specifically because of their
difference, and their eventual, hard-won inclusion in a later version of
that same ritual — achieved through a demonstrated act the community
couldn't ignore — gives the belonging arc a legible beginning, middle, and
resolution.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This record's framing draws on general character-role reasoning informed
by the broader craft-failure research's treatment of character stakes and
agency ([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]); no dedicated
craft-literature source specifically addressing the outsider-and-belonging
trope was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: The patron and the benefactor
records.summary: A figure who supplies what the protagonist could not obtain alone — resources, access, protection — and whose gift is nearly always attached to something, whether or not the story says so at the time.

citations.label: Morphology of the Folktale
The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers
Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A patron gives the protagonist something they could not get on their own: a
technique, a place at an academy, a weapon, a title, divine favour, capital,
protection. The relationship is asymmetric by definition, and the interesting
questions all follow from that asymmetry — what the patron wants, what the
gift obliges, and whether the protagonist can ever be free of it.

The role is distinct from the mentor, treated separately here. A mentor
teaches, and their gift is capability the protagonist ends up owning. A
patron *provides*, and what they provide can usually be withdrawn. Many
figures are both, and the distinction is worth holding anyway, because the
two produce different plots: mentorship ends in independence, patronage ends
in a settlement.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Patronage is one of the few relationships that scales with a protagonist's
power. Where an opponent can be outgrown, a patron can remain relevant
indefinitely: the debt is social rather than physical, and a character strong
enough to defeat anyone may still owe someone.

It also supplies a very usable kind of unease. A gift the protagonist needed
and cannot repay sits under every subsequent scene with the giver, and a
reader will keep turning pages partly to find out what it was for.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The institutional sponsor** — a sect, guild, or house that invests in the
  protagonist and expects a return, usually formalized.
- **The divine patron** — a god or entity whose favour is power and whose
  interest is rarely disinterested; overlaps with oath and binding mechanics.
- **The private benefactor** — an individual acting from motives the story
  reveals gradually.
- **The compromised gift** — help offered by someone the protagonist should
  not accept help from, where taking it is the decision.
- **The absent patron** — a benefactor never met, whose gifts arrive and whose
  purpose is a standing question.
- **The inherited patron** — a relationship the protagonist did not enter,
  attached to a family or a title. Overlaps the heir record.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A gift accepted with a full understanding of its cost, dramatized as a
  choice.
- A patron calling in something small early, so the reader learns the debt is
  real before it is large.
- A protagonist declining help and paying for the refusal.
- Conversely: a benefactor who provides steadily, wants nothing, and is never
  wrong — which functions as a supply line rather than a character.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The vending machine.** A patron who exists to deliver what the plot
  requires, with no interest of their own.
- **The costless gift.** Resources arriving without obligation, which removes
  the only thing the relationship was for.
- **The obviously sinister patron.** A benefactor so plainly untrustworthy
  that the protagonist accepting anything makes them look foolish rather than
  compromised.
- **Debt without a due date.** Obligation asserted and never called in, so the
  tension the relationship creates never resolves into anything.
- **Agency laundering.** The patron making the story's decisions while the
  protagonist executes them, which quietly removes the protagonist from their
  own book.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
The plain version — a benefactor who helps, wants something reasonable, and
eventually asks for it — works well and does not require a twist. The
suspicion that every patron must be secretly malevolent is itself a
convention, and a story where the sponsor is exactly what they appear to be
can be more interesting than one where they are not, because the tension
moves to what the protagonist owes rather than to whether they have been
deceived.

Cultivation and academy settings in particular use straightforward patronage
constantly: a sect invests, a disciple owes service, and the arrangement is
openly understood by everyone. That is not a naive version of the trope. It is
the version where the obligation is the subject.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this patron want, and would they say so if asked directly?
- What would it cost the protagonist to refuse — and has that been shown?
- Can this gift be withdrawn? What happens the first time it is threatened?
- Is the protagonist making decisions, or executing someone else's?
- How does this relationship end — repayment, rupture, inheritance, or
  never?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the patron's own objective in one sentence, without reference to the
   protagonist. If it cannot be written, the patron is currently a mechanism.
2. Have the patron ask for something small and inconvenient early, and see how
   much weight it gives every later scene between them.
3. Draft the refusal: the protagonist declines the gift, and the story
   continues. What that costs is usually the measure of the relationship.
4. Check who decided the protagonist's last three major actions.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories where the benefactor is deliberately a plot device — a brief donor
  figure in a fast-moving structure — and interrogating them would slow the
  book for no gain.
- Deliberate wish-fulfilment, where an uncomplicated benefactor is part of
  the comfort the story is offering.
- Structures where the patron is the antagonist from the start and the
  relationship is openly adversarial rather than obligating.
- Systems that grant boons impersonally, with no giver — which is a mechanic
  rather than a relationship and belongs to the system records.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe which characters supply resources or access to the
protagonist, how often, and whether anything is described as being asked in
return. Repeated one-directional giving is detectable in a loose sense and is
the closest thing here to a signal.

Everything else is interpretation. Whether a patron has an agenda is
frequently withheld deliberately, and an apparently costless gift may be a
setup rather than a flaw. The agency question — whether the protagonist is
making their own decisions — is a semantic judgment the coach should raise as
a question rather than answer from the text.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Vending machine:* Master Yun provided the pill, the technique manual, and
the introduction to the outer sect, and asked for nothing, and was pleased
whenever Wei succeeded.

*Patron with an interest:* Master Yun provided the pill and mentioned, on the
way out, that the Yun family had not placed a disciple in the outer sect for
eleven years and that people had noticed. Wei took the pill. He understood he
had just become a piece of someone's argument.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Vladimir Propp's function-based analysis
([[src.book.propp-morphology-of-the-folktale]]) supplies the underlying
structural observation that a *donor* figure — who tests and then equips the
hero — is a recurring narrative function distinct from other helper roles;
Christopher Vogler ([[src.book.vogler-writers-journey]]) supplies the
popularized treatment of helper and mentor figures this record separates;
Orson Scott Card ([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supplies the
argument about protagonist agency that underpins the agency-laundering
failure mode.

`source_confidence` is `mixed`, with a limit worth stating: Propp studied a
specific corpus of Russian folktales, and his donor function is used here as
a structural lens rather than a universal claim, in keeping with how this
library treats him elsewhere. Vogler's framework is itself a synthesis of
Campbell and is contested as a universal model. The patron-versus-mentor
distinction, the obligation-as-scaling-constraint argument, and the failure
taxonomy are this drafting pass's synthesis rather than any source's claim.

records.title: The tyrant and the institution
records.summary: Opposition that is a structure rather than a person — and the tyrant who personifies it, which is the convention's usual solution and its usual weakness.

citations.label: Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)
The Seven Basic Plots: Why We Tell Stories
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Some opposition has no face. A corrupt sect, an extractive empire, a guild
that has decided the protagonist should not succeed — these obstruct through
procedure, numbers, and inertia rather than intent. The genre's standard
solution is to give the institution a tyrant: a sect elder, a noble, a
governor who embodies it and can be confronted.

That solution is effective and has a cost. Institutions and individuals fail
differently, and defeating a person rarely changes a structure — so a story
that personifies its institutional antagonist has usually committed to an
ending where killing someone fixes a system.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Institutional opposition produces a specific and useful frustration. The
reader feels what the character feels: that being right is not sufficient,
that the rules are the weapon, and that there is nobody to hit. That is a
real experience, and fiction that renders it well is doing something power
fantasy usually cannot.

The tyrant supplies what the institution cannot: a face, a scene, and a
confrontation with an end. Most stories want both, and the interesting
question is how they relate — whether the tyrant made the institution or the
institution produced the tyrant, and whether removing them changes anything.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The personified institution** — one figure standing for the whole,
  confrontable and defeatable.
- **The faceless structure** — no single antagonist; the obstacle is
  procedure, and victory means changing or escaping the system.
- **The reasonable functionary** — someone doing their job, not cruel,
  whose ordinary competence is the obstacle. Frequently the most unsettling
  version.
- **The captured institution** — a structure with a legitimate purpose,
  currently serving someone else's interest, which allows reform as an
  ending.
- **The tyrant who is genuinely load-bearing** — an individual whose removal
  actually would change the structure, which the story has to earn rather
  than assume.
- **The institution as protagonist's own** — the sect, guild, or state the
  protagonist belongs to and is compromised by.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A refusal delivered politely by someone with no stake in it.
- A rule applied selectively, and the impossibility of proving that.
- The tyrant replaced, and the next occupant behaving identically.
- Conversely: an empire whose entire evil is one man, dissolving the moment
  he does.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Decapitation as resolution.** The tyrant killed and the institution
  reforming instantly, which readers experience as the story declining to
  finish its own argument.
- **Cartoon institutions.** Structures staffed entirely by people who enjoy
  cruelty, which is less frightening than one staffed by people following
  procedure.
- **The unopposable structure.** Institutional power so total that the
  protagonist has no available action, which is despair rather than conflict.
- **No internal disagreement.** An institution with a single view, when the
  interesting thing about institutions is that they contain factions.
- **The tyrant with no institution.** A villain described as embodying a
  system the story never shows operating.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
The corrupt elder, the arrogant noble house, the sect that protects its
favorites — these are staples of cultivation and progression fiction and they
work plainly. Readers enjoy this confrontation, and the satisfaction of a
deserved comeuppance is a legitimate thing for a book to deliver.

Straightforward execution is improved by one small addition rather than a
subversion: let the institution outlast the tyrant in some visible way. The
comeuppance still lands, the reader still gets the scene, and the world stays
real because the structure that produced this person is still standing and
will produce another. That costs a paragraph and buys most of what the
sophisticated version offers.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Would removing this person change anything structural, and does the story
  claim it would?
- Who inside this institution disagrees with it, and what does dissent cost
  them?
- What legitimate function does this institution serve? Even extractive ones
  usually do something.
- What can the protagonist do here that is not violence?
- If the protagonist wins, what does the institution look like a year later?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Write the functionary scene: an obstacle delivered by someone with no
   malice, doing their job correctly.
2. Replace the tyrant offstage and let the next one behave the same way.
3. Give the institution one internal faction that agrees with the
   protagonist and cannot help them.
4. Write what the institution is *for*, then check whether the story's
   opposition is to the purpose or to its current holders.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories whose promise is straightforward comeuppance, where a satisfying
  defeat of a hateful individual is the contract and structural realism would
  work against it.
- Personal-scale conflicts where the antagonist is genuinely an individual and
  no institution is in play.
- Comedy and satire, where an absurdly monolithic institution is the joke.
- Very short work, where institutional texture has no room to develop.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
A coach can observe whether an institution is referred to by name across a
manuscript, whether more than one member is individuated, and whether
opposition is attributed to a person or a body. Those are weak signals and
easily misread — a well-run story may keep an institution deliberately
faceless.

Whether decapitation is an unearned resolution is a semantic judgment about
an ending, and readers legitimately disagree about how much structural
realism a genre story owes. The coach should raise the question — what does
this institution look like afterward? — rather than treat a satisfying
personal victory as a flaw.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Decapitation:* Elder Hu was killed, and the sect's disciples were freed, and
the practice of selling outer-court places ended with him.

*Structure that outlasts:* Elder Hu was killed, and within the month the
outer-court places were being sold again at a slightly higher price, by
someone who had disapproved of Hu personally.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Orson Scott Card ([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supplies the
craft argument that antagonism needs a face for a reader to engage with it;
Christopher Booker ([[src.book.booker-seven-basic-plots]]) supplies the
recurring shape of tyrant-overthrow narratives, used as an observation about
recurrence rather than as an authority on execution, given his framework's
contested status. This library's genre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation that
corrupt sects and noble houses are standing conventions in cultivation and
progression fiction.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense. The
characterization principle is sourced; the record's central argument — that
personifying an institution commits a story to an ending where killing
someone fixes a structure, and that letting the structure visibly outlast the
tyrant is a cheap fix — is this drafting pass's synthesis. No source cited
here addresses institutional antagonists directly, and the political reasoning
follows this library's own institutions record rather than any external
authority.

records.title: The trickster
records.summary: A character who operates through cunning, deception, or rule-bending rather than direct confrontation — useful for generating plot through cleverness, and prone to a specific failure where cleverness is asserted rather than demonstrated.

citations.label: Morphology of the Folktale

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A trickster character operates primarily through cunning, deception,
misdirection, or creative rule-bending rather than direct confrontation or
raw capability. The role has deep roots across many storytelling
traditions (figures who outwit rather than overpower), and functionally, a
trickster generates plot through cleverness — their solutions to problems
should surprise the reader with an approach that wasn't the obvious one,
which places a specific burden on the author to actually demonstrate that
cleverness on the page rather than asserting it through other characters'
reactions.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A trickster offers a distinct pleasure from a purely strength-based
protagonist or ally: the satisfaction of watching a problem solved through
wit rather than force, often with an element of surprise or reversal that a
head-on approach couldn't produce. This works especially well as a
counterbalance in ensemble casts built around combat-forward or
strength-based protagonists, giving the group a different kind of solution
available to them.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Benevolent trickster**, using cunning in service of the protagonist's
  goals or a broader good, common as an ally or supporting-cast role.
- **Amoral or self-interested trickster**, whose schemes serve their own
  ends and may or may not align with the protagonist's, adding
  unpredictability to their alliance.
- **Trickster antagonist**, opposing the protagonist through deception and
  misdirection rather than direct confrontation, often requiring a
  different kind of victory (out-thinking rather than out-fighting) for the
  antagonist to be defeated.
- **Trickster protagonist**, where the story's central character operates
  primarily through cunning, shifting the whole narrative's problem-solving
  register toward cleverness rather than confrontation.
- **Chaotic or amoral-comedy trickster**, whose scheming produces comic
  chaos rather than serving a clear strategic goal — a legitimate,
  lighter-toned variant.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A specific, demonstrated clever solution to a problem — a plan the reader
  can follow and verify actually works, rather than a solution asserted as
  clever by other characters' reactions.
- A trickster's scheme with visible moving parts, ideally traceable in
  hindsight to specific setup (closely related to the heist trope's
  fair-play principle).
- The inverse, as a warning sign: other characters repeatedly describing the
  trickster as brilliant or cunning without the reader ever seeing a
  specific clever plan actually executed and working.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Asserted rather than demonstrated cleverness**, where a trickster's
  reputation for cunning isn't backed by specific, verifiable clever
  solutions on the page.
- **Plans that work for no clear reason**, where a scheme succeeds through
  narrative convenience rather than a traceable, fair mechanism.
- **A trickster who never actually risks anything**, where their
  cleverness always works perfectly with no cost or setback, removing
  tension from their scenes.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Can you point to a specific, verifiable clever solution the trickster
  has executed, rather than other characters simply calling them clever?
- Does a trickster's scheme have traceable setup, so an attentive reader
  could follow how it worked?
- Does the trickster ever fail, or pay a cost for a scheme gone wrong?
- If this is a trickster antagonist, does defeating them require
  out-thinking rather than simply out-fighting them?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Find a scene where the trickster's cleverness is asserted by another
   character's reaction rather than demonstrated through a specific plan;
   replace the assertion with an actual demonstrated scheme.
2. Trace a trickster's successful scheme backward to confirm it has fair,
   traceable setup rather than working through convenience.
3. Introduce a scheme that partially fails or costs the trickster something,
   to keep their cleverness from reading as effortless and risk-free.
4. For a trickster antagonist, check whether their eventual defeat comes
   through outsmarting them, not just overpowering them.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- A trickster used briefly for comic relief, without extensive
  page time, may not need the full demonstrated-cleverness treatment this
  pattern describes.
- A story explicitly depicting a trickster's reputation as exaggerated or
  undeserved (a character who talks a bigger game than they deliver) is
  using the gap between reputation and demonstrated ability as its own
  characterization, not failing to earn a trickster reputation.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A trickster whose cleverness is reliably demonstrated and consistently
effective, without needing failure or cost to feel earned, is a satisfying
and reliable structure in lighter or more comedic registers, where the
pleasure is watching competent scheming unfold smoothly rather than
watching it strain against real risk.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a trickster's cleverness is demonstrated through a specific,
traceable plan versus merely asserted through other characters' reactions
requires reading and interpreting the manuscript's plot mechanics — a
judgment no structured data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Asserted cleverness:* Other characters repeatedly call a trickster "the
smartest person in the room," but the story never shows a specific plan of
theirs actually working through demonstrated cunning rather than luck or
other characters' incompetence.

*Demonstrated cleverness:* The same trickster instead is shown planting a
false rumor two chapters earlier, specifically calculated to make a rival
faction distrust their own scout at the exact moment it matters — the
payoff traces to a specific, verifiable setup the reader could follow.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The trickster's cross-traditional character-function grounding draws on
Vladimir Propp's structuralist analysis of character functions
([[src.book.propp-morphology-of-the-folktale]]), a study of a specific
corpus (Russian folktales) used here for function-based framing rather than
as a universal claim about all trickster figures across all traditions;
`source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly, and this record avoids treating
Propp's specific taxonomy as directly transferable to modern genre fiction
without adaptation.

records.title: The villain protagonist
records.summary: A protagonist the story does not ask the reader to approve of — which changes what holds attention, since sympathy is no longer available and something else has to do its work.

citations.label: Characters & Viewpoint (Elements of Fiction Writing)
Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A villain protagonist is a viewpoint character whose aims the story does not
present as good, and does not expect the reader to endorse. This is a
stronger position than the antihero, which this library treats separately:
an antihero is unadmirable in method while broadly aligned with something the
reader wants, whereas a villain protagonist may want what the reader hopes
they do not get.

The distinction that matters in practice is between *sympathy* and
*investment*. A reader does not need to approve of a character to want to
know what they do next, but the story has to supply something in place of
approval — competence, coherence, honesty about what the character is, or
the specific pleasure of watching a plan work.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Approval is only one of several things that holds a reader. Craft writing on
character tends to identify others: a character who wants something intensely
is interesting nearly regardless of what it is; a character who is good at
something is compelling to watch; a character whose logic is internally
consistent invites the reader to follow it even while disagreeing.

There is also a specific pleasure in being allowed inside a mind the reader
would ordinarily be protected from, and in a story that does not pretend to
be shocked by its own protagonist. Progression fiction has its own version
of this — the dungeon core, the monster protagonist, the ruthless optimizer —
where the appeal often lies in a frank amorality the genre otherwise avoids.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **The competent villain** — held by skill and planning; the reader watches
  a difficult thing done well.
- **The sympathetic-cause villain** — wrong methods, comprehensible aim,
  where the reader's discomfort is the design.
- **The unrepentant villain** — no arc toward redemption offered, which is
  the hardest version and the most honest about what it is.
- **The monstrous viewpoint** — a non-human protagonist whose values are
  genuinely alien rather than merely wicked.
- **The villain in decline** — a character whose logic is coherent early and
  visibly deteriorates, which supplies an arc without a redemption.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A protagonist whose plans work, narrated with the same satisfaction a
  heroic story gives to a rescue.
- Victims who are specific people rather than obstacles — a choice that
  makes the book harder and usually better.
- A narration that does not editorialize, letting the reader supply the
  judgment the character will not.
- Conversely: a villain protagonist who is repeatedly excused by
  circumstance, which usually indicates a story that wants the aesthetics of
  villainy without its cost.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The softened villain.** Cruelty established and then continuously
  mitigated, so the reader is asked to enjoy the transgression and forgive it
  simultaneously.
- **Victims as furniture.** Harm done to unnamed, uncharacterized people,
  which makes the transgression weightless and the story less interesting
  rather than more comfortable.
- **Incoherent values.** A character whose ruthlessness is inconsistent,
  applied when the plot needs menace and abandoned when it needs sympathy.
- **Nothing to watch.** A protagonist who is unpleasant without being
  competent, interesting, or coherent — cruelty as characterization.
- **The unearned redemption.** A late turn toward goodness that the book has
  not paid for, which readers often experience as the story losing its nerve.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
This convention needs no inversion. A story about a genuinely villainous
person, executed plainly and without apology, is a legitimate and durable
form — it does not require an ironic frame, a redemptive arc, or a
sympathetic backstory to justify itself, and adding those defensively is one
of the more common ways the form is weakened.

The one thing straightforward execution does require is that the story mean
it. A villain protagonist whose villainy is real, whose harm lands on people
the book has bothered to make real, and who is not quietly excused, gives the
reader a clear contract. It is the half-committed version — transgression
with the costs edited out — that tends to disappoint.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What holds a reader here in place of sympathy, and is it on the page in
  chapter one?
- Does the story ever pretend to disapprove of something it is inviting the
  reader to enjoy?
- Are the people this character harms specific enough that the harm registers?
- Is this character's logic consistent when it is inconvenient for the plot?
- Does the book intend a redemption, and has it been paid for — or is it
  arriving because the ending felt uncomfortable?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Name what the reader is being offered besides approval — competence,
   insight, spectacle, honesty. If it is hard to name, that is the work.
2. Give one victim a page of their own before the harm, and see what the
   scene costs afterward.
3. Remove the story's most recent excuse for the protagonist and read the
   chapter again. If it becomes unreadable, the excuses may be carrying the
   book.
4. Write the protagonist's values as three rules, then find the scene where
   the plot asked them to break one for convenience.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Comedy and satire, where a monstrous protagonist's harm is deliberately
  weightless and making victims real would break the register.
- Stories where the protagonist is villainous by circumstance rather than
  disposition, which are usually antihero or redemption structures and are
  treated in the related record.
- Non-human viewpoints whose alien values are the subject rather than a
  moral position — the dungeon-core profile covers the genre's common case.
- Any story whose intent is to make the reader complicit rather than
  comfortable, where several of the failure modes above may be deliberate
  effects.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Very little of this is computable. A coach can observe whether harmed
characters are named and given dialogue, whether the narration applies
evaluative language to the protagonist's acts, and whether a redemptive turn
occurs late relative to the book's length. None of these establishes the
record's central question.

Whether a reader has been given something in place of sympathy is a semantic
judgment and a reader-dependent one — the same book can be gripping or
repellent to two readers with no disagreement about its content. A coach
should describe what the text does and avoid concluding that a protagonist
is unsympathetic, which is a response rather than a property.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Softened:* he had no choice; they would have killed him first; the guard was
cruel to prisoners anyway. Three excuses in one paragraph, and the reader is
being asked not to notice.

*Committed:* the guard had a daughter at the barracks school and talked about
her while he worked. Kel let him finish the sentence before he did it,
because interrupting would have been rude.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Orson Scott Card's treatment of character and viewpoint
([[src.book.card-characters-and-viewpoint]]) supplies the underlying
distinction between reader sympathy and reader interest, and the argument
that attachment can be built on curiosity and competence rather than
approval; Janet Burroway ([[src.book.burroway-writing-fiction]]) supplies the
general principles about characterization and narrative distance this record
relies on. This library's genre research
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) supplies the observation about
monstrous and amoral protagonists in dungeon-core and dark subgenres.

`source_confidence` is `mixed` in the handoff's second sense: the
character-craft principles are supported by established sources, while the
application to villain protagonists specifically — the failure taxonomy, the
"softened villain" pattern, the argument about specific victims — is this
drafting pass's synthesis. Neither craft source addresses villain
protagonists directly. No claim is made about how readers in aggregate
respond to morally repellent viewpoints; that varies widely and no study is
cited.

records.title: Romantic subplot conventions
records.summary: Romance woven into a larger plot follows recognizable shapes (slow burn, rivals-to-partners, established relationship under strain) that work across relationship models and orientations — the coaching value is in the shape and its promise, not in assuming any one configuration of partners.

citations.label: Story Genius: How to Use Brain Science to Go Beyond Outlining

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A romantic subplot is a relationship arc, romantic or intimate in nature,
that develops alongside a story's primary plot. This record treats the
shape of romantic subplots — how attraction, obstacle, and resolution are
structured — as the coaching subject, deliberately without assuming any
particular configuration of gender, orientation, or relationship model.
The craft questions (does the relationship have real obstacles, does it
change both characters, is its resolution earned) apply the same way
regardless of who the partners are or how many.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
A romantic subplot works when it creates genuine risk and change for the
characters involved — when the relationship costs something to pursue, and
when both people are changed by it. Readers report fatigue with romantic
subplots that feel obligatory (present because the genre expects one) rather
than integrated with the story's actual stakes, and with love triangles or
manufactured obstacles that exist only to generate conflict rather than
reveal character.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Slow burn**, where attraction is established early but deliberately
  delayed, building tension through anticipation and small escalations.
- **Rivals or antagonists to partners**, where the relationship develops out
  of initial opposition, common in progression-fantasy and academy settings.
- **Established relationship under strain**, where the story begins with an
  existing partnership and tests it, rather than building one from scratch.
- **Ensemble or non-exclusive structures**, where the story explores
  relationships that aren't organized around a single exclusive pairing —
  a legitimate structure, not an inherent complication device.
- **Quiet or background romance**, where the relationship develops mostly
  off the story's main stage, given weight through a few well-chosen scenes
  rather than sustained focus.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A relationship obstacle rooted in the characters' actual values, fears, or
  circumstances, rather than a misunderstanding that could be resolved with
  one honest conversation.
- Scenes where the relationship's development changes what a character
  wants or is willing to risk in the main plot, integrating the subplot with
  the story's larger stakes.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a relationship that develops in scenes
  disconnected from the main plot, with no bearing on either character's
  choices elsewhere in the story.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **The manufactured misunderstanding**, an obstacle that exists only
  because characters won't communicate, rather than a genuine incompatible
  want or circumstance.
- **The obligatory romance**, present because the genre or format seems to
  expect one, with no organic development or bearing on the main plot.
- **A love triangle used only to generate tension**, where one or more
  romantic options exist mainly as plot device rather than as a fully
  realized character with independent stakes.
- **Romance that never intersects with the main plot**, developing in a
  narratively isolated track that could be cut without affecting anything
  else in the story.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What is the actual obstacle to this relationship, and could it be
  resolved with a single honest conversation? If so, is that itself part of
  the point, or is the story treating an easily solvable problem as
  a real one?
- Does this relationship change what either character wants or risks in the
  main plot?
- If there's a love triangle or multiple romantic options, does the
  non-chosen option have wants and stakes independent of being a romantic
  option?
- Would cutting the romantic subplot entirely change anything about the
  main plot's outcome?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify the relationship's central obstacle and check whether it's
   rooted in genuine incompatible wants or circumstances, or only in
   miscommunication.
2. Find one scene where the relationship's development directly affects a
   choice in the main plot, or add one if none currently exists.
3. For a love-triangle structure, give the non-chosen character an
   independent want unrelated to the romance, and a scene where it surfaces.
4. If the romance feels obligatory, consider whether the story is better
   served by cutting it, or by deepening its connection to the main plot's
   stakes.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories not centered on romance may include a very minor romantic thread
  with little development, as texture rather than subplot — this pattern
  applies once a relationship is positioned as a subplot with its own arc.
- A story deliberately depicting an unresolved or unrequited relationship as
  its point (not every romantic thread needs to resolve into partnership)
  is using the form differently, not failing to complete it.

sections.title: When straightforward execution is the right choice
sections.content:
A classical slow-burn or rivals-to-partners arc, played without subversion,
remains a reliable and satisfying structure precisely because its shape is
legible — a reader who wants that specific promise (earned tension resolving
into commitment) is well served by a story that delivers it cleanly, as long
as the obstacle along the way is genuine.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a relationship's obstacle is genuine or manufactured, and whether it
intersects meaningfully with the main plot, requires reading and
interpreting characterization and plot structure — a judgment no structured
data substitutes for.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Manufactured obstacle:* Two characters are kept apart for a dozen chapters
by a secret that either could resolve in one sentence, with no reason given
for why neither says it.

*Genuine obstacle:* The same characters are kept apart because one has a
binding, structurally enforced obligation (a contract, a vow, a
command-bound service) that would cost real, dramatized harm to break —
the obstacle is external and consequential, not a withheld sentence.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The want/obstacle framing for relationship subplots draws on established
character-arc craft writing ([[src.book.cron-story-genius]]), applied here
specifically to romantic subplots rather than quoted from a source
