  mechanical fact with no bearing on the setting's politics or inequality.
- **Nominal universality with no practical examination**, where a system
  is stated to be open to anyone but the story never shows or
  acknowledges the practical barriers (resources, opportunity, training
  access) that would realistically limit who actually succeeds.
- **Access criteria that shift for plot convenience**, where a
  bloodline-gated system suddenly grants access to a non-lineage character
  with no explanation, undermining the stated rule's credibility.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is access to this world's power system universal, class-bound, or
  nominally universal but practically gated — and does the story treat
  that distinction as meaningful?
- If access is gated by birth or institution, does the story engage what
  that implies about the setting's social structure, even briefly?
- If access is nominally universal, are there characters who are
  technically eligible but practically excluded by resource or opportunity
  constraints?
- Are the system's stated access rules honored consistently, or does an
  exception occur with no explanation?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. State explicitly whether this world's power access is universal,
   gated, or nominally universal, and check whether the story's actual
   depicted cast reflects that choice consistently.
2. For a gated system with no examined social consequence, add a scene
   showing a character excluded by the gate, and let their exclusion
   matter to the plot.
3. For a nominally universal system, find or add a character who
   illustrates the gap between technical and practical access.
4. Audit any exception to the stated access rule for a credible
   explanation.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight settings where the power system is never load-bearing
  for social or political plot don't need the full examination this
  pattern describes.
- A story explicitly satirizing meritocratic myths (a "universal access"
  system revealed to be quietly gated in practice, as the story's actual
  point) is using the gap between stated and practical access
  deliberately.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a system's stated access rules are honored consistently across the
manuscript is close to deterministic where explicitly tracked. Whether the
story adequately engages the social implications of its access model
requires interpreting the worldbuilding and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unexamined gating:* A magic system is established as available only to a
specific bloodline, and the story never shows or mentions anyone outside
that bloodline reacting to, resenting, or being affected by the
exclusion — the gate exists but does no social work.

*Examined gating:* The same bloodline-gated system instead is shown
sustaining an entrenched aristocracy, with a specific non-lineage character
whose resentment of the system (or whose discovery of an unexpected,
unexplained access to it) drives real plot tension.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The access-versus-structure distinction and its systemic implications draw
on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`'s general survey of genre conventions
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) and Andrew Rowe's writing on
society applying its own powers ([[src.rowe.progression-fantasy]]);
`source_confidence` is `mixed` because the specific universal/gated
taxonomy presented here is this drafting pass's synthesis rather than a
direct claim from either source.

records.title: Pools versus thresholds
records.summary: A resource tracked as a depleting pool (mana points spent and refilled) and one tracked as a binary threshold (either you qualify or you don't) create different tactical textures and different kinds of tension around the same underlying capability.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A pool tracks a resource as a continuous, depleting quantity — a mana bar
spent down and refilled, health lost and restored — where the interesting
tension is how much remains and how it's allocated across multiple
demands. A threshold tracks a resource as a binary or stepped
qualification — a character either has met a prerequisite (enough
accumulated qi to attempt a breakthrough) or hasn't, with no meaningful
in-between state — where the interesting tension is whether and when the
threshold will be crossed, not how much buffer remains above it. The same
underlying capability can be modeled either way, and the choice changes
what kind of moment-to-moment decisions a story's characters (and its
readers, tracking along) actually make.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Pool-based resources support ongoing tactical allocation — a character
managing a dwindling mana pool across a long fight makes a series of small
decisions about when to spend and when to conserve, generating sustained,
granular tension. Threshold-based resources support a different rhythm:
tension builds toward a single qualifying or disqualifying moment (will
this be enough, has this been reached) rather than accumulating through
many small allocation decisions. Neither is superior; they produce
different reading experiences, and a story that treats a threshold
resource with pool-style granular tracking (or vice versa) can create a
mismatch between how a mechanic is presented and how it actually functions
dramatically.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Pure pool**, a continuously trackable quantity spent and replenished
  across many uses, the default model for most combat resources (mana,
  stamina).
- **Pure threshold**, a single qualify/don't-qualify state with no
  meaningful gradation, common in breakthrough or advancement-gate
  mechanics (has enough experience accumulated to level up).
- **Threshold-with-visible-approach**, a hybrid where the underlying state
  is binary but the character can track how close they are to the
  threshold, blending some of the granular tension of a pool with the
  binary payoff of a threshold.
- **Pool with a threshold event**, where continuous accumulation
  (a filling pool) triggers a distinct, binary event once a cap is reached
  (a resource that "overflows" into a transformation or special ability at
  full capacity) — combining both models deliberately.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character allocating a visibly tracked, depleting resource across
  multiple demands within a single scene, weighing how much to spend now
  against what might be needed later.
- A character's progress toward a qualifying threshold tracked and
  anticipated across a longer stretch of the story, with the actual
  crossing functioning as a single significant event.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a resource introduced as a threshold
  (you either qualify or you don't) later treated as though partial
  progress toward it grants partial benefit, blurring the two models
  without acknowledgment.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Model confusion**, where a resource's underlying nature (pool or
  threshold) isn't consistently honored, creating reader confusion about
  what actually determines success.
- **A threshold treated with false granularity**, implying that being
  "close" to a threshold provides some benefit when the system's actual
  rule is binary, misleading the reader about the stakes of any given
  scene.
- **A pool treated as inexhaustible in practice**, undermining the
  granular tactical tension the pool model is meant to provide if it's
  never shown running low enough to matter.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, visibility, and consequences
sections.content:
The two models fail differently, and the difference is felt rather than
calculated. A pool fails gradually: a character runs low, rations, and
finally runs dry, so the drama lives in the descent and the reader can
anticipate it. A threshold fails discretely: the character either qualifies
or does not, so the drama lives in the attempt and its aftermath, and a
failed attempt usually needs its own consequence — lost accumulation, injury,
a closed window — or the threshold becomes a door the character simply knocks
on repeatedly.

Visibility works differently too. Pools invite a legible gauge, whether an
interface or a described sensation, and are easy to make perceivable to
allies and enemies; thresholds are often private until crossed, which is why
breakthrough moments are so often public reveals of a private accumulation.

At the level of a society, pools tend to produce commerce — anything
continuous can be measured, stored, sold, and taxed — while thresholds tend
to produce hierarchy and ceremony, because a stepped qualification invites
institutions to certify, gate, and rank it. A setting can run both at once,
but it is worth noticing which one its economy and its politics actually
grew around.

sections.title: Exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
Each model implies its own abuses. Pools invite stockpiling, borrowing
against future capacity, and topping up mid-fight from consumables — and
anything that refills a pool cheaply quietly deletes the constraint the pool
existed to create. Thresholds invite hovering just below a line to avoid
triggering something, rushing a qualification with borrowed or artificial
accumulation, and the classic cultivation problem of an unstable foundation
bought by crossing too fast. Where the two models coexist — a pool that must
reach a threshold to advance — the interaction is worth stating explicitly,
since readers will otherwise infer a rule from the first example they see
and notice when a later scene contradicts it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- For this resource, is the underlying model a continuous pool or a
  binary threshold, and is that consistently honored across the
  manuscript?
- If it's pool-based, does the story ever show the pool running low enough
  to force a real allocation decision?
- If it's threshold-based, is the character's approach toward the
  threshold tracked in a way the reader can anticipate, or does the
  qualifying moment arrive without buildup?
- Is there a scene where the two models are blurred — partial credit
  implied for a resource that's actually binary?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify the manuscript's key resources and label each as pool or
   threshold; audit for consistency across the scenes where each appears.
2. For a pool resource that's never shown depleting meaningfully, add a
   scene where it runs low enough to force a real decision.
3. For a threshold resource, add tracking or anticipation of the approach
   to the threshold, if the qualifying moment currently arrives without
   buildup.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight or purely narrative-conveyed power systems don't need
  either model made explicit.
- A story deliberately keeping a resource's underlying model ambiguous, as
  a source of tension about whether a character has "enough," may use that
  ambiguity intentionally rather than needing to resolve it.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks a resource's quantity or threshold state
linked to scenes, whether the model is honored consistently is close to
deterministic. Whether the narrative tension matches the resource's actual
underlying model requires interpreting the prose and remains model-
assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Pool tension:* A caster tracks remaining mana across an extended siege,
weighing whether to spend the last reserve on a decisive strike or hold it
in case of a worse threat later — a genuine allocation decision under
uncertainty.

*Threshold tension:* A cultivator instead has accumulated enough qi to
attempt a breakthrough for several chapters, with the tension centered
entirely on whether and when they'll finally attempt it, not on managing a
depleting quantity moment to moment.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The pool/threshold distinction draws on established game-design literature
covering resource representation
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]]); no dedicated craft-
literature source specifically addressing this distinction's application
to prose fiction was available to this drafting pass. `source_confidence`
is set to `limited` accordingly.

records.title: Qi versus mana: choosing a power resource's cultural texture
records.summary: Qi and mana are not interchangeable labels for the same fuel bar — they carry different histories, different relationships to the self, and different narrative textures, and the choice between them (or a third option) should follow the story's promise, not habit.

citations.label: Introducing Daoism
Neidan
Xianxia
LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
The History of Mana: How an Austronesian Concept Became a Video Game Mechanic
How Mana Left the Pacific and Became a Video Game Mechanic
The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-Lore
Rethinking Mana

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
"Mana" and "qi" (also transliterated chi, ki, or qì depending on tradition
and romanization system) are two of the most common vocabulary choices for a
magic or power system's fuel, and they are frequently treated in genre
discussion as interchangeable — a "Western" fuel bar and an "Eastern" one
doing the same job. This record treats that flattening as a mistake.

Mana has a documented route out of the Pacific. The word is Austronesian and
appears across languages spanning the three regions Europeans invented and
imposed — Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia — so calling it simply
"Polynesian" repeats a colonial division the concept crosses. Codrington's
1891 missionary ethnography introduced it to English-language scholarship as
a supernatural power attaching to people and things; Keesing later argued
that reading was a grammatical error, since in Proto-Oceanic mana was
canonically a stative verb — to be efficacious, to work — naming a condition
inferred from an outcome rather than a substance anyone holds. The substance
reading is the one that travelled: through comparative religion, where
Eliade anthologized Codrington for a mass American readership, into the
1960s counterculture, and from there into tabletop spell-point systems and
the video games that inherited them. What fantasy calls mana is therefore a
Victorian misreading of an Oceanic concept, repurposed twice more on its way
to the fuel bar.

Qi, in its historical and philosophical
sense within Chinese thought and Daoist internal alchemy (neidan), refers to
vital energy understood as constitutive of the body and cosmos alike —
not primarily a resource one spends, but a condition one cultivates and
refines. Modern xianxia and cultivation genre fiction uses "qi" in a further,
distinct sense: a game-adjacent, often quantifiable cultivation resource
that borrows the term's prestige and resonance without claiming to represent
the historical or religious concept directly. All three usages are
legitimate; conflating them is the error this record exists to prevent.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The resource label a story chooses signals a promise about the *texture* of
power: is it something a character possesses like a tool, or something a
character *becomes* through refinement? A mana system read as external and
tool-like promises acquisition, allocation, and management — a resource
economy. A qi/cultivation system read as internal and identity-constituting
promises transformation — power as a marker of who a character is becoming,
not just what they can currently spend. Readers of cultivation fiction
specifically are reported to care more about *why* a character advances
(the internal logic and cost of a breakthrough) than about the raw numbers
involved, the inverse of classic LitRPG's number-forward appeal.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Ambient/external mana** — a force drawn from the environment, gods, or a
  cosmic field, existing independently of the caster and merely channeled;
  common in Western high fantasy and many LitRPG systems.
- **Internal, embodied qi** — vital energy cultivated within the body,
  refined through practice, and inseparable from the practitioner's own
  growth and moral/spiritual state; the historical Daoist neidan framing and
  the frame most cultivation fiction gestures toward, even when simplified.
  When using "qi," state which transliteration and tradition you are drawing
  from: Mandarin qì, Cantonese hei, Japanese ki, and Korean gi carry distinct
  histories that one spelling flattens.
- **Hybrid or renamed resources** — invented terms (aether, essence, spirit)
  that borrow structurally from either tradition without claiming either
  culture's vocabulary directly, a common and lower-risk choice for authors
  working outside either tradition's specific cultural context.
- **Dual-resource systems** — mana and qi (or equivalent internal/external
  resources) coexisting in one setting with genuinely different rules,
  useful for stories wanting both an acquisition economy and a cultivation
  arc.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A mana system depicted as a meter that depletes with use and refills with
  rest or environmental access — spend, recover, spend again.
- A qi/cultivation system depicted as a state that deepens through
  disciplined practice, where "how much qi" matters less than "what stage of
  refinement," and where a breakthrough is a narrated event rather than a
  number ticking up.
- A story using "qi" as reskinned mana — a spendable meter with a different
  name and no cultivation-specific behavior. Not wrong; worth choosing
  deliberately rather than defaulting into.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Treating qi and mana as the same resource with different names**,
  discarding the narrative texture each tradition offers and delivering
  neither promise fully.
- **Using "qi" without any signal of which tradition or transliteration is
  meant**, when the setting otherwise gives no context, which can read as
  borrowing prestige from a real cultural and religious tradition without
  engaging its substance. The same applies to mana, whose distance from its
  Oceanic sense is now so wide that most readers do not know it has one.
- **Over-quantifying an internal-cultivation system** into a spendable meter,
  undercutting the "power as identity, not inventory" promise that draws
  cultivation readers to the subgenre in the first place.
- **Under-explaining an ambient mana system's sourcing**, leaving its
  economic and ecological implications unexamined — who else can reach this
  force, and what do they do with it.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Is this story's power meant to feel like something a character has, or
  something a character is becoming? Does the chosen resource label support
  that distinction?
- If "qi" is used, which tradition or transliteration is it drawing from,
  and is that legible to the reader, even implicitly?
- Would this system's promise change if the resource were renamed to a
  fully invented term with no real-world cultural weight?
- Who else in this world has access to the same resource, and what does
  that imply about society, economy, and power structures?

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and visibility
sections.content:
The two framings also progress and fail differently, which is often where a
reskinned system gives itself away. Mana-shaped resources typically grow by
capacity — a larger pool, faster regeneration, cheaper costs — so failure
looks like running out at the wrong moment, and recovery is a matter of time
or access. Qi-shaped resources typically grow by refinement — the same
quantity made purer, or the practitioner made able to hold what would
previously have harmed them — so failure looks like a foundation built too
fast, a stalled stage, or damage taken from one's own power rather than from
an opponent. A story that says "qi" but fails only by running dry has
quietly chosen mana's shape — a legitimate choice, worth making
knowingly.

Visibility differs in the same direction. An ambient resource invites
instruments, wards, and specialists who measure it, and becomes something
institutions can price. An internal, cultivated resource is usually private —
legible to the practitioner, sometimes to a master or a spiritual sense the
setting defines, otherwise inferred from bearing. That privacy is what makes
concealed cultivation, underestimation, and the sudden reveal of a stage
such durable plots, and what makes an appraisal ability change a cultivation
setting more than a mana one.

sections.title: Common exploits, edge cases, and interaction with other mechanics
sections.content:
An externally sourced, ambient resource (mana) raises questions a purely
internal one doesn't: can it be stolen, hoarded, or weaponized as a
resource denial tactic against others? Can it run out at a civilizational
scale? An internally cultivated resource (qi) raises different questions: can
cultivation be accelerated unsafely, is there a risk of "deviation" (a
common trope in cultivation fiction, drawn loosely from real qigong
deviation concerns) from rushing refinement, and does the resource interact
with morality or intent in a way a purely mechanical mana system typically
doesn't. Both interact with class/role systems, crafting (enchantment vs.
alchemy/pill refinement), and social status differently — worth mapping
explicitly rather than assuming either resource behaves like the other once
combined with other mechanics.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Rename the resource, temporarily, to a neutral invented term and reread a
   scene that leans on it. If nothing about the scene changes, the story is
   drawing on the label's borrowed resonance rather than on any behavior the
   system actually has — worth knowing before deciding whether to build the
   behavior or keep the neutral name.
2. Write the resource's failure state as a scene rather than a rule: what a
   character looks like when it runs out, or when refinement goes wrong.
   Whichever comes naturally is usually the tradition the draft actually
   operates in.
3. Draft one paragraph, not for the manuscript, stating which
   transliteration and tradition the term is drawn from and what the story
   does and does not claim about it. Keeping it in the notes tends to keep
   the prose consistent, and makes an eventual author's note easier to write
   honestly.
4. If the setting runs both resources, write the scene where a practitioner
   of one meets a practitioner of the other. Systems that were secretly one
   resource with two names reveal it here: neither character finds anything
   about the other strange.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Stories using neither term, with a fully invented resource vocabulary, sidestep
  this comparison entirely and are not obligated to engage either tradition.
- A deliberate satire or genre mashup may intentionally flatten the
  distinction as its joke or its point — provided that flattening reads as
  authorial choice rather than unexamined default.
- Settings with an explicitly syncretic in-world justification (multiple
  real-world-inspired traditions colliding within the story's own history)
  can justify treating resources as convergent in-world, which is different
  from an author failing to distinguish them at the craft level.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript's resource system reads as ambient/external or
internal/embodied, and whether its vocabulary choices are used with
apparent cultural awareness, requires interpreting the text — no
deterministic check substitutes for this. A coach can surface this
comparison as a framework for the author's own review of a system already in
place, or as a design prompt before one is built, but cannot verify from a
system's stat sheet alone which narrative promise it is actually keeping in
the prose.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Reskinned mana:* A cultivator's "qi pool" depletes by a fixed number per
spell cast and refills after eight hours of rest, functioning identically to
a mana bar with no cultivation-specific behavior — a legitimate choice, but
one that trades away the "power as identity" promise cultivation readers
often want.

*Internal cultivation:* The same character instead measures progress by
named stages (Foundation, Core Formation) reached through sustained,
risk-bearing practice, where a breakthrough is a dramatized turning point
tied to the character's discipline and choices rather than a resource total
crossing a threshold.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The historical and philosophical grounding for qi and Daoist internal
alchemy draws on an academic introduction to Daoism
([[src.book.kohn-introducing-daoism]]) with encyclopedic corroboration
([[src.wikipedia.neidan]], [[src.wikipedia.xianxia]]).

**Mana's history was corrected and sourced on 2026-09-05**, replacing an
earlier unsourced claim that called it "a Polynesian concept... reshaped by
20th-century occultism." Both halves were wrong; the correction and its
audit trail are recorded in `qa/citation-audit.md`. The transmission route
is drawn from Golub's account ([[src.article.golub-history-of-mana]], with
its peer-reviewed version [[src.chapter.golub-peterson-mana-video-game]]),
Codrington cited for what he wrote ([[src.book.codrington-melanesians]]) and
Keesing for the argument that he misread its grammar
([[src.article.keesing-rethinking-mana]]). This pass read Golub in full;
the other three were verified bibliographically and are cited only for
central, well-attested claims — noted so a later pass knows which citations
still want checking at source.

`source_confidence` remains `mixed`, now for a cleaner reason: the
historical claims rest on an academic account and its primary sources, while
the genre-convention and reader-priority material
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]) stays practitioner-level.

One tension is preserved rather than resolved. Golub declines to settle
whether gaming's adoption of mana is appropriation or care, holding that
players borrowed the word, likely exoticized it, and also made it genuinely
their own. This record takes the same position: an author using mana is not
doing something wrong, and is using a word with a history worth knowing.

records.title: Renewable versus finite resources
records.summary: A resource that recovers (mana refilling overnight) and one that doesn't (a limited number of resurrections, a finite well of ancestral favor) create fundamentally different tension shapes — renewable resources create rhythm, finite ones create irreversible stakes.

citations.label: Fundamentals of Game Design
Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
A renewable resource recovers through some in-world process — rest, time,
an action — and can be spent again once restored: mana, stamina, most
cooldown-based abilities. A finite resource exists in a bounded, often
explicitly countable supply that doesn't replenish, or replenishes so
slowly or costly that it functions as effectively finite within the
story's timeframe: a limited number of resurrections, an ancestral
blessing that can only be invoked a set number of times, a body's
irreplaceable years of life spent on a ritual. The distinction is about
recovery, not about how the resource is stored or spent — a resource can be
finite even if it's stored in a large pool, as long as that pool doesn't
refill.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
Renewable resources create rhythm: a reader learns to expect a character's
capacity to rise and fall across scenes, generating tension through timing
(can this character last long enough) rather than through irreversible
loss. Finite resources create a different, often heavier kind of stakes:
every expenditure is a step toward a hard ceiling the character can't walk
back from, which raises the emotional weight of each individual use in a
way a renewable resource's routine spend-and-recover rhythm doesn't.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
- **Fully renewable**, recovering reliably given enough time or the right
  conditions — the default for most combat-relevant resources (mana,
  stamina) in typical systems.
- **Fully finite**, existing in a fixed, non-renewing supply for the
  story's duration — often reserved for the most narratively significant
  resources (a limited number of wishes, resurrections, or irreversible
  transformations).
- **Slow-renewable / effectively finite**, technically recoverable but at a
  rate so slow relative to the story's pace that it functions as finite
  within any given arc, even if it isn't finite across a full series.
- **Convertible resources**, where a renewable resource can be spent to
  extend or refill a finite one at a cost, creating a decision layer about
  when the tradeoff is worth it.
- **Mixed systems**, the most common real-world pattern, using renewable
  resources for routine actions and finite resources for the story's most
  significant capabilities.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A character explicitly tracking a countable, dwindling resource across a
  story, with each use narrated as a meaningful decision rather than a
  routine expenditure.
- A renewable resource depleted and recovered within a single scene or
  chapter, establishing a rhythm the reader can anticipate.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: a resource introduced as finite and
  precious, then used repeatedly with no visible depletion or consequence,
  undermining its stated scarcity.

sections.title: Progression, failure behavior, and cross-mechanic interaction
sections.content:
Finite resources interact powerfully with stakes and character agency: a
choice to spend one of a limited number of resurrections, for instance,
carries weight precisely because it's irreversible, which is why finite
resources are frequently reserved for a story's most significant turning
points rather than routine problem-solving. Renewable resources interact
more with pacing and tension-and-release rhythm, since their recovery
creates natural breathing points. A system combining both needs to make
clear to the reader which category a given resource falls into, since a
reader's felt tension depends on knowing whether an expenditure is routine
or irreversible.

sections.title: Common failure modes
sections.content:
- **Stated finitude that's never honored**, where a resource introduced as
  limited is used repeatedly with no visible depletion, undermining its
  narrative weight.
- **Renewable resources treated with finite-level gravity**, where routine,
  recoverable expenditures are narrated with the same weight as
  irreversible ones, diluting the impact of genuinely finite losses.
- **Unclear category**, where the reader can't tell whether a given
  resource recovers or not, undermining their ability to feel appropriate
  tension about its use.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- For each significant resource in this system, does it recover, and if so,
  how reliably and at what cost?
- Is a resource introduced as finite and precious actually depleted
  visibly across the story, or does its use stay consequence-free?
- Are renewable, routine expenditures narrated with a different weight than
  finite, irreversible ones?
- Would the reader be able to tell, at any point in the story, whether a
  given resource is recoverable or not?

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List the manuscript's key resources and mark each as renewable, finite,
   or effectively finite; check whether the narrative weight given to each
   use matches its category.
2. For a stated finite resource, track its remaining supply explicitly
   across the manuscript and confirm it's honored consistently.
3. Consider converting one routine, renewable resource expenditure into a
   scene that clarifies its recoverable nature, if the reader currently
   can't tell.
4. For a mixed system, find the scene where a character chooses to spend a
   renewable resource to preserve a finite one, and make that tradeoff
   explicit.

sections.title: When this advice does not apply
sections.content:
- Very lightweight magic or power systems with no tracked resource economy
  at all don't need this distinction made explicit.
- A story deliberately keeping a resource's renewability ambiguous, as a
  source of tension or mystery about a character's true limits, is using
  the ambiguity on purpose rather than failing to clarify it.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks a resource's quantity and recovery over
time, whether it behaves as renewable or finite is close to deterministic.
Whether the narrative weight given to its use matches its actual category
requires interpreting the prose and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Unhonored finitude:* A character is granted "one resurrection, and one
only" from a dying deity; two more resurrections occur later in the story
with no acknowledgment of the earlier stated limit.

*Honored finitude:* The same single resurrection is spent early, and the
story subsequently treats every near-death moment with heightened,
irreversible stakes specifically because that safety net is now gone —
the finitude does real narrative work for the rest of the manuscript.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The renewable/finite distinction and its interaction with tension design
draws on established game-design literature covering resource economies
([[src.book.adams-fundamentals-of-game-design]],
[[src.book.salen-zimmerman-rules-of-play]]); both established academic/
practitioner texts. `source_confidence` is `mixed` because this record's
application to prose narrative stakes (rather than interactive game
balance) is this drafting pass's adaptation rather than a direct claim from
either source.

records.title: Subgenre profile: base building and kingdom management
records.summary: Progression applied to a community rather than an individual — watching a campfire become a kingdom — with the characteristic failure of management without personal stakes.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Base building applies progression logic to a growing community rather than
(or in addition to) an individual protagonist: settlement upgrades, NPC
recruitment with roles and loyalty, resource logistics, and siege events
structure the story's escalation.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is macro satisfaction — watching a small, vulnerable start
(a campfire, a single shelter) grow into a thriving settlement or kingdom —
paired with the more intimate satisfaction of individual recruits mattering
as the community grows. The subgenre's central risk is management becoming
an end in itself, disconnected from any character the reader is invested in.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Some base-building stories keep a single protagonist as the settlement's
clear leader and viewpoint; others distribute viewpoint across several
settlement members, closer to a true ensemble structure. Overlap with
dungeon core is common, since both concern managing a growing structure,
though base-building's protagonist is typically mobile and socially
embedded rather than the structure itself.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Found family** applies at particular strength — the recruited cast is
  often the subject of the story, not a supporting structure around a
  single protagonist's arc.
- **Power as sole motivation** needs a variant: the protagonist's goal is
  legitimately communal (the settlement's survival and flourishing) rather
  than personal, and evaluating individual want/need should be applied to
  cast members rather than assumed to require a single unifying personal
  goal.
- **Side-cast obsolescence** (referenced pattern pool concept) fully
  inverts here: the supporting cast is the subject, not a liability, and a
  coach warning about side-cast irrelevance in this subgenre has likely
  misread the book.
- **Vertical versus horizontal progression** applies at the settlement
  level as well as the individual level — new buildings, roles, and
  specializations function as horizontal growth for the community as a
  whole.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Named settlement members with individual roles, loyalty, and stakes that
  develop over time, rather than an undifferentiated population.
- Resource and logistics decisions that carry visible consequences for
  specific characters, not just aggregate settlement statistics.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: settlement growth tracked purely through
  aggregate numbers (population count, building tiers) with no individual
  character affected by or invested in that growth.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
Management without personal stakes — the settlement grows and no one in it
matters, so escalating aggregate numbers substitute for the character
investment that would make the growth feel meaningful.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Name three settlement members with individual stakes in the community's
   growth, and find a scene for each where their specific stake surfaces.
2. Audit a stretch of settlement-management content and check whether
   growth is shown affecting a specific character, or only reported as
   aggregate statistics.
3. For a siege or crisis event, ground the stakes in what it would cost a
   specific named character, not only the settlement in aggregate.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Which specific settlement members does the reader have reason to care
  about individually, distinct from the community as a whole?
- Does settlement growth ever get tracked purely through aggregate numbers
  with no character-level consequence attached?
- If the protagonist's goal is communal rather than personal, is that
  communal goal given the same dramatized weight a personal want would
  receive?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A story with a single mobile protagonist and no recruited, developing
community should use progression-fantasy or another individual-focused
profile instead; applying the side-cast-obsolescence inversion to a
story without a genuine ensemble cast would misapply a modifier meant for
communal structures specifically.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript centers community growth and a recruited cast is
directly observable from its structure. Whether that growth carries
individual character stakes, or remains purely aggregate, requires
interpreting the prose and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Aggregate-only growth:* A settlement's population grows from twelve to two
hundred across a manuscript, reported through periodic status updates, with
no named resident's personal stake in that growth ever dramatized.

*Character-grounded growth:* The same growth instead includes a specific
former refugee who arrived starving in chapter two and is shown, by chapter
thirty, training the settlement's new arrivals in the same skill that once
saved her — the aggregate number and a specific character's arc reinforce
each other.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This subgenre's structural signature and its inversion of the side-cast-
obsolescence pattern draw on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks this material as the
author's own inference. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: classic LitRPG
records.summary: Growth you can track numerically — stat sheets, skill trees, XP, loot tiers — is the reader promise; the characteristic failure is numbers with no worldly weight, and this profile modifies several other library records accordingly.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Complete Guide to LitRPG Subgenres
Subgenre explainer posts (various)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Classic LitRPG is the subgenre where explicit, visible game mechanics — stat
sheets, skill trees, experience points, loot tiers — are not just present
but central to the reading experience. Unlike progression fantasy, which
requires only that power growth drive the story, classic LitRPG specifically
requires that growth be *numeric and displayed*: the reader is meant to see
the numbers, not just infer growth from narrated consequence.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
This subgenre's specific promise is legibility and optimization pleasure: a
reader can track exactly how strong a character is, compare builds, and
anticipate the tactical effect of a new stat or skill. That promise is what
makes stat-block density and presentation choices matter more here than in
almost any other subgenre — the numbers aren't decoration, they're the
point.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Classic LitRPG ranges from lighter, more comedic treatments of game-world
logic to serious, tactically dense builds-focused fiction; it frequently
overlaps with tower climbing (floor-gated numeric progression) and system
apocalypse (numeric systems imposed on a modern setting), and the category
boundary with progression fantasy is genuinely soft — the distinguishing
question is whether growth is displayed as numbers or conveyed narratively.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Stat-block density and interval** applies at full strength here — this
  is the subgenre where the pattern's core complaint (reflexive full-sheet
  reveals) is most reported and most consequential.
- **Hard numbers versus named tiers** — classic LitRPG is the default case
  for the numeric-display side of that comparison; named-tier-only display
  would be an unusual choice worth the author noting deliberately.
- **System-as-narrator intrusion** applies at full strength — the formal
  system voice this pattern addresses is a structural feature of the
  subgenre, not an occasional device.
- **Meaningless numbers** (a related pattern in Family C) is a specific risk
  here precisely because numbers are so central: the subgenre's promise
  depends on numbers mattering tactically, not just appearing.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Explicit stat sheets, skill trees, and level-up notifications appearing
  regularly and driving tactical decisions.
- Combat and problem-solving scenes that reference specific numeric values
  (damage totals, resistances, cooldowns) as part of how a solution is
  reached.
- The inverse, as a signal this profile doesn't fit: a manuscript that
  conveys growth entirely through narrated consequence, with no displayed
  numbers at all — better matched to the progression-fantasy or GameLit
  profile.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
Numbers that never affect tactics, choices, or consequences — the
formulation worth keeping is that without worldly weight, a number is just
inventory. This is the reader-side complaint that pairs most directly with
this subgenre's core promise.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Audit a chapter's displayed numbers and mark which ones affected a
   subsequent tactical decision; consider cutting or consolidating the rest.
2. If stat reveals feel reflexive, apply the reserved-for-consequence
   practice from the related stat-block-density record.
3. Test one scene where a specific numeric value (not just its narrated
   effect) is the deciding factor in a choice, to sharpen the subgenre's
   core promise.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does every displayed stat or skill eventually matter to a tactical
  decision, or are some purely decorative?
- Is the frequency of stat reveals proportional to narrative significance,
  or reflexive?
- If this manuscript were stripped of all displayed numbers, would readers
  still be able to follow what's happening — and if not fully, is that
  acceptable given the subgenre's numeric promise?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A manuscript using LitRPG-adjacent vocabulary without displaying numeric
stat information to the reader is better served by the progression-fantasy
or GameLit profiles instead; applying classic-LitRPG-specific patterns (stat-
block density in particular) to a manuscript with no displayed stat blocks
would misdiagnose a nonexistent problem.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Weightless number:* A character's "Perception +3" stat is announced on
leveling up and never referenced again in any scene involving noticing,
searching, or reacting to danger.

*Weighted number:* The same stat increase is followed, two chapters later,
by the character noticing a specific detail (a mismatched footprint) that a
lower Perception score would plausibly have missed, and that detail changes
the scene's outcome — the number did tactical work.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript displays numeric system information to the reader is
directly observable from the text. Whether that display serves the story's
promise (numbers mattering tactically) requires interpreting the
surrounding prose and remains model-assisted; this profile itself is
`practice`-scoped in the sense that subgenre classification is an author
declaration, not something a coach should infer and assert as fact.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The umbrella taxonomy (GameLit/LitRPG/progression-fantasy nesting, numeric-
versus-narrative distinction) is corroborated across independent sources
([[src.litrpgtools.subgenre-guide]], used for its category skeleton only,
not its promotional author recommendations; [[src.litrpgcritic.subgenre-
explainers]]) and synthesized in `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks the "what this profile
modifies" material as its own inference from the taxonomy, not a directly
sourced claim. `source_confidence` is `mixed` accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: crafting and economy
records.summary: Power without violence — the satisfaction of recipes, discovery, and being indispensable — where combat-escalation patterns largely don't apply and the story lives or dies on whether its economy coheres.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Crafting and economy fiction advances the protagonist without primarily
relying on combat, structuring escalation instead through material tiers,
quality levels, trade routes, and non-combat advancement paths — recipes
discovered, goods produced, markets navigated. Progression here is measured
in what a character can make, source, or trade, not what they can defeat.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is power without violence: the satisfaction of recipes,
discovery, and becoming genuinely indispensable to the people and systems
around you, offering an alternative to combat-driven power fantasy that
still delivers real stakes and real escalation. This makes the subgenre
distinctly non-combat-forward among progression fiction's variants, which
readers specifically seek out for that reason.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Some crafting/economy stories keep the protagonist as an individual artisan
or trader; others scale up toward running a workshop, guild, or trading
operation with employees and competitors. Overlap with base building is
common at the larger end of that scale. The degree to which combat appears
at all (as background threat, occasional obstacle, or genuinely absent)
varies and is a significant tonal choice.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Crafting and economy loops** is this profile's companion system-
  mechanic record and should be read alongside it directly — its guidance
  on scarcity, sinks, and market consistency is the core technical
  toolkit for this subgenre.
- **Systemic social consequences** is central rather than peripheral here —
  per genre research, this subgenre lives or dies on whether society
  plausibly uses what it has; an economy that doesn't cohere with the
  surrounding world's institutions and daily life undermines the
  subgenre's core appeal more directly than it would in a combat-forward
  story.
- **Conflict-escalation patterns built around combat do not apply as
  written** — action-economy, death/respawn, and similar combat-specific
  records should generally be set aside unless the manuscript genuinely
  mixes crafting/economy with combat content; applying them by default
  risks flagging nonexistent problems.
- **Stakes** still applies at full strength, but its concrete-consequence
  framing should be read through economic and social costs (ruin,
  displacement, a ruined reputation) rather than physical danger by
  default.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Consistent material scarcity, pricing, and trade logic honored across
  scenes, with escalating stakes tied to economic rather than combat
  outcomes.
- A protagonist's growing indispensability shown through specific
  relationships and dependencies (a village that now relies on their
  goods, a guild that can't function without their recipe) rather than only
  raw output numbers.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: an economy that behaves inconsistently
  across scenes, or advancement that reads as combat-forward progression
  with crafting vocabulary layered on top.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
An economy that doesn't cohere — prices, supply, and scarcity that exist
only when the plot needs them, breaking the internal consistency this
subgenre's non-combat stakes depend on to feel real.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. List established material scarcity and prices across the manuscript and
   check each mention for consistency, per the companion crafting-and-
   economy-loops record's own experiments.
2. Identify one social or institutional consequence of the protagonist's
   economic activity (a guild's response, a market shift affecting other
   characters) and make sure at least one is dramatized.
3. Audit the manuscript for combat-escalation patterns applied by default;
   remove or reconsider any that don't actually fit a non-combat-forward
   story.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this manuscript's economy behave consistently, or do prices and
  scarcity shift for plot convenience?
- Is the protagonist's growing indispensability shown through specific
  relationships, or only through abstract output numbers?
- If combat appears at all, is it genuinely load-bearing, or does it exist
  because combat escalation felt expected rather than because this story
  needs it?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A story where crafting or trade appears only as minor texture within an
otherwise combat-driven progression narrative should use the progression-
fantasy or classic-LitRPG profile as primary, with the crafting-and-economy-
loops system-mechanic record applied as a supporting element rather than
this profile's full modifier set.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript centers non-combat, economy-driven advancement is
directly observable from its structure. Whether the resulting economy is
internally consistent, and whether social consequences are adequately
engaged, requires interpreting the manuscript's worldbuilding and remains
model-assisted; where material tiers or prices are explicitly tracked as
structured data, consistency checks are closer to deterministic.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Incoherent economy, combat-forward default:* A crafting-focused
protagonist's story escalates almost entirely through fights with rival
crafters over stolen recipes, with the actual economic logic (why a recipe
is valuable, who else wants it and why) left vague.

*Coherent, non-combat escalation:* The same rivalry instead escalates
through undercut pricing, a guild contract dispute, and a supply blockade
that threatens the protagonist's workshop — real economic stakes,
dramatized without requiring physical confrontation to carry the tension.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This subgenre's structural signature, its centrality for systemic social
consequences, and the note that combat-escalation patterns don't apply as
written all draw on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre-profile
material as the author's own inference. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: cultivation
records.summary: Transcendence through internal refinement — readers here care about reasons more than numbers, the inverse of classic LitRPG, and the characteristic failure is breakthroughs that go mechanical while the philosophical half goes vestigial.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
Introducing Daoism

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Cultivation fiction structures power growth as internal refinement toward
transcendence, through named realms, dramatized breakthroughs, sect
politics, and alchemy/refinement practices. The path to power is
conventionally also a path of self-understanding, distinguishing this
subgenre from purely mechanical progression systems.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is that breakthroughs are events with meaning, not just
threshold crossings — readers of this subgenre are reported to care more
about *why* a character advances than about the raw numbers involved, the
inverse of classic LitRPG's number-forward appeal. That inversion is the
single most important thing this profile changes about how other library
patterns should be read.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Cultivation ranges from close adaptations of Chinese xianxia/xuanhuan
conventions to Western cultivation fiction, which conventionally compresses
pacing relative to the source tradition and establishes stakes within the
first few pages — a genre convention associated with Will Wight's influence
on the Western tradition specifically, per genre research, not a claim
about the wider tradition's own pacing norms.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Cultivation realms and breakthroughs** is this profile's companion
  system-mechanic record and should be read alongside it directly.
- **Qi versus mana** applies with qi (in its modern genre-convention sense,
  distinguished from historical Daoist usage) as the default resource
  framing.
- **Meaningless numbers** inverts in framing: the failure here is
  unexplained advancement (a breakthrough with no stated reason) rather than
  weightless numbers specifically, since numbers are frequently secondary or
  absent.
- **Advancement rate**'s widening-interval shape is the explicit convention:
  later realms take longer, and pacing should slow deliberately rather than
  reading as stalled.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A breakthrough scene dramatized with genuine risk, insight, or moral
  weight, not just a threshold crossing.
- Sect politics, alchemy, or philosophical questions given narrative space
  proportional to their conventional centrality in the subgenre.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: realm changes announced with mechanical
  flatness, with no accompanying qualitative or philosophical development.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
Breakthroughs become mechanical and the philosophical half goes vestigial —
realms function as levels with better names, losing the reason-over-numbers
appeal this subgenre's readers are reported to want.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. For each realm change, write one sentence describing what qualitatively
   or philosophically changed, not just what number or rank changed.
2. Check whether sect politics or a mentor-student relationship carries
   real narrative weight, or functions only as background texture.
3. Compare the pacing of a late-book realm to an early one; if the later one
   moves at the same pace, consider whether slowing it (per genre
   convention) would strengthen the sense of escalating difficulty.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does a breakthrough mean for this character beyond a numeric or
  ranked increase?
- Is the philosophical or spiritual dimension of cultivation given narrative
  space, or has it become vestigial?
- Which transliteration and tradition is "qi" (or its equivalent) drawing
  from in this manuscript, and is that legible to the reader?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A numeric, mechanically-focused power system with no qualitative or
philosophical dimension to its advancement is better served by the classic-
LitRPG or progression-fantasy profile; applying cultivation's
reasons-over-numbers framing to such a system would ask it to deliver a
promise it isn't making.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript uses named realms and breakthrough events is directly
observable from its structure. Whether breakthroughs carry genuine
qualitative or philosophical weight, rather than functioning as reskinned
level-ups, requires interpreting the prose and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Vestigial philosophy:* A character reaches Core Formation described purely
in terms of increased power output, with no accompanying change in outlook,
relationships, or self-understanding.

*Present philosophy:* The same breakthrough instead forces the character to
confront a compromise they made to survive an earlier ordeal, and the realm
change is explicitly tied to finally being honest with themselves about it.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
Historical and philosophical grounding for internal cultivation draws on an
academic introduction to Daoism ([[src.book.kohn-introducing-daoism]]);
genre-convention material (Western pacing compression, reader priority on
reasons over numbers) draws on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre-profile
material as the author's own inference. `source_confidence` is `mixed`
accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: dark / horror LitRPG
records.summary: The numbers do not mean safety — real menace and real cost define this subgenre, and its characteristic failure is gore that costs the protagonist nothing durable.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Dark and horror LitRPG uses the genre's familiar mechanical scaffolding —
levels, stats, systems — but inverts its usual reassurance: the system
itself is hostile, indifferent, or actively cruel, and its numbers exist to
make danger legible rather than to promise survival. Structural signature:
permadeath or severe, durable penalties; antagonistic system design (a
system that punishes rather than helps); and morally compromised choices
forced by the mechanics themselves.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is that the numbers do not mean safety — real menace, real cost.
Readers of this subgenre specifically want a LitRPG structure that doesn't
soften its stakes the way lighter, more comedic treatments often do; a
death mechanic or system voice that behaves reassuringly here betrays the
subgenre's core contract more than it would in almost any other LitRPG
variant.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Some dark/horror LitRPG keeps the system itself neutral or mechanical while
the *world* is hostile (survival horror with game mechanics); other, more
distinctive variants make the system itself an antagonist — punishing
curiosity, offering corrupted choices, or lying about its own rules. The
degree of moral compromise forced on the protagonist (not just physical
danger) is often what separates "dark" from merely "difficult."

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Death and respawn** is central here rather than a background design
  choice: permadeath or severe, durable penalties are conventionally core to
  this subgenre's promise, and a soft-respawn system undercuts its core
  appeal more here than in any other subgenre in this corpus.
- **Weak-to-OP honesty** (referenced pattern pool concept, P5) is
  especially load-bearing: this is the subgenre where the protagonist must
  actually lose things, and where readers most reliably notice when they
  don't.
- **Effort equals reward** (referenced pattern pool concept, P9) carries
  similar weight for the same reason — gains that arrive free or by luck are
  particularly damaging to trust in a subgenre built on cost.
- **Fake progression** is a specific risk here: if numeric growth doesn't
  correspond to genuinely rising danger and cost, the subgenre's core
  promise (numbers don't mean safety) collapses into ordinary LitRPG
  reassurance wearing dark aesthetics.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- A death or serious failure that costs the protagonist something durable —
  a resource, a relationship, a piece of themselves — rather than resetting
  cleanly.
- System messages or mechanics that are ambiguous, misleading, or actively
  adversarial, rather than helpfully informative.
- The inverse, as a warning sign: graphic violence or dark imagery paired
  with a death/failure mechanic that costs the protagonist nothing lasting —
  darkness as aesthetic without mechanical teeth.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
Gore substituting for consequence — brutality that costs the protagonist
nothing durable, so stakes are asserted through violent imagery rather than
actually felt through lasting cost.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Audit the manuscript's stated death or failure penalties against what
   actually happens to the protagonist when they fail; close any gap
   between stated and paid cost.
2. For a violent or graphic scene, check whether it changes anything lasting
   about the protagonist's capabilities, relationships, or psychology; if
   not, consider whether the violence is doing narrative work or only
   tonal work.
3. Test one system interaction for genuine ambiguity or hostility — does
   the system ever mislead, withhold, or extract a cost the protagonist
   didn't fully understand they were agreeing to?

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- When the protagonist fails or dies, what do they actually lose, and does
  it last?
- Does this manuscript's system ever behave adversarially, or does it
  remain a helpful, reassuring presence despite the story's dark framing?
- Is the story's violence doing consequential narrative work, or primarily
  tonal work?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A LitRPG manuscript with dark aesthetic dressing but a fundamentally
reassuring, low-permanent-cost system should be evaluated under the
classic-LitRPG profile instead, with dark imagery treated as a tonal choice
rather than evidence this subgenre's structural conventions apply.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Where a project explicitly tracks death, failure, or resource-loss
penalties, whether stated costs were actually applied is close to
deterministic. Whether violence in the prose does genuine consequential work
versus purely tonal work requires interpreting the manuscript and remains
model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Costless darkness:* A character is graphically maimed in combat, described
across a full page of visceral detail, and is shown fully healed and
unaffected by the next chapter with no lasting physical, psychological, or
narrative trace.

*Costly darkness:* The same injury instead permanently reduces a tracked
stat, and three chapters later the character is shown adapting their combat
approach around the loss — the graphic moment bought something the story
keeps paying for.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This subgenre's structural signature (permadeath, antagonistic system
design, morally compromised choices) draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-genre.md` ([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]),
which marks its subgenre-profile material as the author's own inference; the
pattern-modifier framing (P5, P9 centrality) draws on
`docs/research-litrpg-craft-failures.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-craft-failures-research]]), itself citing practitioner
essays rather than controlled research. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: dungeon core
records.summary: An inverted power fantasy where the protagonist is the place, not a traveler through it — the most heavily modified subgenre in this corpus, requiring variants of several agency- and motivation-related patterns.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Dungeon core casts the protagonist as the place itself — a dungeon core
generating rooms, monsters, and traps rather than a traveling adventurer.
Its resource loop is characteristically closed: mana in, rooms and monsters
out, stronger invaders drawn in response, more mana generated in turn.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is an inverted power fantasy: base-building satisfaction in
narrative form, with the reader rooting for what would conventionally be the
"dungeon" antagonists of another story. It asks readers to relate to
architecture and strategy rather than a mobile, socially embedded
protagonist, which is a genuinely different pleasure from most progression
fiction.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
Some dungeon-core stories grant the core limited mobility or an avatar
partway through, shifting toward more conventional agency; others keep the
core fully immobile throughout, leaning further into the inversion. Overlap
with base-building is common, since both concern managing a growing
structure and its inhabitants.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Character agency** needs a dungeon-core variant: choices about what to
  build, who to trust among invaders, and how to interpret ambiguous
  threats carry real agency without physical mobility. Don't mistake
  immobility for a lack of choice.
- **Power as sole motivation** needs a variant: growth is legitimately the
  protagonist's condition and situation here, not an unexamined default —
  look instead for whether the core has any want beyond growth once growth
  stops being urgent.
- **Negative space: problems power cannot solve** is unusually strong here —
  a dungeon literally cannot leave, which is one of the richest built-in
  sets of problems power cannot solve in any subgenre in this corpus.
- **Side-cast obsolescence** (referenced pattern pool concept) inverts:
  adventurers are conventionally antagonists here, and the recurring cast
  may be the invaders rather than allies who need to keep pace.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Scenes built around room design, monster placement, and resource
  allocation as the primary strategic activity, rather than travel or
  direct combat by the protagonist.
- A core's "choices" expressed through what it builds or which invader it
  spares, rather than through physical action.
- The inverse, as a signal this profile doesn't fit: a mobile protagonist
  who merely commands a dungeon from outside it — likely closer to a
  base-building or general progression-fantasy profile.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
A core with no goal beyond growing — the loop runs (mana in, rooms out,
stronger invaders, more mana) without a story attached to it, since growth
alone doesn't generate stakes once its initial novelty wears off.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Identify the core's want beyond survival and growth, and find a scene
   where that want, not growth, drives a decision.
2. List the built-in problems the core's immobility creates (can't leave,
   can't choose its neighbors, can't verify a threat's intentions from a
   safe distance) and check whether the manuscript engages at least one.
3. For a recurring "adventurer" cast, decide deliberately whether they
   function as invaders, potential allies, or something in between, and let
   that relationship develop rather than staying static.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- What does this core want, beyond continued growth and survival?
- Does the core's immobility create real, engaged narrative problems, or
  does the story route around the constraint?
- Is the recurring "invader" cast treated with individual stakes, or as an
  undifferentiated threat?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A story with a mobile protagonist who merely oversees a dungeon or
settlement from outside it should use the base-building profile instead;
applying dungeon-core's agency and motivation variants to a conventionally
mobile protagonist would misapply modifiers meant for immobility
specifically.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a protagonist is structurally immobile (a dungeon core rather than a
traveling character) is directly observable from the premise. Whether the
core has a want beyond growth, and whether its agency is meaningfully
exercised despite immobility, requires interpreting the manuscript and
remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Growth with no attached story:* A dungeon core spends fifteen chapters
building progressively larger rooms and stronger monsters with no
articulated want beyond "grow stronger," and no built-in problem (isolation,
inability to verify intentions, forced proximity to a nearby village)
engaged directly.

*Growth with attached story:* The same core instead wants specifically to
protect a small village it has grown attached to, which creates a direct
tension between "grow stronger" (which requires drawing in dangerous
invaders) and "keep the village safe" (which growth itself endangers).

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
This subgenre's structural signature and its status as the most heavily
modified profile in the taxonomy draw on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks this material as the
author's own inference connecting the taxonomy to the pattern pool rather
than a directly sourced claim. `source_confidence` is set to `limited`
accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: GameLit
records.summary: Game-adjacent fun without the crunch — the widest umbrella subgenre, where several LitRPG-specific patterns simply do not apply because there's no stat screen to misuse.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
GameLit is the widest umbrella subgenre: game-like worlds with quests,
respawns, and NPCs, where mechanics are thematic rather than numerical and
there's no obligation to show a stat screen at all. LitRPG sits inside this
umbrella as the subset that does require explicit, visible mechanics.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is game-world fun without parsing stat tables — readers who want
the flavor and structure of a game-like world without LitRPG's numeric
density are specifically served by this subgenre, and applying LitRPG
conventions to a GameLit manuscript risks serving a promise the story never
made.

sections.title: Common forms and variants
sections.content:
GameLit ranges from stories with almost no game-mechanical vocabulary at all
(quests and NPCs as narrative framing devices) to stories that gesture at
mechanics thematically without ever displaying numbers. The boundary with
classic LitRPG is the single clearest dividing line in the whole taxonomy:
numeric versus narrative progression.

sections.title: What this profile modifies in other records
sections.content:
- **Stat-block density**, **system-as-narrator intrusion**, and
  **meaningless numbers** (referenced pattern) largely do not apply — a book
  with no stat blocks has no stat-block density problem, and a book with no
  system voice has nothing to intrude. This is the subgenre where a coach
  assuming LitRPG conventions will be most obviously and immediately wrong.
- **Hard numbers versus named tiers** resolves toward neither pole in the
  usual sense — GameLit frequently uses neither precise numbers nor formal
  tier names, conveying growth entirely through action and consequence.
- **Visible versus hidden systems** may not apply either, if there is no
  formal "system" to make visible or hidden in the first place.

sections.title: What it can look like on the page
sections.content:
- Quests, NPCs, and game-adjacent structure conveyed through narrative
  action, with no displayed numeric or formally tiered progression.
- Game vocabulary used loosely and thematically (a character "grinding" a
  skill through practice, narrated without any stat readout).
- The inverse, as a signal this profile doesn't fit: displayed stat sheets
  or explicit level-up notifications — likely better matched to the
  classic-LitRPG profile instead.

sections.title: Characteristic failure mode
sections.content:
Neither fish nor fowl — too gamey for general fantasy readers, too soft for
LitRPG readers who want visible mechanics, satisfying neither promise fully.
This is a tonal and expectation-management risk more than a structural
craft failure.

sections.title: Revision or design experiments
sections.content:
1. Confirm early in the manuscript whether numeric mechanics will ever be
   displayed; if not, make that clear to the reader quickly so LitRPG-
   trained expectations don't set in and then go unmet.
2. If the manuscript sits uneasily between GameLit and LitRPG, consider
   which promise is primary and lean the opening chapters toward
   establishing that promise clearly.
3. Audit any coaching notes generated for this manuscript and discard any
   that assume a stat screen or system voice that doesn't exist in the text.

sections.title: Questions for the author
sections.content:
- Does this manuscript ever display explicit numeric mechanics, or is all
  progression conveyed narratively?
- If a reader arrived expecting classic LitRPG's numeric density, would the
  opening chapters correct that expectation quickly enough?
- Is game vocabulary used consistently as theme/flavor, or does it
  intermittently promise mechanical specificity the story doesn't deliver?

sections.title: When this profile does not apply
sections.content:
A manuscript with any meaningful displayed numeric mechanics should be
evaluated primarily under the classic-LitRPG or progression-fantasy profile
instead; treating a numerically explicit manuscript as GameLit would
suppress genuinely applicable stat-presentation coaching.

sections.title: Evidence and detection limits
sections.content:
Whether a manuscript displays numeric mechanics is directly observable from
the text. Whether the resulting tonal positioning (game-adjacent but not
numeric) serves the story's intended readership requires interpreting genre
expectations and remains model-assisted.

sections.title: Original micro-examples
sections.content:
*Numeric drift into unclear territory:* A GameLit-framed story occasionally
mentions a character's "level" in passing dialogue without ever displaying
a number or a formal tier name, creating ambiguity about whether the system
is meant to be tracked or purely atmospheric.

*Clear GameLit framing:* The same story instead consistently narrates growth
through demonstrated capability only ("she could finally hold the heavier
blade steady") with no numeric or tier vocabulary at all, giving the reader
a clear, consistent signal about what kind of progression story this is.

sections.title: Sources and confidence notes
sections.content:
The umbrella taxonomy and this subgenre's boundary case (numeric vs.
narrative progression as the clearest dividing line in the whole framework)
draw on `docs/research-litrpg-genre.md`
([[src.internal.litrpg-genre-research]]), which marks its subgenre-profile
material as the author's own inference. `source_confidence` is set to
`limited` accordingly.

records.title: Subgenre profile: isekai / portal fantasy
records.summary: A transported protagonist's modern knowledge becomes their edge — the subgenre's signature failure is the protagonist solving problems an entire world of intelligent people somehow missed, with no explanation for the gap.

citations.label: LitRPG Genre Research — Taxonomy and Platform
LitRPG Craft-Failure Pattern Research (Part A–D)

sections.title: What it is
sections.content:
Isekai and portal fantasy transport a protagonist from a familiar (usually
contemporary, real-world) setting into an unfamiliar one, structuring the
story around fish-out-of-water adaptation and the creative application of
real-world knowledge or expertise the new world lacks. Structural signature:
a transported protagonist, a cultural-learning arc, and real-world expertise
(a modern skill, a piece of common knowledge, a practical habit) applied as
a genuine advantage.

sections.title: Why readers may care
sections.content:
The promise is that modern knowledge is a real edge, and that the
protagonist's confusion navigating the new world mirrors the reader's own
unfamiliarity with it — the two learn the setting together. This creates a
distinctive intimacy between reader and protagonist that other subgenres
